ECON-SP-EASY-1.q: Which function of money is being used when dollars are accepted to buy groceries?
options: Store of value
Medium of exchange
Unit of account
Reserve requirement
ECON-SP-EASY-1.feedback: Money is a medium of exchange when it is used to buy goods and services.

ECON-SP-EASY-2.q: Which function of money is being used when a store lists a phone price as $900?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
ECON-SP-EASY-2.feedback: Money is a unit of account when it measures and compares prices.

ECON-SP-EASY-4.q: Which item is counted in M1?
options: Large time deposits
Currency held by the public
Credit card balances
Money market mutual funds held by businesses
ECON-SP-EASY-4.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

ECON-SP-EASY-5.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item is included in M2 but not M1?
options: Checkable deposits
Coins held by households
Savings deposits
Currency held by the public
ECON-SP-EASY-5.commonError: Treating M1 and M2 as identical.
ECON-SP-EASY-5.feedback: M2 includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

options: Money backed fully by gold
Accepted money with no intrinsic value
Money used only by banks
Money that cannot lose value
ECON-SP-EASY-6.commonError: Thinking fiat money must be backed by gold.
ECON-SP-EASY-6.feedback: Fiat money has value because people accept it, not because it has intrinsic value.

LG-Q-1.q: A farmer wants shoes, but the shoemaker does not want wheat. Both are willing to accept dollars. Which feature of money solves the immediate trading problem?
options: It serves as a medium of exchange, so the two traders do not need a double coincidence of wants
It serves only as a store of value, so neither trader has to exchange anything
It makes every good part of M1, so barter becomes unnecessary
It guarantees that the relative price of wheat and shoes never changes
LG-Q-1.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
LG-Q-1.feedback: Money serves as a medium of exchange because dollars let the farmer trade without finding a shoemaker who wants wheat.

LG-Q-2.q: A repair shop compares a $450 used laptop with a $900 new laptop before deciding which to buy. Which function of money makes that comparison straightforward?
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Bank reserve
LG-Q-2.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
LG-Q-2.feedback: Money serves as a unit of account because quoting both laptops in dollars provides a common measure for comparing their prices.

LG-Q-3.q: A household keeps $600 in cash for emergencies. If prices rise substantially before the cash is spent, which statement is most accurate?
options: The cash serves as a store of value, but its purchasing power can fall
The cash stops being money because a store of value must keep purchasing power constant
The cash is serving only as a unit of account because it is not being spent today
Inflation converts the cash from M1 into a nonmonetary financial asset
LG-Q-3.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
LG-Q-3.feedback: Cash is a store of value because it carries purchasing power into the future, although inflation can reduce that purchasing power before it is spent.

LG-Q-4.q: Customers accept paper currency even though the paper itself has little intrinsic value and cannot be redeemed for a commodity. Which explanation best fits?
options: It is fiat money whose usefulness depends on general acceptance rather than commodity value
It is commodity money because the paper can be physically held
It is bank capital because it supports financial transactions
It is not money unless every note is backed one-for-one by gold
LG-Q-4.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
LG-Q-4.feedback: The currency is fiat money: it is accepted as payment even though the paper has little intrinsic value and is not redeemable for a commodity.

LG-Q-5.q: Commodity money differs from fiat money because commodity money
options: has intrinsic value
is created only through bank lending
cannot be used as a medium of exchange
is always part of M2 but never M1
LG-Q-5.commonError: treating all money as fiat money
LG-Q-5.feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself, like gold or silver. Fiat money does not.

LG-Q-6.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is included in M1?
options: Currency held by the public
Small time deposits
Savings deposits
Money market mutual funds held by individuals
LG-Q-6.commonError: including all near monies in M1
LG-Q-6.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public, checkable deposits, and similar highly liquid transaction balances.

LG-Q-7.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is part of M2 but not M1?
options: Savings deposits
Currency
Checkable deposits
Traveler's checks
LG-Q-7.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes near monies
LG-Q-7.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies, so they are included in M2 but not M1.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-100.q: A student says credit card balances should be counted in M1 because people use cards to buy goods. What is the best correction?
options: Credit cards are borrowing, not money balances
Credit cards are currency held by the public
Credit cards are checkable deposits
Credit cards are savings deposits
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-100.feedback: Credit cards allow borrowing. They are not money balances like currency or checkable deposits.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-101.q: A household keeps cash because it wants to make purchases quickly, compare prices, and save some value for later. Which answer matches all three functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, fiat money
Unit of account, leverage, discount rate
Medium of exchange, multiplier, bank capital
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-101.commonError: Mixing money functions with banking tools.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-101.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and can transfer purchasing power into the future.

LG-Q-100.q: A student says, 'Money is valuable because the dollar bill itself has valuable paper.' What is the best correction?
options: Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
Fiat money has value because its paper is worth more than its face value.
Commodity money and fiat money are the same thing.
Money only has value if it can be exchanged for gold.
LG-Q-100.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
LG-Q-100.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. Its value comes from general acceptance and government backing.

LG-Q-101.q: A grocery store lists apples at $2 per pound. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Fractional reserve
LG-Q-101.commonError: choosing medium of exchange whenever prices involve money
LG-Q-101.feedback: The price tag uses money to measure value, so money is acting as a unit of account.

LG-Q-102.q: A person keeps $500 in cash for emergencies. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Store of value
Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
LG-Q-102.commonError: thinking money only matters when it is spent immediately
LG-Q-102.feedback: The cash is preserving purchasing power for later, so it is serving as a store of value.

LG-Q-103.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item would be counted in M2 but not in M1?
options: A savings deposit
Currency in your wallet
A checking account deposit
A traveler's check
LG-Q-103.commonError: putting all liquid assets into M1
LG-Q-103.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies. They belong in M2, not M1.

LG-Q-106.q: Why does money make specialization easier?
options: It removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
It makes all goods cost the same amount.
It prevents prices from changing.
It eliminates scarcity.
LG-Q-106.commonError: thinking money eliminates scarcity rather than reducing transaction costs
LG-Q-106.feedback: Money reduces transaction costs because people no longer need to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.

LG-Q-107.q: Which statement best explains why currency held by a bank does not count the same way as currency held by the public?
options: Currency held by banks is part of bank reserves, not currency circulating among the public.
Currency held by banks is automatically counted twice in M1.
Currency held by banks is commodity money.
Currency held by banks is never money.
LG-Q-107.feedback: Currency held by banks is treated as reserves. Currency in the money supply refers to currency held by the public.

ECON-SP-HARD-200.q: A student says M2 is smaller than M1 because M2 excludes currency. What is the best correction?
options: M2 includes M1 plus near monies
M2 includes only bank reserves
M1 includes savings deposits only
M1 equals credit card balances
ECON-SP-HARD-200.commonError: Reversing the relationship between M1 and M2.
ECON-SP-HARD-200.feedback: M2 is broader than M1 because it includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

LG-Q-200.q: A farmer accepts dollars for corn, uses dollars to compare seed prices, and saves some dollars for next month. Which answer correctly matches the three functions of money?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, medium of exchange, unit of account
Unit of account, store of value, medium of exchange
Money multiplier, reserve requirement, federal funds rate
LG-Q-200.commonError: mixing up using money to buy with using money to measure value
LG-Q-200.feedback: Buying uses money as a medium of exchange, comparing prices uses it as a unit of account, and saving it uses it as a store of value.

LG-Q-201.q: A country uses paper currency that has no intrinsic value, is not convertible into gold, but is accepted for payment. What kind of money is this?
options: Fiat money
Commodity money
Barter money
Reserve money only
LG-Q-201.commonError: thinking money must be backed by a commodity to have value
LG-Q-201.feedback: That is fiat money: it has value because it is accepted, not because the paper itself has intrinsic value.

LG-Q-203.q: Currency held by the public rises because households withdraw funds from checking accounts. What happens to banks' ability to create deposits, other things equal?
options: It falls because banks have fewer deposits to support lending.
It rises because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves.
It is unchanged because currency and deposits are identical for banks.
It becomes unlimited because reserve requirements no longer matter.
LG-Q-203.commonError: thinking public currency holdings help banks lend more
LG-Q-203.feedback: When households hold more currency and fewer deposits, banks have fewer deposits available to support loans.

P52B-S3-MFM-H-001.q: A household moves $4,000 from a checking account into a retail money-market mutual fund. Under standard textbook definitions, what happens?
options: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.
P52B-S3-MFM-H-001.commonError: Treating movement between M1 and non-M1 M2 assets as a change in total M2.
P52B-S3-MFM-H-001.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.

P52B-S3-MFM-H-002.q: Which asset is included in M2 but normally excluded from M1?
options: Currency held by the public.
A small-denomination time deposit.
Funds in a checking account.
Traveler’s checks held by households.
P52B-S3-MFM-H-002.commonError: Placing every liquid financial asset in M1.
P52B-S3-MFM-H-002.feedback: Small time deposits are near-money assets included in M2 but not in the narrower M1 measure.

LG-Q-300.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists public currency as $600, checkable deposits as $1,400, savings deposits as $1,800, small time deposits as $500, and retail money market mutual funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
LG-Q-300.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
LG-Q-300.feedback: M1 is currency plus checkable deposits: $600 + $1,400 = $2,000. M2 adds savings, small time deposits, and retail money market funds: $4,600.

P52B-S3-MFM-EL-001.q: A payment app transfers balances instantly from users’ checking accounts but holds no separate monetary balance. How should the app affect measured money?
options: Every transfer through the app permanently increases the measured M1 stock.
The app balance enters M2 even though no separate monetary balance exists.
It changes payment convenience without creating a new money balance.
Using the app removes the linked checking deposits from measured money.
P52B-S3-MFM-EL-001.commonError: Counting a payment method as a separate stock of money when it only accesses an existing deposit.
P52B-S3-MFM-EL-001.feedback: A payment platform that merely accesses checking deposits changes how money is used, not how much money exists.

P52B-S3-MFM-EL-002.q: A store lists prices in dollars, accepts dollars at checkout, and households keep dollars for future purchases. Which statement is correct?
options: Money is serving only as a medium of exchange during the checkout transaction.
Money is serving as a unit of account and barter device, but not as stored value.
Money is serving only as a store of value because households retain some dollars.
Money is serving as unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value.
P52B-S3-MFM-EL-002.commonError: Assuming one transaction can illustrate only one function of money.
P52B-S3-MFM-EL-002.feedback: Money can perform all three functions in the same setting: quoting prices, settling purchases, and carrying purchasing power forward.

P52B-S3-MFM-EL-003.q: Inflation accelerates, but dollars remain widely accepted and prices continue to be quoted in dollars. Which money function is most directly weakened?
options: Store of value, because purchasing power erodes more quickly.
Medium of exchange, because dollars can no longer buy anything.
Unit of account, because prices cannot be stated in dollars.
Standard of deferred payment, because all credit disappears.
P52B-S3-MFM-EL-003.commonError: Assuming inflation eliminates every function of money equally.
P52B-S3-MFM-EL-003.feedback: Rapid inflation most directly weakens money’s ability to preserve purchasing power over time.

LG-Q-9011.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $3,000, savings deposits are $2,500, small time deposits are $1,200, retail money market funds are $800, and large time deposits are $900. If large time deposits are not counted in M2, what is M2?
LG-Q-9011.commonError: including large time deposits when the course definition excludes them
LG-Q-9011.feedback: M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $3,000 + $2,500 + $1,200 + $800 = $7,500.

LG-Q-9012.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A household moves $10,000 from a checking account to a savings account. What happens to M1 and M2, using standard course definitions?
options: M1 falls, while M2 is unchanged.
Both M1 and M2 fall.
M1 is unchanged, while M2 rises.
Both M1 and M2 rise.
LG-Q-9012.commonError: thinking every movement between accounts changes M2
LG-Q-9012.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2; savings deposits are in M2 but not M1. Moving funds to savings lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

LG-Q-9023.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks lend more, and the public redeposits most loan proceeds. Which money measures are most likely affected first?
options: Bank deposits and M1 rise, with broader effects on M2 depending on where funds are held.
Commodity-money holdings rise because bond purchases convert financial assets into physical commodity money
Real GDP rises immediately while the quantity of bank deposits is unaffected by the lending and redeposit process
M1 falls because additional bank lending reduces the checkable deposits held by households and businesses
LG-Q-9023.commonError: thinking bank-created deposits are not part of money measures
LG-Q-9023.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits, and checkable deposits are part of M1. M2 can also be affected depending on where funds are held.

P52B-S3-MFM-L-001.q: Currency held by the public rises by $20 billion, checking deposits fall by $20 billion, and small time deposits are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2?
options: M1 rises by $20 billion while M2 remains unchanged because currency is broader money.
Both aggregates are unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
M1 and M2 both fall by $20 billion because checking deposits decline.
M1 remains unchanged while M2 rises by $20 billion because currency increases.
P52B-S3-MFM-L-001.commonError: Adding gross component changes without recognizing an offset within both aggregates.
P52B-S3-MFM-L-001.feedback: Currency and checking deposits are both in M1 and M2. An equal transfer between them changes composition but not either total.

P52B-S3-MFM-L-002.q: A new digital wallet stores claims on bank checking deposits and the same balances are still reported as checking deposits. How should statisticians avoid double counting?
options: Count both the checking deposit and the wallet claim as separate M1 balances.
Exclude the checking deposit and count only the wallet claim as part of M2.
Count the underlying deposit once and do not add the wallet claim again.
Remove both records because digitally accessed balances cannot qualify as money.
P52B-S3-MFM-L-002.commonError: Counting two records of the same underlying monetary claim as two balances.
P52B-S3-MFM-L-002.feedback: A wallet claim backed one-for-one by an already-counted checking deposit is another access channel, not a second stock of money.

P52B-S3-MFM-L-003.q: An economy replaces an unstable commodity money with fiat currency. Which condition is most important for the fiat currency to function well?
options: The currency must possess substantial nonmonetary commodity value in every use.
Every note must remain redeemable for a fixed quantity of gold or silver.
The government must prohibit bank deposits and all competing payment methods.
Users must trust its acceptance and the institutions supporting its value.
P52B-S3-MFM-L-003.commonError: Assuming fiat money requires intrinsic commodity value.
P52B-S3-MFM-L-003.feedback: Fiat money works because of general acceptability, legal and institutional support, and confidence in its purchasing power.

LG-Q-104.q: Currency held by the public is $800 billion and checkable deposits are $1,200 billion. Assume these are the only M1 components with nonzero balances. What is M1?
options: $2,000 billion
$1,200 billion
$800 billion
$400 billion
LG-Q-104.commonError: leaving out either currency or checkable deposits
LG-Q-104.feedback: M1 includes currency plus checkable deposits: $800 billion + $1,200 billion = $2,000 billion.

LG-Q-105.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $2,000 billion, savings deposits are $900 billion, small time deposits are $300 billion, and retail money market mutual funds are $200 billion. M2 is
options: $3,400 billion
$2,000 billion
$1,400 billion
$2,300 billion
LG-Q-105.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
LG-Q-105.feedback: M2 equals M1 plus near monies: $2,000 + $900 + $300 + $200 = $3,400 billion.

LG-Q-202.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists currency held by the public as $900, checkable deposits as $1,600, savings deposits as $2,000, small time deposits as $700, and retail money market funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
LG-Q-202.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
LG-Q-202.feedback: M1 = currency + checkable deposits = $2,500. M2 = M1 + savings + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $5,500.

LG-Q-2000.q: Which statement correctly describes fiat money?
options: It has value because people accept it and government supports its use.
It has value because the material itself is valuable.
It can only serve as a store of value.
It is excluded from the money supply.
LG-Q-2000.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
LG-Q-2000.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. It works because people accept it.

LG-Q-2001.q: A person uses dollars to buy groceries, compare prices, and save for next month. Which functions of money are being used?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value
Store of value only
Unit of account only
Reserve requirement and money multiplier
LG-Q-2001.commonError: thinking money only has one function at a time
LG-Q-2001.feedback: Buying, comparing prices, and saving line up with the three core functions of money.

LG-Q-2002.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Currency held by the public is $900, checkable deposits are $1,100, savings deposits are $1,500, and small time deposits are $500. What are M1 and M2?
LG-Q-2002.commonError: forgetting M2 includes M1 plus near monies
LG-Q-2002.feedback: M1 is $900 + $1,100 = $2,000. M2 adds savings and small time deposits, so M2 = $4,000.

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-001.q: Which item belongs in M1 under standard textbook definitions?
options: A balance in a checking account.
A small time deposit.
A retail money-market mutual fund.
A long-term corporate bond.
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-001.commonError: Including broad near-money assets in the narrow M1 measure.
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-001.feedback: Checking deposits are immediately spendable and are included in M1.

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-002.q: A restaurant posts every menu price in dollars. Which function of money is being used?
options: Medium of exchange.
Unit of account.
Store of value.
Commodity backing.
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-002.commonError: Confusing the act of quoting prices with settling a transaction.
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-002.feedback: Money serves as a unit of account when it provides the common measurement used to state prices.

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-003.q: A saver moves funds from checking to a small time deposit. Which result is correct?
options: M1 and M2 both decrease.
M1 does not change, but M2 increases.
M1 decreases, but M2 does not change.
M1 and M2 both increase.
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-003.commonError: Treating an internal transfer within M2 as a change in M2.
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-003.feedback: Checking is in M1 and M2; a small time deposit is in M2 only. The transfer lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

P52B-S3-MFM-B3-001.q: A bank customer withdraws $500 from checking and holds the cash. What happens to M1?
options: M1 falls by $500 because checking deposits decline.
M1 rises by $500 because currency increases.
M1 falls while M2 rises by $500.
M1 is unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-001.commonError: Looking at one component change without accounting for the offsetting M1 component.
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-001.feedback: Currency held by the public and checking deposits are both in M1, so the transfer changes composition rather than the total.

P52B-S3-MFM-B3-002.q: An online service lets users pay merchants directly from savings accounts. What is the safest conclusion about money measurement?
options: Classification still depends on the official definition of the account.
Every savings balance automatically moves into M1 once direct payments are possible.
The payment service creates new money each time a customer completes a purchase.
Savings accounts must be removed from M2 because they are now easier to spend.
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-002.commonError: Assuming technology alone automatically changes official monetary definitions.
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-002.feedback: A new payment channel can make an asset more usable without automatically changing how statistical agencies classify the underlying account.

P52B-S3-MFM-B3-003.q: Prices are quoted in dollars, workers accept dollars as wages, and households save dollars for emergencies. What does this example show?
options: Money is performing only as a medium of exchange.
Money is performing all three primary functions.
Money is performing only as a unit of account.
Money is performing only as a store of value.
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-003.commonError: Selecting one function when the scenario demonstrates several.
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-003.feedback: The dollar measures value, settles transactions, and transfers purchasing power over time.

LG-Q-9110.q: Use current U.S. definitions, in which savings deposits are part of M1. A household shifts $75,000 from checking to savings at the same bank. Later the bank originates a $12,000 loan by crediting another customer’s checking account; no loan is repaid and no other balance changes. Relative to the starting totals, how do M1 and M2 change?
options: Both rise by $12,000.
M1 falls by $63,000; M2 rises by $12,000.
Both rise by $87,000.
Both remain unchanged.
LG-Q-9110.commonError: thinking moving funds within M2 must change M2
LG-Q-9110.feedback: The checking-to-savings transfer changes neither aggregate and does not release reserves. The new loan adds a $12,000 deposit, raising both M1 and M2 by that amount.

P52B-S3-MFM-LB-001.q: M1 equals $900 billion and M2 equals $3.4 trillion. Households transfer $80 billion from checking deposits to small time deposits. What are the new values?
options: M1 remains $900 billion and M2 becomes $3.48 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 is $3.32 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
M1 becomes $980 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
P52B-S3-MFM-LB-001.commonError: Subtracting the transfer from both aggregates instead of recognizing it remains inside M2.
P52B-S3-MFM-LB-001.feedback: The transfer leaves the broad M2 total unchanged but removes $80 billion from the narrower M1 measure.

P52B-S3-MFM-LB-002.q: A wallet provider reports $10 billion of customer balances that are fully backed by $10 billion already counted in bank checking deposits. What is the correct measurement treatment?
options: Add the full wallet balance to both M1 and M2 even though the deposit is counted.
Remove the bank deposit and count only the wallet balance in the money stock.
Exclude both balances because electronic monetary claims cannot be measured.
Do not add the wallet balance unless it is a separate monetary liability.
P52B-S3-MFM-LB-002.commonError: Double counting an access claim and the underlying deposit.
P52B-S3-MFM-LB-002.feedback: If the wallet balance is simply a claim on an already-counted deposit, adding both would overstate the money stock.

options: Government acceptance and public trust, not intrinsic commodity value
Its gold content alone
A fixed reserve requirement
Its use only in foreign trade
ECON-SP-COMMODITY-VS-FIAT-MONEY-5067.feedback: Fiat money has value because it is accepted in exchange, not because the paper itself is valuable.

options: Currency held by the public
Large time deposits
Credit card debt
Corporate bonds
ECON-SP-DISTINGUISH-M1-M2-5002.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

ECON-SP-DISTINGUISH-M1-M2-5003.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item is in M2 but not M1?
options: Savings deposits
Currency
Checkable deposits
Coins
ECON-SP-DISTINGUISH-M1-M2-5003.feedback: M2 includes near monies such as savings deposits.

ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-MONEY-FUNCTIONS-5000.q: Money used to buy goods and services is serving which function?
options: Medium of exchange
Store of value
Unit of account
Reserve ratio
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-MONEY-FUNCTIONS-5000.feedback: Buying goods and services uses money as a medium of exchange.

ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-MONEY-FUNCTIONS-5001.q: Money used to compare prices is serving which function?
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Discount rate
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-MONEY-FUNCTIONS-5001.feedback: Listing prices uses money as a unit of account.

LG-R-5000.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
LG-R-5000.q: A household owns a home and stocks and earns a salary, but keeps very little currency or checking deposits. Which statement is correct?
options: Wealth and income can be high even when the household holds little money
All household wealth is counted in M1 because it can eventually be sold
Salary income is automatically part of the money supply before it is paid
Only physical currency can count as money, so checking deposits are wealth instead
LG-R-5000.feedback: Money is the stock of spendable balances, not total wealth or income; a household can own valuable assets and earn a high salary while holding little currency or checking deposits.

LG-R-5001.commonError: Mixing up the three functions of money.
LG-R-5001.q: Money used to list the price of a laptop is serving as:
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Federal funds rate
LG-R-5001.feedback: Money is a unit of account when it is used to measure and quote value.

LG-R-5002.commonError: Thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value.
LG-R-5002.q: Fiat money has value mainly because:
options: People accept it and government supports its use
The paper itself is valuable
It is always backed by gold
It is never used in modern economies
LG-R-5002.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. It works because people accept it.

LG-R-5003.commonError: Confusing fiat money and commodity money.
LG-R-5003.q: Which feature distinguishes commodity money from fiat money?
options: Has intrinsic value
Cannot be used to buy goods
Is created only by banks
Is excluded from M1
LG-R-5003.feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself. Fiat money does not.

LG-R-5004.commonError: Forgetting that M1 includes currency and checkable deposits.
options: Currency and checkable deposits
Savings deposits only
Small time deposits only
All financial assets
LG-R-5004.feedback: M1 is the narrow money measure with currency and checkable deposits.

LG-R-5005.commonError: Forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies.
LG-R-5005.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. M2 equals:
options: M1 plus near monies like savings deposits
Only currency
Only checkable deposits
Only government bonds
LG-R-5005.feedback: M2 includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

ECON-SP-DISTINGUISH-M1-M2-6001.q: Households move cash from wallets into checking accounts. The composition of M1 changes little, but what banking consequence can the shift create?
options: Banks receive deposits and reserves that can support lending under the banking model
The deposits stop counting in M1 because checking accounts are not money
The central bank must create matching bank capital before any deposit can be accepted
The shift guarantees the maximum simple money multiplier regardless of bank behavior
ECON-SP-DISTINGUISH-M1-M2-6001.feedback: Moving cash into checking changes little in M1, but it gives banks deposits and reserves that can support lending under the banking model.
ECON-SP-DISTINGUISH-M1-M2-6001.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-MONEY-FUNCTIONS-6000.q: A grocery store accepts dollars for food, lists prices in dollars, and saves cash overnight. Which set matches the functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, money multiplier
Unit of account, discount rate, federal funds rate
Medium of exchange, LRAS, inflation tax
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-MONEY-FUNCTIONS-6000.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and stores purchasing power over time.

LG-B-6000.commonError: Mixing up the three functions of money.
LG-B-6000.q: A store lists coffee at $6, accepts dollars for payment, and the owner saves some cash for later. Which functions appear?
options: Unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value
Medium of exchange only
Store of value only
Reserve requirement and multiplier
LG-B-6000.feedback: The price is unit of account, payment is medium of exchange, and saving is store of value.

LG-B-6001.commonError: Forgetting M2 includes M1 plus near monies.
LG-B-6001.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Currency is $800, checkable deposits are $1,200, and savings deposits are $1,500. What are M1 and M2?
LG-B-6001.feedback: M1 = currency + checkable deposits = $2,000. M2 adds savings deposits, so M2 = $3,500.

ECON-SP-EASY-7.q: What is the central bank of the United States?
options: The Treasury Department
Congress
The Federal Reserve
The FDIC
ECON-SP-EASY-7.commonError: Confusing the Fed with fiscal agencies.
ECON-SP-EASY-7.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.

options: Federal Open Market Committee
Congressional Budget Office
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Internal Revenue Service
ECON-SP-EASY-8.commonError: Confusing monetary policy agencies with data or tax agencies.
ECON-SP-EASY-8.feedback: The FOMC directs open-market operations as part of monetary policy.

LG-Q-61.q: One major role of the Federal Reserve is to act as
options: a lender of last resort for banks
the agency that collects personal income taxes
the branch of government that writes spending bills
the organization that produces real GDP data
LG-Q-61.commonError: confusing the Federal Reserve with fiscal agencies
LG-Q-61.feedback: The Fed can serve as a lender of last resort by lending to banks when they need liquidity.

LG-Q-62.q: The discount rate is the interest rate
options: the Fed charges banks for loans
banks charge each other on overnight loans
households earn on checking accounts
Congress pays on tax refunds
LG-Q-62.commonError: confusing the discount rate with the federal funds rate
LG-Q-62.feedback: The discount rate is the interest rate the Fed charges banks when it lends to them.

LG-Q-63.q: The federal funds rate is best described as the interest rate
options: banks charge each other for short-term overnight loans
the Fed charges households for mortgages
Congress sets on government spending
firms pay workers as a wage
LG-Q-63.commonError: thinking the federal funds rate is directly charged to consumers by the Fed
LG-Q-63.feedback: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.

LG-Q-8.q: The Federal Reserve is best described as
options: the central bank of the United States
the agency that writes the federal budget
a private commercial bank that lends only to households
the part of Congress that sets tax rates
LG-Q-8.commonError: confusing the Fed with fiscal policymakers
LG-Q-8.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States and conducts monetary policy.

LG-Q-9.q: The Federal Open Market Committee is most directly responsible for
options: conducting open-market operations
setting federal income tax rates
writing government spending bills
calculating the unemployment rate
LG-Q-9.commonError: confusing monetary policy with fiscal policy
LG-Q-9.feedback: The FOMC conducts monetary policy largely through buying and selling government bonds.

LG-Q-113.q: Which statement best describes the FOMC's role?
options: It guides monetary policy and open-market operations.
It sets federal income tax brackets.
It calculates the CPI.
It decides how much Congress spends.
LG-Q-113.commonError: confusing the FOMC with fiscal policymakers
LG-Q-113.feedback: The FOMC is central to monetary policy, especially open-market operations.

LG-Q-114.q: The Fed is called a lender of last resort because it can
options: lend to banks facing liquidity problems
lend directly to every household for groceries
write spending bills for Congress
set all market prices
LG-Q-114.commonError: thinking lender of last resort means normal consumer lending
LG-Q-114.feedback: The Fed can lend to banks when they face liquidity stress, which is why it is called a lender of last resort.

LG-Q-115.q: Why does central bank independence matter?
options: It can help monetary policy avoid short-run political pressure.
It lets the Fed collect income taxes.
It prevents banks from holding reserves.
It means the Fed is owned by Congress.
LG-Q-115.commonError: thinking independence means no public role or accountability
LG-Q-115.feedback: Central bank independence can help keep monetary policy from being driven by short-run political incentives.

P52B-S1-FED-M-001.q: Which distinction between the Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury is correct?
options: The Treasury sets the federal funds rate, while the Fed writes tax laws.
The Fed passes the federal budget, while the Treasury regulates inflation expectations.
The Fed conducts monetary policy, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
Both institutions perform exactly the same functions.
P52B-S1-FED-M-001.commonError: Treating the central bank and fiscal authority as the same institution.
P52B-S1-FED-M-001.feedback: The Fed is the monetary authority; the Treasury is part of the executive branch and manages federal finances.

PM2C1-FED-M-001.q: A commercial bank approves a loan and credits the borrower’s checking account. In a separate transaction, the Federal Reserve credits a bank’s reserve account during an asset purchase. Which distinction is correct?
options: The commercial bank creates a deposit liability; the Fed creates central-bank reserves
The Fed creates the borrower’s commercial-bank deposit, while the bank creates central-bank reserves
Both transactions create only physical currency held by the public
Neither transaction changes any bank liability or reserve balance
PM2C1-FED-M-001.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
PM2C1-FED-M-001.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

PM2C1-FED-M-002.q: A headline says, “The Treasury raised the federal funds rate to conduct monetary policy.” What is the best correction?
options: The statement is correct because the Treasury and Federal Reserve are the same institution
The federal funds rate is set by commercial banks with no connection to Federal Reserve policy
The Treasury sets monetary policy while the Federal Reserve determines tax rates and federal spending
Monetary policy and the federal funds rate are associated with the Federal Reserve, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations
PM2C1-FED-M-002.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
PM2C1-FED-M-002.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

P52B-S1-FED-H-001.q: During a panic, a solvent bank cannot obtain short-term funding even though its assets exceed its liabilities. What central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort role?
options: Guarantee every bank loss without conditions.
Finance a permanent tax cut.
Raise reserve requirements solely to remove liquidity.
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral.
P52B-S1-FED-H-001.commonError: Confusing liquidity support with an unconditional bailout of insolvent institutions.
P52B-S1-FED-H-001.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems while safeguards limit losses and moral hazard.

P52B-S1-FED-H-002.q: Which institutional arrangement best combines central-bank independence with democratic accountability?
options: Public officials set the mandate; the central bank chooses instruments and reports transparently.
The central bank chooses national goals and never explains its decisions to the public.
Elected officials directly set policy interest rates before every national election.
The Treasury secretly directs monetary operations without a published mandate.
P52B-S1-FED-H-002.commonError: Treating independence as freedom from any public mandate or oversight.
P52B-S1-FED-H-002.feedback: Instrument independence can coexist with a legislated mandate, transparency, and public accountability.

P52B-S1-FED-H-003.q: When the central bank buys a large quantity of longer-term securities, what happens directly on its balance sheet?
options: Tax revenue rises while currency liabilities disappear from the balance sheet.
Its securities assets and reserve liabilities usually both rise.
Government purchases of goods rise automatically with the securities purchase.
Commercial-bank capital is converted directly into federal tax receipts.
P52B-S1-FED-H-003.commonError: Treating asset purchases as ordinary fiscal spending.
P52B-S1-FED-H-003.feedback: A central-bank asset purchase expands its asset holdings and typically creates reserve liabilities.

P52B-S1-FED-H-004.q: The short-term policy rate is near its effective lower bound. Which action is still a monetary-policy option?
options: Change federal income-tax rates through the banking system.
Authorize a new congressional spending program immediately.
Use forward guidance or buy longer-term securities.
Set private-sector wages and prices by administrative order.
P52B-S1-FED-H-004.commonError: Assuming monetary policy has no remaining tools when a short-term rate is very low.
P52B-S1-FED-H-004.feedback: Central banks may use communication and balance-sheet tools when conventional rate cuts are constrained.

PM2C1-FED-H-001.q: During a panic, a bank has valuable assets but cannot obtain enough short-term funding to meet payments. Later analysis shows another bank’s assets are worth less than its liabilities. Why should a central bank treat the two cases differently?
options: Liquidity can address the first bank’s funding problem, but it cannot erase the second bank’s insolvency
Both banks should receive unlimited central-bank loans because any funding problem proves that losses and insolvency are irrelevant
The insolvent bank needs only a lower reserve requirement, while the solvent bank must be closed immediately
The central bank should finance both banks permanently because recognizing losses is a fiscal-policy function
PM2C1-FED-H-001.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
PM2C1-FED-H-001.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

PM2C1-FED-H-002.q: A central-bank asset purchase sharply increases reserve balances, yet commercial-bank lending changes little. Which statement best separates the institutions’ roles?
options: The central bank failed to create any reserve balances because commercial banks did not expand loans after the asset purchase
Commercial banks create central-bank reserves whenever they choose not to lend
Reserve balances are identical to bank capital, so unchanged lending proves capital was unchanged
The central bank creates reserves; commercial-bank deposit creation still depends on lending and borrowing
PM2C1-FED-H-002.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
PM2C1-FED-H-002.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

P52B-S1-FED-EL-001.q: A government persistently pressures its central bank to create money to finance large deficits. What institutional risk is most relevant?
options: The natural rate of unemployment automatically becomes zero.
The money supply becomes unrelated to the central bank.
Budget deficits cease to have opportunity costs.
Fiscal dominance can weaken price stability and central-bank credibility.
P52B-S1-FED-EL-001.commonError: Ignoring how fiscal pressure can compromise monetary-policy objectives.
P52B-S1-FED-EL-001.feedback: Under fiscal dominance, debt-financing pressure can subordinate monetary policy and raise inflation risk.

P52B-S1-FED-EL-002.q: Emergency lending stops a bank run, but banks now expect rescue whenever they take large risks. What tradeoff does the central bank face?
options: Financial stability today versus greater moral hazard tomorrow.
Lower inflation today versus a permanently lower natural rate.
Higher taxes today versus lower government spending tomorrow.
More exports today versus fewer imports tomorrow.
P52B-S1-FED-EL-002.commonError: Evaluating emergency lending without considering future risk-taking incentives.
P52B-S1-FED-EL-002.feedback: Liquidity support can stabilize the system, but poorly designed guarantees can encourage excessive risk.

LG-Q-9020.q: A country has no central bank independence. Before elections, policymakers pressure the central bank to buy bonds and expand money aggressively. Which long-run risk is most consistent with the course logic?
options: Political pressure may create excessive money growth and inflation.
Political pressure guarantees higher real output forever.
Bond purchases permanently lower the price level.
Money becomes commodity money.
LG-Q-9020.commonError: thinking central bank independence is irrelevant to inflation outcomes
LG-Q-9020.feedback: Central bank independence can help reduce politically motivated money growth that risks inflation.

P52B-S1-FED-L-001.q: Why does central-bank independence not mean the central bank should be free to choose any social objective it wants?
options: Independence requires all monetary-policy decisions to remain secret.
Independence covers instrument choice within a publicly established mandate.
The central bank must directly control federal taxes and spending.
Independence means elected institutions have no legitimate policy role.
P52B-S1-FED-L-001.commonError: Equating instrument independence with unlimited policy authority.
P52B-S1-FED-L-001.feedback: A legitimate framework separates public goal setting from day-to-day instrument choices and requires accountability.

P52B-S1-FED-L-002.q: Inflation is well above target and output is near potential, but elected officials demand easier money before an election. What is the strongest case for central-bank independence?
options: It guarantees that monetary tightening has no short-run output cost.
It allows the central bank to eliminate every federal budget deficit.
It resists election-driven easing and protects price-stability credibility.
It permanently fixes unemployment below the natural rate.
P52B-S1-FED-L-002.commonError: Assuming independence removes policy tradeoffs rather than improving commitment.
P52B-S1-FED-L-002.feedback: Independence can support credible commitment to price stability even when near-term political incentives favor expansion.

PM2C1-FED-L-001.q: A crisis program has two parts: the central bank lends temporarily against sound collateral to solvent banks, while the fiscal authority injects taxpayer capital into an insolvent institution. What principle best distinguishes the two actions?
options: Central-bank liquidity support addresses funding; fiscal recapitalization addresses losses and solvency
Both actions are ordinary open-market operations because each changes a financial balance sheet
The central bank is conducting fiscal policy in both cases because all emergency lending uses tax revenue
The fiscal authority is acting as lender of last resort while the central bank is collecting taxes
PM2C1-FED-L-001.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
PM2C1-FED-L-001.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

PM2C1-FED-L-002.q: The central bank expands its balance sheet and reserve balances surge. Banks, however, tighten underwriting and firms postpone borrowing because sales prospects are weak. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The central bank did not actually create reserves because bank lending failed to rise
Weak borrowing proves that commercial banks, not the central bank, issue reserve balances
The simple multiplier guarantees the same deposit expansion regardless of banks or borrowers
Creating reserves does not mechanically force commercial-bank lending or deposit expansion
PM2C1-FED-L-002.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
PM2C1-FED-L-002.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

PM2C1-FED-L-003.q: A student argues that the Federal Reserve must be part of the Treasury because its actions can affect government-security markets. Which response is most accurate?
options: The Treasury conducts monetary policy whenever the Fed buys a government security
Government securities cannot appear on a central-bank balance sheet unless Congress sets the policy rate directly
The Fed is a distinct central bank even though its operations can involve government securities
The Fed is legally just a Treasury checking account because both institutions handle government securities
PM2C1-FED-L-003.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
PM2C1-FED-L-003.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

LG-Q-2003.q: Which description correctly identifies the Federal Reserve?
options: the central bank of the United States
the agency that writes federal spending bills
the agency that collects income taxes
a private household lender
LG-Q-2003.commonError: confusing the Fed with fiscal agencies
LG-Q-2003.feedback: The Fed is the U.S. central bank. It handles monetary policy, not tax law.

LG-Q-2004.q: The FOMC is most directly connected to
options: open-market operations and monetary policy
writing the federal budget
calculating the CPI
setting income tax brackets
LG-Q-2004.commonError: confusing FOMC actions with fiscal policy
LG-Q-2004.feedback: The FOMC conducts monetary policy largely through open-market operations.

LG-Q-2005.q: A central bank faces political pressure to expand money before an election. Why does central bank independence matter here?
options: It limits political pressure for excessive money growth.
It lets the Fed set income tax rates.
It prevents all inflation forever.
It makes banks stop lending.
LG-Q-2005.commonError: thinking Fed independence has nothing to do with inflation risk
LG-Q-2005.feedback: Independence can help keep monetary policy from being pushed around for short-run political gain.

PM2C1-FED-FB-004.q: A solvent bank cannot obtain overnight funding during a panic, while an insolvent bank has losses larger than its capital. Which central-bank principle is most important?
options: Neither bank can receive liquidity because central banks deal only with government budgets
Liquidity lending can help the solvent bank, but it cannot by itself restore the insolvent bank’s capital
Both problems are identical and can be solved by unlimited reserve creation
Only the insolvent bank qualifies for lender-of-last-resort support because it has larger losses
PM2C1-FED-FB-004.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
PM2C1-FED-FB-004.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

PM2C1-FED-FB-005.q: The government establishes the central bank’s mandate, but elected officials cannot order a pre-election interest-rate change. The bank must explain its decisions publicly. What does this arrangement combine?
options: Instrument independence with democratic accountability
Complete independence from any public mandate
Fiscal dominance with no central-bank discretion
Commercial-bank control of the monetary-policy mandate
PM2C1-FED-FB-005.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
PM2C1-FED-FB-005.feedback: Elected institutions establish the public mandate, while the central bank retains day-to-day instrument choice and reports its decisions, combining operational independence with accountability.

PM2C1-FED-FB-006.q: The central bank adds reserves through an asset purchase, but banks and borrowers do not expand credit. What can still be said with confidence?
options: The asset purchase could not have occurred because every reserve increase must create the maximum amount of loans
Commercial banks must have created the reserve balances before the central bank could buy the asset
The lack of new lending means the action was fiscal rather than monetary
The central bank changed reserve conditions even though broader deposit creation did not respond mechanically
PM2C1-FED-FB-006.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
PM2C1-FED-FB-006.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

PM2C1-FED-MB-001.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Federal Reserve from a commercial bank?
options: The Fed can create reserve balances; a commercial bank creates deposits when it makes loans
The commercial bank creates Federal Reserve reserve liabilities for the payment system, while the Fed creates private bank capital for each lender
Both institutions issue only physical currency and neither creates account balances
The Fed accepts household checking deposits in the same way as a retail bank
PM2C1-FED-MB-001.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
PM2C1-FED-MB-001.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

PM2C1-FED-MB-002.q: Which statement best distinguishes the Federal Reserve from the U.S. Treasury?
options: The Treasury conducts monetary policy and determines bank reserve conditions; the Fed sets federal tax rates for Congress
The two names refer to the same institution
The Fed manages congressional spending while the Treasury supplies bank reserves
The Fed conducts monetary policy; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations
PM2C1-FED-MB-002.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
PM2C1-FED-MB-002.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

PM2C1-FED-MB-003.q: A central-bank committee decides to change monetary conditions. Which institutional description is most accurate?
options: The committee determines federal tax rates and appropriations for the entire national budget
The committee measures M1 but has no connection to monetary policy
The policy-making body chooses monetary actions within the central bank’s mandate
The committee directly approves household mortgages at commercial banks
PM2C1-FED-MB-003.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
PM2C1-FED-MB-003.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

LG-Q-9111.q: A central bank under political pressure buys bonds aggressively before an election. Banks lend most of the new reserves, and output is already near potential. Which long-run risk is most consistent with the chapter logic?
options: Excessive money growth creates inflation pressure without lasting real-output gains.
Real output permanently rises because more money creates more resources.
The price level falls because bond purchases reduce reserves.
Money demand becomes zero.
LG-Q-9111.commonError: thinking money growth permanently raises real output
LG-Q-9111.feedback: If output is near potential, aggressive money growth mainly risks inflation rather than permanent real gains.

PM2C1-FED-LB-001.q: A commercial bank makes a loan by crediting a deposit, while the Federal Reserve supplies reserve balances to banks. Which statement best separates the two forms of money creation?
options: Commercial banks create deposits; the central bank creates reserves and base money
Commercial banks issue reserve balances; the central bank issues all checking deposits
Both institutions can create only physical currency
Neither institution can create a financial liability
PM2C1-FED-LB-001.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
PM2C1-FED-LB-001.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

PM2C1-FED-LB-002.q: A bank is solvent but temporarily unable to meet payments because short-term funding markets freeze. Which central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort principle?
options: Use tax revenue to replace every risky bank asset permanently
Refuse all liquidity because a funding shortage proves assets are worthless
Order the Treasury to guarantee every future bank loss
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral to an otherwise solvent bank
PM2C1-FED-LB-002.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
PM2C1-FED-LB-002.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

ECON-SP-CENTRAL-BANK-ROLE-5004.q: What is the central bank of the United States?
options: The Federal Reserve
The Treasury
Congress
The IRS
ECON-SP-CENTRAL-BANK-ROLE-5004.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.

options: FOMC
IRS
BLS
CBO
ECON-SP-FOMC-ROLE-5005.feedback: The Federal Open Market Committee directs open-market operations.

LG-R-5006.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
LG-R-5006.q: A solvent bank has sound assets but cannot obtain short-term funding during a panic. Which central-bank role is designed for this situation?
options: Lender of last resort
Collector of federal income taxes
Issuer of corporate stock
Manager of the congressional budget
LG-R-5006.feedback: A lender of last resort provides temporary liquidity to a solvent bank facing a funding panic.

LG-R-5007.commonError: Confusing monetary policy with fiscal policy.
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Tax collection
LG-R-5007.feedback: The Fed handles monetary policy, not taxes and government spending.

LG-R-5008.q: The FOMC is most closely tied to:
options: Open-market operations
Income tax rates
Federal spending bills
GDP measurement
LG-R-5008.feedback: The FOMC helps direct monetary policy through open-market operations.

LG-R-5009.commonError: Thinking FOMC decisions are fiscal policy.
LG-R-5009.q: When the FOMC buys or sells bonds, it is using:
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Labor policy
LG-R-5009.feedback: Buying and selling bonds is monetary policy.

LG-R-5010.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
LG-R-5010.q: Elected officials establish a central bank’s mandate, while the bank chooses how to use its policy instruments and reports its decisions publicly. What principle does this arrangement illustrate?
options: Instrument independence combined with public accountability
Complete independence from any publicly established mandate
Fiscal dominance because elected officials choose tax rates
Abolition of central-bank discretion over policy instruments
LG-R-5010.feedback: The arrangement gives the bank instrument independence within a public mandate and requires it to explain its decisions, preserving democratic accountability.

LG-R-5011.commonError: Missing the link between political pressure and inflation risk.
LG-R-5011.q: Political pressure to print money can create risk of:
options: Inflation
Deflation always
Zero money demand
No nominal prices
LG-R-5011.feedback: Politically driven money growth can create inflation pressure.

ECON-SP-CENTRAL-BANK-ROLE-6002.q: A financial panic hits and the banking system needs a lender-of-last-resort institution. Which institution fits?
options: Federal Reserve
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Congressional Budget Office
Internal Revenue Service
ECON-SP-CENTRAL-BANK-ROLE-6002.feedback: The Fed acts as the central bank and lender of last resort.

ECON-SP-FOMC-ROLE-6003.q: The FOMC decides that monetary conditions should be easier and authorizes purchases of securities. What connection is being made?
options: The FOMC is choosing a monetary-policy tool that adds reserves
The Treasury is using fiscal policy to change government purchases
A commercial bank is deciding how much capital to issue to shareholders
Households are changing M1 by moving funds from checking to savings
ECON-SP-FOMC-ROLE-6003.feedback: When the FOMC authorizes securities purchases, it is using an expansionary monetary-policy tool that adds reserve balances to banks.
ECON-SP-FOMC-ROLE-6003.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

LG-B-6002.commonError: Confusing the Fed with Congress or the Treasury.
LG-B-6002.q: If a policy changes bank reserves and interest rates, it is most likely:
options: Monetary policy by the Fed
Fiscal policy by Congress
Trade policy
GDP accounting
LG-B-6002.feedback: Changes in reserves and interest rates are monetary policy territory.

LG-Q-13.q: In a fractional reserve banking system, banks
options: hold only part of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest
must keep 100 percent of deposits as cash
cannot affect the money supply
create money by printing currency
LG-Q-13.commonError: thinking banks create money by printing currency
LG-Q-13.feedback: Fractional reserve banking means banks keep some deposits as reserves and lend the rest.

LG-Q-16.q: The money multiplier becomes larger when the reserve ratio
options: falls
rises
equals the inflation rate
equals the nominal interest rate
LG-Q-16.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more lending
LG-Q-16.feedback: A lower reserve ratio lets banks lend more of each deposit, which increases the money multiplier.

P52A-BANK-E-001.q: For a commercial bank, customer deposits are recorded as:
options: Revenue because deposits increase cash.
Liabilities because the bank owes the funds to depositors.
Bank capital because deposits belong to shareholders.
Assets because the bank physically holds the money.
P52A-BANK-E-001.feedback: Deposits are liabilities: the bank has an obligation to repay depositors.

P52A-BANK-E-002.q: A 10 percent reserve rule applies to a $50,000 deposit base. How much must the bank keep rather than lend?
P52A-BANK-E-002.commonError: Multiplying by the lending share instead of the reserve ratio.

P52A-BANK-E-003.q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, the loan is recorded as:
options: Bank capital only.
An asset of the bank.
A reduction in deposits with no matching asset.
A liability of the bank.
P52A-BANK-E-003.feedback: Borrowers owe repayment to the bank, so loans are bank assets.

P52A-BANK-M-001.q: A bank has $300,000 in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $50,000 in actual reserves. Excess reserves are:
P52A-BANK-M-001.commonError: Forgetting to subtract required reserves from actual reserves.
P52A-BANK-M-001.feedback: Required reserves are $36,000, leaving $14,000 in excess reserves.

P52A-BANK-M-002.q: A new $2,000 deposit enters a bank with a 20 percent reserve requirement. The bank’s maximum first-round loan is:
P52A-BANK-M-002.commonError: Using required reserves as lending or applying the multiplier to the first round.
P52A-BANK-M-002.feedback: The bank keeps $400 and may lend $1,600.

P52A-BANK-M-005.q: A bank reports $14 million in assets and $12.9 million in liabilities. What is its capital cushion?
options: $26.9 million.
$1.1 million.
$14 million.
$12.9 million.
P52A-BANK-M-005.commonError: Adding assets and liabilities or using liabilities alone.
P52A-BANK-M-005.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $1.1 million.

LG-Q-221.q: Why does leverage make banks riskier?
options: A small percentage loss on assets can wipe out a large share of capital.
It guarantees assets never fall in value.
It prevents banks from making loans.
It makes reserves unnecessary.
LG-Q-221.commonError: thinking leverage only increases returns and not risk
LG-Q-221.feedback: Leverage magnifies gains and losses. A small asset loss can hit capital hard.

LG-Q-222.q: A bank originates a loan by crediting its borrower’s checking account. The borrower then pays a supplier at a different bank, and the payment settles in reserves. Which comparison correctly separates origination from settlement?
options: Origination adds a loan and a deposit; settlement reduces the originating bank’s reserves and its borrower’s deposit.
Origination reduces reserves; settlement creates the loan and increases bank capital.
Origination adds reserves and a deposit; settlement leaves both banks’ reserves unchanged.
Origination reduces deposits; settlement cancels the originating bank’s loan asset.
LG-Q-222.commonError: thinking loans reduce assets instead of changing asset composition
LG-Q-222.feedback: Crediting the account initially adds a loan asset and a deposit liability. The later outgoing payment reduces reserves and the deposit liability; the loan remains an asset.

P52A-BANK-H-001.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a 10 percent reserve requirement, and $95,000 in reserves. If deposits increase by $100,000 and reserves rise by $20,000, the bank’s new excess reserves are:
P52A-BANK-H-001.commonError: Updating deposits or reserves but not both.
P52A-BANK-H-001.feedback: New deposits are $900,000, required reserves are $90,000, and actual reserves are $115,000.

P52A-BANK-H-002.q: A bank has $25 million in assets and $1.5 million in capital. An 8 percent asset loss occurs. What is the new capital position?
options: $0.5 million.
-$0.5 million.
-$2.0 million.
$1.5 million.
P52A-BANK-H-002.commonError: Applying the loss to capital instead of assets.
P52A-BANK-H-002.feedback: An 8 percent asset loss is $2 million, reducing $1.5 million of capital to -$0.5 million.

P52A-BANK-H-003.q: A banking system has a 10 percent reserve requirement, but banks hold an additional 5 percent of deposits as excess reserves and the public holds no currency. A simple effective deposit multiplier is closest to:
P52A-BANK-H-003.feedback: If 15 percent of deposits is retained, the simple effective multiplier is about 1/0.15 = 6.67.

LG-Q-301.q: Assume the bank cannot obtain extra reserves, sell assets, or retain any new loan proceeds as deposits; every new loan payment would leave the bank. A bank has $900,000 in deposits, a 15 percent reserve requirement, and $135,000 in actual reserves. What can the bank do immediately?
options: It cannot lend more because actual reserves equal required reserves.
It can lend $135,000 because all reserves are excess reserves.
It can lend $765,000 because deposits minus reserves are lendable.
It must borrow $15,000 from the Fed.
LG-Q-301.commonError: treating required reserves as lendable reserves
LG-Q-301.feedback: Required reserves are 0.15 x $900,000 = $135,000. Actual reserves equal required reserves, so there are no excess reserves to lend.

LG-Q-302.q: A bank has $1,200,000 in deposits, $210,000 in reserves, and a 12.5 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, how much can it lend?
LG-Q-302.commonError: lending all reserves instead of only excess reserves
LG-Q-302.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $1,200,000 = $150,000. Excess reserves are $210,000 - $150,000 = $60,000.

LG-Q-307.q: A bank has assets of $50 million and liabilities of $47 million. Asset values fall by 8 percent. What happens to bank capital?
options: Capital falls from $3 million to negative $1 million.
Capital falls from $3 million to $2.76 million.
Capital rises from $3 million to $7 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb losses first.
LG-Q-307.commonError: applying the percentage loss to capital instead of assets
LG-Q-307.feedback: Initial capital is $3 million. An 8 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4 million, so capital becomes negative $1 million.

LG-Q-313.q: A bank has $100 million in assets and $92 million in liabilities. If asset values fall by 6 percent, what percentage of initial capital is lost?
options: 75 percent
6 percent
8 percent
60 percent
LG-Q-313.commonError: thinking a 6 percent asset loss means a 6 percent capital loss
LG-Q-313.feedback: Initial capital is $8 million. A 6 percent asset loss is $6 million, which is 75 percent of capital.

LG-Q-318.q: A bank has $1 million in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The reserve requirement is 10 percent. What is the bank's reserve problem?
options: It is short $10,000 in required reserves.
It has $90,000 in excess reserves.
It can lend $10,000 immediately.
It has exactly enough reserves.
LG-Q-318.commonError: thinking reserves below required levels are still lendable
LG-Q-318.feedback: Required reserves are $100,000. The bank has $90,000, so it is short $10,000.

LG-Q-322.q: If required reserves are $75,000 and the reserve ratio is 15 percent, what are deposits?
LG-Q-322.commonError: multiplying required reserves by the reserve ratio instead of dividing
LG-Q-322.feedback: Required reserves = r x deposits, so deposits = $75,000 / 0.15 = $500,000.

LG-Q-323.q: If excess reserves are $25,000, actual reserves are $85,000, and the reserve ratio is 12 percent, what are deposits?
LG-Q-323.commonError: forgetting to find required reserves before solving deposits
LG-Q-323.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $85,000 - $25,000 = $60,000. Deposits = $60,000 / 0.12 = $500,000.

LG-Q-326.q: A commercial bank wants to increase lending but is below its required reserves. Which action most directly fixes the reserve shortfall?
options: Borrow reserves or attract new deposits before expanding loans.
Make new loans immediately from required reserves.
Reduce assets by increasing liabilities.
Ignore reserve requirements because lending creates reserves.
LG-Q-326.commonError: thinking banks can lend when already short of required reserves
LG-Q-326.feedback: A bank below required reserves needs reserves before it can safely expand lending.

LG-Q-9004.q: A bank has $50 million in assets, $46 million in liabilities, and then suffers a 9 percent asset loss. What is the new capital position?
options: Capital falls from $4 million to negative $500,000.
Capital falls from $4 million to $3.64 million.
Capital rises from $4 million to $8.5 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb asset losses first.
LG-Q-9004.commonError: applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets
LG-Q-9004.feedback: Initial capital is $4 million. A 9 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4.5 million, so capital becomes negative $500,000.

LG-Q-9007.q: A bank has actual reserves of $96,000, excess reserves of $24,000, and a reserve requirement of 12 percent. What are deposits?
LG-Q-9007.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves
LG-Q-9007.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $96,000 - $24,000 = $72,000. Deposits are $72,000 / 0.12 = $600,000.

LG-Q-9016.q: A bank's assets fall by 4 percent. Its capital ratio before the loss was 5 percent of assets. What happens to most of the bank's capital?
options: Most capital is wiped out because the asset loss is almost as large as the capital cushion.
Capital falls by only 4 percent.
Capital rises because liabilities fall first.
Capital is unaffected because reserves absorb all losses.
LG-Q-9016.commonError: thinking a 4 percent asset loss means only 4 percent of capital is lost
LG-Q-9016.feedback: If capital is only 5 percent of assets, a 4 percent asset loss wipes out four-fifths of the capital cushion.

ECON-SP-EASY-10.q: If a bank receives a $1,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 20 percent, required reserves are:
ECON-SP-EASY-10.commonError: Subtracting instead of multiplying by the reserve requirement.
ECON-SP-EASY-10.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement, so $1,000 x 0.20 = $200.

ECON-SP-HARD-201.q: A bank receives $5,000 in new deposits, holds 15 percent required reserves, and lends the rest. What is the maximum first-round loan?
ECON-SP-HARD-201.commonError: Lending required reserves or using the multiplier too early.
ECON-SP-HARD-201.feedback: Required reserves are $750, so the bank can lend $4,250 in the first round.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-102.q: A bank receives $2,000 in new deposits and faces a 10 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, its first new loan can be:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-102.feedback: Required reserves are $200, so excess reserves are $1,800.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-103.q: A bank has $50,000 in deposits and must hold 8 percent in reserves. Required reserves equal:
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-103.commonError: Dividing deposits by the reserve requirement.

LG-Q-116.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Required reserves equal
LG-Q-116.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve ratio: $500,000 x 0.10 = $50,000.

LG-Q-117.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits, $80,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Excess reserves equal
LG-Q-117.commonError: treating all reserves as excess reserves
LG-Q-117.feedback: Required reserves are $50,000, so excess reserves are $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000.

LG-Q-118.q: A bank receives a new $2,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 25 percent. How much can the bank initially lend?
LG-Q-118.commonError: lending the entire deposit despite reserve requirements
LG-Q-118.feedback: Required reserves are 0.25 x $2,000 = $500, so the bank can initially lend $1,500.

LG-Q-14.q: If a bank has $1,000 in deposits and the reserve requirement is 10 percent, required reserves are
LG-Q-14.feedback: Required reserves equal the reserve ratio times deposits: 0.10 x $1,000 = $100.

LG-Q-15.q: If a bank receives a new $1,000 deposit and must hold $100 in required reserves, the bank can initially lend
LG-Q-15.commonError: thinking the full deposit can be lent when reserves are required
LG-Q-15.feedback: The bank can lend excess reserves. $1,000 minus $100 leaves $900 available to lend.

LG-Q-204.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a required reserve ratio of 12.5 percent, and actual reserves of $140,000. How much can it lend before hitting its required reserve level?
LG-Q-204.commonError: treating all actual reserves as lendable reserves
LG-Q-204.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $800,000 = $100,000. Excess reserves are $140,000 - $100,000 = $40,000.

LG-Q-207.q: Use the textbook reserve-constrained model, with no other changes. A bank has $300,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It currently holds $45,000 in reserves. If it lends all excess reserves, what will its reserves and loans change by? Assume the borrower immediately pays someone at another bank and the entire payment settles in reserves.
options: Reserves fall by $15,000 and loans rise by $15,000.
Reserves fall by $30,000 and loans rise by $30,000.
Reserves fall by $45,000 and loans rise by $45,000.
Reserves rise by $15,000 and loans fall by $15,000.
LG-Q-207.commonError: lending required reserves as if they were excess reserves
LG-Q-207.feedback: Required reserves are $30,000, so excess reserves are $15,000. Lending those lowers reserves by $15,000 and raises loans by $15,000.

LG-Q-219.q: A bank has assets of $10 million and liabilities of $9.4 million. What is bank capital?
options: $9.4 million
$10 million
$19.4 million
LG-Q-219.commonError: adding assets and liabilities instead of subtracting
LG-Q-219.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $10 million - $9.4 million = $600,000.

LG-Q-220.q: A bank has $2 million in assets and $100,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 5 percent, what happens to capital?
options: It falls to zero.
It falls by $5,000.
It rises to $200,000.
It stays at $100,000.
LG-Q-220.commonError: applying the percentage loss to capital instead of assets
LG-Q-220.feedback: Five percent of $2 million is $100,000. That wipes out the bank's $100,000 in capital.

LG-Q-2007.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, $110,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. How much can it lend?
LG-Q-2007.commonError: treating all reserves as lendable reserves
LG-Q-2007.feedback: Required reserves are $80,000. Excess reserves are $110,000 - $80,000 = $30,000.

P52A-BANK-B2-001.q: Deposits are $600,000, the reserve requirement is 10 percent, and actual reserves are $90,000. Excess reserves are:

P52A-BANK-B2-003.q: A bank makes a loan from excess reserves. On the bank’s balance sheet, the new loan is:
options: A withdrawal.
Capital.
An asset.
A liability.
P52A-BANK-B2-003.feedback: The borrower owes the bank, so the loan is an asset.

P52A-BANK-B3-001.q: A bank has $1.5 million in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $240,000 in reserves. Its maximum immediate new lending is:
options: $1.32 million.
P52A-BANK-B3-001.commonError: Confusing required reserves with excess reserves.
P52A-BANK-B3-001.feedback: Required reserves are $180,000, so excess reserves are $60,000.

P52A-BANK-B3-002.q: A bank has $30 million in assets and $28.5 million in liabilities. Assets fall 6 percent. New capital is:
options: $1.5 million.
-$1.8 million.
-$0.3 million.
$0.3 million.
P52A-BANK-B3-002.commonError: Applying the asset loss to the wrong base.
P52A-BANK-B3-002.feedback: Initial capital is $1.5 million; the asset loss is $1.8 million.

LG-Q-9104.q: A bank has $80 million in assets and $74 million in liabilities. Asset values fall by 9 percent. What is the new capital position?
options: Negative $1.2 million
$6 million
$7.2 million
Negative $7.2 million
LG-Q-9104.commonError: applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets
LG-Q-9104.feedback: Initial capital is $6 million. A 9 percent loss on $80 million is $7.2 million, leaving capital at negative $1.2 million.

LG-Q-9105.q: A bank has actual reserves of $180,000 and excess reserves of $45,000. The reserve requirement is 9 percent. What are deposits?
LG-Q-9105.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-EXCESS-RESERVES-5007.q: A bank gets $1,000 in deposits and must hold $100. How much can it lend?
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-EXCESS-RESERVES-5007.feedback: The bank can lend deposits minus required reserves: $1,000 - $100 = $900.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-REQUIRED-RESERVES-5006.q: Deposits are $1,000 and the reserve requirement is 10 percent. Required reserves are:
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-REQUIRED-RESERVES-5006.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement: $1,000 x 0.10 = $100.
