AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

LG-Q-360.q: If the Fed shifts money supply right, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS rises, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MD rises, r rises, investment rises, AD shifts right.
LG-Q-360.commonError: reversing the effect of money supply on interest rates
LG-Q-360.feedback: More money lowers the interest rate, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

LG-Q-361.q: If the Fed shifts money supply left, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MD falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
LG-Q-361.commonError: thinking less money lowers interest rates
LG-Q-361.feedback: Less money raises the interest rate, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

LG-Q-365.q: If the Fed increases money supply but investment barely responds to the lower interest rate, what happens to the AD shift?
options: AD shifts right by less than usual because the investment channel is weak.
AD shifts right by more because investment does not matter.
AD must shift left because lower r reduces investment.
AD cannot move because money supply changed.
LG-Q-365.commonError: assuming the money-supply shift mechanically creates the same AD response every time
LG-Q-365.feedback: Monetary policy works through investment. If investment barely responds, AD shifts right less.

LG-Q-366.q: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, which part of the normal expansionary monetary-policy chain weakens?
options: The ability of extra money to lower r enough to boost investment
The identity that AD includes investment
The fact that money demand exists
The ability of government spending to enter AD
LG-Q-366.commonError: thinking liquidity trap means money demand disappears
LG-Q-366.feedback: In a liquidity trap, additional money may not lower interest rates enough to stimulate investment.

LG-Q-369.q: If money supply rises and AD shifts right, what is the correct distinction between the money-market movement and the AD-AS outcome?
options: The money market shows r falling; the AD-AS model shows higher demand for output at each price level.
The money market shows P falling; the AD-AS model shows money demand disappearing.
The money market shows taxes falling; the AD-AS model shows reserves rising.
The money market shows real output fixed by bank reserves.
LG-Q-369.commonError: blending the money-market graph and AD graph into one axis system
LG-Q-369.feedback: The money market determines the interest rate. The AD-AS model then reflects how lower rates raise spending and shift AD.

PG4-MPT-EL-001.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes what changes in the two panels?
options: MD shifts right and MS is traversed; SRAS shifts right along fixed AD.
MS shifts left and MD is traversed; AD shifts left along fixed SRAS.
MS shifts right and MD is traversed; AD shifts right along fixed SRAS.
Both panels show movements along fixed demand and supply curves.
PG4-MPT-EL-001.feedback: Different markets are being linked. Money supply shifts first; the resulting rate change affects spending and shifts AD.
PG4-MPT-EL-001.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
PG4-MPT-EL-001.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (100,6) and dashed MS1 at B (150,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and upper dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (100,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (125,56.25). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

PG4-MPT-EL-002.q: A student says AD1 is lower because the central bank directly reduced real GDP. What is the better interpretation?
options: Lower MS raises rates; lower interest-sensitive spending shifts AD left.
Lower MS lowers rates; higher interest-sensitive spending shifts AD right.
The central bank directly sets real GDP and moves AD to that quantity.
A rightward MD shift raises rates and directly shifts SRAS to the left.
PG4-MPT-EL-002.feedback: Monetary policy works through a transmission mechanism. The central bank acts on money/financial conditions, which influence spending and AD.
PG4-MPT-EL-002.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
PG4-MPT-EL-002.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (125,2.75) and dashed MS1 at B (100,4). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9014.q: The Fed shifts MS left while the economy is already below potential. What is the likely policy risk?
options: Interest rates rise, AD falls, and the recessionary gap worsens.
Interest rates fall, AD rises, and inflation disappears cleanly.
Interest rates rise, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to potential.
Interest rates fall, LRAS shifts left, and unemployment returns to natural.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9014.commonError: Missing the danger of tightening into weak demand.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9014.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates and shifts AD left, which can worsen a recessionary gap.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9022.q: A student says expansionary monetary policy raises AD by directly increasing government purchases. What is the best correction?
options: Monetary policy works mainly through money supply, interest rates, and investment.
Monetary policy works by changing G before interest rates can move.
Monetary policy works only by shifting LRAS through technology.
Monetary policy works by raising taxes and lowering consumption.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9022.commonError: Confusing monetary and fiscal policy channels.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9022.feedback: Monetary policy affects AD primarily through money supply, interest rates, and investment spending.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9052.q: A student says, 'If the Fed buys bonds, inflation must rise immediately and real output cannot move.' Which correction is strongest?
options: In the short run, lower rates can raise AD and output before long-run price adjustment dominates.
Bond purchases only change fiscal spending, so inflation and output are unaffected.
Bond purchases lower AD because reserves rise and lending must fall.
In the long run, bond purchases permanently reduce unemployment.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9052.feedback: Open-market purchases lower interest rates and can raise AD and output in the short run.

LG-Q-9051.q: Refer to the graph. What policy movement is shown across the two panels?
options: Money supply shifts left from MS1 to MS2, r rises from r1 to r2, AD shifts left from AD1 to AD2, and output falls from Y1 to Y2.
Money supply shifts right from MS2 to MS1, r falls from r2 to r1, AD shifts right from AD2 to AD1, and output rises from Y2 to Y1.
Money demand shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
The price level falls and the economy moves along AD1 from Y1 to Y2.
LG-Q-9051.commonError: reading the leftward money-supply shift as expansionary policy
LG-Q-9051.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy: MS shifts left, r rises, AD shifts left, and output falls.
LG-Q-9051.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
LG-Q-9051.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

LG-Q-9052.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment change caused by the MS1 to MS2 movement is $80 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct full AD effect?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $80 billion.
LG-Q-9052.commonError: using the multiplier correctly but reading the graph direction backward
LG-Q-9052.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left and r rising, so investment falls. MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5, so AD falls by $200 billion.
LG-Q-9052.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
LG-Q-9052.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

LG-Q-9053.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed moves the money supply from MS1 to MS2. If the resulting investment change is $60 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the correct full effect on AD?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $240 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.

options: Output falls from Y1 to Y2.

Money demand moves left and AD stays fixed.
The price level falls along AD1.

LG-Q-9072.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment response to the MS1 to MS2 movement is $50 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct order of effects?

MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises $50 billion, and AD shifts right by $125 billion.
MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls $50 billion, and AD shifts left by $50 billion only.
LG-Q-9072.commonError: stopping at the investment decline instead of applying the multiplier

PG4-MPT-L-001.q: Refer to the two-panel graph. Between A and B, the central bank expands money supply while SRAS stays fixed. A commentator says output and prices rose by the same percentage because they both rose. Which numerical comparison and inference are supported?
options: Output rises 12.5 percent and the price level 25 percent; their responses must be proportional.
Both rise 25 percent; equal directions establish equal percentage changes.
Both rise 6.25 percent; a common point label establishes a common percentage change.
Output rises 25 percent and the price level 12.5 percent; their responses need not be proportional.
PG4-MPT-L-001.feedback: Read output 100 to 125 and P 50 to 56.25. Their percentage changes are 25/100 = 25 percent and 6.25/50 = 12.5 percent. The diagram supplies distinct responses along fixed SRAS.

PG4-MPT-L-002.q: What macroeconomic conclusion is supported by the contractionary A-to-B movement across both panels?

The illustrated tightening raises rates and lowers both GDP and the price level.
The illustrated tightening lowers potential GDP by shifting LRAS to the left.
The illustrated tightening lowers GDP while raising the price level.

LG-Q-4003.q: Through the interest-rate channel, expansionary monetary policy shifts aggregate demand in which direction?
options: right
left
nowhere
only along short-run aggregate supply
LG-Q-4003.commonError: thinking expansionary money shifts AD left
LG-Q-4003.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

LG-Q-4004.q: If the Fed increases money supply, what chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
Interest rates rise, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates fall, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates rise, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
LG-Q-4004.commonError: thinking more money raises interest rates in this model
LG-Q-4004.feedback: More money lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

LG-Q-4005.q: The Fed increases money supply and investment rises by $70 billion. If MPC = 0.6, what is the total AD increase?
options: $175 billion
$70 billion
$42 billion
$116.7 billion
LG-Q-4005.commonError: stopping at the investment increase without applying the multiplier
LG-Q-4005.feedback: MPC 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. A $70 billion investment increase raises AD by $175 billion.

P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-001.q: The central bank buys government bonds from the public. What is the first link in the usual expansionary transmission chain?
options: Reserves and the money supply rise, pushing interest rates down.
Bank reserves fall and interest rates rise immediately.
Government purchases increase before the money market changes.
Aggregate supply shifts right because banks hold more bonds.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-001.commonError: Skipping the money-supply and interest-rate links after an open-market purchase.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-001.feedback: A bond purchase adds reserves to the banking system, supports money creation, and tends to lower market interest rates.

P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-002.q: Why can lower interest rates increase aggregate demand in the short run?
options: They automatically reduce all product prices.
They increase investment and other rate-sensitive spending.
They raise required reserve ratios for banks.
They directly increase government purchases.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-002.commonError: Treating monetary policy as a direct change in government spending or product prices.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-002.feedback: Lower borrowing costs encourage investment and some durable consumption, shifting aggregate demand to the right.

P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-003.q: Money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged. What happens at the new money-market equilibrium?
options: The equilibrium interest rate rises.
The price level must fall immediately.
The equilibrium interest rate falls.
Real output must remain permanently fixed.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-003.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B1-003.feedback: With money demand fixed, a larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate.

P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-001.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold most of them as excess reserves. How does this affect the transmission mechanism?
options: Money and credit expand more, making aggregate demand rise farther.
The policy becomes contractionary because excess reserves reduce taxes.
Aggregate demand rises by the same amount because reserve use never matters.
Money and credit expand less, weakening the interest-rate and aggregate-demand response.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-001.commonError: Assuming reserve injections always create the same money and credit expansion.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-001.feedback: When banks hold added reserves rather than lending them, money creation and the downstream spending response are weaker.

P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-002.q: Interest rates fall after an expansionary policy, but firms believe future sales will remain weak. What is the likely result?
options: Investment responds only modestly, so the rightward shift of aggregate demand is limited.
Investment surges because interest rates are the only influence on firms.
Aggregate demand shifts left because lower rates reduce borrowing.
The money supply contracts automatically when firms are pessimistic.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-002.commonError: Assuming lower rates guarantee a large investment response regardless of expectations.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-002.feedback: Weak expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing costs fall, weakening policy transmission.

P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-003.q: Which sequence correctly traces a contractionary open-market operation through aggregate demand?
options: Bond sales raise reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
Bond sales drain reserves, raise interest rates, reduce investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Bond purchases reduce reserves, raise investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Higher taxes reduce reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-003.commonError: Reversing the reserve, interest-rate, or spending links in contractionary policy.
P52B-S4-MPTX-B2-003.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, contracts money and credit, raises rates, reduces interest-sensitive spending, and lowers aggregate demand.

LG-Q-9131.q: Refer to the graph showing MS1 to MS2. In a fixed-price spending model, the resulting investment loss is $90 billion, while an independent recovery in business expectations adds $30 billion of autonomous investment. MPC is 0.6; there are no taxes, imports or further interest-rate feedbacks. What is the net shift in aggregate demand, and what independent investment recovery would exactly cancel the monetary effect?
options: AD shifts left $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $225 billion; a $30 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $60 billion; a $150 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts right $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
LG-Q-9131.commonError: multiplying before finding the net spending impulse or reading the graph backward
LG-Q-9131.feedback: The graph supplies contractionary direction. Net autonomous investment is −90 + 30 = −60. With multiplier 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5, AD shifts left $150 billion. Exact cancellation requires a $90 billion independent recovery, before multiplication.

LG-Q-9132.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed wants AD to move left by $300 billion using the policy direction shown. MPC = 0.75. Each 1-point rise in r lowers investment by $25 billion. How much must r rise?
options: 3 percentage points
4 percentage points
12 percentage points
1 percentage point

LG-Q-9132.feedback: The graph shows r rising. Multiplier is 4, so investment must fall $75 billion. At $25 billion per point, r must rise 3 points.

LG-Q-9138.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement best explains why this is not a liquidity-trap graph?
options: A leftward money-supply shift raises r from r1 to r2.
The graph shows money demand disappearing at low interest rates.
The graph shows investment rising when r rises.
The graph shows AD shifting right after a money-supply decrease.
LG-Q-9138.commonError: calling any money-market graph a liquidity trap
LG-Q-9138.feedback: A liquidity trap would show weak or flat interest-rate response. This graph shows r rising clearly from r1 to r2.

PM2C3-MPTX-LB-001.q: An expansionary policy clearly lowers the market interest rate, but firms expect very weak future sales and barely change investment. Where does the usual transmission chain primarily weaken?
options: At the link from the lower interest rate to interest-sensitive spending, so aggregate demand shifts by less than the standard chain would predict.
At the initial money-supply link, because a lower interest rate proves money supply did not change.
At the price-level definition, because expectations about sales determine whether money is a medium of exchange.
At the long-run neutrality link, which requires aggregate demand to shift by a fixed amount immediately.
PM2C3-MPTX-LB-001.commonError: Assumes a change in the policy instrument guarantees a fixed-size aggregate-demand response.
PM2C3-MPTX-LB-001.feedback: Transmission can weaken if rates respond little or if households and firms are not very responsive to the resulting borrowing-cost change.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-AD-SHIFT-5082.q: If the Fed decreases the money supply, aggregate demand usually:
options: Shifts left as interest rates rise and spending falls
Shifts right as interest rates fall
Does not change under any circumstance
Becomes vertical
ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-AD-SHIFT-5082.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy tends to raise interest rates and reduce interest-sensitive spending, shifting AD left.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-TRANSMISSION-504.q: Expansionary monetary policy usually lowers interest rates and shifts AD:
options: Right
Left
Nowhere
Into SRAS
ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-TRANSMISSION-504.feedback: Lower interest rates raise investment and shift AD right.

ECON-SP-READ-MONEY-MARKET-SHIFT-5089.q: If the money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged, the equilibrium interest rate tends to:
options: Fall
Rise
Stay fixed by definition
Equal the inflation rate
ECON-SP-READ-MONEY-MARKET-SHIFT-5089.feedback: More money supplied at each interest rate creates downward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

LG-R-5044.commonError: Thinking more money raises interest rates in liquidity preference theory.
LG-R-5044.q: If the Fed increases money supply, interest rates usually:
options: Fall
Rise
Stay fixed forever
Become inflation
LG-R-5044.feedback: More money lowers the equilibrium interest rate in the liquidity preference model.

LG-R-5045.commonError: Missing how lower rates shift AD.
LG-R-5045.q: Lower interest rates usually shift AD right because they increase:
options: Investment
Taxes
Imports only
Required reserves
LG-R-5045.feedback: Lower rates increase investment spending, shifting AD right.

LG-R-5046.commonError: Thinking less money lowers interest rates.
LG-R-5046.q: If the Fed decreases money supply, interest rates usually:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
LG-R-5046.feedback: Less money raises the equilibrium interest rate.

LG-R-5047.commonError: Thinking tighter money shifts AD right.
LG-R-5047.q: Higher interest rates usually shift AD left because they reduce:
options: Investment
Taxes
Money demand
Government purchases automatically
LG-R-5047.feedback: Higher interest rates reduce investment, shifting AD left.

PM2C3-MPTX-R-001.q: A student writes only “the central bank increases money supply, so aggregate demand rises.” Which missing links are essential to the standard short-run transmission mechanism?
options: The equilibrium interest rate falls and interest-sensitive spending such as investment rises before aggregate demand shifts right.
Government purchases automatically rise and then the money supply increases.
The price level falls first, which directly forces aggregate demand to shift right.
The natural rate of unemployment falls permanently, which mechanically raises aggregate demand.
PM2C3-MPTX-R-001.commonError: Jumps directly from a central-bank action to aggregate demand and skips the interest-rate and spending links.
PM2C3-MPTX-R-001.feedback: Trace the chain explicitly: money conditions change, the interest rate changes, interest-sensitive spending responds, and aggregate demand shifts.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-TRANSMISSION-603.q: The Fed increases the money supply. Which chain is correct?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates fall, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates rise, investment rises, AD shifts right
ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-TRANSMISSION-603.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

LG-B-6019.q: The Fed increases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Taxes fall, consumption rises, AD shifts right
Money demand disappears, AD is unchanged
LG-B-6019.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

LG-B-6020.q: The Fed decreases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Taxes rise, consumption falls, AD shifts left
Money demand disappears, AD rises
LG-B-6020.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

ECON-SP-EASY-13.q: In the quantity equation MV = PY, what does PY represent?
options: Real GDP
Nominal GDP
Money demand
Bank reserves
ECON-SP-EASY-13.commonError: Confusing nominal GDP with real GDP.
ECON-SP-EASY-13.feedback: P times Y is nominal GDP.

ECON-SP-EASY-15.q: If the money supply rises while velocity and output are unchanged, the quantity theory predicts that:
options: Real output doubles
The price level rises
Velocity becomes zero
The price level falls
ECON-SP-EASY-15.commonError: Thinking money growth must raise real output in the long run.
ECON-SP-EASY-15.feedback: With velocity and output fixed, more money means a higher price level.

ECON-SP-EASY-16.q: If the price level rises, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises
It stays fixed
It falls
It becomes real GDP
ECON-SP-EASY-16.commonError: Thinking a higher price level means money is more valuable.
ECON-SP-EASY-16.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so a higher price level lowers the value of money.

LG-Q-18.q: The value of money is measured as
options: 1 divided by the price level
the price level divided by real GDP
nominal GDP divided by velocity
money supply times output
LG-Q-18.commonError: thinking the value of money equals the price level
LG-Q-18.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it moves in the opposite direction of the price level.

LG-Q-19.q: If the price level rises, the value of money
options: falls
rises
stays constant
becomes equal to velocity
LG-Q-19.commonError: thinking the price level and value of money rise together
LG-Q-19.feedback: When the price level rises, each dollar buys fewer goods, so the value of money falls.

LG-Q-20.q: If the price level falls, the value of money
options: rises
falls
becomes zero
equals nominal GDP
LG-Q-20.commonError: forgetting that 1/P rises when P falls
LG-Q-20.feedback: A lower price level means each dollar buys more goods, so the value of money rises.

LG-Q-21.q: According to the quantity theory of money, persistent growth in the money supply leads mainly to
options: inflation
higher real output forever
lower nominal wages
a permanent fall in the price level
LG-Q-21.commonError: thinking money growth permanently raises real output
LG-Q-21.feedback: The quantity theory connects persistent money growth to inflation, especially in the long run.

options: M x V = P x Y
M + V = P + Y
P / Y = M / V
Y = M - P
LG-Q-22.commonError: mixing up multiplication and addition in the quantity equation
LG-Q-22.feedback: The quantity equation is M x V = P x Y.

LG-Q-23.q: In the quantity equation, P x Y equals
options: nominal GDP
real GDP
velocity
the real interest rate
LG-Q-23.commonError: confusing nominal GDP with real GDP alone
LG-Q-23.feedback: P x Y is the price level times real output, which equals nominal GDP.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-111.q: If velocity is stable and real output is fixed, a one-time doubling of the money supply should eventually:
options: Double the price level
Cut the price level in half
Double real output
Eliminate inflation costs
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-111.commonError: Thinking money growth creates long-run real output growth.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-111.feedback: With velocity and output fixed, doubling money doubles the price level.

LG-Q-126.q: If the value of money falls, what must have happened to the price level?
options: The price level rose.
The price level fell.
The price level stayed fixed.
The price level became real GDP.
LG-Q-126.commonError: thinking value of money and price level move together
LG-Q-126.feedback: Value of money and price level move in opposite directions. If the value of money falls, the price level rises.

LG-Q-127.q: Which curve is fixed by the Fed in the money supply-money demand model?
options: Money supply
Money demand
Aggregate demand
Short-run aggregate supply
LG-Q-127.commonError: thinking money demand is fixed by the Fed
LG-Q-127.feedback: In this model, the Fed fixes the money supply, so the money supply curve is vertical.

LG-Q-128.q: The vertical axis labeled value of money is best understood as
options: 1 divided by the price level
the price level itself only
real GDP divided by money supply
the reserve ratio
LG-Q-128.commonError: treating the value of money as the same thing as the price level
LG-Q-128.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, which is why it moves opposite the price level.

LG-Q-129.q: If money supply increases, the new equilibrium moves toward
options: a lower value of money and a higher price level
a higher value of money and a lower price level
a lower money demand curve only
a higher reserve requirement
LG-Q-129.commonError: forgetting that value of money falls when price level rises
LG-Q-129.feedback: An increase in money supply lowers the value of money and raises the price level.

LG-Q-131.q: If velocity and output are constant, a 10 percent increase in money supply should lead to approximately
options: a 10 percent increase in the price level
a 10 percent decrease in the price level
a 10 percent increase in real output
no change in nominal variables
LG-Q-131.commonError: thinking money growth raises real output when velocity and output are fixed
LG-Q-131.feedback: If V and Y are constant, money growth shows up as price-level growth.

LG-Q-133.q: If central bank money growth continues year after year faster than real output growth, the likely long-run result is
options: ongoing inflation
permanent unemployment below zero
a permanent fall in all nominal wages
no change in prices
LG-Q-133.commonError: thinking repeated money growth has no price-level consequence
LG-Q-133.feedback: Persistent money growth faster than output growth is a recipe for inflation.

LG-Q-228.q: If the Fed increases the money supply from MS1 to MS2, what happens to the equilibrium value of money and the price level?
options: The value of money falls and the price level rises.
The value of money rises and the price level falls.
Both the value of money and the price level rise.
Both the value of money and the price level fall.
LG-Q-228.commonError: forgetting value of money and price level move opposite directions
LG-Q-228.feedback: A monetary injection lowers the value of money and raises the price level.

LG-Q-229.q: Why does money demand slope downward when the value-of-money model places the value of money on the vertical axis?
options: A lower value of money means a higher price level, so people need more money for transactions.
A lower value of money means a lower price level, so people need less money.
A higher value of money means money supply must rise.
Money demand is fixed by the Fed.
LG-Q-229.commonError: missing the inverse relationship between value of money and price level
LG-Q-229.feedback: When the value of money falls, the price level is higher, so more dollars are needed to buy goods and services.

LG-Q-230.q: At the original price level, a monetary injection creates an excess supply of money. According to the adjustment process, people try to get rid of excess money by
options: spending it or lending it, pushing up demand for goods and prices
holding it forever, pushing prices down
destroying it, lowering nominal GDP
turning it into real output automatically
LG-Q-230.commonError: thinking excess money supply disappears without spending or price changes
LG-Q-230.feedback: People spend or lend excess money. That raises demand for goods and services, which pushes prices up.

LG-Q-255.q: Which statement best combines quantity theory and monetary neutrality?
options: Money growth mainly affects prices in the long run, while real output depends on real factors.
Money growth permanently raises real output and leaves prices unchanged.
Money growth lowers all nominal variables and raises real wages.
Money growth has no effect on nominal or real variables.
LG-Q-255.commonError: thinking long-run money growth is mainly a real-output policy
LG-Q-255.feedback: In the long run, money growth mainly shows up in nominal variables like prices, while real output depends on real resources and productivity.

P52B-S4-QTM-H-001.q: Money supply grows 9 percent, velocity falls 2 percent, and real output grows 3 percent. Using the growth-rate form of MV = PY, what inflation rate is implied?
options: Approximately 2 percent.
Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 8 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.
P52B-S4-QTM-H-001.commonError: Ignoring velocity growth or adding real-output growth instead of subtracting it.
P52B-S4-QTM-H-001.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth plus velocity growth minus real-output growth: 9 + (-2) - 3 = 4 percent.

P52B-S4-QTM-H-002.q: The money supply rises once by 10 percent while velocity and real output remain fixed. What does the quantity theory predict?
options: The inflation rate remains 10 percent every year even if money stops growing.
Real output rises permanently by 10 percent with no price change.
The price level rises once; continued inflation needs continued money growth.
Velocity must fall by 10 percent to preserve the equation.
P52B-S4-QTM-H-002.commonError: Confusing a one-time increase in the price level with a permanently higher inflation rate.
P52B-S4-QTM-H-002.feedback: With velocity and real output fixed, a one-time money increase produces a one-time proportional price-level increase.

ECON-SP-ELITE-304.q: Money growth rises, velocity falls, and output rises. Which statement is safest?
options: Inflation depends on all three changes
Inflation must equal money growth
Inflation must be zero
Inflation must exceed output growth
ECON-SP-ELITE-304.commonError: Using money growth alone when V and Y change.
ECON-SP-ELITE-304.feedback: The quantity equation connects money, velocity, prices, and output, so inflation depends on changes in all of them.

LG-Q-328.q: Starting at the original equilibrium, the Fed increases money supply. Which complete chain is correct?
options: MS shifts right, excess money appears at the old price level, spending rises, P rises, and the value of money falls.
MS shifts left, excess money appears, spending rises, P falls, and the value of money rises.
MD shifts right, money supply stays fixed, P falls, and value of money rises.
MS shifts right, spending falls, P falls, and the value of money rises.
LG-Q-328.commonError: getting the direction of value of money backward
LG-Q-328.feedback: A monetary injection shifts MS right. At the old price level there is excess money, which fuels spending, raises P, and lowers the value of money.

LG-Q-329.q: If the economy moves from the original equilibrium to the new equilibrium after a monetary injection, why does the price level rise rather than output permanently rise in the long-run model?
options: The model holds real output fixed in the long run, so extra money mainly changes nominal prices.
Money demand becomes vertical and real output doubles.
The Fed directly raises real GDP by shifting MD right.
The price level rises because the value of money rises.
LG-Q-329.commonError: thinking monetary injection permanently raises real output in the long-run money market model
LG-Q-329.feedback: In the long-run model, real output is determined by real factors, so more money mainly raises the price level.

LG-Q-330.q: If the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4 after the money supply shift, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 2 to 4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays unchanged because only money supply shifted.
LG-Q-330.commonError: treating value of money as the price level itself
LG-Q-330.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. A fall from 1/2 to 1/4 means P rises from 2 to 4.

LG-Q-331.q: At the old equilibrium value of money after MS shifts right, what disequilibrium exists and what removes it?
options: Excess supply of money; people spend or lend excess balances until prices rise.
Excess demand for money; people sell goods until prices fall.
Excess supply of goods; people hoard money until the price level falls.
No disequilibrium; the value of money changes without behavior.
LG-Q-331.commonError: missing why prices rise after excess money appears
LG-Q-331.feedback: At the old price level, the higher money supply creates excess money balances. People spend or lend them, pushing prices up.

LG-Q-332.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply is unchanged in the value-of-money model, what is the likely new equilibrium?
options: Higher value of money and lower price level
Lower value of money and higher price level
Higher money supply and higher price level
Lower money demand and lower value of money
LG-Q-332.commonError: treating all rightward shifts as inflationary regardless of axis meaning
LG-Q-332.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes up the value of money, which means the price level falls.

LG-Q-333.q: If money supply shifts left from the higher money supply back to the original level, what happens to the value of money and the price level?
options: The value of money rises and the price level falls.
The value of money falls and the price level rises.
Both rise because money is scarcer.
Both fall because money is scarcer.
LG-Q-333.commonError: forgetting that money scarcity raises the value of money but lowers P
LG-Q-333.feedback: A lower money supply makes money scarcer, raising its value and lowering the price level.

LG-Q-334.q: A student says the new equilibrium after MS rises means money is more valuable because there is more of it. What is wrong?
options: More money makes each dollar less scarce, so the value of money falls.
More money makes each dollar more scarce, so the value of money rises.
Money demand must disappear when money supply rises.
The price level must fall whenever money supply rises.
LG-Q-334.commonError: thinking more money means each dollar has more value
LG-Q-334.feedback: More money makes each dollar less scarce; with the price level higher, each dollar buys fewer goods, so the value of money falls.

LG-Q-335.q: If the Fed doubles money supply while velocity and real output are stable, which quantity-theory result follows?
options: The price level roughly doubles and the value of money roughly halves.
The price level halves and the value of money doubles.
Real output doubles and the price level stays fixed.
Velocity falls to zero and money demand disappears.
LG-Q-335.commonError: forgetting that stable V and Y push money growth into prices
LG-Q-335.feedback: With stable velocity and output, doubled money supply mainly doubles the price level and cuts the value of money in half.

LG-Q-337.q: An economy has M = 1,000, V = 5, and Y = 2,500. Next year M rises 20 percent, V is unchanged, and Y rises 4 percent. What is the approximate inflation rate?
options: 16 percent
20 percent
24 percent
4 percent
LG-Q-337.commonError: adding output growth to money growth instead of subtracting it
LG-Q-337.feedback: With velocity constant, money growth equals inflation plus output growth. Inflation is about 20 - 4 = 16 percent.

LG-Q-338.q: In 2024, M = 500, V = 4, and Y = 1,000. In 2025, M = 600, V = 4, and Y = 1,200. What happens to the price level?
options: It stays at 2.
It rises from 2 to 2.4.
It falls from 2 to 1.6.
It rises from 4 to 6.
LG-Q-338.commonError: seeing money rise and assuming P must rise without checking Y
LG-Q-338.feedback: 2024 P = 500 x 4 / 1,000 = 2. 2025 P = 600 x 4 / 1,200 = 2. Output rose enough to keep P unchanged.

LG-Q-353.q: If money growth is 12 percent, velocity growth is -2 percent, and real output growth is 3 percent, what is approximate inflation using the quantity equation growth form?
options: 7 percent
11 percent
17 percent
13 percent
LG-Q-353.commonError: ignoring velocity growth when it is explicitly given
LG-Q-353.feedback: Money growth plus velocity growth equals inflation plus output growth. Inflation = 12 + (-2) - 3 = 7 percent.

LG-Q-9025.q: Money supply shifts from MS1 to MS2. If the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4, which price-level change and interpretation are correct?
options: P rises from 2 to 4; each dollar buys half as much.
P falls from 2 to 4; each dollar buys twice as much.
P rises from 1/2 to 1/4; each dollar buys more.
P stays at 2 because only money supply shifted.
LG-Q-9025.commonError: treating the value of money as the price level
LG-Q-9025.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. A fall from 1/2 to 1/4 means P rises from 2 to 4, so a dollar buys half as much.

LG-Q-9026.q: Starting at the original equilibrium, the Fed doubles money supply. If output and velocity are unchanged, which answer matches quantity theory?
options: The price level doubles and the value of money halves.
The price level halves and the value of money doubles.
Real output doubles and the price level is unchanged.
Velocity doubles and money demand disappears.
LG-Q-9026.commonError: thinking a doubled money supply doubles real output
LG-Q-9026.feedback: With V and Y fixed, doubling M doubles P. Since value of money is 1/P, it falls by half.

LG-Q-9027.q: After MS shifts right, there is excess money at the old price level. Which adjustment process restores equilibrium?
options: People spend or lend excess balances, raising demand for goods and pushing prices up until money demand equals supply.
People destroy excess balances, lowering prices until value of money falls.
The Fed automatically shifts money demand left.
Output permanently doubles, leaving prices unchanged.
LG-Q-9027.commonError: identifying the shift but not explaining the adjustment process
LG-Q-9027.feedback: People spend or lend excess balances, increasing demand for goods and services; prices rise until money demand equals the higher money supply.

LG-Q-9028.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, and the value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, what happens to the price level?
options: It falls from 4 to 2.
It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays at 4.
LG-Q-9028.commonError: thinking higher value of money means a higher price level
LG-Q-9028.feedback: If the value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, P falls from 4 to 2.

LG-Q-9029.q: Refer to the graph. An analyst describes the move from a to b as a rightward shift of money demand and says that doubling the money quantity proves a doubling of the price level. Which diagnosis uses both curve evidence and the vertical-axis scale?
options: MD is unchanged; the price level rises by one-third, so constant output would require velocity to fall.
MD shifts right; the price level doubles, so velocity can remain fixed.
MD is unchanged; the price level falls by one-quarter, so velocity must rise.
MD shifts left; the price level is unchanged because the money supply is vertical.
LG-Q-9029.feedback: The same MD contains both a and b. Money doubles from 2,500 to 5,000, while P rises from 1/2 to 2/3, a factor of 4/3. With Y fixed, MV = PY requires velocity to change by (4/3)/2 = 2/3, so it falls.
LG-Q-9029.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
LG-Q-9029.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

LG-Q-9030.q: An economy has M = 2,000, V = 3, and Y = 1,500. Next year M rises to 2,400, V falls to 2.5, and Y rises to 1,600. What happens to the price level?
options: It falls from 4.0 to 3.75.
It rises from 3.75 to 4.0.
It rises from 4.0 to 4.8.
It stays at 4.0.
LG-Q-9030.commonError: assuming money growth raises prices without checking velocity and output

LG-Q-9031.q: An economy plans for real output to grow 4 percent and the price level to grow 2 percent over one year. A payments change is expected to reduce velocity by 3 percent. Using the exact multiplicative quantity equation, approximately what money-growth rate meets both targets, and why would simply adding 2 and 4 be insufficient?
options: 9.36 percent; money must also offset the velocity decline.
6 percent; velocity has no effect when output growth is given.
3 percent; declining velocity reduces the money needed.
9 percent exactly; percentage growth rates always add exactly.
LG-Q-9031.commonError: ignoring velocity growth even though it is given
LG-Q-9031.feedback: The required money growth factor is (1.02 × 1.04)/0.97 = 1.093608..., so growth is about 9.36 percent. The sum approximation gives 9 percent, but is not the exact multiplicative result.

LG-Q-9049.q: If the Fed contracts money supply and the value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, which statement correctly describes the result?
options: P falls from 4 to 2, so each dollar buys more.
P rises from 2 to 4, so each dollar buys less.
P stays fixed because money demand did not shift.
P falls from 1/2 to 1/4, so each dollar buys less.
LG-Q-9049.commonError: forgetting that higher value of money means lower P
LG-Q-9049.feedback: If value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, P falls from 4 to 2. Each dollar buys more.

LG-Q-9050.q: A student says, 'Inflation means the money demand curve slopes up.' What is the best correction?
options: Inflation means a higher price level and lower value of money.
Inflation means money demand is always vertical.
Inflation means money supply must slope down.
Inflation means quantity of money cannot change.
LG-Q-9050.commonError: misreading the value-of-money axis and money demand slope
LG-Q-9050.feedback: The MD curve slopes downward against value of money because lower money value means higher P and more dollars demanded.

ECON-SP-HARD-206.q: If M grows 8 percent, V grows 1 percent, and Y grows 3 percent, predicted inflation is approximately:
options: 4 percent
6 percent
9 percent
12 percent
ECON-SP-HARD-206.commonError: Ignoring output growth or velocity growth.
ECON-SP-HARD-206.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth plus velocity growth minus output growth: 8 + 1 - 3 = 6 percent.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-110.q: In the quantity equation, if M rises 5 percent, V is constant, and Y rises 2 percent, inflation is approximately:
options: 2 percent
3 percent
5 percent
7 percent
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-110.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth plus velocity growth minus output growth: 5 + 0 - 2 = 3 percent.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-112.q: If P rises from 2 to 4, the value of money changes from:
options: 2 to 4
4 to 8
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-112.commonError: Treating a higher price level as higher money value.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-112.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it falls from 1/2 to 1/4.

LG-Q-125.q: What happens to the value of money when the price level rises from 2 to 4?
options: It falls from 1/2 to 1/4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays at 1/2.
It doubles from 2 to 4.
LG-Q-125.commonError: forgetting that value of money equals 1 divided by price level
LG-Q-125.feedback: The value of money is 1/P. When P rises from 2 to 4, value falls from 1/2 to 1/4.

LG-Q-130.q: Using the quantity equation, if M = 400, V = 5, and Y = 1,000, then P equals
LG-Q-130.commonError: dividing by velocity instead of output
LG-Q-130.feedback: M x V = P x Y, so 400 x 5 = P x 1,000. P = 2.

LG-Q-132.q: If nominal GDP is $20,000 and the money supply is $5,000, velocity equals
LG-Q-132.commonError: multiplying nominal GDP by money supply
LG-Q-132.feedback: Velocity equals nominal GDP divided by money supply: $20,000 / $5,000 = 4.

LG-Q-231.q: If M rises by 8 percent, V is constant, and Y rises by 2 percent, the quantity theory predicts inflation of approximately
options: 6 percent
8 percent
10 percent
2 percent
LG-Q-231.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth from money growth
LG-Q-231.feedback: With constant velocity, money growth equals inflation plus output growth. Inflation is about 8 - 2 = 6 percent.

LG-Q-232.q: If M = 1,000, V = 3, and Y = 600, what is the price level?
LG-Q-232.commonError: dividing by M instead of Y when solving for P
LG-Q-232.feedback: M x V = P x Y, so 1,000 x 3 = P x 600. P = 5.

LG-Q-233.q: If nominal GDP is $60,000 and velocity is 5, what money supply is required?
LG-Q-233.commonError: multiplying nominal GDP by velocity instead of dividing
LG-Q-233.feedback: Velocity = nominal GDP / money supply, so money supply = $60,000 / 5 = $12,000.

LG-Q-234.q: If the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 2 to 4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays at 2.
LG-Q-234.commonError: treating the value of money as the price level itself
LG-Q-234.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. If value falls from 1/2 to 1/4, P rises from 2 to 4.

LG-Q-235.q: An economy has M = 500, V = 4, and Y = 1,000. Next year M rises to 600, V stays at 4, and Y stays at 1,000. What happens to P?
options: It rises from 2.0 to 2.4.
It falls from 2.4 to 2.0.
It stays at 2.0.
It rises from 4.0 to 6.0.
LG-Q-235.commonError: forgetting to solve both years before comparing

LG-Q-24.q: If M = 500, V = 2, and Y = 1,000, then P equals
LG-Q-24.commonError: multiplying by output instead of dividing by output
LG-Q-24.feedback: Using M x V = P x Y gives 500 x 2 = P x 1,000, so P = 1.

LG-Q-3000.q: Which equation links the money supply, velocity, the price level, and real output?
options: M x V = P x Y
M + V = P + Y
P x M = V x Y
M / V = P / Y
LG-Q-3000.commonError: mixing up the parts of the quantity equation
LG-Q-3000.feedback: The quantity equation is M x V = P x Y.

LG-Q-3001.q: If M = 600, V = 5, and Y = 1,000, what is P?
LG-Q-3001.commonError: dividing by velocity instead of output
LG-Q-3001.feedback: M x V = P x Y, so 600 x 5 = P x 1,000. P = 3.

LG-Q-3002.q: If money supply shifts right and the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 2 to 4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays fixed.
LG-Q-3002.commonError: reading value of money as the price level
LG-Q-3002.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. A fall from 1/2 to 1/4 means P rises from 2 to 4.

P52B-S4-QTM-B1-001.q: In the equation MV = PY, what does velocity measure?
options: The percentage rate at which the overall price level changes.
The amount of real output produced by each unit of labor.
The interest rate the central bank pays on reserve balances.
The average turnover of money in purchases of final output.
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-001.commonError: Confusing velocity with inflation, productivity, or an interest rate.
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-001.feedback: Velocity links the money stock to nominal spending by measuring the average turnover of money.

P52B-S4-QTM-B1-002.q: Money grows 10 percent, real output grows 4 percent, and velocity is stable. What inflation rate is predicted?
options: Approximately 6 percent.
Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-002.commonError: Failing to subtract real-output growth from money growth.
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-002.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is approximately money growth minus real-output growth: 10 - 4 = 6 percent.

P52B-S4-QTM-B1-003.q: If money supply and velocity are unchanged while real output rises, what must happen to the price level in MV = PY?
options: The price level rises.
The price level falls.
The price level stays fixed by definition.
Nominal GDP doubles.
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-003.commonError: Assuming higher real output always raises the price level when nominal spending is fixed.
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-003.feedback: If MV is unchanged and Y rises, P must fall so that PY continues to equal nominal spending.

P52B-S4-QTM-B3-001.q: Money supply grows 12 percent, velocity falls 2 percent, and real output grows 3 percent. What inflation rate follows from the quantity equation?
options: Approximately 3 percent.
Approximately 11 percent.
Approximately 7 percent.
Approximately 17 percent.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-001.commonError: Adding all growth rates or ignoring the decline in velocity.

P52B-S4-QTM-B3-002.q: Money supply grows 5 percent and velocity grows 1 percent. What is the implied growth rate of nominal GDP?
options: Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 5 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
Approximately 6 percent.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-002.commonError: Subtracting velocity growth from money growth when calculating nominal-spending growth.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-002.feedback: Because MV equals nominal GDP, its growth is approximately money growth plus velocity growth: 5 + 1 = 6 percent.

P52B-S4-QTM-B3-003.q: A student claims that faster money growth can permanently raise real output at the same rate. What is the best long-run correction?
options: In the long run, sustained money growth mainly raises inflation, not real output.
Sustained money growth permanently raises real output but never prices.
Money growth has no effect on either nominal or real variables.
Velocity always adjusts to eliminate every effect of money growth.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-003.commonError: Extending short-run output effects into a permanent long-run relationship.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-003.feedback: In the long run, real output is determined mainly by real factors, so sustained excess money growth appears largely as inflation.

LG-Q-9116.q: After MS shifts right, P rises from 2 to 4. If M doubled and Y was constant, what must have happened to velocity for these changes to satisfy the quantity equation?
options: Velocity stayed constant.
Velocity doubled.
Velocity fell by half.
Velocity became zero.
LG-Q-9116.commonError: missing that doubled M and doubled P with fixed Y implies stable V
LG-Q-9116.feedback: With Y constant, doubled M and doubled P are consistent with velocity staying constant.

LG-Q-9118.q: Money growth rises from 7 percent to 22 percent, velocity growth rises from 0 to 3 percent, and real output growth stays at 4 percent. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 3 percent to about 21 percent.
It rises from about 7 percent to about 22 percent.
It falls from about 21 percent to about 3 percent.
It stays at 4 percent.
LG-Q-9118.commonError: ignoring velocity growth in the second period
LG-Q-9118.feedback: Inflation equals money growth plus velocity growth minus output growth. It rises from 7 + 0 - 4 = 3 percent to 22 + 3 - 4 = 21 percent.

LG-Q-9122.q: A country has M = 1,500, V = 6, and Y = 3,000. Next year M = 2,100, V = 5, and Y = 3,500. What happens to the price level?
options: It stays at 3.
It rises from 3 to 3.5.
It falls from 3 to 2.5.
It rises from 5 to 6.
LG-Q-9122.commonError: assuming higher M must raise P without checking V and Y

LG-Q-9126.q: If the value of money falls from 1 to 1/2, then later to 1/4, what happens to the price level over those two moves?
options: It rises from 1 to 2 to 4.
It falls from 1 to 1/2 to 1/4.
It rises from 1/4 to 1/2 to 1.
It stays unchanged because value of money is not related to P.
LG-Q-9126.commonError: reading the value-of-money axis as the price-level axis
LG-Q-9126.feedback: P is the inverse of value of money. Values 1, 1/2, and 1/4 correspond to price levels 1, 2, and 4.

ECON-SP-MONEY-GROWTH-TO-INFLATION-5015.q: If money grows while velocity and output are fixed, the price level should:
options: Rise
Fall
Stay zero
Become unemployment
ECON-SP-MONEY-GROWTH-TO-INFLATION-5015.feedback: With velocity and output fixed, more money raises the price level.

ECON-SP-QUANTITY-EQUATION-5013.q: In MV = PY, what does P represent?
options: Price level
Population
Profit
Public debt

ECON-SP-QUANTITY-EQUATION-5014.q: In MV = PY, what does Y represent?
options: Real output
Nominal interest rate
Money supply
Expected inflation

ECON-SP-VALUE-OF-MONEY-5016.q: If the price level rises, the value of money:
options: Falls
Rises
Stays fixed
Becomes GDP

LG-R-5024.commonError: Thinking value of money equals the price level.
options: 1 divided by the price level
The price level itself
Money supply times output
Velocity divided by GDP

LG-R-5025.q: What happens to money's purchasing power when the price level increases?
options: Falls
Rises
Stays fixed
Becomes velocity

LG-R-5026.commonError: Forgetting to subtract output growth from money growth.
LG-R-5026.q: If velocity is stable, inflation is approximately:
options: Money growth minus real output growth
Money growth plus real output growth
Real output growth minus money growth
MPC times money growth

LG-R-5027.commonError: Using money growth alone as inflation.
LG-R-5027.q: Money grows 10%, output grows 3%, and velocity is stable. Inflation is about:

ECON-SP-MONEY-GROWTH-TO-INFLATION-6011.q: Money grows 6 percent, velocity is stable, and output grows 2 percent. Approximate inflation is:
options: 4 percent
6 percent
8 percent
2 percent
ECON-SP-MONEY-GROWTH-TO-INFLATION-6011.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth minus output growth: 6 - 2 = 4 percent.

ECON-SP-QUANTITY-EQUATION-6010.q: If M = 200, V = 5, and Y = 500, then P equals:
ECON-SP-QUANTITY-EQUATION-6010.feedback: MV = PY, so 200 x 5 = P x 500, which gives P = 2.

ECON-SP-VALUE-OF-MONEY-6012.q: If the price level rises from 2 to 5, the value of money changes from:
options: 2 to 5
5 to 2
ECON-SP-VALUE-OF-MONEY-6012.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it falls from 1/2 to 1/5.

LG-B-6009.commonError: Reading value of money as the price level.
LG-B-6009.q: Use value of money = 1/P. If value falls from 1/2 to 1/4, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4
It falls from 2 to 4
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4
It stays fixed
LG-B-6009.feedback: Value of money is 1/P, so 1/2 means P = 2 and 1/4 means P = 4.

LG-B-6010.q: Money grows 12%, output grows 4%, and velocity is stable. Inflation is about:

options: Real GDP
Nominal wage

ECON-SP-EASY-17.commonError: Confusing money-measured variables with real variables.

options: Nominal GDP
Dollar wage
Relative price
Price level
ECON-SP-EASY-18.commonError: Treating all prices as nominal variables.
ECON-SP-EASY-18.feedback: A relative price compares one good to another, so it is a real variable.

ECON-SP-EASY-19.q: Monetary neutrality says that in the long run, a change in the money supply affects:
options: Nominal variables, not real variables
Real output only
The natural rate only
Technology only
ECON-SP-EASY-19.commonError: Thinking money changes real variables permanently in the long run.
ECON-SP-EASY-19.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables in the long run, not real output or employment.

LG-Q-25.q: A nominal variable is measured in
options: monetary units
physical units
hours only
percent changes only
LG-Q-25.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in monetary units, such as dollars.

LG-Q-26.q: A real variable is measured in
options: physical units or purchasing power
only current dollars
only bank deposits
only government bonds
LG-Q-26.commonError: thinking all economic variables are nominal
LG-Q-26.feedback: Real variables are measured in physical units or purchasing power, not just dollars.

LG-Q-27.q: Which of the following is a nominal variable?
options: Nominal wage in dollars per hour
Real wage in goods per hour
Real GDP in units of output
Relative price of apples in terms of oranges
LG-Q-27.commonError: mistaking real purchasing power for a dollar amount
LG-Q-27.feedback: A nominal wage is measured in dollars per hour, so it is a nominal variable.

LG-Q-28.q: Which of the following is a real variable?
options: Real GDP
Nominal GDP
Nominal wage
The price level
LG-Q-28.feedback: Real GDP measures output adjusted for prices, so it is a real variable.

LG-Q-29.q: The classical dichotomy separates variables into
options: nominal and real variables
supply and demand variables
public and private variables
short-run and long-run bonds
LG-Q-29.commonError: thinking the dichotomy separates fiscal and monetary policy
LG-Q-29.feedback: The classical dichotomy separates nominal variables from real variables.

LG-Q-30.q: Monetary neutrality means changes in the money supply do not affect
options: real variables in the long run
nominal prices in the long run
the price level
the inflation rate
LG-Q-30.commonError: thinking money neutrality means money has no effect on prices
LG-Q-30.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

PM2C2-NEUT-E-001.q: Over the long run, all dollar wages and prices are twice as high while output per worker and hours worked are unchanged. Which interpretation best fits monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed, but the listed real variables did not.
Real variables doubled because every dollar price doubled.
Output per worker must have doubled because wages doubled.
The price level is a real variable, so nothing nominal changed.
PM2C2-NEUT-E-001.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
PM2C2-NEUT-E-001.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-113.q: If all nominal prices and wages double while relative prices stay unchanged, this illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
A supply shock
A liquidity trap
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-113.commonError: Missing the real versus nominal distinction.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-113.feedback: Monetary neutrality says nominal variables can change while real variables remain unchanged in the long run.

LG-Q-135.q: If all nominal prices double but relative prices stay the same, this illustrates
options: monetary neutrality
crowding out
the multiplier effect
liquidity preference
LG-Q-135.commonError: thinking changes in nominal prices automatically change relative prices
LG-Q-135.feedback: Monetary neutrality says money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

LG-Q-137.q: Which statement is consistent with the classical dichotomy?
options: Money growth can affect nominal wages without changing real wages in the long run.
Money growth changes only real variables and never nominal variables.
Nominal and real variables are always identical.
The price level is a real variable.
LG-Q-137.commonError: thinking nominal and real variables move identically
LG-Q-137.feedback: Under the classical dichotomy, money affects nominal variables, while real variables are determined by real factors in the long run.

LG-Q-138.q: A nominal wage rises from $15 to $30 while the price level doubles. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays the same.
It doubles.
It falls by half.
It becomes zero.
LG-Q-138.commonError: thinking a higher nominal wage always means a higher real wage
LG-Q-138.feedback: If nominal wages and the price level both double, the real wage is unchanged.

PM2C2-NEUT-M-001.q: After a sustained monetary expansion, the long-run price level is higher and nominal wages are higher by roughly the same proportion. What happens to the real wage if productivity is unchanged?
options: It can return to about its previous level because both the wage and price level rose together.
It must rise in the same proportion as the nominal wage because a larger dollar wage always guarantees more purchasing power.
It must fall to zero because money growth raises prices.
It becomes equal to the money-supply growth rate.
PM2C2-NEUT-M-001.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
PM2C2-NEUT-M-001.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

ECON-SP-HARD-207.q: If nominal wages double, prices double, and real output is unchanged, the result best illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky prices
Fiscal stimulus
ECON-SP-HARD-207.commonError: Treating nominal changes as real changes.
ECON-SP-HARD-207.feedback: If nominal variables double while real variables stay unchanged, that is monetary neutrality.

LG-Q-236.q: A textbook says money is neutral in the long run. Which outcome is most consistent with that idea after the money supply doubles?
options: Nominal prices double while relative prices and real output are unchanged.
Real output doubles while nominal prices are unchanged.
Relative prices double while nominal prices are unchanged.
The price level falls and real wages double.
LG-Q-236.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
LG-Q-236.feedback: Money neutrality means money changes nominal variables, not real variables, in the long run.

LG-Q-239.q: If every nominal price and nominal wage doubles, why might employment and output be unchanged in the long run?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged.
Workers receive twice as many physical goods per hour.
Money demand must fall to zero.
The reserve requirement doubles automatically.
LG-Q-239.commonError: thinking nominal doubling changes real incentives by itself
LG-Q-239.feedback: If all nominal values double together, real wages and relative prices do not change, so real decisions need not change.

LG-Q-240.q: Which pair correctly classifies the variables?
options: Nominal GDP is nominal; real GDP is real.
Nominal GDP is real; real GDP is nominal.
The price level is real; real wage is nominal.
Relative price is nominal; dollar wage is real.
LG-Q-240.commonError: labeling anything involving GDP as real
LG-Q-240.feedback: Nominal GDP is measured in dollars. Real GDP is measured in output adjusted for price changes.

LG-Q-241.q: A country doubles its money supply and, in the long run, all dollar prices double. What happens to the value of money?
options: It falls by half.
It doubles.
It stays unchanged.
It becomes equal to real GDP.
LG-Q-241.commonError: thinking money supply doubling doubles the value of money
LG-Q-241.feedback: If the price level doubles, the value of money, 1/P, falls by half.

PM2C2-NEUT-H-001.q: A monetary expansion raises output temporarily, but years later output returns to its prior real trend while the price level remains permanently higher. Why is this consistent with monetary neutrality?
options: Neutrality describes the long-run separation of nominal changes from real output, not the absence of short-run real effects.
Neutrality requires the price level to return fully to its original level after every monetary expansion, even in the long run.
Neutrality means real output must remain permanently above trend after money growth.
Neutrality applies only when both output and prices are unchanged at every horizon.
PM2C2-NEUT-H-001.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
PM2C2-NEUT-H-001.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

ECON-SP-ELITE-303.q: A central bank doubles the money supply, output is unchanged, and all nominal wages and prices double. Which claim is strongest?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged
Real wages double with nominal wages
Relative prices double with prices
Output must double with money
ECON-SP-ELITE-303.commonError: Confusing nominal doubling with real doubling.
ECON-SP-ELITE-303.feedback: If wages and prices double together, real wages and relative prices remain unchanged.

ECON-SP-ELITE-305.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 6 percent while the price level rises 9 percent. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls by about 3 percent
It rises by about 3 percent
It rises by about 15 percent
It stays unchanged
ECON-SP-ELITE-305.commonError: Treating nominal wage growth as real wage growth.
ECON-SP-ELITE-305.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so 6 - 9 = -3 percent.

LG-Q-336.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. The economy moves from a to b. In a long-run comparison, a nominal wage rises by the same proportion as the price level inferred from those points, and technology and labor supplies are unchanged. Which comparison fits monetary neutrality?
options: The price level and nominal wage rise by one-third; the real wage need not change.
The price level falls by one-quarter; the real wage must rise.
The price level doubles; unchanged real resources require output to double.
The price level rises by one-third; the real wage must also rise by one-third.
LG-Q-336.commonError: confusing nominal price-level changes with real-output changes
LG-Q-336.feedback: The graph gives value of money 2 at a and 1.5 at b. Their reciprocal price levels are 1/2 and 2/3, a one-third increase. Proportional nominal wage growth leaves the real wage unchanged; nominal changes alone do not raise real productive capacity.

Crowding out
The liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs

options: It rises by about 4 percent.
It falls by about 4 percent.
It rises by about 20 percent.
It is unchanged.
LG-Q-340.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
LG-Q-340.feedback: Real wage growth is roughly nominal wage growth minus inflation: 12 percent - 8 percent = 4 percent.

LG-Q-354.q: If nominal GDP rises 10 percent while real GDP rises 4 percent, what happened to the price level approximately?
options: It rose about 6 percent.
It rose about 14 percent.
It fell about 6 percent.
It stayed fixed.

LG-Q-354.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price level growth is about 10 - 4 = 6 percent.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9027.q: A student says nominal wages rose 8 percent, so workers are better off. Inflation was 11 percent. What correction survives?

Real wages were unchanged because all inflation is neutral immediately.
Real wages doubled because nominal wages are measured in dollars.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9027.commonError: Confusing nominal wage growth with real wage growth.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9027.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so workers lost purchasing power.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9051.q: A student says, 'Since money is neutral, monetary policy cannot affect output during recessions.' Which correction is strongest?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run sticky prices allow AD effects on output.
Neutrality means money changes output permanently but not prices.
Neutrality applies only to fiscal policy and never to money.
Neutrality means the Phillips curve slopes downward in the long run.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9051.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to every short-run case.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9051.feedback: Money is neutral in the long run, but monetary policy can affect output in the short run through aggregate demand.

LG-Q-9032.q: Nominal GDP rises 12 percent while real GDP rises 5 percent. What happened to the price level, and which kind of variable changed?
options: The price level rose about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level rose about 17 percent; that is a real change.
The price level fell about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level was unchanged; only real output changed.
LG-Q-9032.commonError: adding nominal and real growth instead of subtracting
LG-Q-9032.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price growth is about 12 - 5 = 7 percent. The price level is nominal.

LG-Q-9033.q: A worker's nominal wage rises from $24 to $30 while the price level rises from 6 to 10. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls from 4 units to 3 units.
It rises from 4 units to 5 units.
It stays at 4 units.
It rises from 6 units to 10 units.
LG-Q-9033.commonError: looking only at the nominal wage increase
LG-Q-9033.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It falls from 24/6 = 4 to 30/10 = 3 units.

LG-Q-9034.q: All nominal prices double except wages, which rise only 50 percent. What happens to real wages?
options: Real wages fall because nominal wages rise less than the price level.
Real wages rise because nominal wages rose.
Real wages are unchanged because all prices rose.
Real wages double because prices doubled.
LG-Q-9034.commonError: thinking any nominal wage increase raises the real wage
LG-Q-9034.feedback: Real wages depend on wages relative to prices. If wages rise 50 percent while prices double, real wages fall.

LG-Q-9045.q: A country's price level rises from 100 to 140, nominal wages rise from $20 to $24, and workers complain their purchasing power fell. What happened to real wages?

They rose because nominal wages rose.
They stayed the same because both wages and prices rose.
They doubled because the price level rose.
LG-Q-9045.commonError: thinking nominal wage growth automatically raises purchasing power
LG-Q-9045.feedback: Nominal wages rose 20 percent, but prices rose 40 percent. Real wages fell.

LG-Q-9046.q: A policy causes all nominal prices, nominal wages, and nominal debts to double, but output and employment remain unchanged. Which outcome best fits long-run monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed while real variables stayed unchanged.
Real variables changed while nominal variables stayed unchanged.
Money had no effect on the price level.
Relative prices doubled.
LG-Q-9046.commonError: thinking monetary neutrality means money has no nominal effects
LG-Q-9046.feedback: Long-run monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real output or employment.

LG-Q-134.q: A worker earns $20 per hour, and the price level is 5. The real wage is
options: 4 units of output per hour
$25 per hour
100 units of output per hour
0.25 units of output per hour
LG-Q-134.commonError: multiplying wage by price level instead of dividing
LG-Q-134.feedback: Real wage equals nominal wage divided by price level: 20 / 5 = 4 units of output per hour.

LG-Q-136.q: If the price of pizza rises from $10 to $20 and the price of soda rises from $2 to $4, the relative price of pizza in terms of soda

doubles
falls by half
becomes zero
