LG-Q-136.feedback: Pizza was 5 sodas before and 5 sodas after. The relative price is unchanged.

LG-Q-237.q: A worker's nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 5. What happens to the real wage?
options: It rises from 5 to 6 units of output.
It falls from 5 to 4 units of output.
It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 4 to 5 units of output.
LG-Q-237.commonError: looking only at the nominal wage increase
LG-Q-237.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It rises from 20/4 = 5 to 30/5 = 6.

LG-Q-238.q: The price of coffee rises from $4 to $8 while the price of tea rises from $2 to $3. What happens to the relative price of coffee in terms of tea?
options: It rises from 2 teas to about 2.67 teas.
It stays at 2 teas.
It falls from 2 teas to 1.5 teas.
It becomes 8 teas.
LG-Q-238.commonError: thinking all nominal price increases leave relative prices unchanged
LG-Q-238.feedback: Coffee was 4/2 = 2 teas. It becomes 8/3, or about 2.67 teas.

LG-Q-3003.q: Which unit is used to express a nominal variable?
options: monetary units
physical units
real output units
labor hours only
LG-Q-3003.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in money terms, such as dollars.

LG-Q-3004.q: A nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 5 to 6 units.
It falls from 5 to 3.33 units.
It doubles.
LG-Q-3004.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
LG-Q-3004.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It starts at 20/4 = 5 and ends at 30/6 = 5.

LG-Q-3005.q: A country's money supply doubles, and in the long run all nominal prices and wages double while output is unchanged. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs
LG-Q-3005.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
LG-Q-3005.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

PM2C2-NEUT-EB-001.q: Which outcome is most consistent with long-run monetary neutrality after a one-time increase in the money supply?
options: A higher price level with real output determined by real productive factors.
Permanently higher real output with no change in nominal prices.
Permanently lower prices because more money makes each dollar more valuable.
A permanently higher real wage solely because the number of dollars increased.
PM2C2-NEUT-EB-001.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
PM2C2-NEUT-EB-001.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

PM2C2-NEUT-EB-002.q: A worker’s nominal wage and the price level both rise 10 percent while productivity is unchanged. What happens to the worker’s real wage approximately?
options: It rises about 20 percent.
It rises exactly 10 percent.
It falls exactly 10 percent.
It is roughly unchanged.
PM2C2-NEUT-EB-002.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
PM2C2-NEUT-EB-002.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

PM2C2-NEUT-EB-003.q: Which variable is nominal rather than real?
options: Hours of labor used to produce haircuts.
Haircuts produced per worker.
The dollar price of a haircut.
The quantity of haircuts produced.
PM2C2-NEUT-EB-003.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
PM2C2-NEUT-EB-003.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

PM2C2-NEUT-FB-004.q: Money growth accelerates for several years. In the long-run neutrality framework, which comparison is most defensible?
options: Neutrality requires money growth to leave every nominal price and wage unchanged in the long run.
Nominal prices can be persistently higher even though money growth does not permanently raise productive capacity.
Productive capacity must rise one-for-one with the price level.
A higher price level proves long-run real output rose by the same percentage.
PM2C2-NEUT-FB-004.commonError: Treats a one-time nominal level change as permanent real growth.
PM2C2-NEUT-FB-004.feedback: A one-time monetary expansion can raise nominal levels; long-run real growth requires changes in real productive capacity.

PM2C2-NEUT-FB-005.q: A country redenominates so every old 100-unit price becomes 1 new unit, with contracts and wages converted proportionally. What has changed economically?
options: The nominal unit of account changed, while real quantities and relative prices need not change.
Real output fell by 99 percent because smaller numbers on price tags necessarily mean less production.
Productivity rose because fewer currency units are needed per transaction.
The natural rate of unemployment must fall because nominal wages were converted.
PM2C2-NEUT-FB-005.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
PM2C2-NEUT-FB-005.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

PM2C2-NEUT-FB-006.q: The central bank unexpectedly expands money, real activity rises for a time, and later output returns to potential while nominal prices remain higher. Which statement best reconciles the episode?
options: Long-run neutrality is disproved whenever any short-run real effect occurs.
Neutrality requires output to remain permanently above potential.
The episode can be neutral only if the price level eventually falls below its starting point.
Short-run real effects can coexist with long-run monetary neutrality.
PM2C2-NEUT-FB-006.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
PM2C2-NEUT-FB-006.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

LG-Q-9115.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. A worker earns $24 at point a and $30 at point b. Treat each point’s price level as the reciprocal of its displayed value of money. LG-Q-9123.q: Nominal GDP rises 15 percent, real GDP rises 6 percent, and nominal wages rise 8 percent. What happens to the price level and real wages approximately?

PM2C2-NEUT-LB-001.q: A country doubles the number of currency units used to quote every wage and price, while production technology, labor, and relative prices are unchanged. What is the best first inference?
options: The change is nominal; the economy has not doubled its real productive capacity.
Real productive capacity doubled because every nominal amount doubled.
The natural rate of unemployment doubled because the currency unit changed.
The country necessarily experienced a permanent doubling of output per worker because every quoted nominal price and wage also doubled.
PM2C2-NEUT-LB-001.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-5019.q: A student says, “If money is neutral, monetary policy can never affect real output.” What is the best correction?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run real effects can occur even if long-run real output returns to a level set by real factors.
Neutrality means money changes only real output and never prices at any horizon, so even temporary short-run changes in prices, spending, or production cannot occur.
Neutrality applies only during recessions, not in long-run comparisons of nominal and real economic variables.
Neutrality means every monetary-policy action has exactly zero effect on prices, output, employment, and interest rates at every horizon.
ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-5019.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.
ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-5019.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.

ECON-SP-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-VARIABLES-5017.q: A wage measured in dollars is:
options: Nominal
Real
Relative
Imported
ECON-SP-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-VARIABLES-5017.feedback: A dollar wage is a nominal variable.

ECON-SP-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-VARIABLES-5018.q: A wage adjusted for the price level is:
options: Real
Nominal
Fiat
Reserve
ECON-SP-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-VARIABLES-5018.feedback: A wage adjusted for prices is a real wage.

LG-R-5028.commonError: Looking only at the nominal wage.
options: Nominal wage divided by price level
Nominal wage times price level
Price level divided by nominal wage
Money supply divided by wage
LG-R-5028.feedback: Real wage adjusts the dollar wage for the price level.

LG-R-5029.commonError: Thinking a higher nominal wage always means higher purchasing power.
LG-R-5029.q: If nominal wage is $20 and the price level is 4, real wage is:
options: 5 units
80 units
16 units
24 units

LG-R-5030.commonError: Thinking neutrality means money has no effect on prices.
LG-R-5030.q: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects:
options: Long-run nominal variables
Only real variables
Neither prices nor wages
Only unemployment
LG-R-5030.feedback: Money neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

LG-R-5031.commonError: Thinking money neutrality means prices are fixed.
LG-R-5031.q: If all nominal prices double but real output is unchanged, this fits:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs only
LG-R-5031.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-6014.q: If all nominal prices and wages double but real output is unchanged, this supports:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky wage theory only
A liquidity trap
ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-6014.feedback: Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run.

ECON-SP-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-VARIABLES-6013.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 5 percent while inflation is 8 percent. The real wage:
options: Falls by about 3 percent
Rises by about 3 percent
Rises by about 13 percent
Does not change
ECON-SP-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-VARIABLES-6013.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation: 5 - 8 = -3 percent.

LG-B-6011.commonError: Looking only at nominal wage growth.
LG-B-6011.q: Nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 and the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units
It rises to 6 units
It falls to 3.33 units
It doubles

LG-B-6012.commonError: Thinking neutrality means no price changes.
LG-B-6012.q: Money supply doubles, all nominal prices double, and real output is unchanged. This illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
LG-B-6012.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

PM2C2-NEUT-BR-001.q: The quantity theory predicts that sustained money growth faster than real output growth can raise inflation. In the long-run neutrality framework, what should a student infer about real productive capacity?
options: Faster money growth can raise nominal prices without permanently increasing productive capacity.
Faster money growth must permanently raise productive capacity by the same percentage.
Higher inflation proves output per worker rose by the same amount.
Long-run neutrality requires inflation to be zero whenever money growth exceeds output growth.
PM2C2-NEUT-BR-001.commonError: Stops after predicting the price-level effect and does not separate nominal from real outcomes.
PM2C2-NEUT-BR-001.feedback: Use the quantity-theory result for nominal spending and prices, then apply long-run neutrality to ask which real variables need not rise permanently.

ECON-SP-EASY-21.q: If expected inflation rises and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should:
options: Fall
Rise
Become zero
Equal real GDP
ECON-SP-EASY-21.feedback: Nominal interest rates include expected inflation, so they rise when expected inflation rises.

LG-Q-31.q: The Fisher effect says that when expected inflation rises, the nominal interest rate tends to
options: rise
fall
stay fixed forever
become equal to real GDP growth
LG-Q-31.commonError: thinking inflation lowers nominal interest rates
LG-Q-31.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

LG-Q-72.q: The Fisher equation is most commonly written as
options: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation
real interest rate = nominal interest rate + expected inflation
expected inflation = real GDP + money supply
nominal interest rate = velocity divided by output
LG-Q-72.commonError: adding inflation to the wrong side of the equation
LG-Q-72.feedback: The Fisher equation links nominal rates, real rates, and expected inflation: nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation.

LG-Q-74.q: If expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should
options: rise by about 3 percentage points
fall by about 3 percentage points
stay exactly the same
fall to zero
LG-Q-74.commonError: thinking nominal rates ignore expected inflation
LG-Q-74.feedback: If the real rate is unchanged, a 3-point rise in expected inflation raises the nominal rate by about 3 points.

LG-Q-75.q: Under the Fisher effect, a country with persistently higher inflation will tend to have
options: higher nominal interest rates
lower nominal interest rates
no nominal interest rates
unchanged price levels forever
LG-Q-75.commonError: thinking high inflation means low nominal rates
LG-Q-75.feedback: Higher expected inflation tends to be built into higher nominal interest rates.

PM2C2-FISH-E-001.q: Lenders begin expecting inflation to be 4 percentage points higher, while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Nominal interest rates tend to rise by about 4 percentage points.
Nominal interest rates tend to fall by about 4 percentage points.
Real interest rates must rise by exactly 4 percentage points.
Actual inflation must immediately equal the new nominal interest rate.
PM2C2-FISH-E-001.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
PM2C2-FISH-E-001.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

PM2C2-FISH-E-002.q: A bank sets a fixed nominal loan rate today for next year. Which inflation concept is most relevant to the Fisher effect when that rate is chosen?
options: Only inflation that has already occurred.
The current unemployment rate by itself.
Only the realized inflation rate known after repayment.
Expected inflation over the loan period.
PM2C2-FISH-E-002.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
PM2C2-FISH-E-002.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

LG-Q-141.q: If expected inflation rises while the real interest rate is unchanged, lenders will require
options: a higher nominal interest rate
a lower nominal interest rate
no repayment
a lower price level
LG-Q-141.feedback: Lenders care about purchasing power, so higher expected inflation is built into higher nominal interest rates.

PM2C2-FISH-M-001.q: Two otherwise similar economies have the same long-run real interest rate, but expected inflation is 2 percent in one and 7 percent in the other. What should differ under the Fisher effect?
options: The second economy should tend to have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher.
The first economy should have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher instead because lower expected inflation raises nominal rates.
Both nominal rates must be identical because real rates match.
The second economy must have a real rate 5 points higher.
PM2C2-FISH-M-001.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
PM2C2-FISH-M-001.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

PM2C2-FISH-M-002.q: Expected inflation falls from 6 percent to 2 percent while the long-run real interest rate remains 3 percent. What nominal-rate change is predicted?
options: The nominal rate rises from about 5 percent to about 9 percent.
The real rate falls from 3 percent to negative 1 percent automatically.
The nominal rate stays at 9 percent because only actual inflation matters.
The nominal rate falls from about 9 percent to about 5 percent.
PM2C2-FISH-M-002.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
PM2C2-FISH-M-002.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

PM2C2-FISH-M-003.q: A one-year loan is priced when inflation is expected to be 3 percent. Actual inflation later turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement separates the Fisher effect from the realized return?
options: The Fisher effect uses actual inflation only and ignores expectations.
Unexpected inflation raises both parties’ realized real returns by the same amount.
The nominal rate reflected expected inflation when set; the unexpectedly high actual inflation changes the ex post real return.
The nominal rate must be rewritten after actual inflation is observed so the original expected rate no longer matters.
PM2C2-FISH-M-003.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
PM2C2-FISH-M-003.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

PM2C2-FISH-H-001.q: Expected inflation rises 6 percentage points while the equilibrium real interest rate falls 2 percentage points. What happens to the nominal interest rate approximately?
options: It rises about 4 percentage points because both expected inflation and the real rate matter.
It rises exactly 6 percentage points because the Fisher effect requires the real rate to remain fixed in every comparison.
It falls about 8 percentage points because expected inflation lowers nominal rates.
It is unchanged because the two components must always offset completely.
PM2C2-FISH-H-001.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
PM2C2-FISH-H-001.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

PM2C2-FISH-H-002.q: Country A has expected inflation of 8 percent and a real interest rate of 1 percent. Country B has expected inflation of 3 percent and a real interest rate of 5 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Country A must have a nominal rate exactly 5 points above Country B.
Country B must have the lower nominal interest rate because lower expected inflation always dominates any real-rate difference.
The Fisher effect says real interest rates are always identical across countries.
A one-for-one comparison of nominal rates cannot use expected inflation alone because the real rates differ too.
PM2C2-FISH-H-002.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
PM2C2-FISH-H-002.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

PM2C2-FISH-H-003.q: Expected inflation falls sharply after a credible long-run policy change, but productive opportunities and saving behavior leave the real rate roughly unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Real interest rates must fall by exactly the same amount as expected inflation.
Nominal rates should stay fixed because only realized inflation affects contracts.
Nominal interest rates should fall as the inflation premium falls.
Nominal interest rates should rise because lower expected inflation raises the inflation premium.
PM2C2-FISH-H-003.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
PM2C2-FISH-H-003.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

PM2C2-FISH-H-004.q: A lender receives a 10 percent nominal rate that was set when expected inflation was 4 percent. Actual inflation is later 9 percent. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Expected inflation is irrelevant once a fixed nominal rate has been written.
The ex ante pricing reflected roughly a 6 percent real return, but the realized real return is much lower.
The Fisher effect predicted a 1 percent real return when the loan was made.
The nominal rate automatically rises to 15 percent after inflation is observed because fixed-rate contracts always adjust retroactively after the fact.
PM2C2-FISH-H-004.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
PM2C2-FISH-H-004.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

PM2C2-FISH-H-005.q: Nominal interest rates rise from 7 to 11 percent at the same time expected inflation rises from 3 to 8 percent. Can we conclude the real rate was unchanged?
options: No. The nominal rate rose 4 points while expected inflation rose 5, so the implied real rate actually fell about 1 point.
Yes. Any rise in nominal rates alongside expected inflation proves the real rate is unchanged.
Yes. The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to rise exactly half as much as expected inflation regardless of changes in real rates.
No. The implied real rate rose about 9 percentage points.
PM2C2-FISH-H-005.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
PM2C2-FISH-H-005.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

ECON-SP-ELITE-306.q: A lender expected 4 percent inflation and charged 9 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 8 percent. What happened to the realized real return?
options: It was lower than expected
It was higher than expected
It was unchanged
It became nominal GDP
ECON-SP-ELITE-306.commonError: Ignoring unexpected inflation after a loan is written.
ECON-SP-ELITE-306.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real return to lenders.

LG-Q-341.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower signs a loan at 9 percent nominal interest when expected inflation is 4 percent. Actual inflation is 7 percent. What happened to the realized real interest rate compared with what the lender expected?
options: It fell from 5 percent expected to 2 percent realized.
It rose from 5 percent expected to 7 percent realized.
It stayed at 5 percent because nominal interest was fixed.
It fell from 9 percent expected to 4 percent realized.
LG-Q-341.commonError: using expected inflation for the realized real rate
LG-Q-341.feedback: Expected real rate was 9 - 4 = 5 percent. Realized real rate was 9 - 7 = 2 percent.

LG-Q-342.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate is stable at 3 percent, what should happen to the nominal interest rate under the Fisher effect?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 12 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 3 percent.
It rises from 2 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 3 percent.
LG-Q-342.commonError: forgetting the real interest rate is part of nominal interest
LG-Q-342.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 3 + 2 = 5 to 3 + 9 = 12 percent.

LG-Q-9035.q: A lender’s one-year fixed nominal contract pays 12 percent. Expected inflation when written was 5 percent, but actual inflation is 9 percent. Use exact gross returns. What are the expected and realized real returns, and what nominal rate on a new loan would preserve the original expected real return if expected inflation is now 9 percent?
options: About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 16.27 percent.
7 percent, 3 percent, and 16 percent exactly.
About 2.75 percent, 6.67 percent, and 12 percent.
About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 12 percent.
LG-Q-9035.commonError: using expected inflation for both expected and realized real rates
LG-Q-9035.feedback: Expected real return is 1.12/1.05 − 1 = 6.67 percent; realized is 1.12/1.09 − 1 = 2.75 percent. Preserving the original gross real return on a new loan requires (1.12/1.05) × 1.09 − 1 = 16.27 percent nominal.

LG-Q-9036.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 11 percent. The real interest rate falls from 3 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 13 percent.
It rises from 4 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
LG-Q-9036.commonError: assuming the real rate is constant when it is explicitly changed
LG-Q-9036.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 3 + 4 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 11 = 13 percent.

LG-Q-9047.q: A one-time monetary expansion lowers the value of money today. Credible guidance says the money-growth rate will then return to its previous path. The long-run real interest rate is unchanged. An analyst concludes that nominal interest rates must remain permanently higher. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: A one-time price-level rise does not establish permanently higher expected inflation, so the lasting nominal-rate claim is unsupported.
The higher price level guarantees permanently higher inflation, so the nominal-rate claim follows.
The lower value of money proves the real interest rate falls permanently, so nominal rates must fall.
Monetary neutrality makes expected inflation irrelevant to nominal rates, so the Fisher relationship does not apply.
LG-Q-9047.commonError: confusing short-run liquidity effects with long-run Fisher effect
LG-Q-9047.feedback: The Fisher effect relates nominal rates to expected inflation over the loan horizon. A level adjustment alone does not establish a continuing inflation-rate increase. The real-rate assumption therefore does not complete the analyst’s argument.

LG-Q-9048.q: Money growth rises from 8 percent to 20 percent. Velocity growth is zero and output growth is 4 percent. If expected inflation adjusts fully, what happens to nominal rates when the real rate stays at 3 percent?
options: Nominal rates rise from about 7 percent to about 19 percent.
Nominal rates fall from 7 percent to 3 percent.
Nominal rates rise from 8 percent to 20 percent exactly.
Nominal rates stay at 3 percent.
LG-Q-9048.commonError: not converting money growth into inflation before applying Fisher
LG-Q-9048.feedback: Inflation rises from 8 - 4 = 4 percent to 20 - 4 = 16 percent. With real rate 3 percent, nominal rates rise from 7 to 19 percent.

PM2C2-FISH-L-001.q: A country establishes a credible low-inflation regime. Expected inflation falls from 9 percent to 3 percent, while saving and investment conditions leave the long-run real interest rate near 2 percent. Which outcome best fits the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate tends to fall from about 11 percent to about 5 percent.
The nominal interest rate tends to rise from about 5 percent to about 11 percent.
The real interest rate must fall from 2 percent to negative 4 percent.
The nominal interest rate should stay near 11 percent because credibility affects only actual inflation.
PM2C2-FISH-L-001.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
PM2C2-FISH-L-001.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

PM2C2-FISH-L-002.q: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?
options: It must be unchanged because identical expected inflation always forces identical nominal interest rates even when real saving and investment conditions differ.
It must be lower because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.
It must equal expected inflation because real rates disappear in the long run.
It should also be higher, showing that Fisher comparisons must account for the real-rate component as well as expected inflation.
PM2C2-FISH-L-002.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
PM2C2-FISH-L-002.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

ECON-SP-HARD-209.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 9 percent, the Fisher effect predicts the nominal rate rises by:
options: 3 points
4 points
5 points
9 points
ECON-SP-HARD-209.commonError: Using the final inflation rate instead of the change.
ECON-SP-HARD-209.feedback: Expected inflation rises by 5 percentage points, so the nominal rate rises by 5 points.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-115.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 6 percent while the real interest rate stays at 2 percent. The nominal rate becomes:
options: 3 percent
5 percent
6 percent
8 percent
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-115.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-115.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

LG-Q-139.q: If the nominal interest rate is 9 percent and expected inflation is 4 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
13 percent
4 percent
36 percent
LG-Q-139.commonError: adding inflation when solving for the real rate
LG-Q-139.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal rate minus expected inflation: 9 - 4 = 5 percent.

LG-Q-140.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 8 percent
4 percent
3 percent
12 percent
LG-Q-140.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
LG-Q-140.feedback: Nominal interest rate is approximately real interest rate plus expected inflation: 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

LG-Q-242.q: Use the Fisher approximation. The nominal interest rate is 11 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent. If actual inflation turns out to be 10 percent, what is the realized real interest rate?
options: 1 percent
4 percent
3 percent
21 percent
LG-Q-242.commonError: using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate
LG-Q-242.feedback: The realized real rate uses actual inflation: 11 - 10 = 1 percent.

LG-Q-243.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent and the real interest rate remains 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 2 percent.
LG-Q-243.commonError: forgetting to include the real interest rate in both periods
LG-Q-243.feedback: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 8 = 10.

LG-Q-32.q: If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 2 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
1 percent
2 percent
6 percent
LG-Q-32.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
LG-Q-32.feedback: The nominal interest rate is approximately the real interest rate plus expected inflation: 3 + 2 = 5 percent.

LG-Q-73.q: If the nominal interest rate is 7 percent and expected inflation is 3 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 4 percent
10 percent
3 percent
21 percent
LG-Q-73.commonError: adding expected inflation when solving for the real interest rate
LG-Q-73.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal interest rate minus expected inflation: 7 - 3 = 4 percent.

LG-Q-3006.q: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to
options: nominal interest rates
real GDP only
reserve requirements
M1 only
LG-Q-3006.commonError: thinking expected inflation is unrelated to nominal rates
LG-Q-3006.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

LG-Q-3007.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent, the nominal interest rate is about
options: 9 percent
5 percent
7 percent
14 percent
LG-Q-3007.commonError: subtracting expected inflation when solving for nominal rate
LG-Q-3007.feedback: Nominal interest is real interest plus expected inflation: 2 + 7 = 9 percent.

LG-Q-3008.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent while the real interest rate falls from 4 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
LG-Q-3008.commonError: tracking only expected inflation and ignoring the real rate change
LG-Q-3008.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 3 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 8 = 10 percent.

PM2C2-FISH-EB-001.q: If expected inflation rises while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged, the Fisher effect predicts that the nominal interest rate will:
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to real GDP growth.
PM2C2-FISH-EB-001.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
PM2C2-FISH-EB-001.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

PM2C2-FISH-EB-002.q: Which inflation rate matters when lenders set a nominal rate today for a future loan period?
options: Only last year’s inflation.
Only inflation observed after repayment.
The unemployment rate instead of inflation.
Expected inflation.
PM2C2-FISH-EB-002.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
PM2C2-FISH-EB-002.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

PM2C2-FISH-EB-003.q: The real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 5 percent. The Fisher approximation gives a nominal rate near:
options: 3 percent.
15 percent.
8 percent.
2 percent.
PM2C2-FISH-EB-003.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
PM2C2-FISH-EB-003.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

PM2C2-FISH-FB-004.q: Expected inflation rises from 4 to 10 percent while the equilibrium real rate falls from 3 to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal rate approximately?
options: It remains at about 7 percent because expected inflation and real rates always offset.
It rises from about 7 to about 11 percent.
It rises from about 7 to about 13 percent because the real-rate change is irrelevant.
It falls from about 7 to about 5 percent.
PM2C2-FISH-FB-004.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
PM2C2-FISH-FB-004.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

PM2C2-FISH-FB-005.q: A fixed-rate loan was written when expected inflation was 2 percent, but actual inflation turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Expected inflation helped determine the original nominal rate; the surprise changes the realized real return.
The Fisher effect requires the bank to retroactively reset the nominal rate to actual inflation.
Unexpected inflation leaves the realized real return unchanged on a fixed-rate contract.
The nominal rate was based only on actual inflation, which was already known.
PM2C2-FISH-FB-005.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
PM2C2-FISH-FB-005.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

PM2C2-FISH-FB-006.q: Nominal interest rates rise 3 percentage points while expected inflation rises 5 points. What does the Fisher decomposition imply about the real-rate component?
options: It rose by about 8 percentage points.
It rose by exactly 5 percentage points.
It must have remained unchanged because nominal rates increased.
It fell by about 2 percentage points.
PM2C2-FISH-FB-006.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
PM2C2-FISH-FB-006.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

LG-Q-9117.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If MS shifts right and the value of money falls, expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate stays at 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 5 percent.
LG-Q-9117.commonError: forgetting to add the real interest rate to expected inflation
LG-Q-9117.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 9 = 11 percent.

LG-Q-9127.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 10 percent while the real rate falls from 4 percent to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate, and why is this not a contradiction?
options: It rises from 6 percent to 11 percent because expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.
It falls from 6 percent to 1 percent because the real rate fell.
It stays at 6 percent because changes cancel exactly.
It rises from 2 percent to 10 percent because real rates do not matter.
LG-Q-9127.commonError: tracking only the real rate or only expected inflation
LG-Q-9127.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 2 = 6 percent. New nominal rate is 1 + 10 = 11 percent. Expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.

LG-Q-9128.q: A country’s nominal loan rate falls from 16 to 9 percent while expected inflation falls from 12 to 4 percent. Using the Fisher approximation, what happens to the expected real rate, and by how much would the new nominal rate have had to fall further to preserve its original expected real rate?
options: The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate falls from 4 to 3 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate stays at 4 percent; no further nominal change was needed.
The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 5-point nominal cut was needed.
LG-Q-9128.commonError: assuming lower nominal rates always mean lower real rates
LG-Q-9128.feedback: Subtract expected inflation: 16 − 12 = 4 initially and 9 − 4 = 5 later. Preserving a real rate of 4 with expected inflation of 4 requires a nominal rate of 8, one point below 9.

ECON-SP-FISHER-EFFECT-5020.q: A borrower says the Fisher effect is found by subtracting this year’s actual inflation from a loan rate set last year. What is the key mistake?
options: The Fisher effect concerns expected inflation when the nominal rate is set, not merely realized inflation afterward.
The Fisher effect uses only the unemployment rate when a loan is made, so expected inflation has no role in nominal-rate setting.
The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to stay fixed when expected inflation changes.
The Fisher effect says actual inflation and expected inflation must always be identical.

LG-Q-77.feedback: An inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money balances held by the public.

options: very rapid growth in the money supply
a fixed money supply forever
falling prices every year
a permanent drop in nominal wages only
LG-Q-78.commonError: thinking hyperinflation happens without excessive money creation
LG-Q-78.feedback: Hyperinflation is usually tied to extremely rapid money growth, often when governments print money to finance spending.

LG-Q-79.q: Deflation means the economy is experiencing
options: a falling overall price level
a rising overall price level
zero interest rates only
a larger money multiplier only
LG-Q-79.feedback: Deflation means the overall price level is falling.

LG-Q-80.q: A major danger of heavy reliance on printing money to finance government spending is
options: high inflation or hyperinflation
a guaranteed rise in real output
a permanent fall in nominal prices
the end of money demand
LG-Q-80.commonError: thinking printing money creates real resources without inflation costs
LG-Q-80.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but heavy reliance on it can produce high inflation or hyperinflation.

PM2C2-ITAX-E-001.q: A government creates money to finance purchases, the price level rises, and households’ existing cash buys less. What burden is illustrated?
options: The real purchasing power of money balances is being eroded by the inflation tax.
A statutory income-tax rate automatically rose on every household.
Deflation increased the real value of cash balances.
The natural rate of unemployment fell permanently because the government created more money and raised the overall price level.
PM2C2-ITAX-E-001.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
PM2C2-ITAX-E-001.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-119.q: Why can heavy reliance on printing money become dangerous?
options: It can create rapid inflation and reduce money's value
It guarantees higher real GDP forever
It eliminates all tax burdens
It makes nominal variables real
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-119.commonError: Thinking printing money is costless financing.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-119.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but it reduces the value of money and can create high inflation.

LG-Q-146.q: A government repeatedly prints money to pay its bills. Which risk is most directly connected to this policy?
options: Inflation tax and possible hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real output
Permanent monetary neutrality failure
A lower price level forever
LG-Q-146.commonError: thinking printing money creates real resources without inflation pressure
LG-Q-146.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but repeated reliance on it can create inflation or hyperinflation.

LG-Q-147.q: Why is the inflation tax called a tax even though Congress may not pass a tax law?
options: It reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.
It raises real GDP automatically.
It only applies to people who owe income taxes.
It directly increases the real wage.
LG-Q-147.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit and legislative
LG-Q-147.feedback: Inflation acts like a tax on money holders by reducing the purchasing power of their cash balances.

LG-Q-148.q: A country with runaway money creation and rapidly rising prices is experiencing
options: hyperinflation
monetary neutrality only
deflation
crowding out
LG-Q-148.commonError: confusing high inflation with falling prices
LG-Q-148.feedback: Rapid money creation paired with rapidly rising prices is hyperinflation territory.

LG-Q-149.q: If prices are falling across the economy, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises.
It falls.
It becomes zero.
It becomes the nominal interest rate.
LG-Q-149.commonError: thinking falling prices reduce the purchasing power of money
LG-Q-149.feedback: Deflation means falling prices, so each dollar buys more. The value of money rises.

PM2C2-ITAX-M-001.q: Inflation falls from 7 percent to 2 percent, but the overall price level is still rising. Which description is correct?
options: The economy is experiencing disinflation, not deflation.
The economy is experiencing deflation because inflation is lower.
The economy is experiencing hyperinflation because prices are still rising.
The price level must be falling by 5 percent.
PM2C2-ITAX-M-001.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
PM2C2-ITAX-M-001.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

ECON-SP-HARD-210.q: A country prints money to cover deficits, prices rise rapidly, and people rush to spend cash before it loses value. Which idea is most central?
options: Inflation tax and falling money value
Crowding out and rising investment
LRAS growth and lower inflation
Commodity money and stable prices
ECON-SP-HARD-210.commonError: Treating money printing as costless financing.
ECON-SP-HARD-210.feedback: Printing money can finance spending through an inflation tax, reducing the value of money.

LG-Q-249.q: A household keeps a fixed $720 cash balance while the price level rises from 1.2 to 1.5 during money-financed government spending. How much purchasing power, measured in units of the composite good, does this unchanged balance lose?
options: 120 units.
180 units.
144 units.
No units, because the nominal balance is fixed.
LG-Q-249.commonError: thinking inflation tax affects only people who file taxes
LG-Q-249.feedback: The cash initially buys 720/1.2 = 600 units and later buys 720/1.5 = 480 units. The loss is 120 units; an unchanged dollar balance need not preserve purchasing power.

LG-Q-250.q: A country has no ability to borrow and keeps financing deficits by creating money. What is the likely risk if this continues?
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real GDP without inflation
Permanent deflation
A lower money supply
LG-Q-250.commonError: thinking money printing solves fiscal problems without inflation consequences
LG-Q-250.feedback: Persistent money creation to finance deficits can trigger high inflation or hyperinflation.

LG-Q-251.q: If inflation falls from 8 percent to 3 percent but remains positive, this is best described as
options: disinflation
deflation
hyperinflation
monetary neutrality
LG-Q-251.commonError: calling falling inflation deflation when prices are still rising
LG-Q-251.feedback: Disinflation means inflation is falling but still positive. Deflation means the price level is falling.

LG-Q-253.q: Which policy concern is strongest when a government relies heavily on seigniorage?
options: Money growth may create inflation that erodes purchasing power.
Real output must permanently double.
Nominal interest rates must fall to zero.
The quantity equation stops applying.
LG-Q-253.feedback: Seigniorage can raise revenue, but it risks inflation by expanding the money supply.

PM2C2-ITAX-H-001.q: An economy enters unexpected deflation while households carry fixed nominal mortgage debt. What happens to the real debt burden, other things equal?
options: It rises because each repayment dollar has greater purchasing power.
It falls because lower prices make nominal debts shrink automatically.
It is unchanged because the price level cannot affect fixed nominal contracts.
It disappears because deflation forces lenders to cancel nominal debt.
PM2C2-ITAX-H-001.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
PM2C2-ITAX-H-001.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

ECON-SP-ELITE-307.q: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise with expected inflation. Which two ideas are linked?
options: Inflation tax and Fisher effect
Crowding out and SRAS
Multiplier and LRPC
M1 and sacrifice ratio
ECON-SP-ELITE-307.commonError: Separating deficit money creation from expected inflation effects.
ECON-SP-ELITE-307.feedback: Printing money can act as an inflation tax, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

LG-Q-348.q: If a government prints money to cover spending and the public starts expecting higher future inflation, what happens to nominal interest rates under the Fisher effect?
options: They rise as expected inflation rises.
They fall because money supply rose.
They stay fixed because real rates cannot change.
They become equal to the reserve ratio.
LG-Q-348.commonError: thinking more money always lowers every interest rate in every model and horizon
LG-Q-348.feedback: If money finance raises expected inflation, nominal interest rates tend to rise through the Fisher effect.

LG-Q-349.q: A country raises money growth from 5 percent to 25 percent while real output growth stays at 3 percent and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 2 percent to about 22 percent.
It rises from about 5 percent to about 25 percent exactly.
It falls from 25 percent to 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth is unchanged.
LG-Q-349.commonError: forgetting to subtract real output growth
LG-Q-349.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth: initially 2 percent, then 22 percent.

LG-Q-350.q: Deflation lowers the price level from 200 to 180. What happens to the value of money, and why can this matter for debtors?
options: The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth more.
The value of money falls; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
The value of money is unchanged; debtors are unaffected.
The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
LG-Q-350.commonError: thinking falling prices help borrowers with fixed nominal debts
LG-Q-350.feedback: Deflation raises the value of money. Fixed nominal debts become harder for debtors to repay.

LG-Q-351.q: Which result best distinguishes disinflation from deflation?
options: Inflation falls from 8 percent to 3 percent during disinflation, while the price level falls during deflation.
The price level falls during disinflation, while inflation rises during deflation.
Both mean the price level rises faster.
Both mean money has no value.
LG-Q-351.commonError: calling any fall in inflation deflation
LG-Q-351.feedback: Disinflation means inflation slows. Deflation means the price level actually falls.

LG-Q-352.q: A country uses seigniorage heavily during a fiscal crisis. Which combination is most likely if confidence erodes?
options: Rapid money growth, rising expected inflation, and higher nominal interest rates
Falling money growth, falling expected inflation, and lower nominal interest rates
No change in inflation because money is neutral in the short run
Lower price levels and higher money value immediately
LG-Q-352.commonError: thinking seigniorage is free revenue with no expectations effect
LG-Q-352.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations, and higher expected inflation pushes nominal interest rates up.

LG-Q-9039.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth rises from 6 percent to 26 percent, output growth remains 3 percent, and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 3 percent to about 23 percent.
It rises from about 6 percent to about 26 percent exactly.
It falls from about 23 percent to about 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth did not change.
LG-Q-9039.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth from money growth
LG-Q-9039.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth. It rises from 3 percent to 23 percent.

LG-Q-9040.q: A government uses inflation tax finance, expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise. Which concepts are being connected?
options: Inflation tax, expected inflation, and the Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and commodity money
Menu costs, M1, and fiscal multipliers
Liquidity trap, real wage, and barter
LG-Q-9040.commonError: not connecting money finance to expected inflation and nominal rates
LG-Q-9040.feedback: Printing money can create inflation expectations, and the Fisher effect links expected inflation to nominal interest rates.

LG-Q-9041.q: Unexpected deflation reduces the price level from 1.25 to 1.00. A firm’s fixed nominal debt is $48,000. Its sales volume is unchanged, and its $12,000 nominal operating cash flow falls in the same proportion as the price level. Which pair describes the debt burden and the cash-flow pressure?
options: Real debt rises from 38,400 to 48,000 units; debt/cash flow rises from 4 to 5.
Real debt falls from 48,000 to 38,400 units; debt/cash flow falls from 5 to 4.
Real debt rises from 38,400 to 48,000 units; debt/cash flow stays at 4.
Real debt stays at 48,000 units; debt/cash flow rises from 4 to 5.
LG-Q-9041.commonError: thinking falling prices always help borrowers
LG-Q-9041.feedback: Real debt rises from 48,000/1.25 = 38,400 to 48,000/1 = 48,000. Nominal cash flow becomes 12,000 × 1/1.25 = 9,600. Debt/cash flow therefore rises from 4 to 5, despite unchanged sales volume.

PM2C2-ITAX-L-001.q: A government increasingly finances deficits by creating money. As inflation expectations rise, households try to hold smaller real money balances. Why can continued reliance on seigniorage become increasingly disruptive?
options: The shrinking demand to hold real balances can require still more money creation to extract a given amount of real resources, worsening inflation pressure.
Lower money demand guarantees the government can finance the same amount of real spending with progressively less money creation and steadily less inflation forever.
Seigniorage becomes costless once households expect inflation.
The quantity theory implies real output must rise one-for-one with the extra money creation.
PM2C2-ITAX-L-001.commonError: Treats money creation as a costless financing source regardless of public money demand.
PM2C2-ITAX-L-001.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

PM2C2-ITAX-L-002.q: A heavily indebted economy experiences an unexpected 6 percent fall in the overall price level while nominal debts are fixed. Which balance-sheet effect is most likely?
options: Debtors receive an automatic reduction in the nominal face value of their debts.
Creditors lose because every repayment dollar is worth less in real terms.
The fall in the price level is disinflation and therefore cannot affect real debt burdens.
Debtors face a higher real repayment burden, which can weaken spending and financial positions.
PM2C2-ITAX-L-002.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
PM2C2-ITAX-L-002.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

PM2C2-ITAX-L-003.q: Inflation drops from 12 percent to 4 percent after a stabilization program, but the price level continues to rise. A student calls this deflation. What is the best evaluation?
options: The student is correct only if nominal interest rates also fall.
The student is wrong because disinflation requires inflation to become negative.
The student is wrong: inflation slowed, but deflation requires the overall price level to fall.
The student is correct because any decline in the inflation rate means the overall price level must also be falling.
PM2C2-ITAX-L-003.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
PM2C2-ITAX-L-003.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

LG-Q-252.q: If the price level falls from 125 to 120, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises because 1/P is larger.
It falls because 1/P is smaller.
It stays constant because P changed by less than 10.
It becomes equal to velocity.
LG-Q-252.commonError: thinking falling prices reduce the value of money
LG-Q-252.feedback: When the price level falls, each dollar buys more, so the value of money rises.

LG-Q-3012.q: When a government finances spending by printing money, this is called
options: an inflation tax
crowding out
a liquidity trap
a reserve requirement
LG-Q-3012.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit
LG-Q-3012.feedback: Printing money can act like an inflation tax by reducing the purchasing power of money.

LG-Q-3013.q: Use the quantity-equation growth approximation. A government prints money heavily to pay bills. Money growth rises to 18 percent, velocity is stable, and real output grows 4 percent. What inflation rate is predicted?
options: 14 percent
18 percent
22 percent
4 percent
LG-Q-3013.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is about money growth minus output growth: 18 - 4 = 14 percent.

LG-Q-3014.q: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates increase. Which concepts are linked?
options: Inflation tax, quantity theory, and Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and M1
Liquidity trap, real GDP, and commodity money
Menu costs, unemployment, and barter
LG-Q-3014.commonError: not connecting money creation to inflation expectations and nominal rates
LG-Q-3014.feedback: Money-financed deficits can raise inflation, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

PM2C2-ITAX-EB-001.q: When money-financed government spending reduces the purchasing power of existing money balances, the burden is called:
options: The inflation tax.
Crowding out.
The money multiplier.
The natural rate.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-001.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-001.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

PM2C2-ITAX-EB-002.q: Inflation falls from 6 percent to 3 percent while prices continue to rise. This is:
options: Deflation.
Hyperinflation.
Monetary neutrality.
Disinflation.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-002.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-002.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

PM2C2-ITAX-EB-003.q: If the overall price level falls, the value of money generally:
options: Becomes zero.
Equals the inflation rate.
Rises.
Falls.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-003.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-003.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

PM2C2-ITAX-FB-004.q: A government prints money to finance spending, expected inflation rises, and households reduce desired real cash balances. Which concern is most complete?
options: Households holding less money automatically raises real output enough to offset the inflation-tax burden and preserve seigniorage revenue.
Inflation-tax finance can erode real balances and become harder to sustain as people avoid holding money.
Lower money demand guarantees a stable price level despite continued money creation.
Printing money eliminates the need to consider inflation because seigniorage is a real resource.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-004.commonError: Treats money creation as a costless financing source regardless of public money demand.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-004.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

PM2C2-ITAX-FB-005.q: Unexpected deflation occurs while firms and households owe large fixed nominal debts. Which distributional effect is most likely?
options: The real burden shifts against debtors and toward creditors.
The real burden shifts against creditors because repayment dollars buy less.
Both sides are unaffected because nominal debt cannot have a real value.
All nominal debts automatically fall at the same rate as the price level.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-005.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-005.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

PM2C2-ITAX-FB-006.q: A stabilization program reduces inflation from 20 percent to 5 percent without making inflation negative. Which statement is correct?
options: The program created deflation because any large decline in the inflation rate makes the price level fall.
The price level must have fallen 15 percent.
Disinflation requires the inflation rate to be below zero.
The program achieved disinflation; the price level can still be rising.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-006.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-006.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

LG-Q-9121.q: If money demand shifts right while MS is fixed and the value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, what happens to P, and what inflation term does this imply?
options: P falls from 5 to 4; this is deflation.
P rises from 4 to 5; this is inflation.
P falls from 1/4 to 1/5; this is disinflation.
P is unchanged; this is monetary neutrality.
LG-Q-9121.commonError: thinking higher value of money means higher price level
LG-Q-9121.feedback: Value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, so P falls from 5 to 4. A falling price level is deflation.

LG-Q-9124.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth jumps, expected inflation rises, nominal rates rise, and people hold less cash. Which chain is most complete?
options: Expected inflation raises nominal rates and shoeleather costs.
Crowding out lowers nominal rates and eliminates inflation costs.
Reserve requirements rise automatically and make money neutral.
Commodity money replaces fiat money and ends inflation.
LG-Q-9124.commonError: not connecting money finance to expectations and behavior
LG-Q-9124.feedback: Money finance can act as an inflation tax, raise expected inflation and nominal rates, and make people spend resources avoiding cash holdings.

PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.q: A government finances part of its budget by creating money, and the public’s existing money balances lose purchasing power as prices rise. What is the core mechanism?
options: Money creation transfers real purchasing power away from holders of money balances through the inflation tax.
A statutory tax authority directly debits an inflation-tax line from every bank account.
Deflation raises the real value of balances and transfers purchasing power to debtors.
The policy can finance the same amount of real spending indefinitely without reducing the purchasing power of existing money balances held by the public.
PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-5023.q: A student looks for an “inflation tax” line on a tax return. What is the best correction?
options: The inflation tax is the loss of purchasing power on money balances when money-financed spending contributes to inflation.
It is a statutory percentage surcharge collected only from commercial banks whenever the central bank expands the money supply to finance government spending.
It is the interest payment the Treasury makes on government bonds.
It is the fall in real debt burdens caused by unexpected deflation.
ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-5023.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.
ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-5023.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.

LG-R-5038.commonError: Thinking printing money is costless government revenue.
LG-R-5038.q: The inflation tax comes from government financing by:
options: Printing money
Cutting money supply
Lowering prices
Reducing nominal wages
LG-R-5038.feedback: Printing money can act like a tax by reducing the value of money people already hold.

LG-R-5039.commonError: Thinking heavy money creation has no inflation risk.
LG-R-5039.q: Heavy reliance on printing money can lead to:
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
Permanent deflation
Zero nominal interest rates forever
A higher value of money
LG-R-5039.feedback: Persistent money creation can create high inflation.

ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-6018.q: A government prints money to pay bills and the value of existing money falls. This is closest to:
options: Inflation tax
Reserve requirement
Crowding out
Sacrifice ratio
ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-6018.feedback: The inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.

LG-B-6016.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
LG-B-6016.q: A government relies heavily on money creation. Inflation rises, households reduce cash balances, and they make more frequent transfers to avoid holding money. Which connection is most accurate?
options: Money finance creates an inflation-tax burden on money balances and also generates shoeleather costs.
Money finance eliminates the inflation tax because households hold less cash.
Shoeleather costs occur only during deflation, so the two effects cannot occur together.
The policy changes only real output and has no effect on nominal money balances, cash-management decisions, or the purchasing power of money.
LG-B-6016.feedback: Money creation erodes the purchasing power of money balances (the inflation tax) and encourages people to make more frequent transfers or otherwise avoid holding cash (shoeleather costs).

money-functions-and-measures.title: Money Functions and Measures
money-functions-and-measures.description: Identify money’s functions, forms, and M1/M2 measurement.

easy.q: Which function of money is being used when dollars are accepted to buy groceries?
options: Store of value
Medium of exchange
Unit of account
Reserve requirement
easy.commonError: Confusing the functions of money.
easy.feedback: Money is a medium of exchange when it is used to buy goods and services.

easy.q: Which function of money is being used when a store lists a phone price as $900?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
easy.commonError: Confusing pricing with payment.
easy.feedback: Money is a unit of account when it measures and compares prices.

easy.q: Which item is counted in M1?
options: Large time deposits
Currency held by the public
Credit card balances
Money market mutual funds held by businesses
easy.commonError: Counting credit cards as money.
easy.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item is included in M2 but not M1?
options: Checkable deposits
Coins held by households
Savings deposits
Currency held by the public
easy.commonError: Treating M1 and M2 as identical.
easy.feedback: M2 includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

easy.q: What is fiat money?
options: Money backed fully by gold
Accepted money with no intrinsic value
Money used only by banks
Money that cannot lose value
easy.commonError: Thinking fiat money must be backed by gold.
easy.feedback: Fiat money has value because people accept it, not because it has intrinsic value.

easy.q: A farmer wants shoes, but the shoemaker does not want wheat. Both are willing to accept dollars. Which feature of money solves the immediate trading problem?
options: It serves as a medium of exchange, so the two traders do not need a double coincidence of wants
It serves only as a store of value, so neither trader has to exchange anything
It makes every good part of M1, so barter becomes unnecessary
It guarantees that the relative price of wheat and shoes never changes
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Money serves as a medium of exchange because dollars let the farmer trade without finding a shoemaker who wants wheat.

easy.q: A repair shop compares a $450 used laptop with a $900 new laptop before deciding which to buy. Which function of money makes that comparison straightforward?
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Bank reserve
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Money serves as a unit of account because quoting both laptops in dollars provides a common measure for comparing their prices.

easy.q: A household keeps $600 in cash for emergencies. If prices rise substantially before the cash is spent, which statement is most accurate?
options: The cash serves as a store of value, but its purchasing power can fall
The cash stops being money because a store of value must keep purchasing power constant
The cash is serving only as a unit of account because it is not being spent today
Inflation converts the cash from M1 into a nonmonetary financial asset
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Cash is a store of value because it carries purchasing power into the future, although inflation can reduce that purchasing power before it is spent.

easy.q: Customers accept paper currency even though the paper itself has little intrinsic value and cannot be redeemed for a commodity. Which explanation best fits?
options: It is fiat money whose usefulness depends on general acceptance rather than commodity value
It is commodity money because the paper can be physically held
It is bank capital because it supports financial transactions
It is not money unless every note is backed one-for-one by gold
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: The currency is fiat money: it is accepted as payment even though the paper has little intrinsic value and is not redeemable for a commodity.

easy.q: Commodity money differs from fiat money because commodity money
options: has intrinsic value
is created only through bank lending
cannot be used as a medium of exchange
is always part of M2 but never M1
easy.commonError: treating all money as fiat money
easy.feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself, like gold or silver. Fiat money does not.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is included in M1?
options: Currency held by the public
Small time deposits
Savings deposits
Money market mutual funds held by individuals
easy.commonError: including all near monies in M1
easy.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public, checkable deposits, and similar highly liquid transaction balances.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is part of M2 but not M1?
options: Savings deposits
Currency
Checkable deposits
Traveler's checks
easy.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes near monies
easy.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies, so they are included in M2 but not M1.

medium.q: A student says credit card balances should be counted in M1 because people use cards to buy goods. What is the best correction?
options: Credit cards are borrowing, not money balances
Credit cards are currency held by the public
Credit cards are checkable deposits
Credit cards are savings deposits
medium.commonError: Counting credit cards as money.
medium.feedback: Credit cards allow borrowing. They are not money balances like currency or checkable deposits.

medium.q: A household keeps cash because it wants to make purchases quickly, compare prices, and save some value for later. Which answer matches all three functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, fiat money
Unit of account, leverage, discount rate
Medium of exchange, multiplier, bank capital
medium.commonError: Mixing money functions with banking tools.
medium.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and can transfer purchasing power into the future.

medium.q: A student says, 'Money is valuable because the dollar bill itself has valuable paper.' What is the best correction?
options: Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
Fiat money has value because its paper is worth more than its face value.
Commodity money and fiat money are the same thing.
Money only has value if it can be exchanged for gold.
medium.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
medium.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. Its value comes from general acceptance and government backing.

medium.q: A grocery store lists apples at $2 per pound. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Fractional reserve
medium.commonError: choosing medium of exchange whenever prices involve money
medium.feedback: The price tag uses money to measure value, so money is acting as a unit of account.

medium.q: A person keeps $500 in cash for emergencies. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Store of value
Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
medium.commonError: thinking money only matters when it is spent immediately
medium.feedback: The cash is preserving purchasing power for later, so it is serving as a store of value.

medium.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item would be counted in M2 but not in M1?
options: A savings deposit
Currency in your wallet
A checking account deposit
A traveler's check
medium.commonError: putting all liquid assets into M1
medium.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies. They belong in M2, not M1.

medium.q: Why does money make specialization easier?
options: It removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
It makes all goods cost the same amount.
It prevents prices from changing.
It eliminates scarcity.
medium.commonError: thinking money eliminates scarcity rather than reducing transaction costs
medium.feedback: Money reduces transaction costs because people no longer need to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.

medium.q: Which statement best explains why currency held by a bank does not count the same way as currency held by the public?
options: Currency held by banks is part of bank reserves, not currency circulating among the public.
Currency held by banks is automatically counted twice in M1.
Currency held by banks is commodity money.
Currency held by banks is never money.
medium.commonError: double-counting currency held inside banks
medium.feedback: Currency held by banks is treated as reserves. Currency in the money supply refers to currency held by the public.

hard.q: A student says M2 is smaller than M1 because M2 excludes currency. What is the best correction?
options: M2 includes M1 plus near monies
M2 includes only bank reserves
M1 includes savings deposits only
M1 equals credit card balances
hard.commonError: Reversing the relationship between M1 and M2.
hard.feedback: M2 is broader than M1 because it includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

hard.q: A farmer accepts dollars for corn, uses dollars to compare seed prices, and saves some dollars for next month. Which answer correctly matches the three functions of money?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, medium of exchange, unit of account
Unit of account, store of value, medium of exchange
Money multiplier, reserve requirement, federal funds rate
hard.commonError: mixing up using money to buy with using money to measure value
hard.feedback: Buying uses money as a medium of exchange, comparing prices uses it as a unit of account, and saving it uses it as a store of value.

hard.q: A country uses paper currency that has no intrinsic value, is not convertible into gold, but is accepted for payment. What kind of money is this?
options: Fiat money
Commodity money
Barter money
Reserve money only
hard.commonError: thinking money must be backed by a commodity to have value
hard.feedback: That is fiat money: it has value because it is accepted, not because the paper itself has intrinsic value.

hard.q: Currency held by the public rises because households withdraw funds from checking accounts. What happens to banks' ability to create deposits, other things equal?
options: It falls because banks have fewer deposits to support lending.
It rises because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves.
It is unchanged because currency and deposits are identical for banks.
It becomes unlimited because reserve requirements no longer matter.
hard.commonError: thinking public currency holdings help banks lend more
hard.feedback: When households hold more currency and fewer deposits, banks have fewer deposits available to support loans.

hard.q: A household moves $4,000 from a checking account into a retail money-market mutual fund. Under standard textbook definitions, what happens?
options: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.
hard.commonError: Treating movement between M1 and non-M1 M2 assets as a change in total M2.
hard.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.

hard.q: Which asset is included in M2 but normally excluded from M1?
options: Currency held by the public.
A small-denomination time deposit.
Funds in a checking account.
Traveler’s checks held by households.
hard.commonError: Placing every liquid financial asset in M1.
hard.feedback: Small time deposits are near-money assets included in M2 but not in the narrower M1 measure.

elite.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists public currency as $600, checkable deposits as $1,400, savings deposits as $1,800, small time deposits as $500, and retail money market mutual funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
elite.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
