monetary-neutrality.title: Monetary Neutrality
monetary-neutrality.description: Distinguish nominal and real variables and analyze long-run neutrality.

easy.q: Which variable is nominal?
options: Real GDP
Nominal wage
Relative price
Quantity of labor
easy.commonError: Confusing money-measured variables with real variables.
easy.feedback: A nominal wage is measured in dollars.

easy.q: Which variable is real?
options: Nominal GDP
Dollar wage
Relative price
Price level
easy.commonError: Treating all prices as nominal variables.
easy.feedback: A relative price compares one good to another, so it is a real variable.

easy.q: Monetary neutrality says that in the long run, a change in the money supply affects:
options: Nominal variables, not real variables
Real output only
The natural rate only
Technology only
easy.commonError: Thinking money changes real variables permanently in the long run.
easy.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables in the long run, not real output or employment.

easy.q: A nominal variable is measured in
options: monetary units
physical units
hours only
percent changes only
easy.commonError: confusing nominal with real
easy.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in monetary units, such as dollars.

easy.q: A real variable is measured in
options: physical units or purchasing power
only current dollars
only bank deposits
only government bonds
easy.commonError: thinking all economic variables are nominal
easy.feedback: Real variables are measured in physical units or purchasing power, not just dollars.

easy.q: Which of the following is a nominal variable?
options: Nominal wage in dollars per hour
Real wage in goods per hour
Real GDP in units of output
Relative price of apples in terms of oranges
easy.commonError: mistaking real purchasing power for a dollar amount
easy.feedback: A nominal wage is measured in dollars per hour, so it is a nominal variable.

easy.q: Which of the following is a real variable?
options: Real GDP
Nominal GDP
Nominal wage
The price level
easy.commonError: thinking GDP is always nominal
easy.feedback: Real GDP measures output adjusted for prices, so it is a real variable.

easy.q: The classical dichotomy separates variables into
options: nominal and real variables
supply and demand variables
public and private variables
short-run and long-run bonds
easy.commonError: thinking the dichotomy separates fiscal and monetary policy
easy.feedback: The classical dichotomy separates nominal variables from real variables.

easy.q: Monetary neutrality means changes in the money supply do not affect
options: real variables in the long run
nominal prices in the long run
the price level
the inflation rate
easy.commonError: thinking money neutrality means money has no effect on prices
easy.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

easy.q: Over the long run, all dollar wages and prices are twice as high while output per worker and hours worked are unchanged. Which interpretation best fits monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed, but the listed real variables did not.
Real variables doubled because every dollar price doubled.
Output per worker must have doubled because wages doubled.
The price level is a real variable, so nothing nominal changed.
easy.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
easy.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

medium.q: If all nominal prices and wages double while relative prices stay unchanged, this illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
A supply shock
A liquidity trap
medium.commonError: Missing the real versus nominal distinction.
medium.feedback: Monetary neutrality says nominal variables can change while real variables remain unchanged in the long run.

medium.q: If all nominal prices double but relative prices stay the same, this illustrates
options: monetary neutrality
crowding out
the multiplier effect
liquidity preference
medium.commonError: thinking changes in nominal prices automatically change relative prices
medium.feedback: Monetary neutrality says money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

medium.q: Which statement is consistent with the classical dichotomy?
options: Money growth can affect nominal wages without changing real wages in the long run.
Money growth changes only real variables and never nominal variables.
Nominal and real variables are always identical.
The price level is a real variable.
medium.commonError: thinking nominal and real variables move identically
medium.feedback: Under the classical dichotomy, money affects nominal variables, while real variables are determined by real factors in the long run.

medium.q: A nominal wage rises from $15 to $30 while the price level doubles. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays the same.
It doubles.
It falls by half.
It becomes zero.
medium.commonError: thinking a higher nominal wage always means a higher real wage
medium.feedback: If nominal wages and the price level both double, the real wage is unchanged.

medium.q: After a sustained monetary expansion, the long-run price level is higher and nominal wages are higher by roughly the same proportion. What happens to the real wage if productivity is unchanged?
options: It can return to about its previous level because both the wage and price level rose together.
It must rise in the same proportion as the nominal wage because a larger dollar wage always guarantees more purchasing power.
It must fall to zero because money growth raises prices.
It becomes equal to the money-supply growth rate.
medium.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
medium.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

hard.q: If nominal wages double, prices double, and real output is unchanged, the result best illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky prices
Fiscal stimulus
hard.commonError: Treating nominal changes as real changes.
hard.feedback: If nominal variables double while real variables stay unchanged, that is monetary neutrality.

hard.q: A textbook says money is neutral in the long run. Which outcome is most consistent with that idea after the money supply doubles?
options: Nominal prices double while relative prices and real output are unchanged.
Real output doubles while nominal prices are unchanged.
Relative prices double while nominal prices are unchanged.
The price level falls and real wages double.
hard.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
hard.feedback: Money neutrality means money changes nominal variables, not real variables, in the long run.

hard.q: If every nominal price and nominal wage doubles, why might employment and output be unchanged in the long run?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged.
Workers receive twice as many physical goods per hour.
Money demand must fall to zero.
The reserve requirement doubles automatically.
hard.commonError: thinking nominal doubling changes real incentives by itself
hard.feedback: If all nominal values double together, real wages and relative prices do not change, so real decisions need not change.

hard.q: Which pair correctly classifies the variables?
options: Nominal GDP is nominal; real GDP is real.
Nominal GDP is real; real GDP is nominal.
The price level is real; real wage is nominal.
Relative price is nominal; dollar wage is real.
hard.commonError: labeling anything involving GDP as real
hard.feedback: Nominal GDP is measured in dollars. Real GDP is measured in output adjusted for price changes.

hard.q: A country doubles its money supply and, in the long run, all dollar prices double. What happens to the value of money?
options: It falls by half.
It doubles.
It stays unchanged.
It becomes equal to real GDP.
hard.commonError: thinking money supply doubling doubles the value of money
hard.feedback: If the price level doubles, the value of money, 1/P, falls by half.

hard.q: A monetary expansion raises output temporarily, but years later output returns to its prior real trend while the price level remains permanently higher. Why is this consistent with monetary neutrality?
options: Neutrality describes the long-run separation of nominal changes from real output, not the absence of short-run real effects.
Neutrality requires the price level to return fully to its original level after every monetary expansion, even in the long run.
Neutrality means real output must remain permanently above trend after money growth.
Neutrality applies only when both output and prices are unchanged at every horizon.
hard.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
hard.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

elite.q: A central bank doubles the money supply, output is unchanged, and all nominal wages and prices double. Which claim is strongest?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged
Real wages double with nominal wages
Relative prices double with prices
Output must double with money
elite.commonError: Confusing nominal doubling with real doubling.
elite.feedback: If wages and prices double together, real wages and relative prices remain unchanged.

elite.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 6 percent while the price level rises 9 percent. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls by about 3 percent
It rises by about 3 percent
It rises by about 15 percent
It stays unchanged
elite.commonError: Treating nominal wage growth as real wage growth.
elite.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so 6 - 9 = -3 percent.

elite.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. The economy moves from a to b. In a long-run comparison, a nominal wage rises by the same proportion as the price level inferred from those points, and technology and labor supplies are unchanged. Which comparison fits monetary neutrality?
options: The price level and nominal wage rise by one-third; the real wage need not change.
The price level falls by one-quarter; the real wage must rise.
The price level doubles; unchanged real resources require output to double.
The price level rises by one-third; the real wage must also rise by one-third.
elite.commonError: confusing nominal price-level changes with real-output changes
elite.feedback: The graph gives value of money 2 at a and 1.5 at b. Their reciprocal price levels are 1/2 and 2/3, a one-third increase. Proportional nominal wage growth leaves the real wage unchanged; nominal changes alone do not raise real productive capacity.
elite.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

elite.q: A country doubles all nominal wages and prices, while output, employment, and relative prices are unchanged. Which concept explains this outcome?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
The liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
elite.commonError: thinking nominal doubling must increase real output
elite.feedback: If nominal variables change but real variables do not, that is monetary neutrality.

elite.q: Nominal wages rise 12 percent while the price level rises 8 percent. Approximately what happens to the real wage?
options: It rises by about 4 percent.
It falls by about 4 percent.
It rises by about 20 percent.
It is unchanged.
elite.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
elite.feedback: Real wage growth is roughly nominal wage growth minus inflation: 12 percent - 8 percent = 4 percent.

elite.q: If nominal GDP rises 10 percent while real GDP rises 4 percent, what happened to the price level approximately?
options: It rose about 6 percent.
It rose about 14 percent.
It fell about 6 percent.
It stayed fixed.
elite.commonError: adding real growth to nominal growth instead of subtracting
elite.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price level growth is about 10 - 4 = 6 percent.

legendary.q: A student says nominal wages rose 8 percent, so workers are better off. Inflation was 11 percent. What correction survives?
options: Real wages fell because prices rose faster than nominal wages.
Real wages rose because nominal wages increased above zero.
Real wages were unchanged because all inflation is neutral immediately.
Real wages doubled because nominal wages are measured in dollars.
legendary.commonError: Confusing nominal wage growth with real wage growth.
legendary.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so workers lost purchasing power.

legendary.q: A student says, 'Since money is neutral, monetary policy cannot affect output during recessions.' Which correction is strongest?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run sticky prices allow AD effects on output.
Neutrality means money changes output permanently but not prices.
Neutrality applies only to fiscal policy and never to money.
Neutrality means the Phillips curve slopes downward in the long run.
legendary.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to every short-run case.
legendary.feedback: Money is neutral in the long run, but monetary policy can affect output in the short run through aggregate demand.

legendary.q: Nominal GDP rises 12 percent while real GDP rises 5 percent. What happened to the price level, and which kind of variable changed?
options: The price level rose about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level rose about 17 percent; that is a real change.
The price level fell about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level was unchanged; only real output changed.
legendary.commonError: adding nominal and real growth instead of subtracting
legendary.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price growth is about 12 - 5 = 7 percent. The price level is nominal.

legendary.q: A worker's nominal wage rises from $24 to $30 while the price level rises from 6 to 10. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls from 4 units to 3 units.
It rises from 4 units to 5 units.
It stays at 4 units.
It rises from 6 units to 10 units.
legendary.commonError: looking only at the nominal wage increase
legendary.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It falls from 24/6 = 4 to 30/10 = 3 units.

legendary.q: All nominal prices double except wages, which rise only 50 percent. What happens to real wages?
options: Real wages fall because nominal wages rise less than the price level.
Real wages rise because nominal wages rose.
Real wages are unchanged because all prices rose.
Real wages double because prices doubled.
legendary.commonError: thinking any nominal wage increase raises the real wage
legendary.feedback: Real wages depend on wages relative to prices. If wages rise 50 percent while prices double, real wages fall.

legendary.q: A country's price level rises from 100 to 140, nominal wages rise from $20 to $24, and workers complain their purchasing power fell. What happened to real wages?
options: They fell because wages rose 20 percent while prices rose 40 percent.
They rose because nominal wages rose.
They stayed the same because both wages and prices rose.
They doubled because the price level rose.
legendary.commonError: thinking nominal wage growth automatically raises purchasing power
legendary.feedback: Nominal wages rose 20 percent, but prices rose 40 percent. Real wages fell.

legendary.q: A policy causes all nominal prices, nominal wages, and nominal debts to double, but output and employment remain unchanged. Which outcome best fits long-run monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed while real variables stayed unchanged.
Real variables changed while nominal variables stayed unchanged.
Money had no effect on the price level.
Relative prices doubled.
legendary.commonError: thinking monetary neutrality means money has no nominal effects
legendary.feedback: Long-run monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real output or employment.

calculation.q: A worker earns $20 per hour, and the price level is 5. The real wage is
options: 4 units of output per hour
$25 per hour
100 units of output per hour
0.25 units of output per hour
calculation.commonError: multiplying wage by price level instead of dividing
calculation.feedback: Real wage equals nominal wage divided by price level: 20 / 5 = 4 units of output per hour.

calculation.q: If the price of pizza rises from $10 to $20 and the price of soda rises from $2 to $4, the relative price of pizza in terms of soda
options: is unchanged
doubles
falls by half
becomes zero
calculation.commonError: thinking nominal price increases always change relative prices
calculation.feedback: Pizza was 5 sodas before and 5 sodas after. The relative price is unchanged.

calculation.q: A worker's nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 5. What happens to the real wage?
options: It rises from 5 to 6 units of output.
It falls from 5 to 4 units of output.
It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 4 to 5 units of output.
calculation.commonError: looking only at the nominal wage increase
calculation.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It rises from 20/4 = 5 to 30/5 = 6.

calculation.q: The price of coffee rises from $4 to $8 while the price of tea rises from $2 to $3. What happens to the relative price of coffee in terms of tea?
options: It rises from 2 teas to about 2.67 teas.
It stays at 2 teas.
It falls from 2 teas to 1.5 teas.
It becomes 8 teas.
calculation.commonError: thinking all nominal price increases leave relative prices unchanged
calculation.feedback: Coffee was 4/2 = 2 teas. It becomes 8/3, or about 2.67 teas.

boss.q: Which unit is used to express a nominal variable?
options: monetary units
physical units
real output units
labor hours only
boss.commonError: confusing nominal with real
boss.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in money terms, such as dollars.

boss.q: A nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 5 to 6 units.
It falls from 5 to 3.33 units.
It doubles.
boss.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
boss.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It starts at 20/4 = 5 and ends at 30/6 = 5.

boss.q: A country's money supply doubles, and in the long run all nominal prices and wages double while output is unchanged. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs
boss.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
boss.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

boss.q: Which outcome is most consistent with long-run monetary neutrality after a one-time increase in the money supply?
options: A higher price level with real output determined by real productive factors.
Permanently higher real output with no change in nominal prices.
Permanently lower prices because more money makes each dollar more valuable.
A permanently higher real wage solely because the number of dollars increased.
boss.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
boss.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

boss.q: A worker’s nominal wage and the price level both rise 10 percent while productivity is unchanged. What happens to the worker’s real wage approximately?
options: It rises about 20 percent.
It rises exactly 10 percent.
It falls exactly 10 percent.
It is roughly unchanged.
boss.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
boss.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

boss.q: Which variable is nominal rather than real?
options: Hours of labor used to produce haircuts.
Haircuts produced per worker.
The dollar price of a haircut.
The quantity of haircuts produced.
boss.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
boss.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

boss.q: Money growth accelerates for several years. In the long-run neutrality framework, which comparison is most defensible?
options: Neutrality requires money growth to leave every nominal price and wage unchanged in the long run.
Nominal prices can be persistently higher even though money growth does not permanently raise productive capacity.
Productive capacity must rise one-for-one with the price level.
A higher price level proves long-run real output rose by the same percentage.
boss.commonError: Treats a one-time nominal level change as permanent real growth.
boss.feedback: A one-time monetary expansion can raise nominal levels; long-run real growth requires changes in real productive capacity.

boss.q: A country redenominates so every old 100-unit price becomes 1 new unit, with contracts and wages converted proportionally. What has changed economically?
options: The nominal unit of account changed, while real quantities and relative prices need not change.
Real output fell by 99 percent because smaller numbers on price tags necessarily mean less production.
Productivity rose because fewer currency units are needed per transaction.
The natural rate of unemployment must fall because nominal wages were converted.
boss.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
boss.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

boss.q: The central bank unexpectedly expands money, real activity rises for a time, and later output returns to potential while nominal prices remain higher. Which statement best reconciles the episode?
options: Long-run neutrality is disproved whenever any short-run real effect occurs.
Neutrality requires output to remain permanently above potential.
The episode can be neutral only if the price level eventually falls below its starting point.
Short-run real effects can coexist with long-run monetary neutrality.
boss.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
boss.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. A worker earns $24 at point a and $30 at point b. Treat each point’s price level as the reciprocal of its displayed value of money. What happens to the worker’s real wage, and what nominal wage at b would instead preserve the original purchasing power?
options: Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $32 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 12 to 20 output units; $18 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 48 to 60 output units; $24 would preserve it.
Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $36 would preserve it.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not converting value of money into price level before calculating real wage
legendaryBoss.feedback: P is 1/2 at a and 2/3 at b. Real wages are 24/(1/2) = 48 and 30/(2/3) = 45. To retain 48 units at b requires 48 × 2/3 = $32.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

legendaryBoss.q: Nominal GDP rises 15 percent, real GDP rises 6 percent, and nominal wages rise 8 percent. What happens to the price level and real wages approximately?
options: P rises about 9 percent; real wages fall about 1 percent.
P rises about 21 percent; real wages rise about 8 percent.
P falls about 9 percent; real wages rise about 17 percent.
P rises about 6 percent; real wages rise about 2 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not comparing nominal wage growth to inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Inflation is about 15 - 6 = 9 percent. Nominal wages rise 8 percent, so real wages fall about 1 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: A country doubles the number of currency units used to quote every wage and price, while production technology, labor, and relative prices are unchanged. What is the best first inference?
options: The change is nominal; the economy has not doubled its real productive capacity.
Real productive capacity doubled because every nominal amount doubled.
The natural rate of unemployment doubled because the currency unit changed.
The country necessarily experienced a permanent doubling of output per worker because every quoted nominal price and wage also doubled.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

repairQuestions.q: A student says, “If money is neutral, monetary policy can never affect real output.” What is the best correction?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run real effects can occur even if long-run real output returns to a level set by real factors.
Neutrality means money changes only real output and never prices at any horizon, so even temporary short-run changes in prices, spending, or production cannot occur.
Neutrality applies only during recessions, not in long-run comparisons of nominal and real economic variables.
Neutrality means every monetary-policy action has exactly zero effect on prices, output, employment, and interest rates at every horizon.
repairQuestions.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.

repairQuestions.q: A wage measured in dollars is:
options: Nominal
Real
Relative
Imported
repairQuestions.feedback: A dollar wage is a nominal variable.

repairQuestions.q: A wage adjusted for the price level is:
options: Real
Nominal
Fiat
Reserve
repairQuestions.feedback: A wage adjusted for prices is a real wage.

repairQuestions.commonError: Looking only at the nominal wage.
repairQuestions.q: Real wage equals:
options: Nominal wage divided by price level
Nominal wage times price level
Price level divided by nominal wage
Money supply divided by wage
repairQuestions.feedback: Real wage adjusts the dollar wage for the price level.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking a higher nominal wage always means higher purchasing power.
repairQuestions.q: If nominal wage is $20 and the price level is 4, real wage is:
options: 5 units
80 units
16 units
24 units
repairQuestions.feedback: Real wage is 20 / 4 = 5 units.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking neutrality means money has no effect on prices.
repairQuestions.q: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects:
options: Long-run nominal variables
Only real variables
Neither prices nor wages
Only unemployment
repairQuestions.feedback: Money neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking money neutrality means prices are fixed.
repairQuestions.q: If all nominal prices double but real output is unchanged, this fits:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs only
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

bridgeQuestions.q: If all nominal prices and wages double but real output is unchanged, this supports:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky wage theory only
A liquidity trap
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run.

bridgeQuestions.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 5 percent while inflation is 8 percent. The real wage:
options: Falls by about 3 percent
Rises by about 3 percent
Rises by about 13 percent
Does not change
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation: 5 - 8 = -3 percent.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Looking only at nominal wage growth.
bridgeQuestions.q: Nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 and the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units
It rises to 6 units
It falls to 3.33 units
It doubles
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Real wage is 20/4 = 5 and 30/6 = 5.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Thinking neutrality means no price changes.
bridgeQuestions.q: Money supply doubles, all nominal prices double, and real output is unchanged. This illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

bridgeQuestions.q: The quantity theory predicts that sustained money growth faster than real output growth can raise inflation. In the long-run neutrality framework, what should a student infer about real productive capacity?
options: Faster money growth can raise nominal prices without permanently increasing productive capacity.
Faster money growth must permanently raise productive capacity by the same percentage.
Higher inflation proves output per worker rose by the same amount.
Long-run neutrality requires inflation to be zero whenever money growth exceeds output growth.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops after predicting the price-level effect and does not separate nominal from real outcomes.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Use the quantity-theory result for nominal spending and prices, then apply long-run neutrality to ask which real variables need not rise permanently.

fisher-effect.title: Fisher Effect
fisher-effect.description: Connect expected inflation to nominal and real interest rates.

easy.q: If expected inflation rises and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should:
options: Fall
Rise
Become zero
Equal real GDP
easy.commonError: Reversing the Fisher effect.
easy.feedback: Nominal interest rates include expected inflation, so they rise when expected inflation rises.

easy.q: The Fisher effect says that when expected inflation rises, the nominal interest rate tends to
options: rise
fall
stay fixed forever
become equal to real GDP growth
easy.commonError: thinking inflation lowers nominal interest rates
easy.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

easy.q: The Fisher equation is most commonly written as
options: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation
real interest rate = nominal interest rate + expected inflation
expected inflation = real GDP + money supply
nominal interest rate = velocity divided by output
easy.commonError: adding inflation to the wrong side of the equation
easy.feedback: The Fisher equation links nominal rates, real rates, and expected inflation: nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation.

easy.q: If expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should
options: rise by about 3 percentage points
fall by about 3 percentage points
stay exactly the same
fall to zero
easy.commonError: thinking nominal rates ignore expected inflation
easy.feedback: If the real rate is unchanged, a 3-point rise in expected inflation raises the nominal rate by about 3 points.

easy.q: Under the Fisher effect, a country with persistently higher inflation will tend to have
options: higher nominal interest rates
lower nominal interest rates
no nominal interest rates
unchanged price levels forever
easy.commonError: thinking high inflation means low nominal rates
easy.feedback: Higher expected inflation tends to be built into higher nominal interest rates.

easy.q: Lenders begin expecting inflation to be 4 percentage points higher, while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Nominal interest rates tend to rise by about 4 percentage points.
Nominal interest rates tend to fall by about 4 percentage points.
Real interest rates must rise by exactly 4 percentage points.
Actual inflation must immediately equal the new nominal interest rate.
easy.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
easy.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

easy.q: A bank sets a fixed nominal loan rate today for next year. Which inflation concept is most relevant to the Fisher effect when that rate is chosen?
options: Only inflation that has already occurred.
The current unemployment rate by itself.
Only the realized inflation rate known after repayment.
Expected inflation over the loan period.
easy.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
easy.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

medium.q: If expected inflation rises while the real interest rate is unchanged, lenders will require
options: a higher nominal interest rate
a lower nominal interest rate
no repayment
a lower price level
medium.commonError: thinking lenders ignore expected inflation
medium.feedback: Lenders care about purchasing power, so higher expected inflation is built into higher nominal interest rates.

medium.q: Two otherwise similar economies have the same long-run real interest rate, but expected inflation is 2 percent in one and 7 percent in the other. What should differ under the Fisher effect?
options: The second economy should tend to have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher.
The first economy should have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher instead because lower expected inflation raises nominal rates.
Both nominal rates must be identical because real rates match.
The second economy must have a real rate 5 points higher.
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
medium.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

medium.q: Expected inflation falls from 6 percent to 2 percent while the long-run real interest rate remains 3 percent. What nominal-rate change is predicted?
options: The nominal rate rises from about 5 percent to about 9 percent.
The real rate falls from 3 percent to negative 1 percent automatically.
The nominal rate stays at 9 percent because only actual inflation matters.
The nominal rate falls from about 9 percent to about 5 percent.
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
medium.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

medium.q: A one-year loan is priced when inflation is expected to be 3 percent. Actual inflation later turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement separates the Fisher effect from the realized return?
options: The Fisher effect uses actual inflation only and ignores expectations.
Unexpected inflation raises both parties’ realized real returns by the same amount.
The nominal rate reflected expected inflation when set; the unexpectedly high actual inflation changes the ex post real return.
The nominal rate must be rewritten after actual inflation is observed so the original expected rate no longer matters.
medium.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
medium.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

hard.q: Expected inflation rises 6 percentage points while the equilibrium real interest rate falls 2 percentage points. What happens to the nominal interest rate approximately?
options: It rises about 4 percentage points because both expected inflation and the real rate matter.
It rises exactly 6 percentage points because the Fisher effect requires the real rate to remain fixed in every comparison.
It falls about 8 percentage points because expected inflation lowers nominal rates.
It is unchanged because the two components must always offset completely.
hard.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
hard.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

hard.q: Country A has expected inflation of 8 percent and a real interest rate of 1 percent. Country B has expected inflation of 3 percent and a real interest rate of 5 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Country A must have a nominal rate exactly 5 points above Country B.
Country B must have the lower nominal interest rate because lower expected inflation always dominates any real-rate difference.
The Fisher effect says real interest rates are always identical across countries.
A one-for-one comparison of nominal rates cannot use expected inflation alone because the real rates differ too.
hard.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
hard.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

hard.q: Expected inflation falls sharply after a credible long-run policy change, but productive opportunities and saving behavior leave the real rate roughly unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Real interest rates must fall by exactly the same amount as expected inflation.
Nominal rates should stay fixed because only realized inflation affects contracts.
Nominal interest rates should fall as the inflation premium falls.
Nominal interest rates should rise because lower expected inflation raises the inflation premium.
hard.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
hard.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

hard.q: A lender receives a 10 percent nominal rate that was set when expected inflation was 4 percent. Actual inflation is later 9 percent. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Expected inflation is irrelevant once a fixed nominal rate has been written.
The ex ante pricing reflected roughly a 6 percent real return, but the realized real return is much lower.
The Fisher effect predicted a 1 percent real return when the loan was made.
The nominal rate automatically rises to 15 percent after inflation is observed because fixed-rate contracts always adjust retroactively after the fact.
hard.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
hard.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

hard.q: Nominal interest rates rise from 7 to 11 percent at the same time expected inflation rises from 3 to 8 percent. Can we conclude the real rate was unchanged?
options: No. The nominal rate rose 4 points while expected inflation rose 5, so the implied real rate actually fell about 1 point.
Yes. Any rise in nominal rates alongside expected inflation proves the real rate is unchanged.
Yes. The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to rise exactly half as much as expected inflation regardless of changes in real rates.
No. The implied real rate rose about 9 percentage points.
hard.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
hard.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

elite.q: A lender expected 4 percent inflation and charged 9 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 8 percent. What happened to the realized real return?
options: It was lower than expected
It was higher than expected
It was unchanged
It became nominal GDP
elite.commonError: Ignoring unexpected inflation after a loan is written.
elite.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real return to lenders.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower signs a loan at 9 percent nominal interest when expected inflation is 4 percent. Actual inflation is 7 percent. What happened to the realized real interest rate compared with what the lender expected?
options: It fell from 5 percent expected to 2 percent realized.
It rose from 5 percent expected to 7 percent realized.
It stayed at 5 percent because nominal interest was fixed.
It fell from 9 percent expected to 4 percent realized.
elite.commonError: using expected inflation for the realized real rate
elite.feedback: Expected real rate was 9 - 4 = 5 percent. Realized real rate was 9 - 7 = 2 percent.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate is stable at 3 percent, what should happen to the nominal interest rate under the Fisher effect?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 12 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 3 percent.
It rises from 2 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 3 percent.
elite.commonError: forgetting the real interest rate is part of nominal interest
elite.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 3 + 2 = 5 to 3 + 9 = 12 percent.

legendary.q: A lender’s one-year fixed nominal contract pays 12 percent. Expected inflation when written was 5 percent, but actual inflation is 9 percent. Use exact gross returns. What are the expected and realized real returns, and what nominal rate on a new loan would preserve the original expected real return if expected inflation is now 9 percent?
options: About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 16.27 percent.
7 percent, 3 percent, and 16 percent exactly.
About 2.75 percent, 6.67 percent, and 12 percent.
About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 12 percent.
legendary.commonError: using expected inflation for both expected and realized real rates
legendary.feedback: Expected real return is 1.12/1.05 − 1 = 6.67 percent; realized is 1.12/1.09 − 1 = 2.75 percent. Preserving the original gross real return on a new loan requires (1.12/1.05) × 1.09 − 1 = 16.27 percent nominal.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 11 percent. The real interest rate falls from 3 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 13 percent.
It rises from 4 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
legendary.commonError: assuming the real rate is constant when it is explicitly changed
legendary.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 3 + 4 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 11 = 13 percent.

legendary.q: A one-time monetary expansion lowers the value of money today. Credible guidance says the money-growth rate will then return to its previous path. The long-run real interest rate is unchanged. An analyst concludes that nominal interest rates must remain permanently higher. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: A one-time price-level rise does not establish permanently higher expected inflation, so the lasting nominal-rate claim is unsupported.
The higher price level guarantees permanently higher inflation, so the nominal-rate claim follows.
The lower value of money proves the real interest rate falls permanently, so nominal rates must fall.
Monetary neutrality makes expected inflation irrelevant to nominal rates, so the Fisher relationship does not apply.
legendary.commonError: confusing short-run liquidity effects with long-run Fisher effect
legendary.feedback: The Fisher effect relates nominal rates to expected inflation over the loan horizon. A level adjustment alone does not establish a continuing inflation-rate increase. The real-rate assumption therefore does not complete the analyst’s argument.

legendary.q: Money growth rises from 8 percent to 20 percent. Velocity growth is zero and output growth is 4 percent. If expected inflation adjusts fully, what happens to nominal rates when the real rate stays at 3 percent?
options: Nominal rates rise from about 7 percent to about 19 percent.
Nominal rates fall from 7 percent to 3 percent.
Nominal rates rise from 8 percent to 20 percent exactly.
Nominal rates stay at 3 percent.
legendary.commonError: not converting money growth into inflation before applying Fisher
legendary.feedback: Inflation rises from 8 - 4 = 4 percent to 20 - 4 = 16 percent. With real rate 3 percent, nominal rates rise from 7 to 19 percent.

legendary.q: A country establishes a credible low-inflation regime. Expected inflation falls from 9 percent to 3 percent, while saving and investment conditions leave the long-run real interest rate near 2 percent. Which outcome best fits the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate tends to fall from about 11 percent to about 5 percent.
The nominal interest rate tends to rise from about 5 percent to about 11 percent.
The real interest rate must fall from 2 percent to negative 4 percent.
The nominal interest rate should stay near 11 percent because credibility affects only actual inflation.
legendary.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
legendary.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

legendary.q: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?
options: It must be unchanged because identical expected inflation always forces identical nominal interest rates even when real saving and investment conditions differ.
It must be lower because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.
It must equal expected inflation because real rates disappear in the long run.
It should also be higher, showing that Fisher comparisons must account for the real-rate component as well as expected inflation.
legendary.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
legendary.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 9 percent, the Fisher effect predicts the nominal rate rises by:
options: 3 points
4 points
5 points
9 points
calculation.commonError: Using the final inflation rate instead of the change.
calculation.feedback: Expected inflation rises by 5 percentage points, so the nominal rate rises by 5 points.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 6 percent while the real interest rate stays at 2 percent. The nominal rate becomes:
options: 3 percent
5 percent
6 percent
8 percent
calculation.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
calculation.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

calculation.q: If the nominal interest rate is 9 percent and expected inflation is 4 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
13 percent
4 percent
36 percent
calculation.commonError: adding inflation when solving for the real rate
calculation.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal rate minus expected inflation: 9 - 4 = 5 percent.

calculation.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 8 percent
4 percent
3 percent
12 percent
calculation.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
calculation.feedback: Nominal interest rate is approximately real interest rate plus expected inflation: 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. The nominal interest rate is 11 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent. If actual inflation turns out to be 10 percent, what is the realized real interest rate?
options: 1 percent
4 percent
3 percent
21 percent
calculation.commonError: using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate
calculation.feedback: The realized real rate uses actual inflation: 11 - 10 = 1 percent.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent and the real interest rate remains 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 2 percent.
calculation.commonError: forgetting to include the real interest rate in both periods
calculation.feedback: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 8 = 10.

calculation.q: If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 2 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
1 percent
2 percent
6 percent
calculation.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
calculation.feedback: The nominal interest rate is approximately the real interest rate plus expected inflation: 3 + 2 = 5 percent.

calculation.q: If the nominal interest rate is 7 percent and expected inflation is 3 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 4 percent
10 percent
3 percent
21 percent
calculation.commonError: adding expected inflation when solving for the real interest rate
calculation.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal interest rate minus expected inflation: 7 - 3 = 4 percent.

boss.q: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to
options: nominal interest rates
real GDP only
reserve requirements
M1 only
boss.commonError: thinking expected inflation is unrelated to nominal rates
boss.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

boss.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent, the nominal interest rate is about
options: 9 percent
5 percent
7 percent
14 percent
boss.commonError: subtracting expected inflation when solving for nominal rate
boss.feedback: Nominal interest is real interest plus expected inflation: 2 + 7 = 9 percent.

boss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent while the real interest rate falls from 4 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
boss.commonError: tracking only expected inflation and ignoring the real rate change
boss.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 3 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 8 = 10 percent.

boss.q: If expected inflation rises while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged, the Fisher effect predicts that the nominal interest rate will:
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to real GDP growth.
boss.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
boss.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

boss.q: Which inflation rate matters when lenders set a nominal rate today for a future loan period?
options: Only last year’s inflation.
Only inflation observed after repayment.
The unemployment rate instead of inflation.
Expected inflation.
boss.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
boss.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

boss.q: The real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 5 percent. The Fisher approximation gives a nominal rate near:
options: 3 percent.
15 percent.
8 percent.
2 percent.
boss.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
boss.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

boss.q: Expected inflation rises from 4 to 10 percent while the equilibrium real rate falls from 3 to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal rate approximately?
options: It remains at about 7 percent because expected inflation and real rates always offset.
It rises from about 7 to about 11 percent.
It rises from about 7 to about 13 percent because the real-rate change is irrelevant.
It falls from about 7 to about 5 percent.
boss.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
boss.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

boss.q: A fixed-rate loan was written when expected inflation was 2 percent, but actual inflation turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Expected inflation helped determine the original nominal rate; the surprise changes the realized real return.
The Fisher effect requires the bank to retroactively reset the nominal rate to actual inflation.
Unexpected inflation leaves the realized real return unchanged on a fixed-rate contract.
The nominal rate was based only on actual inflation, which was already known.
boss.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
boss.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

boss.q: Nominal interest rates rise 3 percentage points while expected inflation rises 5 points. What does the Fisher decomposition imply about the real-rate component?
options: It rose by about 8 percentage points.
It rose by exactly 5 percentage points.
It must have remained unchanged because nominal rates increased.
It fell by about 2 percentage points.
boss.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
boss.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If MS shifts right and the value of money falls, expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate stays at 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 5 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: forgetting to add the real interest rate to expected inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 9 = 11 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 10 percent while the real rate falls from 4 percent to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate, and why is this not a contradiction?
options: It rises from 6 percent to 11 percent because expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.
It falls from 6 percent to 1 percent because the real rate fell.
It stays at 6 percent because changes cancel exactly.
It rises from 2 percent to 10 percent because real rates do not matter.
legendaryBoss.commonError: tracking only the real rate or only expected inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 2 = 6 percent. New nominal rate is 1 + 10 = 11 percent. Expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.

legendaryBoss.q: A country’s nominal loan rate falls from 16 to 9 percent while expected inflation falls from 12 to 4 percent. Using the Fisher approximation, what happens to the expected real rate, and by how much would the new nominal rate have had to fall further to preserve its original expected real rate?
options: The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate falls from 4 to 3 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate stays at 4 percent; no further nominal change was needed.
The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 5-point nominal cut was needed.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming lower nominal rates always mean lower real rates
legendaryBoss.feedback: Subtract expected inflation: 16 − 12 = 4 initially and 9 − 4 = 5 later. Preserving a real rate of 4 with expected inflation of 4 requires a nominal rate of 8, one point below 9.

repairQuestions.q: A borrower says the Fisher effect is found by subtracting this year’s actual inflation from a loan rate set last year. What is the key mistake?
options: The Fisher effect concerns expected inflation when the nominal rate is set, not merely realized inflation afterward.
The Fisher effect uses only the unemployment rate when a loan is made, so expected inflation has no role in nominal-rate setting.
The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to stay fixed when expected inflation changes.
The Fisher effect says actual inflation and expected inflation must always be identical.
repairQuestions.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.

repairQuestions.q: A nominal interest rate is 8 percent and inflation is 3 percent. The approximate real interest rate is:
options: 5 percent
11 percent
8 percent
-5 percent
repairQuestions.feedback: Approximate real interest equals nominal interest minus inflation: 8% − 3% = 5%.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
repairQuestions.q: The Fisher equation says nominal interest is approximately:
options: Real interest plus expected inflation
Real interest minus expected inflation
Expected inflation minus money growth
MPC times inflation
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is approximately real interest plus expected inflation.

repairQuestions.commonError: Subtracting when solving for nominal interest.
repairQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If real interest is 3% and expected inflation is 5%, nominal interest is:
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is 3% + 5% = 8%.

bridgeQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is:
options: 8 percent
6 percent
4 percent
2 percent
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting expected inflation in nominal rates.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Real interest is 2% and expected inflation is 6%. Nominal interest is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is 2% + 6% = 8%.

bridgeQuestions.q: Suppose long-run money growth raises expected inflation while real productive conditions leave the real interest rate unchanged. Which next step connects monetary neutrality to the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate rises to incorporate the higher expected inflation while the real-rate component stays unchanged.
The real interest rate must rise one-for-one because all nominal variables are neutral and expected inflation cannot influence nominal contract rates.
The nominal interest rate stays fixed because expected inflation affects only the price level.
Actual inflation must be known before lenders can set any nominal interest rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Recognizes nominal neutrality but does not connect expected inflation to nominal interest rates.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Once long-run real and nominal variables are separated, the Fisher effect explains why higher expected inflation is reflected in higher nominal interest rates.
