inflation-costs.title: Costs of Inflation
inflation-costs.description: Analyze redistribution, shoeleather costs, menu costs, and price distortions.

easy.q: Shoeleather costs of inflation come from:
options: Changing menus often
Holding less cash and making more transactions
Higher unemployment benefits
Falling expected prices
easy.commonError: Confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs.
easy.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from efforts to reduce money holdings when inflation is high.

easy.q: Menu costs of inflation refer to the cost of:
options: Printing more money
Changing posted prices
Measuring real GDP
Buying bonds
easy.commonError: Confusing menu costs with restaurant spending.
easy.feedback: Menu costs are the costs firms face when changing listed prices.

easy.q: Shoe-leather costs of inflation come from people
options: trying to reduce money holdings when inflation is high
wearing out shoes because factories produce less
paying higher menu prices at restaurants
borrowing less because taxes are lower
easy.commonError: taking shoe-leather costs literally
easy.feedback: Shoe-leather costs refer to the time and effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high.

easy.q: Menu costs of inflation are the costs of
options: changing listed prices
buying more food at restaurants
holding too many government bonds
printing money at the central bank
easy.commonError: thinking menu costs only apply to restaurants
easy.feedback: Menu costs are the costs firms face when they change posted prices.

easy.q: Unexpected inflation tends to help
options: debtors
creditors
people holding only cash
workers with fixed nominal wages and no adjustment
easy.commonError: thinking lenders always benefit from inflation
easy.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps debtors because they repay loans with dollars that are worth less than expected.

easy.q: Unexpected inflation tends to hurt
options: creditors
debtors
borrowers with fixed-rate loans
people whose debts are repaid with cheaper dollars
easy.commonError: forgetting that creditors are repaid in money with lower value
easy.feedback: Unexpected inflation hurts creditors because the dollars they are repaid have less purchasing power than expected.

medium.q: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders when:
options: Loans were written before the inflation surprise
All contracts are indexed perfectly
Real wages rise automatically
Nominal prices cannot change
medium.commonError: Missing redistribution from unexpected inflation.
medium.feedback: Borrowers repay with dollars that are worth less than lenders expected.

medium.q: Which example best fits menu costs?
options: A firm pays to update price lists after inflation rises
A household visits the bank more often
A lender loses from unexpected inflation
A central bank buys bonds
medium.commonError: Confusing menu costs with shoeleather costs.
medium.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices.

medium.q: Which example best fits shoeleather costs?
options: A firm prints new menus
A worker compares nominal and real wages
A household makes extra bank transfers to hold less cash
A creditor gains from unexpected deflation
medium.commonError: Confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs.
medium.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from actions people take to reduce money holdings during inflation.

medium.q: Unexpected inflation benefits borrowers because
options: they repay loans with dollars worth less than expected
they repay loans with dollars worth more than expected
their nominal debt automatically disappears
creditors receive more purchasing power than expected
medium.commonError: thinking inflation always hurts borrowers
medium.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers because their fixed nominal repayments are made with less valuable dollars.

medium.q: Unexpectedly low inflation hurts borrowers because
options: they repay loans with dollars worth more than expected
they repay loans with dollars worth less than expected
their debts are erased
nominal interest rates instantly become negative
medium.commonError: forgetting that unexpectedly low inflation benefits creditors
medium.feedback: When inflation is lower than expected, borrowers repay with dollars that have more purchasing power than expected.

medium.q: Which situation is the clearest example of menu costs?
options: A firm spends money updating price tags and online menus after inflation.
A worker walks to the bank more often to avoid holding cash.
A borrower repays debt with less valuable dollars.
A bank holds excess reserves.
medium.commonError: confusing menu costs with shoeleather costs
medium.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices.

medium.q: Which situation is the clearest example of shoeleather costs?
options: People make more frequent trips to reduce cash holdings during high inflation.
A restaurant prints new menus after raising prices.
A debtor repays a fixed loan with less valuable dollars.
A firm buys new equipment because interest rates fall.
medium.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
medium.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from the effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high.

medium.q: Inflation is fully anticipated, so fixed-rate contracts are written with the expected inflation built in. Which cost can still remain?
options: Firms may still spend resources changing posted prices more often.
Unexpected borrower-creditor redistribution must become larger even though the inflation rate was correctly anticipated by both sides.
The nominal interest rate must become zero.
All relative prices become permanently fixed.
medium.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
medium.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

hard.q: A borrower signs a loan expecting 2 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 7 percent. Who is helped?
options: The borrower
The lender
Both equally
Neither side
hard.commonError: Reversing unexpected inflation redistribution.
hard.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers because they repay in dollars worth less than expected.

hard.q: A lender expected 2 percent inflation and charged 6 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 5 percent. Who is helped by the surprise, and why?
options: Borrowers, because they repay with dollars worth less than expected.
Lenders, because they receive dollars worth more than expected.
Borrowers, because the nominal interest rate rises after the loan is signed.
Lenders, because real repayment rises automatically.
hard.commonError: thinking lenders benefit from unexpectedly high inflation
hard.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders because repayment occurs in less valuable dollars.

hard.q: A lender expected 6 percent inflation and charged 10 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 2 percent. Who is helped by the surprise?
options: Lenders
Borrowers
Both equally because nominal interest was fixed
Neither because inflation never redistributes wealth
hard.commonError: thinking all inflation outcomes help borrowers
hard.feedback: Lower-than-expected inflation helps lenders because they are repaid with dollars worth more than expected.

hard.q: Which sequence best explains shoeleather costs during high inflation?
options: Inflation raises the cost of holding money, so people spend resources reducing cash balances.
Inflation lowers interest rates, so people hold more cash forever.
Inflation makes all prices stable, so no one changes behavior.
Inflation eliminates the need for banks.
hard.commonError: treating shoeleather costs as literal shoe damage only
hard.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the wasted time and effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.

hard.q: Which sequence best explains menu costs during inflation?
options: Inflation changes desired prices, so firms spend resources updating posted prices.
Inflation reduces borrowing costs, so firms buy more menus.
Inflation eliminates relative price changes.
Inflation makes prices unnecessary.
hard.commonError: thinking menu costs apply only to restaurants
hard.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices, not just restaurant menus.

hard.q: Why can inflation make relative prices harder to interpret?
options: Because not all prices adjust at the same time or by the same amount.
Because all real prices are legally fixed.
Because inflation makes money demand disappear.
Because every nominal price changes perfectly together every second.
hard.commonError: thinking inflation only changes the average price level without affecting signals
hard.feedback: Inflation can distort price signals because different prices adjust unevenly.

hard.q: If all prices rise but incomes rise by the same percentage, why can inflation still be costly?
options: It causes shoe-leather, menu, tax, signal, and redistribution costs.
It has no costs if incomes rise at all.
It only affects people who never buy goods.
It permanently raises real wages.
hard.commonError: thinking inflation is harmless whenever nominal incomes rise
hard.feedback: Inflation can still impose real costs through behavior changes, price adjustment costs, distortions, and redistribution.

hard.q: A fixed-rate lender expected 3 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 8 percent. At the same time firms repeatedly update prices. Which statement separates the two costs?
options: The inflation surprise redistributes toward the borrower, while repricing uses real resources even if inflation had been anticipated.
Both effects are examples only of shoeleather costs.
The surprise benefits the lender, while repricing raises real output automatically.
Neither effect is an inflation cost unless the price level actually falls, because rising prices cannot redistribute purchasing power or use real resources.
hard.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
hard.feedback: The surprise redistributes purchasing power toward the borrower, while repeated price changes are menu costs that use real resources even when inflation is anticipated.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 6 percent inflation and charged 11 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 3 percent. Who gains from the surprise and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 14 percent.
elite.commonError: missing that lower-than-expected inflation helps lenders
elite.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so the lender gains. Realized real rate is 11 - 3 = 8 percent.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower expected 3 percent inflation on a loan with a 7 percent nominal rate. Actual inflation was 10 percent. Who gains and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 4 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 7 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
elite.commonError: thinking borrowers are hurt by unexpectedly high inflation
elite.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 7 - 10 = -3 percent.

elite.q: Why can high inflation distort relative prices even if the average price level is what gets reported?
options: Individual prices do not all adjust instantly or proportionally, so signals get noisy.
All individual prices change by exactly the same amount every second.
Relative prices are nominal variables only.
Inflation eliminates scarcity.
elite.commonError: thinking inflation only changes the average price level with no signal distortion
elite.feedback: Inflation can make price signals harder to read because prices adjust unevenly across goods and time.

elite.q: A government funds a deficit by printing money. People respond by holding less cash and visiting banks more often. Which inflation cost is most directly shown?
options: Shoeleather costs from reducing money holdings
Menu costs from changing posted prices
Crowding out from higher interest rates
Monetary neutrality from unchanged real variables
elite.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
elite.feedback: The extra effort to reduce money holdings is the shoeleather cost of inflation.

elite.q: A government funds a deficit by printing money. Firms then repeatedly update catalogs, labels, and online prices. Which inflation cost is most directly shown?
options: Menu costs
Shoeleather costs
Unexpected inflation redistribution
Liquidity trap
elite.commonError: thinking menu costs are only restaurant costs
elite.feedback: The cost of updating prices is menu cost. Not glamorous. Still real.

elite.q: A student says inflation makes everyone poorer because all prices rise. What is the best elite-level correction?
options: Inflation still causes distortions, behavior changes, and redistribution.
Inflation never has costs if any wage rises.
Inflation only affects creditors and no one else.
Inflation lowers all nominal incomes by definition.
elite.commonError: thinking inflation's only effect is higher prices with no nominal income adjustment
elite.feedback: Inflation is costly, but not simply because prices rise. The real damage comes through distortions, wasted effort, confusion, and redistribution.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 3 percent inflation and charged 8 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 12 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
legendary.feedback: Actual inflation exceeded expected inflation, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 8 - 12 = -4 percent.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 8 percent inflation and charged 13 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 2 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking borrowers always gain when inflation is positive
legendary.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so lenders gain. The realized real rate is 13 - 2 = 11 percent.

legendary.q: If MS shifts right and the price level rises from 2 to 4, what inflation cost would become more likely if firms must repeatedly update prices?
options: Menu costs
Crowding out
Reserve shortfall
Liquidity preference equilibrium
legendary.commonError: identifying inflation but not connecting it to a specific cost
legendary.feedback: The graph shows inflation after monetary expansion. Firms repeatedly changing posted prices is menu cost.

legendary.q: If MS shifts right, the price level rises, and people reduce cash balances by making more frequent transfers, what inflation cost is described?
options: Shoeleather costs
Menu costs
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
legendary.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
legendary.feedback: When inflation makes people spend effort reducing money holdings, that is shoeleather cost.

legendary.q: A country experiences 18 percent money growth, 2 percent velocity growth, and 5 percent real output growth. Inflation is high, and borrowers with fixed-rate debt gain unexpectedly. What is the approximate inflation rate?
options: 15 percent
25 percent
21 percent
11 percent
legendary.commonError: forgetting velocity growth or subtracting it incorrectly
legendary.feedback: Inflation = money growth + velocity growth - output growth = 18 + 2 - 5 = 15 percent.

legendary.q: A country perfectly indexes many long-term contracts to the price level, greatly reducing unexpected debtor-creditor redistribution. Inflation nevertheless remains high and predictable. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Indexation can reduce redistribution without eliminating costs such as frequent repricing, cash management, or tax distortions.
Once contracts are indexed, high expected inflation becomes economically costless.
Indexation guarantees the price level stops rising because once nominal contracts are indexed, firms and households no longer face any inflation-related decisions.
Indexation converts inflation into deflation by raising the real value of money.
legendary.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

boss.q: Shoeleather costs of inflation come from people
options: spending resources to reduce money holdings
changing posted prices
borrowing from the Fed
holding required reserves
boss.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
boss.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.

boss.q: A borrower expected inflation to be 2 percent, but actual inflation is 8 percent. Who benefits?
options: Borrowers benefit because they repay with less valuable dollars.
Lenders benefit because they receive more purchasing power.
No one is affected by unexpected inflation.
Only workers benefit because real wages rise.
boss.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
boss.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers because they repay with dollars worth less than expected.

boss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan has a 9 percent nominal interest rate. Expected inflation was 3 percent, but actual inflation was 10 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real interest rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 6 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 9 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
boss.commonError: using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate
boss.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. Realized real rate is 9 - 10 = -1 percent.

boss.q: A store must repeatedly change price labels because the overall price level is rising. This is primarily a:
options: Menu cost.
Shoeleather cost.
Natural-rate effect.
Money-multiplier effect.
boss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
boss.feedback: Repeatedly changing price labels is a menu cost because firms spend resources updating posted prices.

boss.q: People make more frequent transfers so they can hold smaller cash balances during inflation. This is primarily a:
options: Menu cost.
Fisher-effect premium.
Reserve requirement.
Shoeleather cost.
boss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
boss.feedback: Extra transfers to keep smaller cash balances are shoeleather costs because households spend time and effort reducing money holdings.

boss.q: Unexpected inflation is higher than lenders anticipated on fixed-rate loans. Who tends to gain?
options: Both sides equally, because unexpected inflation cannot redistribute purchasing power.
Only the central bank, because private contracts are unaffected by inflation.
Borrowers, because repayment dollars have less purchasing power than expected.
Lenders, because inflation always raises realized real returns.
boss.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
boss.feedback: Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between parties to fixed nominal contracts because the realized price level differs from what they expected.

boss.q: Inflation is anticipated and nominal interest rates adjust, but firms still reprice frequently and households economize on cash balances. What does this show?
options: Anticipated inflation necessarily increases real output enough to offset every menu, cash-management, and redistribution cost.
Expected inflation can still impose menu and shoeleather costs even when some redistribution is avoided.
Expected inflation is costless whenever nominal interest rates adjust.
Menu and shoeleather costs occur only when inflation is unexpected.
boss.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
boss.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

boss.q: A pension is fixed in nominal dollars and inflation is unexpectedly high. Which mechanism is most important?
options: The pension’s real purchasing power falls because the nominal payment buys less than expected.
The pension automatically rises one-for-one because every fixed nominal contract is indexed against unexpected inflation.
The price level falls, increasing the pension’s real value.
The inflation surprise affects only banks, not recipients of fixed nominal payments.
boss.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
boss.feedback: Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between parties to fixed nominal contracts because the realized price level differs from what they expected.

boss.q: High inflation causes firms to reprice at different times, making it harder to distinguish relative-price changes from changes in the overall price level. Which cost is being described?
options: A larger money multiplier.
A lower natural unemployment rate by definition.
A statutory inflation-tax payment collected on a tax return.
Relative-price variability and signal confusion.
boss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
boss.feedback: When prices adjust at different times and by different amounts, inflation makes relative-price signals noisier; this is relative-price variability and signal confusion.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan has a 10 percent nominal interest rate. Expected inflation was 4 percent, but actual inflation was 11 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real interest rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 6 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 10 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. Realized real rate is 10 - 11 = -1 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: MS shifts right, P rises, and firms must update thousands of posted prices while households also reduce money balances. Which pair of inflation costs is described?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and the Fisher effect
Reserve shortfalls and capital losses
Liquidity trap and fiscal lag
legendaryBoss.commonError: identifying inflation but missing the specific costs
legendaryBoss.feedback: Updating posted prices is menu cost. Reducing money balances through extra effort is shoeleather cost.

legendaryBoss.q: MS shifts right, P rises from 2 to 5, and a fixed nominal debt of $10,000 is repaid. What happens to the real burden of that debt?
options: It falls because dollars are worth less when repaid.
It rises because dollars are worth more when repaid.
It is unchanged because the nominal debt is fixed.
It rises because inflation helps creditors.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking fixed nominal debt means unchanged real burden
legendaryBoss.feedback: When P rises, money is worth less. Fixed nominal repayments become easier in real terms, helping debtors.

legendaryBoss.q: All long-term debt is fully price-indexed, wage contracts adjust correctly, and inflation is perfectly anticipated. Firms still reprice at different times and households spend time moving funds out of non-interest-bearing cash. Which evaluation separates what indexation resolves from what it leaves?
options: Debt indexation limits surprise redistribution; asynchronous prices and cash management can still consume resources or distort signals.
Debt indexation eliminates all inflation costs because every relative price must adjust at the same instant.
The remaining cash-management costs transfer wealth from borrowers to lenders without using real resources.
Perfect anticipation eliminates repricing costs but creates unexpected redistribution on the indexed debt.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking only unexpected inflation is costly
legendaryBoss.feedback: Indexation protects the real value of the specified debt. It does not make repricing instantaneous or eliminate the effort spent economizing on non-interest-bearing cash.

repairQuestions.q: Unexpected inflation redistributes wealth toward borrowers when:
options: Loans have fixed nominal payments
All loans adjust instantly with inflation
Interest rates are always zero
Prices never change
repairQuestions.feedback: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers and hurting lenders.

repairQuestions.q: Menu costs are the costs of changing:
options: Posted prices
Reserve ratios
Real GDP
Natural unemployment
repairQuestions.feedback: Menu costs are costs firms face when changing posted prices.

repairQuestions.q: Shoeleather costs come from people trying to hold:
options: Less cash during inflation
More capital during recessions
More imports during booms
Less output during deflation
repairQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from efforts to reduce cash holdings during inflation.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation.
repairQuestions.q: Unexpectedly high inflation helps:
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Only banks
No one
repairQuestions.feedback: Borrowers repay with dollars worth less than expected.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking borrowers gain from unexpectedly low inflation.
repairQuestions.q: Unexpectedly low inflation helps:
options: Lenders
Borrowers
Only workers
Only importers
repairQuestions.feedback: Lenders are repaid with dollars worth more than expected.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
repairQuestions.q: A student says, “If everyone correctly expects 6 percent inflation, inflation has no economic costs.” Which response is best?
options: Anticipation reduces some redistribution, but cash-management, repricing, tax, and relative-price costs can remain.
Correct; expected inflation removes every resource and information cost.
Correct; only unexpected deflation can create economic costs.
Incorrect only because expected inflation always lowers real GDP by exactly 6 percent and therefore creates a predictable recession every year.
repairQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing shoeleather and menu costs.
repairQuestions.q: Shoeleather costs come from:
options: Effort spent reducing money holdings
Firms changing posted prices
Banks calculating reserves
The Fed selling bonds
repairQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the time and effort spent avoiding holding too much money during inflation.

bridgeQuestions.q: A restaurant reprints menus every week because prices keep changing. This is:
options: Menu cost
Shoeleather cost
Inflation tax
Money neutrality
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Menu costs are costs of changing posted prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: Inflation makes a household transfer money more often to avoid holding cash. This is:
options: Shoeleather cost
Menu cost
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the costs of reducing money holdings during inflation.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate.
bridgeQuestions.q: Nominal interest is 9%, expected inflation was 3%, but actual inflation is 10%. Who gains?
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Both equally
No one
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers repay with less valuable dollars.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing inflation cost examples.
bridgeQuestions.q: Firms repeatedly update posted prices while households make more transfers to avoid holding cash. Which costs are shown?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and liquidity trap
Reserve shortfall and bank capital loss
M1 and M2
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Price updates are menu costs; reducing cash balances creates shoeleather costs.

inflation-tax-and-deflation.title: Inflation Tax and Deflation
inflation-tax-and-deflation.description: Analyze seigniorage, the inflation tax, disinflation, and deflation burdens.

easy.q: When a government finances spending by printing money, it is using
options: an inflation tax
a real wage subsidy
a reserve requirement
a bond-rating rule
easy.commonError: thinking inflation tax requires an explicit tax bill
easy.feedback: Printing money to finance spending creates an inflation tax because it reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.

easy.q: An inflation tax reduces the value of
options: money held by the public
only physical capital
only imported goods
real GDP by definition
easy.commonError: thinking inflation tax only affects people who owe taxes
easy.feedback: An inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money balances held by the public.

easy.q: Hyperinflation is usually associated with
options: very rapid growth in the money supply
a fixed money supply forever
falling prices every year
a permanent drop in nominal wages only
easy.commonError: thinking hyperinflation happens without excessive money creation
easy.feedback: Hyperinflation is usually tied to extremely rapid money growth, often when governments print money to finance spending.

easy.q: Deflation means the economy is experiencing
options: a falling overall price level
a rising overall price level
zero interest rates only
a larger money multiplier only
easy.commonError: confusing deflation with disinflation
easy.feedback: Deflation means the overall price level is falling.

easy.q: A major danger of heavy reliance on printing money to finance government spending is
options: high inflation or hyperinflation
a guaranteed rise in real output
a permanent fall in nominal prices
the end of money demand
easy.commonError: thinking printing money creates real resources without inflation costs
easy.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but heavy reliance on it can produce high inflation or hyperinflation.

easy.q: A government creates money to finance purchases, the price level rises, and households’ existing cash buys less. What burden is illustrated?
options: The real purchasing power of money balances is being eroded by the inflation tax.
A statutory income-tax rate automatically rose on every household.
Deflation increased the real value of cash balances.
The natural rate of unemployment fell permanently because the government created more money and raised the overall price level.
easy.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
easy.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

medium.q: Why can heavy reliance on printing money become dangerous?
options: It can create rapid inflation and reduce money's value
It guarantees higher real GDP forever
It eliminates all tax burdens
It makes nominal variables real
medium.commonError: Thinking printing money is costless financing.
medium.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but it reduces the value of money and can create high inflation.

medium.q: A government repeatedly prints money to pay its bills. Which risk is most directly connected to this policy?
options: Inflation tax and possible hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real output
Permanent monetary neutrality failure
A lower price level forever
medium.commonError: thinking printing money creates real resources without inflation pressure
medium.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but repeated reliance on it can create inflation or hyperinflation.

medium.q: Why is the inflation tax called a tax even though Congress may not pass a tax law?
options: It reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.
It raises real GDP automatically.
It only applies to people who owe income taxes.
It directly increases the real wage.
medium.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit and legislative
medium.feedback: Inflation acts like a tax on money holders by reducing the purchasing power of their cash balances.

medium.q: A country with runaway money creation and rapidly rising prices is experiencing
options: hyperinflation
monetary neutrality only
deflation
crowding out
medium.commonError: confusing high inflation with falling prices
medium.feedback: Rapid money creation paired with rapidly rising prices is hyperinflation territory.

medium.q: If prices are falling across the economy, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises.
It falls.
It becomes zero.
It becomes the nominal interest rate.
medium.commonError: thinking falling prices reduce the purchasing power of money
medium.feedback: Deflation means falling prices, so each dollar buys more. The value of money rises.

medium.q: Inflation falls from 7 percent to 2 percent, but the overall price level is still rising. Which description is correct?
options: The economy is experiencing disinflation, not deflation.
The economy is experiencing deflation because inflation is lower.
The economy is experiencing hyperinflation because prices are still rising.
The price level must be falling by 5 percent.
medium.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
medium.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

hard.q: A country prints money to cover deficits, prices rise rapidly, and people rush to spend cash before it loses value. Which idea is most central?
options: Inflation tax and falling money value
Crowding out and rising investment
LRAS growth and lower inflation
Commodity money and stable prices
hard.commonError: Treating money printing as costless financing.
hard.feedback: Printing money can finance spending through an inflation tax, reducing the value of money.

hard.q: A household keeps a fixed $720 cash balance while the price level rises from 1.2 to 1.5 during money-financed government spending. How much purchasing power, measured in units of the composite good, does this unchanged balance lose?
options: 120 units.
180 units.
144 units.
No units, because the nominal balance is fixed.
hard.commonError: thinking inflation tax affects only people who file taxes
hard.feedback: The cash initially buys 720/1.2 = 600 units and later buys 720/1.5 = 480 units. The loss is 120 units; an unchanged dollar balance need not preserve purchasing power.

hard.q: A country has no ability to borrow and keeps financing deficits by creating money. What is the likely risk if this continues?
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real GDP without inflation
Permanent deflation
A lower money supply
hard.commonError: thinking money printing solves fiscal problems without inflation consequences
hard.feedback: Persistent money creation to finance deficits can trigger high inflation or hyperinflation.

hard.q: If inflation falls from 8 percent to 3 percent but remains positive, this is best described as
options: disinflation
deflation
hyperinflation
monetary neutrality
hard.commonError: calling falling inflation deflation when prices are still rising
hard.feedback: Disinflation means inflation is falling but still positive. Deflation means the price level is falling.

hard.q: Which policy concern is strongest when a government relies heavily on seigniorage?
options: Money growth may create inflation that erodes purchasing power.
Real output must permanently double.
Nominal interest rates must fall to zero.
The quantity equation stops applying.
hard.commonError: thinking seigniorage is costless revenue
hard.feedback: Seigniorage can raise revenue, but it risks inflation by expanding the money supply.

hard.q: An economy enters unexpected deflation while households carry fixed nominal mortgage debt. What happens to the real debt burden, other things equal?
options: It rises because each repayment dollar has greater purchasing power.
It falls because lower prices make nominal debts shrink automatically.
It is unchanged because the price level cannot affect fixed nominal contracts.
It disappears because deflation forces lenders to cancel nominal debt.
hard.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
hard.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

elite.q: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise with expected inflation. Which two ideas are linked?
options: Inflation tax and Fisher effect
Crowding out and SRAS
Multiplier and LRPC
M1 and sacrifice ratio
elite.commonError: Separating deficit money creation from expected inflation effects.
elite.feedback: Printing money can act as an inflation tax, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

elite.q: If a government prints money to cover spending and the public starts expecting higher future inflation, what happens to nominal interest rates under the Fisher effect?
options: They rise as expected inflation rises.
They fall because money supply rose.
They stay fixed because real rates cannot change.
They become equal to the reserve ratio.
elite.commonError: thinking more money always lowers every interest rate in every model and horizon
elite.feedback: If money finance raises expected inflation, nominal interest rates tend to rise through the Fisher effect.

elite.q: A country raises money growth from 5 percent to 25 percent while real output growth stays at 3 percent and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 2 percent to about 22 percent.
It rises from about 5 percent to about 25 percent exactly.
It falls from 25 percent to 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth is unchanged.
elite.commonError: forgetting to subtract real output growth
elite.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth: initially 2 percent, then 22 percent.

elite.q: Deflation lowers the price level from 200 to 180. What happens to the value of money, and why can this matter for debtors?
options: The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth more.
The value of money falls; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
The value of money is unchanged; debtors are unaffected.
The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
elite.commonError: thinking falling prices help borrowers with fixed nominal debts
elite.feedback: Deflation raises the value of money. Fixed nominal debts become harder for debtors to repay.

elite.q: Which result best distinguishes disinflation from deflation?
options: Inflation falls from 8 percent to 3 percent during disinflation, while the price level falls during deflation.
The price level falls during disinflation, while inflation rises during deflation.
Both mean the price level rises faster.
Both mean money has no value.
elite.commonError: calling any fall in inflation deflation
elite.feedback: Disinflation means inflation slows. Deflation means the price level actually falls.

elite.q: A country uses seigniorage heavily during a fiscal crisis. Which combination is most likely if confidence erodes?
options: Rapid money growth, rising expected inflation, and higher nominal interest rates
Falling money growth, falling expected inflation, and lower nominal interest rates
No change in inflation because money is neutral in the short run
Lower price levels and higher money value immediately
elite.commonError: thinking seigniorage is free revenue with no expectations effect
elite.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations, and higher expected inflation pushes nominal interest rates up.

legendary.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth rises from 6 percent to 26 percent, output growth remains 3 percent, and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 3 percent to about 23 percent.
It rises from about 6 percent to about 26 percent exactly.
It falls from about 23 percent to about 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth did not change.
legendary.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth from money growth
legendary.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth. It rises from 3 percent to 23 percent.

legendary.q: A government uses inflation tax finance, expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise. Which concepts are being connected?
options: Inflation tax, expected inflation, and the Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and commodity money
Menu costs, M1, and fiscal multipliers
Liquidity trap, real wage, and barter
legendary.commonError: not connecting money finance to expected inflation and nominal rates
legendary.feedback: Printing money can create inflation expectations, and the Fisher effect links expected inflation to nominal interest rates.

legendary.q: Unexpected deflation reduces the price level from 1.25 to 1.00. A firm’s fixed nominal debt is $48,000. Its sales volume is unchanged, and its $12,000 nominal operating cash flow falls in the same proportion as the price level. Which pair describes the debt burden and the cash-flow pressure?
options: Real debt rises from 38,400 to 48,000 units; debt/cash flow rises from 4 to 5.
Real debt falls from 48,000 to 38,400 units; debt/cash flow falls from 5 to 4.
Real debt rises from 38,400 to 48,000 units; debt/cash flow stays at 4.
Real debt stays at 48,000 units; debt/cash flow rises from 4 to 5.
legendary.commonError: thinking falling prices always help borrowers
legendary.feedback: Real debt rises from 48,000/1.25 = 38,400 to 48,000/1 = 48,000. Nominal cash flow becomes 12,000 × 1/1.25 = 9,600. Debt/cash flow therefore rises from 4 to 5, despite unchanged sales volume.

legendary.q: A government increasingly finances deficits by creating money. As inflation expectations rise, households try to hold smaller real money balances. Why can continued reliance on seigniorage become increasingly disruptive?
options: The shrinking demand to hold real balances can require still more money creation to extract a given amount of real resources, worsening inflation pressure.
Lower money demand guarantees the government can finance the same amount of real spending with progressively less money creation and steadily less inflation forever.
Seigniorage becomes costless once households expect inflation.
The quantity theory implies real output must rise one-for-one with the extra money creation.
legendary.commonError: Treats money creation as a costless financing source regardless of public money demand.
legendary.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

legendary.q: A heavily indebted economy experiences an unexpected 6 percent fall in the overall price level while nominal debts are fixed. Which balance-sheet effect is most likely?
options: Debtors receive an automatic reduction in the nominal face value of their debts.
Creditors lose because every repayment dollar is worth less in real terms.
The fall in the price level is disinflation and therefore cannot affect real debt burdens.
Debtors face a higher real repayment burden, which can weaken spending and financial positions.
legendary.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
legendary.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

legendary.q: Inflation drops from 12 percent to 4 percent after a stabilization program, but the price level continues to rise. A student calls this deflation. What is the best evaluation?
options: The student is correct only if nominal interest rates also fall.
The student is wrong because disinflation requires inflation to become negative.
The student is wrong: inflation slowed, but deflation requires the overall price level to fall.
The student is correct because any decline in the inflation rate means the overall price level must also be falling.
legendary.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
legendary.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

calculation.q: If the price level falls from 125 to 120, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises because 1/P is larger.
It falls because 1/P is smaller.
It stays constant because P changed by less than 10.
It becomes equal to velocity.
calculation.commonError: thinking falling prices reduce the value of money
calculation.feedback: When the price level falls, each dollar buys more, so the value of money rises.

boss.q: When a government finances spending by printing money, this is called
options: an inflation tax
crowding out
a liquidity trap
a reserve requirement
boss.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit
boss.feedback: Printing money can act like an inflation tax by reducing the purchasing power of money.

boss.q: Use the quantity-equation growth approximation. A government prints money heavily to pay bills. Money growth rises to 18 percent, velocity is stable, and real output grows 4 percent. What inflation rate is predicted?
options: 14 percent
18 percent
22 percent
4 percent
boss.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth
boss.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is about money growth minus output growth: 18 - 4 = 14 percent.

boss.q: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates increase. Which concepts are linked?
options: Inflation tax, quantity theory, and Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and M1
Liquidity trap, real GDP, and commodity money
Menu costs, unemployment, and barter
boss.commonError: not connecting money creation to inflation expectations and nominal rates
boss.feedback: Money-financed deficits can raise inflation, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

boss.q: When money-financed government spending reduces the purchasing power of existing money balances, the burden is called:
options: The inflation tax.
Crowding out.
The money multiplier.
The natural rate.
boss.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
boss.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

boss.q: Inflation falls from 6 percent to 3 percent while prices continue to rise. This is:
options: Deflation.
Hyperinflation.
Monetary neutrality.
Disinflation.
boss.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
boss.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

boss.q: If the overall price level falls, the value of money generally:
options: Becomes zero.
Equals the inflation rate.
Rises.
Falls.
boss.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
boss.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

boss.q: A government prints money to finance spending, expected inflation rises, and households reduce desired real cash balances. Which concern is most complete?
options: Households holding less money automatically raises real output enough to offset the inflation-tax burden and preserve seigniorage revenue.
Inflation-tax finance can erode real balances and become harder to sustain as people avoid holding money.
Lower money demand guarantees a stable price level despite continued money creation.
Printing money eliminates the need to consider inflation because seigniorage is a real resource.
boss.commonError: Treats money creation as a costless financing source regardless of public money demand.
boss.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

boss.q: Unexpected deflation occurs while firms and households owe large fixed nominal debts. Which distributional effect is most likely?
options: The real burden shifts against debtors and toward creditors.
The real burden shifts against creditors because repayment dollars buy less.
Both sides are unaffected because nominal debt cannot have a real value.
All nominal debts automatically fall at the same rate as the price level.
boss.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
boss.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

boss.q: A stabilization program reduces inflation from 20 percent to 5 percent without making inflation negative. Which statement is correct?
options: The program created deflation because any large decline in the inflation rate makes the price level fall.
The price level must have fallen 15 percent.
Disinflation requires the inflation rate to be below zero.
The program achieved disinflation; the price level can still be rising.
boss.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
boss.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

legendaryBoss.q: If money demand shifts right while MS is fixed and the value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, what happens to P, and what inflation term does this imply?
options: P falls from 5 to 4; this is deflation.
P rises from 4 to 5; this is inflation.
P falls from 1/4 to 1/5; this is disinflation.
P is unchanged; this is monetary neutrality.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking higher value of money means higher price level
legendaryBoss.feedback: Value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, so P falls from 5 to 4. A falling price level is deflation.

legendaryBoss.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth jumps, expected inflation rises, nominal rates rise, and people hold less cash. Which chain is most complete?
options: Expected inflation raises nominal rates and shoeleather costs.
Crowding out lowers nominal rates and eliminates inflation costs.
Reserve requirements rise automatically and make money neutral.
Commodity money replaces fiat money and ends inflation.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not connecting money finance to expectations and behavior
legendaryBoss.feedback: Money finance can act as an inflation tax, raise expected inflation and nominal rates, and make people spend resources avoiding cash holdings.

legendaryBoss.q: A government finances part of its budget by creating money, and the public’s existing money balances lose purchasing power as prices rise. What is the core mechanism?
options: Money creation transfers real purchasing power away from holders of money balances through the inflation tax.
A statutory tax authority directly debits an inflation-tax line from every bank account.
Deflation raises the real value of balances and transfers purchasing power to debtors.
The policy can finance the same amount of real spending indefinitely without reducing the purchasing power of existing money balances held by the public.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

repairQuestions.q: A student looks for an “inflation tax” line on a tax return. What is the best correction?
options: The inflation tax is the loss of purchasing power on money balances when money-financed spending contributes to inflation.
It is a statutory percentage surcharge collected only from commercial banks whenever the central bank expands the money supply to finance government spending.
It is the interest payment the Treasury makes on government bonds.
It is the fall in real debt burdens caused by unexpected deflation.
repairQuestions.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
Thinking printing money is costless government revenue.
repairQuestions.q: The inflation tax comes from government financing by:
options: Printing money
Cutting money supply
Lowering prices
Reducing nominal wages
repairQuestions.feedback: Printing money can act like a tax by reducing the value of money people already hold.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking heavy money creation has no inflation risk.
repairQuestions.q: Heavy reliance on printing money can lead to:
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
Permanent deflation
Zero nominal interest rates forever
A higher value of money
repairQuestions.feedback: Persistent money creation can create high inflation.

bridgeQuestions.q: A government prints money to pay bills and the value of existing money falls. This is closest to:
options: Inflation tax
Reserve requirement
Crowding out
Sacrifice ratio
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
bridgeQuestions.q: A government relies heavily on money creation. Inflation rises, households reduce cash balances, and they make more frequent transfers to avoid holding money. Which connection is most accurate?
options: Money finance creates an inflation-tax burden on money balances and also generates shoeleather costs.
Money finance eliminates the inflation tax because households hold less cash.
Shoeleather costs occur only during deflation, so the two effects cannot occur together.
The policy changes only real output and has no effect on nominal money balances, cash-management decisions, or the purchasing power of money.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Money creation erodes the purchasing power of money balances (the inflation tax) and encourages people to make more frequent transfers or otherwise avoid holding cash (shoeleather costs).

assetMetadata.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
assetMetadata.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

easy.q: Which function of money is being used when dollars are accepted to buy groceries?
options: Store of value
Medium of exchange
Unit of account
Reserve requirement
easy.commonError: Confusing the functions of money.
easy.feedback: Money is a medium of exchange when it is used to buy goods and services.

easy.q: Which function of money is being used when a store lists a phone price as $900?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
easy.commonError: Confusing pricing with payment.
easy.feedback: Money is a unit of account when it measures and compares prices.

easy.q: Which item is counted in M1?
options: Large time deposits
Currency held by the public
Credit card balances
Money market mutual funds held by businesses
easy.commonError: Counting credit cards as money.
easy.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item is included in M2 but not M1?
options: Checkable deposits
Coins held by households
Savings deposits
Currency held by the public
easy.commonError: Treating M1 and M2 as identical.
easy.feedback: M2 includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

easy.q: What is fiat money?
options: Money backed fully by gold
Accepted money with no intrinsic value
Money used only by banks
Money that cannot lose value
easy.commonError: Thinking fiat money must be backed by gold.
easy.feedback: Fiat money has value because people accept it, not because it has intrinsic value.

easy.q: A farmer wants shoes, but the shoemaker does not want wheat. Both are willing to accept dollars. Which feature of money solves the immediate trading problem?
options: It serves as a medium of exchange, so the two traders do not need a double coincidence of wants
It serves only as a store of value, so neither trader has to exchange anything
It makes every good part of M1, so barter becomes unnecessary
It guarantees that the relative price of wheat and shoes never changes
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Money serves as a medium of exchange because dollars let the farmer trade without finding a shoemaker who wants wheat.

easy.q: A repair shop compares a $450 used laptop with a $900 new laptop before deciding which to buy. Which function of money makes that comparison straightforward?
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Bank reserve
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Money serves as a unit of account because quoting both laptops in dollars provides a common measure for comparing their prices.

easy.q: A household keeps $600 in cash for emergencies. If prices rise substantially before the cash is spent, which statement is most accurate?
options: The cash serves as a store of value, but its purchasing power can fall
The cash stops being money because a store of value must keep purchasing power constant
The cash is serving only as a unit of account because it is not being spent today
Inflation converts the cash from M1 into a nonmonetary financial asset
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Cash is a store of value because it carries purchasing power into the future, although inflation can reduce that purchasing power before it is spent.

easy.q: Customers accept paper currency even though the paper itself has little intrinsic value and cannot be redeemed for a commodity. Which explanation best fits?
options: It is fiat money whose usefulness depends on general acceptance rather than commodity value
It is commodity money because the paper can be physically held
It is bank capital because it supports financial transactions
It is not money unless every note is backed one-for-one by gold
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: The currency is fiat money: it is accepted as payment even though the paper has little intrinsic value and is not redeemable for a commodity.

easy.q: Commodity money differs from fiat money because commodity money
options: has intrinsic value
is created only through bank lending
cannot be used as a medium of exchange
is always part of M2 but never M1
easy.commonError: treating all money as fiat money
easy.feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself, like gold or silver. Fiat money does not.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is included in M1?
options: Currency held by the public
Small time deposits
Savings deposits
Money market mutual funds held by individuals
easy.commonError: including all near monies in M1
easy.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public, checkable deposits, and similar highly liquid transaction balances.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is part of M2 but not M1?
options: Savings deposits
Currency
Checkable deposits
Traveler's checks
easy.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes near monies
easy.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies, so they are included in M2 but not M1.

easy.q: What is the central bank of the United States?
options: The Treasury Department
Congress
The Federal Reserve
The FDIC
easy.commonError: Confusing the Fed with fiscal agencies.
easy.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.

easy.q: Which group directs open-market operations?
options: Federal Open Market Committee
Congressional Budget Office
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Internal Revenue Service
easy.commonError: Confusing monetary policy agencies with data or tax agencies.
easy.feedback: The FOMC directs open-market operations as part of monetary policy.

easy.q: One major role of the Federal Reserve is to act as
options: a lender of last resort for banks
the agency that collects personal income taxes
the branch of government that writes spending bills
the organization that produces real GDP data
easy.commonError: confusing the Federal Reserve with fiscal agencies
easy.feedback: The Fed can serve as a lender of last resort by lending to banks when they need liquidity.

easy.q: The discount rate is the interest rate
options: the Fed charges banks for loans
banks charge each other on overnight loans
households earn on checking accounts
Congress pays on tax refunds
easy.commonError: confusing the discount rate with the federal funds rate
easy.feedback: The discount rate is the interest rate the Fed charges banks when it lends to them.

easy.q: The federal funds rate is best described as the interest rate
options: banks charge each other for short-term overnight loans
the Fed charges households for mortgages
Congress sets on government spending
firms pay workers as a wage
easy.commonError: thinking the federal funds rate is directly charged to consumers by the Fed
easy.feedback: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.

easy.q: The Federal Reserve is best described as
options: the central bank of the United States
the agency that writes the federal budget
a private commercial bank that lends only to households
the part of Congress that sets tax rates
easy.commonError: confusing the Fed with fiscal policymakers
easy.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States and conducts monetary policy.

easy.q: The Federal Open Market Committee is most directly responsible for
options: conducting open-market operations
setting federal income tax rates
writing government spending bills
calculating the unemployment rate
easy.commonError: confusing monetary policy with fiscal policy
easy.feedback: The FOMC conducts monetary policy largely through buying and selling government bonds.

easy.q: In a fractional reserve banking system, banks
options: hold only part of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest
must keep 100 percent of deposits as cash
cannot affect the money supply
create money by printing currency
easy.commonError: thinking banks create money by printing currency
easy.feedback: Fractional reserve banking means banks keep some deposits as reserves and lend the rest.

easy.q: The money multiplier becomes larger when the reserve ratio
options: falls
rises
equals the inflation rate
equals the nominal interest rate
easy.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more lending
easy.feedback: A lower reserve ratio lets banks lend more of each deposit, which increases the money multiplier.

easy.q: For a commercial bank, customer deposits are recorded as:
options: Revenue because deposits increase cash.
Liabilities because the bank owes the funds to depositors.
Bank capital because deposits belong to shareholders.
Assets because the bank physically holds the money.
easy.commonError: Treating deposits as bank-owned assets.
easy.feedback: Deposits are liabilities: the bank has an obligation to repay depositors.

easy.q: A 10 percent reserve rule applies to a $50,000 deposit base. How much must the bank keep rather than lend?
easy.commonError: Multiplying by the lending share instead of the reserve ratio.
easy.feedback: Ten percent of $50,000 is $5,000.

easy.q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, the loan is recorded as:
options: Bank capital only.
An asset of the bank.
A reduction in deposits with no matching asset.
A liability of the bank.
easy.commonError: Classifying loans as liabilities.
easy.feedback: Borrowers owe repayment to the bank, so loans are bank assets.

easy.q: If a bank receives a $1,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 20 percent, required reserves are:
easy.commonError: Subtracting instead of multiplying by the reserve requirement.
easy.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement, so $1,000 x 0.20 = $200.

easy.q: If a bank has $1,000 in deposits and the reserve requirement is 10 percent, required reserves are
easy.commonError: multiplying by 10 instead of 0.10
easy.feedback: Required reserves equal the reserve ratio times deposits: 0.10 x $1,000 = $100.

easy.q: If a bank receives a new $1,000 deposit and must hold $100 in required reserves, the bank can initially lend
easy.commonError: thinking the full deposit can be lent when reserves are required
easy.feedback: The bank can lend excess reserves. $1,000 minus $100 leaves $900 available to lend.

easy.q: If the reserve requirement rises, the simple money multiplier generally:
options: Rises.
Stays equal to one.
Falls.
Becomes unrelated to reserves.
easy.commonError: Reversing the relationship between the reserve ratio and multiplier.
easy.feedback: The simple multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio.

easy.q: If the reserve requirement is 10 percent, the simple money multiplier is:
easy.commonError: Using the reserve ratio instead of its reciprocal.
easy.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve requirement, so 1/0.10 = 10.

easy.q: If the reserve ratio is 20 percent, the simple money multiplier is
easy.commonError: using the reserve ratio as the multiplier
easy.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio: 1 / 0.20 = 5.

easy.q: If the Fed buys bonds in open-market operations, what happens first?
options: Bank reserves tend to fall
Bank reserves tend to rise
SRAS shifts left
The natural rate falls
easy.commonError: Reversing bond purchases and bond sales.
easy.feedback: Fed bond purchases inject reserves into the banking system.

easy.q: When the Fed buys government bonds in open-market operations, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed by law
turn into commodity money
easy.commonError: thinking bond purchases reduce the money supply
easy.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it injects money into the banking system, so the money supply tends to increase.

easy.q: When the Fed sells government bonds in open-market operations, the money supply tends to
options: decrease
increase
become equal to real GDP
stop depending on banks
easy.commonError: thinking bond sales add money to the economy
easy.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, buyers pay money to the Fed, so money is pulled out of circulation.

easy.q: A lower discount rate tends to make banks
options: more willing to borrow from the Fed
less willing to lend
hold exactly 100 percent reserves
stop creating deposits
easy.commonError: thinking a lower borrowing cost discourages borrowing
easy.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper, which can encourage bank lending.

easy.q: If the Fed wants to expand the money supply using open-market operations, it should
options: buy government bonds
sell government bonds
raise taxes
cut government purchases
easy.commonError: thinking bond purchases take money out of circulation
easy.feedback: Buying government bonds injects money into the banking system and expands the money supply.

easy.q: If the Fed wants to contract the money supply using open-market operations, it should
options: sell government bonds
buy government bonds
increase government spending
lower income taxes
easy.commonError: thinking bond sales add money to banks
easy.feedback: Selling government bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

easy.q: If the Fed lowers reserve requirements, banks can usually create
options: more money through lending
less money through lending
no deposits at all
commodity money instead of fiat money
easy.commonError: thinking lower reserve requirements reduce bank lending
easy.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free up reserves, allowing banks to lend more and expand deposits.

easy.q: Why is the Fed's control over the money supply not perfect?
options: M1 and M2 are always equal
Currency is not money
The Fed cannot buy bonds
Banks and depositors also influence lending
easy.commonError: Assuming the Fed controls every dollar directly.
easy.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits.

easy.q: The Fed's control over the money supply is imperfect partly because
options: banks may choose to hold excess reserves
Congress directly controls every bank loan
money demand is always zero
currency cannot be held by the public
easy.commonError: thinking the Fed can force banks to lend every excess reserve
easy.feedback: The Fed can influence lending conditions, but banks may still choose to hold excess reserves.

easy.q: The Fed's control over the money supply is imperfect partly because households can choose to hold more money as
options: currency instead of deposits
real GDP instead of inflation
tax revenue instead of government spending
imports instead of exports
easy.commonError: forgetting that currency held by the public affects bank reserves and deposit creation
easy.feedback: If people hold more currency instead of deposits, banks have fewer deposits to lend out, limiting money creation.

easy.q: If banks become nervous and stop lending excess reserves, the money multiplier will
options: be smaller than the simple multiplier predicts
be larger than the simple multiplier predicts
be exactly equal to the inflation rate
stop depending on reserves
easy.commonError: thinking the simple multiplier always predicts the exact real-world result
easy.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves instead of lending them, deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier suggests.

easy.q: Why might a Fed policy action fail to increase the money supply as much as expected?
options: Banks may not lend all available excess reserves.
The Fed cannot buy government bonds.
Fiat money must have intrinsic value.
The price level is always fixed.
easy.commonError: assuming central bank policy mechanically creates lending one-for-one
easy.feedback: Fed actions influence the money supply, but the final effect depends partly on bank lending decisions.

easy.q: Interest on reserves can affect monetary control because it changes banks' incentive to
options: hold reserves instead of lending them
calculate real GDP
set tax rates
issue commodity money
easy.commonError: thinking interest on reserves has nothing to do with bank lending
easy.feedback: Paying interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend them, affecting money creation.

easy.q: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate adjusts to balance:
options: Money supply and money demand
Taxes and spending
Imports and exports
Inflation and unemployment
easy.commonError: Confusing money-market equilibrium with fiscal balance.
easy.feedback: Liquidity preference theory says the interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

easy.q: Liquidity preference theory says the interest rate adjusts to balance
options: money supply and money demand
aggregate supply and aggregate demand
tax revenue and government spending
exports and imports
easy.commonError: confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
easy.feedback: Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the price that balances money supply and money demand.

easy.q: In liquidity preference theory, the money supply is assumed to be fixed by
options: the central bank
household income
the price level alone
consumer confidence
easy.commonError: thinking money supply slopes downward like money demand
easy.feedback: In this model, the central bank fixes the money supply.

easy.q: When the interest rate rises, the opportunity cost of holding money
options: rises
falls
disappears
becomes the price level
easy.commonError: forgetting that bonds pay more when interest rates rise
easy.feedback: A higher interest rate raises the opportunity cost of holding money instead of bonds.

easy.q: When the interest rate rises, money demand tends to
options: fall
rise
become vertical
equal government spending
easy.commonError: thinking higher interest rates increase money demand
easy.feedback: Higher interest rates make holding money more costly, so money demand falls.

easy.q: When real income rises, money demand tends to
options: rise
fall
stay fixed by the Fed
turn into money supply
easy.commonError: thinking higher income reduces transaction demand for money
easy.feedback: Higher income means people buy more goods and services, so they demand more money for transactions.

easy.q: When the price level rises, money demand tends to
options: rise
fall
stay unchanged because prices do not matter
become equal to investment
easy.commonError: thinking a higher price level reduces the dollars needed for purchases
easy.feedback: A higher price level means people need more dollars to buy the same goods, so money demand rises.

easy.q: At point A in the money market, what is the equilibrium nominal interest rate?
options: 6 percent
4 percent
8 percent
12 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: Point A is where MD0 intersects MS0, at a nominal interest rate of 6 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Money market with downward-sloping money demand MD0 and vertical money supply MS0 intersecting at point A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Money demand MD0 slopes downward from an interest rate of 12 at quantity 0 to 0 at quantity 200. Money supply MS0 is vertical at quantity 100. The curves intersect at point A, quantity of money 100 and nominal interest rate 6.

easy.q: The money-supply curve moves from MS0 at 100 to MS1 at 125. What happens to the equilibrium nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
It stays at 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: With money demand fixed, the larger money supply moves equilibrium down MD0 from 4 percent to 2 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 125; its MD0 intersection is at rate 2. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 2.

easy.q: When the money-supply line moves left from 100 to 75, how does the equilibrium interest rate respond?
options: It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
It stays at 4 percent
It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: With money demand fixed, the smaller money supply moves equilibrium up MD0 from 4 percent to 6 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 75; its MD0 intersection is at rate 6. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 6.

easy.q: Which labeled point is the original equilibrium where MD0 intersects MS0?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
Point D
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: The original curves MD0 and MS0 intersect at point B, quantity 75 and interest rate 3.
easy.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with two vertical MS lines, two downward MD lines and labeled points A, B, C and D.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money; the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Solid MS0 is vertical at 75 and dashed MS1 at 100. Solid MD0 is the lower straight downward line, through B (75,3) and D (100,1). Dashed MD1 is the upper parallel line, through A (75,6) and C (100,4). MD1 crosses the vertical axis at 12 and the horizontal axis at 150. MD0 crosses the vertical axis at 9. All four points are marked with black dots.

easy.q: In the left panel, money demand rises from MD0 to MD1 while MS0 stays fixed. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2 percent
It stays at 2 percent
It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: With fixed money supply, the higher money-demand curve raises the equilibrium interest rate from point A to point B.
easy.imageAlt: Two panels with MS0, MD0 and MD1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
easy.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. MS0 is vertical at 75. Solid downward MD0 passes through A (75,2); upper dashed MD1 passes through B (75,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 and SRAS meet at A (150,55); AD1 and SRAS meet at B (105,45). Dashed guides identify the point coordinates.

easy.q: If the Fed increases the money supply, the interest rate usually:
options: Rises
Falls
Becomes the price level
Equals unemployment
easy.commonError: Reversing expansionary monetary policy.
easy.feedback: Increasing the money supply lowers the interest rate in the liquidity-preference model.

easy.q: If the Fed decreases the money supply, aggregate demand usually:
options: Shifts right
Shifts left
