Becomes vertical
Turns into SRAS
easy.commonError: Reversing contractionary monetary policy.
easy.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates, reduces investment, and shifts AD left.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from MS1 to MS2 causes the interest rate to:
options: Rise from r1 to r2
Fall from r2 to r1
Stay at r1
Become the price level
easy.commonError: Reversing money supply shifts and interest rates.
easy.feedback: MS2 is left of MS1, so the money supply falls and the interest rate rises from r1 to r2.
easy.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
easy.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. The move from AD1 to AD2 shows aggregate demand:
options: Shifting right
Shifting left
Becoming SRAS
Becoming LRAS
easy.commonError: Reversing AD shifts.
easy.feedback: AD2 is to the left of AD1, so aggregate demand decreases.
easy.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
easy.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

easy.q: If the Fed increases the money supply in the short run, interest rates tend to
options: fall
rise
stay fixed by Congress
become equal to inflation automatically
easy.commonError: thinking more money raises interest rates in the liquidity preference model
easy.feedback: An increase in money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate in the liquidity preference model.

easy.q: If the Fed decreases the money supply in the short run, interest rates tend to
options: rise
fall
turn negative automatically
stop affecting investment
easy.commonError: thinking less money lowers interest rates
easy.feedback: A decrease in money supply raises the equilibrium interest rate.

easy.q: Lower interest rates tend to make investment spending
options: increase
decrease
stay unchanged by definition
equal money demand
easy.commonError: thinking lower borrowing costs reduce investment
easy.feedback: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, so investment spending tends to increase.

easy.q: Higher interest rates tend to make investment spending
options: decrease
increase
equal consumption
shift money supply right
easy.commonError: thinking higher borrowing costs increase investment
easy.feedback: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so investment spending tends to decrease.

easy.q: Expansionary monetary policy usually shifts aggregate demand
options: right
left
nowhere because AD cannot shift
down along the same curve only
easy.commonError: confusing a shift in AD with a movement along AD
easy.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

easy.q: Contractionary monetary policy usually shifts aggregate demand
options: left
right
up along short-run aggregate supply
only through the labor market
easy.commonError: thinking tighter money increases aggregate demand
easy.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy raises interest rates, reduces investment, and shifts AD left.

easy.q: A liquidity trap occurs when monetary policy may lose power because nominal interest rates are near
options: zero
100 percent
the reserve ratio
the unemployment rate
easy.commonError: thinking liquidity traps happen when inflation is high by itself
easy.feedback: A liquidity trap occurs when interest rates are near zero, limiting the central bank's ability to lower them further.

easy.q: The left panel shows money supply increasing from MS0 to MS1. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
It stays at 6 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 2 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: The increase in money supply moves the money-market equilibrium from A at 6 percent to B at 4 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
easy.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (100,6) and dashed MS1 at B (150,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and upper dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (100,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (125,56.25). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

easy.q: In the contractionary two-panel diagram, what happens to the nominal interest rate after the money-supply change?
options: It rises from 2.75 percent to 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2.75 percent
It stays at 2.75 percent
It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: The smaller money supply moves equilibrium from A at 2.75 percent to B at 4 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
easy.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (125,2.75) and dashed MS1 at B (100,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (125,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (100,45). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

easy.q: In the quantity equation MV = PY, what does PY represent?
options: Real GDP
Nominal GDP
Money demand
Bank reserves
easy.commonError: Confusing nominal GDP with real GDP.
easy.feedback: P times Y is nominal GDP.

easy.q: If the money supply rises while velocity and output are unchanged, the quantity theory predicts that:
options: Real output doubles
The price level rises
Velocity becomes zero
The price level falls
easy.commonError: Thinking money growth must raise real output in the long run.
easy.feedback: With velocity and output fixed, more money means a higher price level.

easy.q: If the price level rises, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises
It stays fixed
It falls
It becomes real GDP
easy.commonError: Thinking a higher price level means money is more valuable.
easy.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so a higher price level lowers the value of money.

easy.q: The value of money is measured as
options: 1 divided by the price level
the price level divided by real GDP
nominal GDP divided by velocity
money supply times output
easy.commonError: thinking the value of money equals the price level
easy.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it moves in the opposite direction of the price level.

easy.q: If the price level rises, the value of money
options: falls
rises
stays constant
becomes equal to velocity
easy.commonError: thinking the price level and value of money rise together
easy.feedback: When the price level rises, each dollar buys fewer goods, so the value of money falls.

easy.q: If the price level falls, the value of money
options: rises
falls
becomes zero
equals nominal GDP
easy.commonError: forgetting that 1/P rises when P falls
easy.feedback: A lower price level means each dollar buys more goods, so the value of money rises.

easy.q: According to the quantity theory of money, persistent growth in the money supply leads mainly to
options: inflation
higher real output forever
lower nominal wages
a permanent fall in the price level
easy.commonError: thinking money growth permanently raises real output
easy.feedback: The quantity theory connects persistent money growth to inflation, especially in the long run.

easy.q: The quantity equation is
options: M x V = P x Y
M + V = P + Y
P / Y = M / V
Y = M - P
easy.commonError: mixing up multiplication and addition in the quantity equation
easy.feedback: The quantity equation is M x V = P x Y.

easy.q: In the quantity equation, P x Y equals
options: nominal GDP
real GDP
velocity
the real interest rate
easy.commonError: confusing nominal GDP with real GDP alone
easy.feedback: P x Y is the price level times real output, which equals nominal GDP.

easy.q: If M = 500, V = 2, and Y = 1,000, then P equals
easy.commonError: multiplying by output instead of dividing by output
easy.feedback: Using M x V = P x Y gives 500 x 2 = P x 1,000, so P = 1.

easy.q: Which variable is nominal?
options: Real GDP
Nominal wage
Relative price
Quantity of labor
easy.commonError: Confusing money-measured variables with real variables.
easy.feedback: A nominal wage is measured in dollars.

easy.q: Which variable is real?
options: Nominal GDP
Dollar wage
Relative price
Price level
easy.commonError: Treating all prices as nominal variables.
easy.feedback: A relative price compares one good to another, so it is a real variable.

easy.q: Monetary neutrality says that in the long run, a change in the money supply affects:
options: Nominal variables, not real variables
Real output only
The natural rate only
Technology only
easy.commonError: Thinking money changes real variables permanently in the long run.
easy.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables in the long run, not real output or employment.

easy.q: A nominal variable is measured in
options: monetary units
physical units
hours only
percent changes only
easy.commonError: confusing nominal with real
easy.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in monetary units, such as dollars.

easy.q: A real variable is measured in
options: physical units or purchasing power
only current dollars
only bank deposits
only government bonds
easy.commonError: thinking all economic variables are nominal
easy.feedback: Real variables are measured in physical units or purchasing power, not just dollars.

easy.q: Which of the following is a nominal variable?
options: Nominal wage in dollars per hour
Real wage in goods per hour
Real GDP in units of output
Relative price of apples in terms of oranges
easy.commonError: mistaking real purchasing power for a dollar amount
easy.feedback: A nominal wage is measured in dollars per hour, so it is a nominal variable.

easy.q: Which of the following is a real variable?
options: Real GDP
Nominal GDP
Nominal wage
The price level
easy.commonError: thinking GDP is always nominal
easy.feedback: Real GDP measures output adjusted for prices, so it is a real variable.

easy.q: The classical dichotomy separates variables into
options: nominal and real variables
supply and demand variables
public and private variables
short-run and long-run bonds
easy.commonError: thinking the dichotomy separates fiscal and monetary policy
easy.feedback: The classical dichotomy separates nominal variables from real variables.

easy.q: Monetary neutrality means changes in the money supply do not affect
options: real variables in the long run
nominal prices in the long run
the price level
the inflation rate
easy.commonError: thinking money neutrality means money has no effect on prices
easy.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

easy.q: Over the long run, all dollar wages and prices are twice as high while output per worker and hours worked are unchanged. Which interpretation best fits monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed, but the listed real variables did not.
Real variables doubled because every dollar price doubled.
Output per worker must have doubled because wages doubled.
The price level is a real variable, so nothing nominal changed.
easy.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
easy.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

easy.q: If expected inflation rises and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should:
options: Fall
Rise
Become zero
Equal real GDP
easy.commonError: Reversing the Fisher effect.
easy.feedback: Nominal interest rates include expected inflation, so they rise when expected inflation rises.

easy.q: The Fisher effect says that when expected inflation rises, the nominal interest rate tends to
options: rise
fall
stay fixed forever
become equal to real GDP growth
easy.commonError: thinking inflation lowers nominal interest rates
easy.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

easy.q: The Fisher equation is most commonly written as
options: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation
real interest rate = nominal interest rate + expected inflation
expected inflation = real GDP + money supply
nominal interest rate = velocity divided by output
easy.commonError: adding inflation to the wrong side of the equation
easy.feedback: The Fisher equation links nominal rates, real rates, and expected inflation: nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation.

easy.q: If expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should
options: rise by about 3 percentage points
fall by about 3 percentage points
stay exactly the same
fall to zero
easy.commonError: thinking nominal rates ignore expected inflation
easy.feedback: If the real rate is unchanged, a 3-point rise in expected inflation raises the nominal rate by about 3 points.

easy.q: Under the Fisher effect, a country with persistently higher inflation will tend to have
options: higher nominal interest rates
lower nominal interest rates
no nominal interest rates
unchanged price levels forever
easy.commonError: thinking high inflation means low nominal rates
easy.feedback: Higher expected inflation tends to be built into higher nominal interest rates.

easy.q: Lenders begin expecting inflation to be 4 percentage points higher, while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Nominal interest rates tend to rise by about 4 percentage points.
Nominal interest rates tend to fall by about 4 percentage points.
Real interest rates must rise by exactly 4 percentage points.
Actual inflation must immediately equal the new nominal interest rate.
easy.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
easy.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

easy.q: A bank sets a fixed nominal loan rate today for next year. Which inflation concept is most relevant to the Fisher effect when that rate is chosen?
options: Only inflation that has already occurred.
The current unemployment rate by itself.
Only the realized inflation rate known after repayment.
Expected inflation over the loan period.
easy.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
easy.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

easy.q: If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 2 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
1 percent
2 percent
6 percent
easy.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
easy.feedback: The nominal interest rate is approximately the real interest rate plus expected inflation: 3 + 2 = 5 percent.

easy.q: If the nominal interest rate is 7 percent and expected inflation is 3 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 4 percent
10 percent
3 percent
21 percent
easy.commonError: adding expected inflation when solving for the real interest rate
easy.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal interest rate minus expected inflation: 7 - 3 = 4 percent.

easy.q: Shoeleather costs of inflation come from:
options: Changing menus often
Holding less cash and making more transactions
Higher unemployment benefits
Falling expected prices
easy.commonError: Confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs.
easy.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from efforts to reduce money holdings when inflation is high.

easy.q: Menu costs of inflation refer to the cost of:
options: Printing more money
Changing posted prices
Measuring real GDP
Buying bonds
easy.commonError: Confusing menu costs with restaurant spending.
easy.feedback: Menu costs are the costs firms face when changing listed prices.

easy.q: Shoe-leather costs of inflation come from people
options: trying to reduce money holdings when inflation is high
wearing out shoes because factories produce less
paying higher menu prices at restaurants
borrowing less because taxes are lower
easy.commonError: taking shoe-leather costs literally
easy.feedback: Shoe-leather costs refer to the time and effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high.

easy.q: Menu costs of inflation are the costs of
options: changing listed prices
buying more food at restaurants
holding too many government bonds
printing money at the central bank
easy.commonError: thinking menu costs only apply to restaurants
easy.feedback: Menu costs are the costs firms face when they change posted prices.

easy.q: Unexpected inflation tends to help
options: debtors
creditors
people holding only cash
workers with fixed nominal wages and no adjustment
easy.commonError: thinking lenders always benefit from inflation
easy.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps debtors because they repay loans with dollars that are worth less than expected.

easy.q: Unexpected inflation tends to hurt
options: creditors
debtors
borrowers with fixed-rate loans
people whose debts are repaid with cheaper dollars
easy.commonError: forgetting that creditors are repaid in money with lower value
easy.feedback: Unexpected inflation hurts creditors because the dollars they are repaid have less purchasing power than expected.

easy.q: When a government finances spending by printing money, it is using
options: an inflation tax
a real wage subsidy
a reserve requirement
a bond-rating rule
easy.commonError: thinking inflation tax requires an explicit tax bill
easy.feedback: Printing money to finance spending creates an inflation tax because it reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.

easy.q: An inflation tax reduces the value of
options: money held by the public
only physical capital
only imported goods
real GDP by definition
easy.commonError: thinking inflation tax only affects people who owe taxes
easy.feedback: An inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money balances held by the public.

easy.q: Hyperinflation is usually associated with
options: very rapid growth in the money supply
a fixed money supply forever
falling prices every year
a permanent drop in nominal wages only
easy.commonError: thinking hyperinflation happens without excessive money creation
easy.feedback: Hyperinflation is usually tied to extremely rapid money growth, often when governments print money to finance spending.

easy.q: Deflation means the economy is experiencing
options: a falling overall price level
a rising overall price level
zero interest rates only
a larger money multiplier only
easy.commonError: confusing deflation with disinflation
easy.feedback: Deflation means the overall price level is falling.

easy.q: A major danger of heavy reliance on printing money to finance government spending is
options: high inflation or hyperinflation
a guaranteed rise in real output
a permanent fall in nominal prices
the end of money demand
easy.commonError: thinking printing money creates real resources without inflation costs
easy.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but heavy reliance on it can produce high inflation or hyperinflation.

easy.q: A government creates money to finance purchases, the price level rises, and households’ existing cash buys less. What burden is illustrated?
options: The real purchasing power of money balances is being eroded by the inflation tax.
A statutory income-tax rate automatically rose on every household.
Deflation increased the real value of cash balances.
The natural rate of unemployment fell permanently because the government created more money and raised the overall price level.
easy.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
easy.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

medium.q: A student says credit card balances should be counted in M1 because people use cards to buy goods. What is the best correction?
options: Credit cards are borrowing, not money balances
Credit cards are currency held by the public
Credit cards are checkable deposits
Credit cards are savings deposits
medium.commonError: Counting credit cards as money.
medium.feedback: Credit cards allow borrowing. They are not money balances like currency or checkable deposits.

medium.q: A household keeps cash because it wants to make purchases quickly, compare prices, and save some value for later. Which answer matches all three functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, fiat money
Unit of account, leverage, discount rate
Medium of exchange, multiplier, bank capital
medium.commonError: Mixing money functions with banking tools.
medium.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and can transfer purchasing power into the future.

medium.q: A student says, 'Money is valuable because the dollar bill itself has valuable paper.' What is the best correction?
options: Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
Fiat money has value because its paper is worth more than its face value.
Commodity money and fiat money are the same thing.
Money only has value if it can be exchanged for gold.
medium.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
medium.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. Its value comes from general acceptance and government backing.

medium.q: A grocery store lists apples at $2 per pound. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Fractional reserve
medium.commonError: choosing medium of exchange whenever prices involve money
medium.feedback: The price tag uses money to measure value, so money is acting as a unit of account.

medium.q: A person keeps $500 in cash for emergencies. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Store of value
Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
medium.commonError: thinking money only matters when it is spent immediately
medium.feedback: The cash is preserving purchasing power for later, so it is serving as a store of value.

medium.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item would be counted in M2 but not in M1?
options: A savings deposit
Currency in your wallet
A checking account deposit
A traveler's check
medium.commonError: putting all liquid assets into M1
medium.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies. They belong in M2, not M1.

medium.q: Why does money make specialization easier?
options: It removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
It makes all goods cost the same amount.
It prevents prices from changing.
It eliminates scarcity.
medium.commonError: thinking money eliminates scarcity rather than reducing transaction costs
medium.feedback: Money reduces transaction costs because people no longer need to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.

medium.q: Which statement best explains why currency held by a bank does not count the same way as currency held by the public?
options: Currency held by banks is part of bank reserves, not currency circulating among the public.
Currency held by banks is automatically counted twice in M1.
Currency held by banks is commodity money.
Currency held by banks is never money.
medium.commonError: double-counting currency held inside banks
medium.feedback: Currency held by banks is treated as reserves. Currency in the money supply refers to currency held by the public.

medium.q: Currency held by the public is $800 billion and checkable deposits are $1,200 billion. Assume these are the only M1 components with nonzero balances. What is M1?
options: $2,000 billion
$1,200 billion
$800 billion
$400 billion
medium.commonError: leaving out either currency or checkable deposits
medium.feedback: M1 includes currency plus checkable deposits: $800 billion + $1,200 billion = $2,000 billion.

medium.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $2,000 billion, savings deposits are $900 billion, small time deposits are $300 billion, and retail money market mutual funds are $200 billion. M2 is
options: $3,400 billion
$2,000 billion
$1,400 billion
$2,300 billion
medium.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
medium.feedback: M2 equals M1 plus near monies: $2,000 + $900 + $300 + $200 = $3,400 billion.

medium.q: Which statement best describes the FOMC's role?
options: It guides monetary policy and open-market operations.
It sets federal income tax brackets.
It calculates the CPI.
It decides how much Congress spends.
medium.commonError: confusing the FOMC with fiscal policymakers
medium.feedback: The FOMC is central to monetary policy, especially open-market operations.

medium.q: The Fed is called a lender of last resort because it can
options: lend to banks facing liquidity problems
lend directly to every household for groceries
write spending bills for Congress
set all market prices
medium.commonError: thinking lender of last resort means normal consumer lending
medium.feedback: The Fed can lend to banks when they face liquidity stress, which is why it is called a lender of last resort.

medium.q: Why does central bank independence matter?
options: It can help monetary policy avoid short-run political pressure.
It lets the Fed collect income taxes.
It prevents banks from holding reserves.
It means the Fed is owned by Congress.
medium.commonError: thinking independence means no public role or accountability
medium.feedback: Central bank independence can help keep monetary policy from being driven by short-run political incentives.

medium.q: Which distinction between the Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury is correct?
options: The Treasury sets the federal funds rate, while the Fed writes tax laws.
The Fed passes the federal budget, while the Treasury regulates inflation expectations.
The Fed conducts monetary policy, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
Both institutions perform exactly the same functions.
medium.commonError: Treating the central bank and fiscal authority as the same institution.
medium.feedback: The Fed is the monetary authority; the Treasury is part of the executive branch and manages federal finances.

medium.q: A commercial bank approves a loan and credits the borrower’s checking account. In a separate transaction, the Federal Reserve credits a bank’s reserve account during an asset purchase. Which distinction is correct?
options: The commercial bank creates a deposit liability; the Fed creates central-bank reserves
The Fed creates the borrower’s commercial-bank deposit, while the bank creates central-bank reserves
Both transactions create only physical currency held by the public
Neither transaction changes any bank liability or reserve balance
medium.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
medium.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

medium.q: A headline says, “The Treasury raised the federal funds rate to conduct monetary policy.” What is the best correction?
options: The statement is correct because the Treasury and Federal Reserve are the same institution
The federal funds rate is set by commercial banks with no connection to Federal Reserve policy
The Treasury sets monetary policy while the Federal Reserve determines tax rates and federal spending
Monetary policy and the federal funds rate are associated with the Federal Reserve, while the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations
medium.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
medium.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

medium.q: A bank has $300,000 in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $50,000 in actual reserves. Excess reserves are:
medium.commonError: Forgetting to subtract required reserves from actual reserves.
medium.feedback: Required reserves are $36,000, leaving $14,000 in excess reserves.

medium.q: A new $2,000 deposit enters a bank with a 20 percent reserve requirement. The bank’s maximum first-round loan is:
medium.commonError: Using required reserves as lending or applying the multiplier to the first round.
medium.feedback: The bank keeps $400 and may lend $1,600.

medium.q: A bank reports $14 million in assets and $12.9 million in liabilities. What is its capital cushion?
options: $26.9 million.
$1.1 million.
$14 million.
$12.9 million.
medium.commonError: Adding assets and liabilities or using liabilities alone.
medium.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $1.1 million.

medium.q: A bank receives $2,000 in new deposits and faces a 10 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, its first new loan can be:
medium.commonError: Lending required reserves.
medium.feedback: Required reserves are $200, so excess reserves are $1,800.

medium.q: A bank has $50,000 in deposits and must hold 8 percent in reserves. Required reserves equal:
medium.commonError: Dividing deposits by the reserve requirement.
medium.feedback: Required reserves are $50,000 x 0.08 = $4,000.

medium.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Required reserves equal
medium.commonError: using 10 instead of 0.10
medium.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve ratio: $500,000 x 0.10 = $50,000.

medium.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits, $80,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Excess reserves equal
medium.commonError: treating all reserves as excess reserves
medium.feedback: Required reserves are $50,000, so excess reserves are $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000.

medium.q: A bank receives a new $2,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 25 percent. How much can the bank initially lend?
medium.commonError: lending the entire deposit despite reserve requirements
medium.feedback: Required reserves are 0.25 x $2,000 = $500, so the bank can initially lend $1,500.

medium.q: The simple money multiplier is 5. The implied reserve ratio is:
options: 50 percent.
25 percent.
20 percent.
5 percent.
medium.commonError: Using the multiplier itself as the reserve percentage.
medium.feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/5, or 20 percent.

medium.q: A bank receives a new deposit and holds all of it as excess reserves instead of lending. Compared with the simple multiplier prediction:
options: Deposit expansion will be larger.
The reserve requirement becomes zero.
Deposit expansion will be smaller.
Deposit expansion must equal the full multiplier.
medium.commonError: Assuming banks always lend all excess reserves.
medium.feedback: The simple multiplier is a maximum that depends on lending and redepositing.

medium.q: A borrower spends a newly created bank loan, and the recipient deposits the payment at another bank. This process:
options: Eliminates the original loan under the stated conditions.
Creates a new deposit that can support another round of lending.
Prevents any further money creation as the relevant economic conclusion.
Turns the loan into bank capital.
medium.commonError: Failing to connect lending, spending, and redepositing.
medium.feedback: Loan proceeds commonly become deposits elsewhere, allowing additional lending.

medium.q: If the reserve requirement falls from 20 percent to 10 percent, the simple money multiplier:
options: Falls from 10 to 5
Rises from 5 to 10
Stays fixed at 20
Falls from 20 to 10
medium.commonError: Thinking a lower reserve requirement lowers the multiplier.
medium.feedback: The multiplier is 1/rr. It rises from 5 to 10 when the reserve requirement falls from 0.20 to 0.10.

medium.q: If the reserve ratio is 12.5 percent, the simple money multiplier is
medium.commonError: using the reserve ratio itself as the multiplier
medium.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1 / 0.125 = 8.

medium.q: If the money multiplier is 5 and the Fed injects $20 million of reserves, the maximum possible increase in the money supply is
options: $100 million
$20 million
$25 million
$4 million
medium.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
medium.feedback: The maximum increase equals multiplier times reserves: 5 x $20 million = $100 million.

medium.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply through open-market operations, it should:
options: Buy bonds from banks
Sell bonds to the public
Lower reserve requirements
Lower the discount rate
medium.commonError: Reversing open-market purchases and sales.
medium.feedback: Selling bonds pulls reserves out of the banking system and reduces the money supply.

medium.q: Which sequence correctly describes an open-market purchase?
options: Fed buys bonds, reserves rise, money supply can expand
Fed sells bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Fed buys bonds, reserves fall, money supply contracts
Fed sells bonds, reserves fall, money demand vanishes
medium.commonError: Breaking the reserves-to-money-supply chain.
medium.feedback: A Fed bond purchase adds reserves and can support money supply expansion.

medium.q: A higher interest rate paid on reserves most directly encourages banks to:
options: Hold more reserves
Hold fewer reserves
Ignore the Fed
Create commodity money
medium.commonError: Thinking interest on reserves always increases lending.
medium.feedback: Paying more on reserves makes holding reserves more attractive to banks.

medium.q: The Fed wants to increase the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Buy government bonds from the public.
Sell government bonds to the public.
Raise taxes on households.
Reduce government purchases.
medium.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases remove money from circulation
medium.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it pays money into the economy, increasing the money supply.

medium.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Sell government bonds to the public.
Buy government bonds from the public.
Cut the discount rate.
Lower reserve requirements.
medium.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales inject money
medium.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, the public pays money to the Fed, reducing the money supply.

medium.q: If the Fed lowers the discount rate, which effect is most likely?
options: Banks find it cheaper to borrow from the Fed.
Banks are required to hold more reserves.
The money supply must fall.
Currency becomes commodity money.
medium.commonError: thinking a lower discount rate discourages borrowing
medium.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper for banks.

medium.q: If the Fed raises reserve requirements, the banking system's ability to create money usually
options: decreases
increases
becomes unlimited
does not depend on deposits anymore
medium.commonError: thinking higher required reserves create more lending
medium.feedback: Higher reserve requirements force banks to hold more reserves and lend less, reducing money creation.

medium.q: If the Fed pays a higher interest rate on reserves, banks may respond by
options: holding more reserves and lending less
holding fewer reserves and lending more
creating commodity money
eliminating demand deposits
medium.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending
medium.feedback: Higher interest on reserves can make banks more willing to hold reserves instead of lending.

medium.q: If banks decide to hold more excess reserves, the money creation process becomes:
options: Stronger because lending rises
Weaker because lending falls
Unchanged because reserves do not matter
Infinite because deposits disappear
medium.commonError: Ignoring bank behavior in monetary control.
medium.feedback: When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.

medium.q: Why is the simple money multiplier only a rough prediction in the real world?
options: Banks may hold excess reserves and people may hold currency.
The Fed cannot affect reserves in any way.
Deposits are not part of the money supply.
Banks always lend exactly zero.
medium.commonError: thinking the simple multiplier always predicts the exact result
medium.feedback: The simple multiplier assumes banks lend all excess reserves and the public holds no currency; excess reserves and currency holdings make actual money creation smaller.

medium.q: If households decide to hold more currency and fewer bank deposits, banks will have
options: fewer deposits available to support loans
more deposits available to support loans
no reserve requirement
a larger required reserve ratio automatically
medium.commonError: thinking currency holdings do not affect bank lending
medium.feedback: When people hold more currency, fewer funds sit in deposits, which limits bank lending and money creation.

medium.q: A bank holds excess reserves during a financial panic. What happens to deposit creation compared with the simple multiplier prediction?
options: Deposit creation is weaker.
Deposit creation is stronger.
Deposit creation is exactly unchanged.
Deposit creation becomes unrelated to reserves.
medium.commonError: ignoring bank behavior in money creation
medium.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

medium.q: Which situation makes the Fed's control over the money supply less precise?
options: Banks change how much they want to lend.
The Fed exists as a central bank.
Money has three functions.
Prices are quoted in dollars.
medium.commonError: thinking central bank control is mechanically perfect
medium.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but bank lending decisions affect the final amount of money created.

medium.q: The central bank supplies ample reserves and banks are willing to lend, but households and firms become reluctant to borrow. What happens to deposit creation relative to the simple multiplier maximum?
options: Weak loan demand can keep deposit creation below the simple-multiplier maximum
It must equal the maximum because reserve supply alone determines every loan
It must exceed the maximum because unborrowed reserves count twice
It becomes fiscal policy because borrowers are not requesting loans
medium.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
medium.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

medium.q: A bank has assets of $1,000,000 and capital of $80,000. If assets fall by $40,000, bank capital becomes:
medium.commonError: Thinking losses reduce liabilities first.
medium.feedback: Losses reduce bank capital. $80,000 - $40,000 = $40,000.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD1 unchanged, money supply increases from MS1 to MS2. Which equilibrium movement follows?
options: g to e
e to g
a to d
c to f
medium.commonError: Using the wrong money demand curve.
medium.feedback: MD1 intersects MS1 at e and MS2 at g. Increasing supply moves equilibrium from e to g and lowers the nominal interest rate.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market graph. If money demand shifts from MD1 to MD2 while money supply remains MS1, equilibrium moves from:
options: e to a
a to e
g to d
f to c
medium.commonError: Confusing money demand shifts with money supply shifts.
medium.feedback: At MS1, MD1 intersects at e and MD2 intersects at a, so the interest rate rises.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market graph. Which point shows MS2 and MD2 in equilibrium?
options: a
b
d
g
medium.commonError: Reading a non-intersection point as equilibrium.
medium.feedback: MS2 and MD2 intersect at point d.

medium.q: If real income rises, money demand increases. In the liquidity preference model, this tends to:
options: Raise the interest rate
Lower the interest rate
Reduce money supply automatically
Shift AD left directly
medium.commonError: Thinking more money demand lowers interest rates.
medium.feedback: Higher money demand pushes the interest rate up when money supply is fixed.

medium.q: Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the variable that balances
options: money supply and money demand
labor supply and labor demand
exports and imports
taxes and spending
medium.commonError: confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
medium.feedback: The interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

medium.q: Which curve shows the amount of money fixed by the central bank?
options: The vertical money supply curve
The downward-sloping money demand curve
The aggregate demand curve
The multiplier curve
medium.commonError: thinking money demand is fixed by the central bank
medium.feedback: The central bank fixes the money supply in this model, so money supply is vertical.

medium.q: Which curve slopes downward because higher interest rates reduce the quantity of money demanded?
options: Money demand
Money supply
Aggregate demand
Long-run aggregate supply
medium.commonError: thinking money supply slopes downward
medium.feedback: Money demand slopes downward because higher interest rates raise the opportunity cost of holding money.

medium.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, the equilibrium interest rate should
options: rise
fall
stay unchanged
become the price level
medium.commonError: thinking higher money demand lowers the interest rate
medium.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes the equilibrium interest rate up.

medium.q: If real income rises, money demand increases because households
options: need more money for transactions
want fewer goods and services
face a lower price level automatically
stop holding liquid assets
medium.commonError: thinking higher income lowers transaction demand for money
medium.feedback: Higher income usually means more buying and selling, so people demand more money for transactions.

medium.q: If the price level rises while output is unchanged, money demand increases because people
options: need more dollars to buy the same goods
need fewer dollars to buy the same goods
earn no income
stop buying bonds forever
medium.commonError: thinking higher prices reduce the dollars needed for transactions
medium.feedback: Higher prices mean people need more money to buy the same amount of goods and services.

medium.q: At point A, what quantity of money clears the market?
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: The vertical money-supply curve MS0 is fixed at quantity 100, and MD0 intersects it at point A.

options: MD0 is downward sloping as the interest rate changes.
Point A lies where the two curves cross in equilibrium.
MS0 is vertical at a fixed money quantity.
The interest rate is measured on the vertical axis.
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: In the standard liquidity-preference model, the central bank fixes the nominal quantity of money, so MS is vertical.

medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: Money supply increases from 100 to 125, a rise of 25 units.

options: An expansionary action that increases the money supply
A contractionary action that decreases the money supply
A rise in real income that shifts money demand right
A higher price level that shifts money demand right
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: The graph shows a rightward shift of the vertical money-supply curve, which is expansionary.

medium.q: Measure the leftward distance from MS0 to MS1. How much smaller is the money supply?
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: Money supply falls from 100 to 75, a decrease of 25 units.

medium.q: Which contractionary central-bank action could produce the displayed money-supply shift?
options: An expansionary action that increases the money supply
A rise in real income that increases money demand
A contractionary action that reduces the money supply
A lower price level that reduces money demand
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: The graph shows a leftward shift of the vertical money-supply curve, which is contractionary.

medium.q: If only money demand increases from MD0 to MD1 while MS0 stays fixed, which point becomes the new equilibrium?
options: Point B
Point C
Point D
Point A
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: Holding MS0 at 75, the higher MD1 curve intersects it at point A, interest rate 6.

options: Point D
Point A
Point B
Point C

medium.feedback: Holding MD0 fixed, the larger MS1 intersects it at point D, quantity 100 and interest rate 1.

options: Aggregate demand shifts right from AD1 to AD0
Aggregate demand shifts left from AD0 to AD1
SRAS shifts left while aggregate demand stays fixed
LRAS shifts right

options: Higher rates directly increase the money supply.
Higher rates increase potential output and LRAS.
Higher rates reduce interest-sensitive spending.
Higher rates lower all production costs and SRAS.
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: The standard link is through interest-sensitive components of spending, especially investment.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market graph. If the Fed moves from MS1 to MS2, the policy is:
options: Expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal policy
A positive supply shock
medium.commonError: Reversing leftward money-supply shifts.
medium.feedback: MS2 is left of MS1, so the money supply falls and interest rates rise.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market and AD graph. The move from MS1 to MS2 leads to:
options: Lower r and higher AD
Higher r and lower AD
Higher r and higher AD
Lower r and lower AD
medium.commonError: Breaking the interest-rate to AD chain.
medium.feedback: A lower money supply raises r, reducing investment and shifting AD left.

medium.q: What is the correct short-run chain from an increase in the money supply to aggregate demand?
options: Money supply rises, interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Money supply rises, interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Money supply rises, taxes rise, consumption falls, AD shifts left.
Money supply rises, reserve requirements rise, AD disappears.
medium.commonError: reversing the interest-rate effect
medium.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

medium.q: What is the correct short-run chain from a decrease in the money supply to aggregate demand?
options: Money supply falls, interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Money supply falls, interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Money supply falls, taxes fall, consumption rises, AD shifts right.
Money supply falls, MPC rises, AD shifts right.
medium.commonError: thinking tighter money lowers interest rates
medium.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy raises interest rates, reduces investment, and shifts AD left.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Which panel represents the money market part of the monetary policy transmission mechanism?
options: The panel with money supply, money demand, and the interest rate
The panel with aggregate demand and output only
The panel with government spending only
The panel with the money multiplier only
medium.commonError: confusing the money market graph with the AD graph
medium.feedback: The money market panel shows money supply, money demand, and the interest rate.

A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

medium.q: In the monetary policy transmission mechanism, a lower interest rate leads most directly to
options: higher investment spending
lower investment spending
lower government spending automatically
a smaller money supply automatically
medium.commonError: thinking lower borrowing costs reduce investment
medium.feedback: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, so investment spending rises.

medium.q: If the Fed increases the money supply, the aggregate demand curve should
options: shift right
shift left
become vertical
turn into money demand
medium.commonError: confusing movement along AD with a shift of AD
medium.feedback: More money lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

medium.q: A liquidity trap limits traditional monetary policy because
options: nominal interest rates cannot be pushed much below zero
money demand is always zero
government spending cannot change
banks cannot hold reserves
medium.commonError: thinking the Fed can always lower nominal rates without limit
medium.feedback: When nominal rates are near zero, the Fed has less room to stimulate spending through further rate cuts.

medium.q: If the economy is weak and the Fed wants to stimulate aggregate demand, which action fits the goal?
options: Increase the money supply to lower interest rates.
Decrease the money supply to raise interest rates.
Raise taxes to reduce consumption.
Lower government spending to reduce AD.
medium.commonError: choosing contractionary money during weak demand
medium.feedback: To stimulate AD, the Fed can increase the money supply, lower interest rates, and encourage investment.

medium.q: If inflation pressure is high because aggregate demand is too strong, which Fed action fits the goal?
options: Decrease the money supply to raise interest rates.
Increase the money supply to lower interest rates.
Buy bonds to increase investment.
Cut interest rates to shift AD right.
medium.commonError: using expansionary monetary policy when AD is already too high
medium.feedback: To cool AD, the Fed can reduce the money supply, raise interest rates, and reduce investment.

medium.q: Which aggregate-demand change accompanies the lower interest rate in the right panel?
options: AD shifts left from AD1 to AD0
SRAS shifts right while AD stays fixed
LRAS shifts left
AD shifts right from AD0 to AD1
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: The lower interest rate stimulates interest-sensitive spending, shifting aggregate demand right.

medium.q: In the expansionary two-panel diagram, how many units does real GDP rise from A to B?
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: Read real GDP at A and B: 125 − 100 = 25 units.

options: AD shifts right from AD1 to AD0
AD shifts left from AD0 to AD1
SRAS shifts left while AD stays fixed
LRAS shifts right
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: The higher interest rate reduces interest-sensitive spending, shifting aggregate demand left.

medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: Read real GDP at A and B: 125 − 100 = 25 units.

medium.q: If velocity is stable and real output is fixed, a one-time doubling of the money supply should eventually:
options: Double the price level
Cut the price level in half
Double real output
Eliminate inflation costs
medium.commonError: Thinking money growth creates long-run real output growth.
medium.feedback: With velocity and output fixed, doubling money doubles the price level.

medium.q: If the value of money falls, what must have happened to the price level?
options: The price level rose.
The price level fell.
The price level stayed fixed.
The price level became real GDP.
medium.commonError: thinking value of money and price level move together
medium.feedback: Value of money and price level move in opposite directions. If the value of money falls, the price level rises.

medium.q: Which curve is fixed by the Fed in the money supply-money demand model?
options: Money supply
Money demand
Aggregate demand
Short-run aggregate supply
medium.commonError: thinking money demand is fixed by the Fed
medium.feedback: In this model, the Fed fixes the money supply, so the money supply curve is vertical.

medium.q: The vertical axis labeled value of money is best understood as
options: 1 divided by the price level
the price level itself only
real GDP divided by money supply
the reserve ratio
medium.commonError: treating the value of money as the same thing as the price level
medium.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, which is why it moves opposite the price level.

medium.q: If money supply increases, the new equilibrium moves toward
options: a lower value of money and a higher price level
a higher value of money and a lower price level
a lower money demand curve only
a higher reserve requirement
medium.commonError: forgetting that value of money falls when price level rises
medium.feedback: An increase in money supply lowers the value of money and raises the price level.

medium.q: If velocity and output are constant, a 10 percent increase in money supply should lead to approximately
options: a 10 percent increase in the price level
a 10 percent decrease in the price level
a 10 percent increase in real output
no change in nominal variables
medium.commonError: thinking money growth raises real output when velocity and output are fixed
medium.feedback: If V and Y are constant, money growth shows up as price-level growth.

medium.q: If central bank money growth continues year after year faster than real output growth, the likely long-run result is
options: ongoing inflation
permanent unemployment below zero
a permanent fall in all nominal wages
no change in prices
medium.commonError: thinking repeated money growth has no price-level consequence
medium.feedback: Persistent money growth faster than output growth is a recipe for inflation.

medium.q: In the quantity equation, if M rises 5 percent, V is constant, and Y rises 2 percent, inflation is approximately:
options: 2 percent
3 percent
5 percent
7 percent
medium.commonError: Ignoring output growth.
medium.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth plus velocity growth minus output growth: 5 + 0 - 2 = 3 percent.

medium.q: If P rises from 2 to 4, the value of money changes from:
options: 2 to 4
4 to 8
medium.commonError: Treating a higher price level as higher money value.
medium.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it falls from 1/2 to 1/4.

medium.q: What happens to the value of money when the price level rises from 2 to 4?
options: It falls from 1/2 to 1/4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays at 1/2.
It doubles from 2 to 4.
medium.commonError: forgetting that value of money equals 1 divided by price level
medium.feedback: The value of money is 1/P. When P rises from 2 to 4, value falls from 1/2 to 1/4.

medium.q: Using the quantity equation, if M = 400, V = 5, and Y = 1,000, then P equals
medium.commonError: dividing by velocity instead of output
medium.feedback: M x V = P x Y, so 400 x 5 = P x 1,000. P = 2.

medium.q: If nominal GDP is $20,000 and the money supply is $5,000, velocity equals
medium.commonError: multiplying nominal GDP by money supply
medium.feedback: Velocity equals nominal GDP divided by money supply: $20,000 / $5,000 = 4.

medium.q: If all nominal prices and wages double while relative prices stay unchanged, this illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
A supply shock
A liquidity trap
medium.commonError: Missing the real versus nominal distinction.
medium.feedback: Monetary neutrality says nominal variables can change while real variables remain unchanged in the long run.

medium.q: If all nominal prices double but relative prices stay the same, this illustrates
options: monetary neutrality
crowding out
the multiplier effect
liquidity preference
medium.commonError: thinking changes in nominal prices automatically change relative prices
medium.feedback: Monetary neutrality says money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

medium.q: Which statement is consistent with the classical dichotomy?
options: Money growth can affect nominal wages without changing real wages in the long run.
Money growth changes only real variables and never nominal variables.
Nominal and real variables are always identical.
The price level is a real variable.
medium.commonError: thinking nominal and real variables move identically
medium.feedback: Under the classical dichotomy, money affects nominal variables, while real variables are determined by real factors in the long run.

medium.q: A nominal wage rises from $15 to $30 while the price level doubles. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays the same.
It doubles.
It falls by half.
It becomes zero.
medium.commonError: thinking a higher nominal wage always means a higher real wage
medium.feedback: If nominal wages and the price level both double, the real wage is unchanged.

medium.q: After a sustained monetary expansion, the long-run price level is higher and nominal wages are higher by roughly the same proportion. What happens to the real wage if productivity is unchanged?
options: It can return to about its previous level because both the wage and price level rose together.
It must rise in the same proportion as the nominal wage because a larger dollar wage always guarantees more purchasing power.
It must fall to zero because money growth raises prices.
It becomes equal to the money-supply growth rate.
medium.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
medium.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

medium.q: A worker earns $20 per hour, and the price level is 5. The real wage is
options: 4 units of output per hour
$25 per hour
100 units of output per hour
0.25 units of output per hour
medium.commonError: multiplying wage by price level instead of dividing
medium.feedback: Real wage equals nominal wage divided by price level: 20 / 5 = 4 units of output per hour.

medium.q: If the price of pizza rises from $10 to $20 and the price of soda rises from $2 to $4, the relative price of pizza in terms of soda
options: is unchanged
doubles
falls by half
becomes zero
medium.commonError: thinking nominal price increases always change relative prices
medium.feedback: Pizza was 5 sodas before and 5 sodas after. The relative price is unchanged.

medium.q: If expected inflation rises while the real interest rate is unchanged, lenders will require
options: a higher nominal interest rate
a lower nominal interest rate
no repayment
a lower price level
medium.commonError: thinking lenders ignore expected inflation
medium.feedback: Lenders care about purchasing power, so higher expected inflation is built into higher nominal interest rates.

medium.q: Two otherwise similar economies have the same long-run real interest rate, but expected inflation is 2 percent in one and 7 percent in the other. What should differ under the Fisher effect?
options: The second economy should tend to have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher.
The first economy should have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher instead because lower expected inflation raises nominal rates.
Both nominal rates must be identical because real rates match.
The second economy must have a real rate 5 points higher.
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
medium.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

medium.q: Expected inflation falls from 6 percent to 2 percent while the long-run real interest rate remains 3 percent. What nominal-rate change is predicted?
options: The nominal rate rises from about 5 percent to about 9 percent.
The real rate falls from 3 percent to negative 1 percent automatically.
The nominal rate stays at 9 percent because only actual inflation matters.
The nominal rate falls from about 9 percent to about 5 percent.
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
medium.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

medium.q: A one-year loan is priced when inflation is expected to be 3 percent. Actual inflation later turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement separates the Fisher effect from the realized return?
options: The Fisher effect uses actual inflation only and ignores expectations.
Unexpected inflation raises both parties’ realized real returns by the same amount.
The nominal rate reflected expected inflation when set; the unexpectedly high actual inflation changes the ex post real return.
The nominal rate must be rewritten after actual inflation is observed so the original expected rate no longer matters.
medium.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
medium.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

medium.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 6 percent while the real interest rate stays at 2 percent. The nominal rate becomes:
options: 3 percent
5 percent
6 percent
8 percent
medium.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
medium.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

medium.q: If the nominal interest rate is 9 percent and expected inflation is 4 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
13 percent
4 percent
36 percent
medium.commonError: adding inflation when solving for the real rate
medium.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal rate minus expected inflation: 9 - 4 = 5 percent.

medium.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 8 percent
4 percent
3 percent
12 percent
medium.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
medium.feedback: Nominal interest rate is approximately real interest rate plus expected inflation: 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

medium.q: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders when:
options: Loans were written before the inflation surprise
All contracts are indexed perfectly
Real wages rise automatically
Nominal prices cannot change
medium.commonError: Missing redistribution from unexpected inflation.
medium.feedback: Borrowers repay with dollars that are worth less than lenders expected.

medium.q: Which example best fits menu costs?
options: A firm pays to update price lists after inflation rises
A household visits the bank more often
A lender loses from unexpected inflation
A central bank buys bonds
medium.commonError: Confusing menu costs with shoeleather costs.
medium.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices.

medium.q: Which example best fits shoeleather costs?
options: A firm prints new menus
A worker compares nominal and real wages
A household makes extra bank transfers to hold less cash
A creditor gains from unexpected deflation
medium.commonError: Confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs.
medium.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from actions people take to reduce money holdings during inflation.

medium.q: Unexpected inflation benefits borrowers because
options: they repay loans with dollars worth less than expected
they repay loans with dollars worth more than expected
their nominal debt automatically disappears
creditors receive more purchasing power than expected
medium.commonError: thinking inflation always hurts borrowers
medium.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers because their fixed nominal repayments are made with less valuable dollars.

medium.q: Unexpectedly low inflation hurts borrowers because
options: they repay loans with dollars worth more than expected
they repay loans with dollars worth less than expected
their debts are erased
nominal interest rates instantly become negative
medium.commonError: forgetting that unexpectedly low inflation benefits creditors
medium.feedback: When inflation is lower than expected, borrowers repay with dollars that have more purchasing power than expected.

medium.q: Which situation is the clearest example of menu costs?
options: A firm spends money updating price tags and online menus after inflation.
A worker walks to the bank more often to avoid holding cash.
A borrower repays debt with less valuable dollars.
A bank holds excess reserves.
medium.commonError: confusing menu costs with shoeleather costs
medium.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices.

medium.q: Which situation is the clearest example of shoeleather costs?
options: People make more frequent trips to reduce cash holdings during high inflation.
A restaurant prints new menus after raising prices.
A debtor repays a fixed loan with less valuable dollars.
A firm buys new equipment because interest rates fall.
medium.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
medium.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from the effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high.

medium.q: Inflation is fully anticipated, so fixed-rate contracts are written with the expected inflation built in. Which cost can still remain?
options: Firms may still spend resources changing posted prices more often.
Unexpected borrower-creditor redistribution must become larger even though the inflation rate was correctly anticipated by both sides.
The nominal interest rate must become zero.
All relative prices become permanently fixed.
medium.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
medium.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

medium.q: Why can heavy reliance on printing money become dangerous?
options: It can create rapid inflation and reduce money's value
It guarantees higher real GDP forever
It eliminates all tax burdens
It makes nominal variables real
medium.commonError: Thinking printing money is costless financing.
medium.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but it reduces the value of money and can create high inflation.

medium.q: A government repeatedly prints money to pay its bills. Which risk is most directly connected to this policy?
options: Inflation tax and possible hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real output
Permanent monetary neutrality failure
A lower price level forever
medium.commonError: thinking printing money creates real resources without inflation pressure
medium.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but repeated reliance on it can create inflation or hyperinflation.

medium.q: Why is the inflation tax called a tax even though Congress may not pass a tax law?
options: It reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.
It raises real GDP automatically.
It only applies to people who owe income taxes.
It directly increases the real wage.
medium.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit and legislative
medium.feedback: Inflation acts like a tax on money holders by reducing the purchasing power of their cash balances.

medium.q: A country with runaway money creation and rapidly rising prices is experiencing
options: hyperinflation
monetary neutrality only
deflation
crowding out
medium.commonError: confusing high inflation with falling prices
medium.feedback: Rapid money creation paired with rapidly rising prices is hyperinflation territory.

medium.q: If prices are falling across the economy, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises.
It falls.
It becomes zero.
It becomes the nominal interest rate.
medium.commonError: thinking falling prices reduce the purchasing power of money
medium.feedback: Deflation means falling prices, so each dollar buys more. The value of money rises.

medium.q: Inflation falls from 7 percent to 2 percent, but the overall price level is still rising. Which description is correct?
options: The economy is experiencing disinflation, not deflation.
The economy is experiencing deflation because inflation is lower.
The economy is experiencing hyperinflation because prices are still rising.
The price level must be falling by 5 percent.
medium.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
medium.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

hard.q: A student says M2 is smaller than M1 because M2 excludes currency. What is the best correction?
options: M2 includes M1 plus near monies
M2 includes only bank reserves
M1 includes savings deposits only
M1 equals credit card balances
hard.commonError: Reversing the relationship between M1 and M2.
hard.feedback: M2 is broader than M1 because it includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

hard.q: A farmer accepts dollars for corn, uses dollars to compare seed prices, and saves some dollars for next month. Which answer correctly matches the three functions of money?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, medium of exchange, unit of account
Unit of account, store of value, medium of exchange
Money multiplier, reserve requirement, federal funds rate
hard.commonError: mixing up using money to buy with using money to measure value
hard.feedback: Buying uses money as a medium of exchange, comparing prices uses it as a unit of account, and saving it uses it as a store of value.

hard.q: A country uses paper currency that has no intrinsic value, is not convertible into gold, but is accepted for payment. What kind of money is this?
options: Fiat money
Commodity money
Barter money
Reserve money only
hard.commonError: thinking money must be backed by a commodity to have value
hard.feedback: That is fiat money: it has value because it is accepted, not because the paper itself has intrinsic value.

hard.q: Currency held by the public rises because households withdraw funds from checking accounts. What happens to banks' ability to create deposits, other things equal?
options: It falls because banks have fewer deposits to support lending.
It rises because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves.
It is unchanged because currency and deposits are identical for banks.
It becomes unlimited because reserve requirements no longer matter.
hard.commonError: thinking public currency holdings help banks lend more
hard.feedback: When households hold more currency and fewer deposits, banks have fewer deposits available to support loans.

hard.q: A household moves $4,000 from a checking account into a retail money-market mutual fund. Under standard textbook definitions, what happens?
options: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.
hard.commonError: Treating movement between M1 and non-M1 M2 assets as a change in total M2.
hard.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.

hard.q: Which asset is included in M2 but normally excluded from M1?
options: Currency held by the public.
A small-denomination time deposit.
Funds in a checking account.
Traveler’s checks held by households.
hard.commonError: Placing every liquid financial asset in M1.
hard.feedback: Small time deposits are near-money assets included in M2 but not in the narrower M1 measure.

hard.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists currency held by the public as $900, checkable deposits as $1,600, savings deposits as $2,000, small time deposits as $700, and retail money market funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
hard.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
hard.feedback: M1 = currency + checkable deposits = $2,500. M2 = M1 + savings + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $5,500.

hard.q: During a panic, a solvent bank cannot obtain short-term funding even though its assets exceed its liabilities. What central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort role?
options: Guarantee every bank loss without conditions.
Finance a permanent tax cut.
Raise reserve requirements solely to remove liquidity.
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral.
hard.commonError: Confusing liquidity support with an unconditional bailout of insolvent institutions.
hard.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems while safeguards limit losses and moral hazard.

hard.q: Which institutional arrangement best combines central-bank independence with democratic accountability?
options: Public officials set the mandate; the central bank chooses instruments and reports transparently.
The central bank chooses national goals and never explains its decisions to the public.
Elected officials directly set policy interest rates before every national election.
The Treasury secretly directs monetary operations without a published mandate.
hard.commonError: Treating independence as freedom from any public mandate or oversight.
hard.feedback: Instrument independence can coexist with a legislated mandate, transparency, and public accountability.

hard.q: When the central bank buys a large quantity of longer-term securities, what happens directly on its balance sheet?
options: Tax revenue rises while currency liabilities disappear from the balance sheet.
Its securities assets and reserve liabilities usually both rise.
Government purchases of goods rise automatically with the securities purchase.
Commercial-bank capital is converted directly into federal tax receipts.
hard.commonError: Treating asset purchases as ordinary fiscal spending.
hard.feedback: A central-bank asset purchase expands its asset holdings and typically creates reserve liabilities.

hard.q: The short-term policy rate is near its effective lower bound. Which action is still a monetary-policy option?
options: Change federal income-tax rates through the banking system.
Authorize a new congressional spending program immediately.
Use forward guidance or buy longer-term securities.
Set private-sector wages and prices by administrative order.
hard.commonError: Assuming monetary policy has no remaining tools when a short-term rate is very low.
hard.feedback: Central banks may use communication and balance-sheet tools when conventional rate cuts are constrained.

hard.q: During a panic, a bank has valuable assets but cannot obtain enough short-term funding to meet payments. Later analysis shows another bank’s assets are worth less than its liabilities. Why should a central bank treat the two cases differently?
options: Liquidity can address the first bank’s funding problem, but it cannot erase the second bank’s insolvency
Both banks should receive unlimited central-bank loans because any funding problem proves that losses and insolvency are irrelevant
The insolvent bank needs only a lower reserve requirement, while the solvent bank must be closed immediately
The central bank should finance both banks permanently because recognizing losses is a fiscal-policy function
hard.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
hard.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

hard.q: A central-bank asset purchase sharply increases reserve balances, yet commercial-bank lending changes little. Which statement best separates the institutions’ roles?
options: The central bank failed to create any reserve balances because commercial banks did not expand loans after the asset purchase
Commercial banks create central-bank reserves whenever they choose not to lend
Reserve balances are identical to bank capital, so unchanged lending proves capital was unchanged
The central bank creates reserves; commercial-bank deposit creation still depends on lending and borrowing
hard.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
hard.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

hard.q: Why does leverage make banks riskier?
options: A small percentage loss on assets can wipe out a large share of capital.
It guarantees assets never fall in value.
It prevents banks from making loans.
It makes reserves unnecessary.
hard.commonError: thinking leverage only increases returns and not risk
hard.feedback: Leverage magnifies gains and losses. A small asset loss can hit capital hard.

hard.q: A bank originates a loan by crediting its borrower’s checking account. The borrower then pays a supplier at a different bank, and the payment settles in reserves. Which comparison correctly separates origination from settlement?
options: Origination adds a loan and a deposit; settlement reduces the originating bank’s reserves and its borrower’s deposit.
Origination reduces reserves; settlement creates the loan and increases bank capital.
Origination adds reserves and a deposit; settlement leaves both banks’ reserves unchanged.
Origination reduces deposits; settlement cancels the originating bank’s loan asset.
hard.commonError: thinking loans reduce assets instead of changing asset composition
hard.feedback: Crediting the account initially adds a loan asset and a deposit liability. The later outgoing payment reduces reserves and the deposit liability; the loan remains an asset.

hard.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a 10 percent reserve requirement, and $95,000 in reserves. If deposits increase by $100,000 and reserves rise by $20,000, the bank’s new excess reserves are:
hard.commonError: Updating deposits or reserves but not both.
hard.feedback: New deposits are $900,000, required reserves are $90,000, and actual reserves are $115,000.

hard.q: A bank has $25 million in assets and $1.5 million in capital. An 8 percent asset loss occurs. What is the new capital position?
options: $0.5 million.
-$0.5 million.
-$2.0 million.
$1.5 million.
