Reduce government spending to make MD vertical.
elite.commonError: thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
elite.feedback: If money demand rises, increasing money supply can prevent the equilibrium interest rate from rising.

elite.q: If P rises, money demand shifts right. If the Fed also increases money supply enough to hold r constant, what happens to the interest-rate effect on AD?
options: It is offset because r does not rise to reduce investment.
It becomes stronger because r rises more.
It reverses because investment must fall more.
It disappears because AD is no longer related to spending.
elite.commonError: ignoring that Fed policy can offset money-demand pressure on r
elite.feedback: If the Fed accommodates the higher money demand, r does not rise, so the investment channel behind the interest-rate effect is muted.

elite.q: A student says a fall in the interest rate from 8 percent to 6 percent would shift MD0 to the right. What is the best correction?
options: Interest-rate changes move along MD0; they do not shift MD0.
Interest-rate changes shift MD0 because the rate is on the axis.
Interest-rate changes shift MS0 while MD0 stays fixed.
Interest-rate changes shift both MD0 and MS0 together.
elite.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
elite.feedback: The interest rate is the price variable on the money-demand curve. Changing it moves the economy along MD0.
elite.imageAlt: Money market with downward-sloping money demand MD0 and vertical money supply MS0 intersecting at point A.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Money demand MD0 slopes downward from an interest rate of 12 at quantity 0 to 0 at quantity 200. Money supply MS0 is vertical at quantity 100. The curves intersect at point A, quantity of money 100 and nominal interest rate 6.

elite.q: A student says the fall in the interest rate from 4 percent to 2 percent proves money demand shifted left. What does the graph actually show?
options: MD0 shifts left while money supply remains fixed at MS0 throughout.
MD0 and money supply both shift right to separate new curves.
MD0 is fixed; MS shifts right and equilibrium moves along MD0.
Neither money demand nor money supply changes in the diagram.
elite.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
elite.feedback: MD0 is unchanged. The new equilibrium is reached by moving along the same money-demand curve after MS shifts right.
elite.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 125; its MD0 intersection is at rate 2. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 2.

elite.q: A student says the rise in the interest rate from 4 percent to 6 percent proves money demand shifted right. What does the graph actually show?
options: MD0 is fixed; MS shifts left and equilibrium moves along MD0.
MD0 shifts right while money supply remains fixed at MS0 throughout.
MD0 and money supply both shift left to separate new curves.
Neither money demand nor money supply changes in the diagram.
elite.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
elite.feedback: MD0 is unchanged. The higher interest rate comes from the smaller money supply, causing a movement along MD0.
elite.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 75; its MD0 intersection is at rate 6. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 6.

elite.q: Compare original point B with simultaneous-shift point C. What happens to quantity of money and the nominal interest rate?
options: Quantity rises from 75 to 100 while the interest rate falls from 3 percent to 1 percent
Quantity stays at 75 while the interest rate rises from 3 percent to 6 percent
Quantity rises from 75 to 100 while the interest rate rises from 3 percent to 4 percent
Quantity falls from 100 to 75 while the interest rate falls from 4 percent to 3 percent
elite.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
elite.feedback: The increase in money supply raises equilibrium quantity, while the simultaneous increase in money demand is strong enough to leave the interest rate one point higher than at B.
elite.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with two vertical MS lines, two downward MD lines and labeled points A, B, C and D.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money; the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Solid MS0 is vertical at 75 and dashed MS1 at 100. Solid MD0 is the lower straight downward line, through B (75,3) and D (100,1). Dashed MD1 is the upper parallel line, through A (75,6) and C (100,4). MD1 crosses the vertical axis at 12 and the horizontal axis at 150. MD0 crosses the vertical axis at 9. All four points are marked with black dots.

elite.q: A student says the money-demand increase should shift aggregate demand right because people want to hold more money. What is the strongest correction using the graph?
options: With MS fixed, higher MD raises rates; spending falls and AD shifts left.
With MS fixed, higher MD lowers rates; spending rises and AD shifts right.
Higher MD creates extra money automatically, so interest rates fall.
Money demand and aggregate demand are the same curve and shift together.
elite.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
elite.feedback: Money demand is demand for liquid balances, not aggregate expenditure. With fixed supply, more money demand raises the interest rate and can reduce spending.
elite.imageAlt: Two panels with MS0, MD0 and MD1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
elite.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. MS0 is vertical at 75. Solid downward MD0 passes through A (75,2); upper dashed MD1 passes through B (75,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 and SRAS meet at A (150,55); AD1 and SRAS meet at B (105,45). Dashed guides identify the point coordinates.

elite.q: Refer to the money-market and AD graph. Which chain correctly explains the movement shown from MS1 to MS2 and AD1 to AD2?
options: Money supply falls, r rises, investment falls, AD falls
Money supply rises, r falls, investment falls, AD falls
Money demand falls, r rises, consumption rises, AD rises
Money supply falls, r falls, investment rises, AD rises
elite.commonError: Breaking the monetary transmission chain.
elite.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates, reduces investment, and shifts AD left.
elite.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
elite.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

elite.q: If the Fed shifts money supply right, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS rises, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MD rises, r rises, investment rises, AD shifts right.
elite.commonError: reversing the effect of money supply on interest rates
elite.feedback: More money lowers the interest rate, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

elite.q: If the Fed shifts money supply left, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MD falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
elite.commonError: thinking less money lowers interest rates
elite.feedback: Less money raises the interest rate, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

elite.q: If the Fed increases money supply but investment barely responds to the lower interest rate, what happens to the AD shift?
options: AD shifts right by less than usual because the investment channel is weak.
AD shifts right by more because investment does not matter.
AD must shift left because lower r reduces investment.
AD cannot move because money supply changed.
elite.commonError: assuming the money-supply shift mechanically creates the same AD response every time
elite.feedback: Monetary policy works through investment. If investment barely responds, AD shifts right less.

elite.q: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, which part of the normal expansionary monetary-policy chain weakens?
options: The ability of extra money to lower r enough to boost investment
The identity that AD includes investment
The fact that money demand exists
The ability of government spending to enter AD
elite.commonError: thinking liquidity trap means money demand disappears
elite.feedback: In a liquidity trap, additional money may not lower interest rates enough to stimulate investment.

elite.q: If money supply rises and AD shifts right, what is the correct distinction between the money-market movement and the AD-AS outcome?
options: The money market shows r falling; the AD-AS model shows higher demand for output at each price level.
The money market shows P falling; the AD-AS model shows money demand disappearing.
The money market shows taxes falling; the AD-AS model shows reserves rising.
The money market shows real output fixed by bank reserves.
elite.commonError: blending the money-market graph and AD graph into one axis system
elite.feedback: The money market determines the interest rate. The AD-AS model then reflects how lower rates raise spending and shift AD.

elite.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes what changes in the two panels?
options: MD shifts right and MS is traversed; SRAS shifts right along fixed AD.
MS shifts left and MD is traversed; AD shifts left along fixed SRAS.
MS shifts right and MD is traversed; AD shifts right along fixed SRAS.
Both panels show movements along fixed demand and supply curves.
elite.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
elite.feedback: Different markets are being linked. Money supply shifts first; the resulting rate change affects spending and shifts AD.
elite.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
elite.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (100,6) and dashed MS1 at B (150,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and upper dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (100,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (125,56.25). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

elite.q: A student says AD1 is lower because the central bank directly reduced real GDP. What is the better interpretation?
options: Lower MS raises rates; lower interest-sensitive spending shifts AD left.
Lower MS lowers rates; higher interest-sensitive spending shifts AD right.
The central bank directly sets real GDP and moves AD to that quantity.
A rightward MD shift raises rates and directly shifts SRAS to the left.
elite.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
elite.feedback: Monetary policy works through a transmission mechanism. The central bank acts on money/financial conditions, which influence spending and AD.
elite.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
elite.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (125,2.75) and dashed MS1 at B (100,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (125,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (100,45). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

elite.q: Money growth rises, velocity falls, and output rises. Which statement is safest?
options: Inflation depends on all three changes
Inflation must equal money growth
Inflation must be zero
Inflation must exceed output growth
elite.commonError: Using money growth alone when V and Y change.
elite.feedback: The quantity equation connects money, velocity, prices, and output, so inflation depends on changes in all of them.

elite.q: Starting at the original equilibrium, the Fed increases money supply. Which complete chain is correct?
options: MS shifts right, excess money appears at the old price level, spending rises, P rises, and the value of money falls.
MS shifts left, excess money appears, spending rises, P falls, and the value of money rises.
MD shifts right, money supply stays fixed, P falls, and value of money rises.
MS shifts right, spending falls, P falls, and the value of money rises.
elite.commonError: getting the direction of value of money backward
elite.feedback: A monetary injection shifts MS right. At the old price level there is excess money, which fuels spending, raises P, and lowers the value of money.

elite.q: If the economy moves from the original equilibrium to the new equilibrium after a monetary injection, why does the price level rise rather than output permanently rise in the long-run model?
options: The model holds real output fixed in the long run, so extra money mainly changes nominal prices.
Money demand becomes vertical and real output doubles.
The Fed directly raises real GDP by shifting MD right.
The price level rises because the value of money rises.
elite.commonError: thinking monetary injection permanently raises real output in the long-run money market model
elite.feedback: In the long-run model, real output is determined by real factors, so more money mainly raises the price level.

elite.q: If the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4 after the money supply shift, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 2 to 4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays unchanged because only money supply shifted.
elite.commonError: treating value of money as the price level itself
elite.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. A fall from 1/2 to 1/4 means P rises from 2 to 4.

elite.q: At the old equilibrium value of money after MS shifts right, what disequilibrium exists and what removes it?
options: Excess supply of money; people spend or lend excess balances until prices rise.
Excess demand for money; people sell goods until prices fall.
Excess supply of goods; people hoard money until the price level falls.
No disequilibrium; the value of money changes without behavior.
elite.commonError: missing why prices rise after excess money appears
elite.feedback: At the old price level, the higher money supply creates excess money balances. People spend or lend them, pushing prices up.

elite.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply is unchanged in the value-of-money model, what is the likely new equilibrium?
options: Higher value of money and lower price level
Lower value of money and higher price level
Higher money supply and higher price level
Lower money demand and lower value of money
elite.commonError: treating all rightward shifts as inflationary regardless of axis meaning
elite.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes up the value of money, which means the price level falls.

elite.q: If money supply shifts left from the higher money supply back to the original level, what happens to the value of money and the price level?
options: The value of money rises and the price level falls.
The value of money falls and the price level rises.
Both rise because money is scarcer.
Both fall because money is scarcer.
elite.commonError: forgetting that money scarcity raises the value of money but lowers P
elite.feedback: A lower money supply makes money scarcer, raising its value and lowering the price level.

elite.q: A student says the new equilibrium after MS rises means money is more valuable because there is more of it. What is wrong?
options: More money makes each dollar less scarce, so the value of money falls.
More money makes each dollar more scarce, so the value of money rises.
Money demand must disappear when money supply rises.
The price level must fall whenever money supply rises.
elite.commonError: thinking more money means each dollar has more value
elite.feedback: More money makes each dollar less scarce; with the price level higher, each dollar buys fewer goods, so the value of money falls.

elite.q: If the Fed doubles money supply while velocity and real output are stable, which quantity-theory result follows?
options: The price level roughly doubles and the value of money roughly halves.
The price level halves and the value of money doubles.
Real output doubles and the price level stays fixed.
Velocity falls to zero and money demand disappears.
elite.commonError: forgetting that stable V and Y push money growth into prices
elite.feedback: With stable velocity and output, doubled money supply mainly doubles the price level and cuts the value of money in half.

elite.q: An economy has M = 1,000, V = 5, and Y = 2,500. Next year M rises 20 percent, V is unchanged, and Y rises 4 percent. What is the approximate inflation rate?
options: 16 percent
20 percent
24 percent
4 percent
elite.commonError: adding output growth to money growth instead of subtracting it
elite.feedback: With velocity constant, money growth equals inflation plus output growth. Inflation is about 20 - 4 = 16 percent.

elite.q: In 2024, M = 500, V = 4, and Y = 1,000. In 2025, M = 600, V = 4, and Y = 1,200. What happens to the price level?
options: It stays at 2.
It rises from 2 to 2.4.
It falls from 2 to 1.6.
It rises from 4 to 6.
elite.commonError: seeing money rise and assuming P must rise without checking Y
elite.feedback: 2024 P = 500 x 4 / 1,000 = 2. 2025 P = 600 x 4 / 1,200 = 2. Output rose enough to keep P unchanged.

elite.q: If money growth is 12 percent, velocity growth is -2 percent, and real output growth is 3 percent, what is approximate inflation using the quantity equation growth form?
options: 7 percent
11 percent
17 percent
13 percent
elite.commonError: ignoring velocity growth when it is explicitly given
elite.feedback: Money growth plus velocity growth equals inflation plus output growth. Inflation = 12 + (-2) - 3 = 7 percent.

elite.q: A central bank doubles the money supply, output is unchanged, and all nominal wages and prices double. Which claim is strongest?
options: Real wages and relative prices are unchanged
Real wages double with nominal wages
Relative prices double with prices
Output must double with money
elite.commonError: Confusing nominal doubling with real doubling.
elite.feedback: If wages and prices double together, real wages and relative prices remain unchanged.

elite.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 6 percent while the price level rises 9 percent. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls by about 3 percent
It rises by about 3 percent
It rises by about 15 percent
It stays unchanged
elite.commonError: Treating nominal wage growth as real wage growth.
elite.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so 6 - 9 = -3 percent.

elite.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. The economy moves from a to b. In a long-run comparison, a nominal wage rises by the same proportion as the price level inferred from those points, and technology and labor supplies are unchanged. Which comparison fits monetary neutrality?
options: The price level and nominal wage rise by one-third; the real wage need not change.
The price level falls by one-quarter; the real wage must rise.
The price level doubles; unchanged real resources require output to double.
The price level rises by one-third; the real wage must also rise by one-third.
elite.commonError: confusing nominal price-level changes with real-output changes
elite.feedback: The graph gives value of money 2 at a and 1.5 at b. Their reciprocal price levels are 1/2 and 2/3, a one-third increase. Proportional nominal wage growth leaves the real wage unchanged; nominal changes alone do not raise real productive capacity.
elite.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
elite.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

elite.q: A country doubles all nominal wages and prices, while output, employment, and relative prices are unchanged. Which concept explains this outcome?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
The liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
elite.commonError: thinking nominal doubling must increase real output
elite.feedback: If nominal variables change but real variables do not, that is monetary neutrality.

elite.q: Nominal wages rise 12 percent while the price level rises 8 percent. Approximately what happens to the real wage?
options: It rises by about 4 percent.
It falls by about 4 percent.
It rises by about 20 percent.
It is unchanged.
elite.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
elite.feedback: Real wage growth is roughly nominal wage growth minus inflation: 12 percent - 8 percent = 4 percent.

elite.q: If nominal GDP rises 10 percent while real GDP rises 4 percent, what happened to the price level approximately?
options: It rose about 6 percent.
It rose about 14 percent.
It fell about 6 percent.
It stayed fixed.
elite.commonError: adding real growth to nominal growth instead of subtracting
elite.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price level growth is about 10 - 4 = 6 percent.

elite.q: A lender expected 4 percent inflation and charged 9 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 8 percent. What happened to the realized real return?
options: It was lower than expected
It was higher than expected
It was unchanged
It became nominal GDP
elite.commonError: Ignoring unexpected inflation after a loan is written.
elite.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real return to lenders.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower signs a loan at 9 percent nominal interest when expected inflation is 4 percent. Actual inflation is 7 percent. What happened to the realized real interest rate compared with what the lender expected?
options: It fell from 5 percent expected to 2 percent realized.
It rose from 5 percent expected to 7 percent realized.
It stayed at 5 percent because nominal interest was fixed.
It fell from 9 percent expected to 4 percent realized.
elite.commonError: using expected inflation for the realized real rate
elite.feedback: Expected real rate was 9 - 4 = 5 percent. Realized real rate was 9 - 7 = 2 percent.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate is stable at 3 percent, what should happen to the nominal interest rate under the Fisher effect?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 12 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 3 percent.
It rises from 2 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 3 percent.
elite.commonError: forgetting the real interest rate is part of nominal interest
elite.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 3 + 2 = 5 to 3 + 9 = 12 percent.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 6 percent inflation and charged 11 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 3 percent. Who gains from the surprise and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 14 percent.
elite.commonError: missing that lower-than-expected inflation helps lenders
elite.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so the lender gains. Realized real rate is 11 - 3 = 8 percent.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower expected 3 percent inflation on a loan with a 7 percent nominal rate. Actual inflation was 10 percent. Who gains and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 4 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 7 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
elite.commonError: thinking borrowers are hurt by unexpectedly high inflation
elite.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 7 - 10 = -3 percent.

elite.q: Why can high inflation distort relative prices even if the average price level is what gets reported?
options: Individual prices do not all adjust instantly or proportionally, so signals get noisy.
All individual prices change by exactly the same amount every second.
Relative prices are nominal variables only.
Inflation eliminates scarcity.
elite.commonError: thinking inflation only changes the average price level with no signal distortion
elite.feedback: Inflation can make price signals harder to read because prices adjust unevenly across goods and time.

elite.q: A government funds a deficit by printing money. People respond by holding less cash and visiting banks more often. Which inflation cost is most directly shown?
options: Shoeleather costs from reducing money holdings
Menu costs from changing posted prices
Crowding out from higher interest rates
Monetary neutrality from unchanged real variables
elite.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
elite.feedback: The extra effort to reduce money holdings is the shoeleather cost of inflation.

elite.q: A government funds a deficit by printing money. Firms then repeatedly update catalogs, labels, and online prices. Which inflation cost is most directly shown?
options: Menu costs
Shoeleather costs
Unexpected inflation redistribution
Liquidity trap
elite.commonError: thinking menu costs are only restaurant costs
elite.feedback: The cost of updating prices is menu cost. Not glamorous. Still real.

elite.q: A student says inflation makes everyone poorer because all prices rise. What is the best elite-level correction?
options: Inflation still causes distortions, behavior changes, and redistribution.
Inflation never has costs if any wage rises.
Inflation only affects creditors and no one else.
Inflation lowers all nominal incomes by definition.
elite.commonError: thinking inflation's only effect is higher prices with no nominal income adjustment
elite.feedback: Inflation is costly, but not simply because prices rise. The real damage comes through distortions, wasted effort, confusion, and redistribution.

elite.q: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise with expected inflation. Which two ideas are linked?
options: Inflation tax and Fisher effect
Crowding out and SRAS
Multiplier and LRPC
M1 and sacrifice ratio
elite.commonError: Separating deficit money creation from expected inflation effects.
elite.feedback: Printing money can act as an inflation tax, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

elite.q: If a government prints money to cover spending and the public starts expecting higher future inflation, what happens to nominal interest rates under the Fisher effect?
options: They rise as expected inflation rises.
They fall because money supply rose.
They stay fixed because real rates cannot change.
They become equal to the reserve ratio.
elite.commonError: thinking more money always lowers every interest rate in every model and horizon
elite.feedback: If money finance raises expected inflation, nominal interest rates tend to rise through the Fisher effect.

elite.q: A country raises money growth from 5 percent to 25 percent while real output growth stays at 3 percent and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 2 percent to about 22 percent.
It rises from about 5 percent to about 25 percent exactly.
It falls from 25 percent to 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth is unchanged.
elite.commonError: forgetting to subtract real output growth
elite.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth: initially 2 percent, then 22 percent.

elite.q: Deflation lowers the price level from 200 to 180. What happens to the value of money, and why can this matter for debtors?
options: The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth more.
The value of money falls; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
The value of money is unchanged; debtors are unaffected.
The value of money rises; debtors repay with dollars worth less.
elite.commonError: thinking falling prices help borrowers with fixed nominal debts
elite.feedback: Deflation raises the value of money. Fixed nominal debts become harder for debtors to repay.

elite.q: Which result best distinguishes disinflation from deflation?
options: Inflation falls from 8 percent to 3 percent during disinflation, while the price level falls during deflation.
The price level falls during disinflation, while inflation rises during deflation.
Both mean the price level rises faster.
Both mean money has no value.
elite.commonError: calling any fall in inflation deflation
elite.feedback: Disinflation means inflation slows. Deflation means the price level actually falls.

elite.q: A country uses seigniorage heavily during a fiscal crisis. Which combination is most likely if confidence erodes?
options: Rapid money growth, rising expected inflation, and higher nominal interest rates
Falling money growth, falling expected inflation, and lower nominal interest rates
No change in inflation because money is neutral in the short run
Lower price levels and higher money value immediately
elite.commonError: thinking seigniorage is free revenue with no expectations effect
elite.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations, and higher expected inflation pushes nominal interest rates up.

legendary.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $3,000, savings deposits are $2,500, small time deposits are $1,200, retail money market funds are $800, and large time deposits are $900. If large time deposits are not counted in M2, what is M2?
legendary.commonError: including large time deposits when the course definition excludes them
legendary.feedback: M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $3,000 + $2,500 + $1,200 + $800 = $7,500.

legendary.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A household moves $10,000 from a checking account to a savings account. What happens to M1 and M2, using standard course definitions?
options: M1 falls, while M2 is unchanged.
Both M1 and M2 fall.
M1 is unchanged, while M2 rises.
Both M1 and M2 rise.
legendary.commonError: thinking every movement between accounts changes M2
legendary.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2; savings deposits are in M2 but not M1. Moving funds to savings lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

legendary.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks lend more, and the public redeposits most loan proceeds. Which money measures are most likely affected first?
options: Bank deposits and M1 rise, with broader effects on M2 depending on where funds are held.
Commodity-money holdings rise because bond purchases convert financial assets into physical commodity money
Real GDP rises immediately while the quantity of bank deposits is unaffected by the lending and redeposit process
M1 falls because additional bank lending reduces the checkable deposits held by households and businesses
legendary.commonError: thinking bank-created deposits are not part of money measures
legendary.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits, and checkable deposits are part of M1. M2 can also be affected depending on where funds are held.

legendary.q: Currency held by the public rises by $20 billion, checking deposits fall by $20 billion, and small time deposits are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2?
options: M1 rises by $20 billion while M2 remains unchanged because currency is broader money.
Both aggregates are unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
M1 and M2 both fall by $20 billion because checking deposits decline.
M1 remains unchanged while M2 rises by $20 billion because currency increases.
legendary.commonError: Adding gross component changes without recognizing an offset within both aggregates.
legendary.feedback: Currency and checking deposits are both in M1 and M2. An equal transfer between them changes composition but not either total.

legendary.q: A new digital wallet stores claims on bank checking deposits and the same balances are still reported as checking deposits. How should statisticians avoid double counting?
options: Count both the checking deposit and the wallet claim as separate M1 balances.
Exclude the checking deposit and count only the wallet claim as part of M2.
Count the underlying deposit once and do not add the wallet claim again.
Remove both records because digitally accessed balances cannot qualify as money.
legendary.commonError: Counting two records of the same underlying monetary claim as two balances.
legendary.feedback: A wallet claim backed one-for-one by an already-counted checking deposit is another access channel, not a second stock of money.

legendary.q: An economy replaces an unstable commodity money with fiat currency. Which condition is most important for the fiat currency to function well?
options: The currency must possess substantial nonmonetary commodity value in every use.
Every note must remain redeemable for a fixed quantity of gold or silver.
The government must prohibit bank deposits and all competing payment methods.
Users must trust its acceptance and the institutions supporting its value.
legendary.commonError: Assuming fiat money requires intrinsic commodity value.
legendary.feedback: Fiat money works because of general acceptability, legal and institutional support, and confidence in its purchasing power.

legendary.q: A country has no central bank independence. Before elections, policymakers pressure the central bank to buy bonds and expand money aggressively. Which long-run risk is most consistent with the course logic?
options: Political pressure may create excessive money growth and inflation.
Political pressure guarantees higher real output forever.
Bond purchases permanently lower the price level.
Money becomes commodity money.
legendary.commonError: thinking central bank independence is irrelevant to inflation outcomes
legendary.feedback: Central bank independence can help reduce politically motivated money growth that risks inflation.

legendary.q: Why does central-bank independence not mean the central bank should be free to choose any social objective it wants?
options: Independence requires all monetary-policy decisions to remain secret.
Independence covers instrument choice within a publicly established mandate.
The central bank must directly control federal taxes and spending.
Independence means elected institutions have no legitimate policy role.
legendary.commonError: Equating instrument independence with unlimited policy authority.
legendary.feedback: A legitimate framework separates public goal setting from day-to-day instrument choices and requires accountability.

legendary.q: Inflation is well above target and output is near potential, but elected officials demand easier money before an election. What is the strongest case for central-bank independence?
options: It guarantees that monetary tightening has no short-run output cost.
It allows the central bank to eliminate every federal budget deficit.
It resists election-driven easing and protects price-stability credibility.
It permanently fixes unemployment below the natural rate.
legendary.commonError: Assuming independence removes policy tradeoffs rather than improving commitment.
legendary.feedback: Independence can support credible commitment to price stability even when near-term political incentives favor expansion.

legendary.q: A crisis program has two parts: the central bank lends temporarily against sound collateral to solvent banks, while the fiscal authority injects taxpayer capital into an insolvent institution. What principle best distinguishes the two actions?
options: Central-bank liquidity support addresses funding; fiscal recapitalization addresses losses and solvency
Both actions are ordinary open-market operations because each changes a financial balance sheet
The central bank is conducting fiscal policy in both cases because all emergency lending uses tax revenue
The fiscal authority is acting as lender of last resort while the central bank is collecting taxes
legendary.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
legendary.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

legendary.q: The central bank expands its balance sheet and reserve balances surge. Banks, however, tighten underwriting and firms postpone borrowing because sales prospects are weak. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The central bank did not actually create reserves because bank lending failed to rise
Weak borrowing proves that commercial banks, not the central bank, issue reserve balances
The simple multiplier guarantees the same deposit expansion regardless of banks or borrowers
Creating reserves does not mechanically force commercial-bank lending or deposit expansion
legendary.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
legendary.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

legendary.q: A student argues that the Federal Reserve must be part of the Treasury because its actions can affect government-security markets. Which response is most accurate?
options: The Treasury conducts monetary policy whenever the Fed buys a government security
Government securities cannot appear on a central-bank balance sheet unless Congress sets the policy rate directly
The Fed is a distinct central bank even though its operations can involve government securities
The Fed is legally just a Treasury checking account because both institutions handle government securities
legendary.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
legendary.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

legendary.q: A bank has $50 million in assets, $46 million in liabilities, and then suffers a 9 percent asset loss. What is the new capital position?
options: Capital falls from $4 million to negative $500,000.
Capital falls from $4 million to $3.64 million.
Capital rises from $4 million to $8.5 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb asset losses first.
legendary.commonError: applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets
legendary.feedback: Initial capital is $4 million. A 9 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4.5 million, so capital becomes negative $500,000.

legendary.q: A bank has actual reserves of $96,000, excess reserves of $24,000, and a reserve requirement of 12 percent. What are deposits?
legendary.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves
legendary.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $96,000 - $24,000 = $72,000. Deposits are $72,000 / 0.12 = $600,000.

legendary.q: A bank's assets fall by 4 percent. Its capital ratio before the loss was 5 percent of assets. What happens to most of the bank's capital?
options: Most capital is wiped out because the asset loss is almost as large as the capital cushion.
Capital falls by only 4 percent.
Capital rises because liabilities fall first.
Capital is unaffected because reserves absorb all losses.
legendary.commonError: thinking a 4 percent asset loss means only 4 percent of capital is lost
legendary.feedback: If capital is only 5 percent of assets, a 4 percent asset loss wipes out four-fifths of the capital cushion.

legendary.q: In a hypothetical system with a fixed 12.5 percent reserve ratio, a household deposits $28,000 of existing public currency. Banks initially have no excess reserves. Every bank lends all new excess reserves, all loan payments are redeposited, and no other constraint binds. An analyst counts the first deposit as new money and reports the full deposit increase as money creation. Which set of results diagnoses the error?
options: First loan $24,500; deposit increase $224,000; net money increase $196,000.
First loan $24,500; deposit increase $196,000; net money increase $224,000.
First loan $3,500; deposit increase $224,000; net money increase $224,000.
First loan $28,000; deposit increase $196,000; net money increase $168,000.
legendary.commonError: confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion
legendary.feedback: The first loan is $28,000 × 0.875 = $24,500. Deposits rise by $28,000/0.125 = $224,000. Subtract the $28,000 decline in public currency to obtain $196,000 of net money creation.

legendary.q: A bank has $1,000,000 in deposits and $140,000 in reserves. The reserve requirement is 10 percent. The bank lends all excess reserves, and that loan is redeposited in another bank facing the same reserve requirement. What is the second bank's maximum loan?
legendary.commonError: using the original deposit instead of the first loan as the second bank's deposit
legendary.feedback: The first bank's required reserves are $100,000, so it lends $40,000. The second bank keeps 10 percent, or $4,000, and can lend $36,000.

legendary.q: In two hypothetical steady states, the public holds no currency and banks have a fixed required-reserve ratio of 10 percent. The observed deposit-to-reserve ratio falls from 8 to 5. Assume all reserves are either required or deliberately held as excess reserves. Which diagnosis fits both observations?
options: The excess-reserve share of deposits rose from 2.5 to 10 percent.
The required-reserve ratio rose from 12.5 to 20 percent.
The excess-reserve share of deposits fell from 10 to 2.5 percent.
The public currency-to-deposit ratio rose from 2.5 to 10 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking a lower multiplier means a lower reserve ratio
legendary.feedback: Total reserves/deposits are the reciprocal of deposits/reserves: 12.5 percent, then 20 percent. Subtract the unchanged 10 percent requirement to infer excess-reserve shares of 2.5 and 10 percent.

legendary.q: Use a hypothetical fixed-ratio reserve model with no currency drain: every loan payment is fully redeposited, credit demand is sufficient, and no other constraint binds. A bank has $5 million in deposits, $700,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It lends all excess reserves, and every later bank does the same. What is the maximum total money expansion created by the excess reserves?
options: $2 million
$5 million
legendary.commonError: multiplying total reserves instead of excess reserves
legendary.feedback: Required reserves are $500,000, so excess reserves are $200,000. With multiplier 10, maximum expansion from excess reserves is $2 million.

legendary.q: A bank has $2,400,000 in deposits, $360,000 in reserves, and a reserve requirement of 10 percent. The reserve requirement then rises to 15 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $120,000 to $0.
They rise from $120,000 to $360,000.
They fall from $360,000 to $240,000.
They rise from $0 to $120,000.
legendary.commonError: forgetting to recalculate required reserves after the policy change
legendary.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $240,000, so excess reserves are $120,000. At 15 percent, required reserves are $360,000, leaving zero excess reserves.

legendary.q: In a hypothetical steady-state banking model, the required-reserve ratio is 10 percent, banks hold excess reserves equal to 5 percent of deposits, and the public holds currency equal to 25 percent of deposits. These ratios remain fixed. Money is currency plus deposits; the monetary base is currency plus total reserves. What base increase is needed for a $250 million money increase, and why is the simple 1/required-ratio estimate too small?
options: $80 million; both currency holdings and excess reserves absorb base money.
$25 million; every base dollar supports ten dollars of money.
$100 million; currency is excluded from the money measure.
$62.5 million; retaining a fixed fraction once describes every lending round.
legendary.commonError: ignoring the 80 percent lending adjustment
legendary.feedback: With deposits D, money is 1.25D and the base is (0.25 + 0.10 + 0.05)D = 0.40D. The money/base ratio is 3.125, so the base must rise $250/3.125 = $80 million. The simple multiplier ignores both leakages.

legendary.q: A hypothetical bank has $600,000 in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The required-reserve ratio rises from 10 to 15 percent. The bank cannot obtain new reserves, and any additional loan payment would settle at another bank. Which conclusion distinguishes its reserve position from its ability to expand?
options: It meets the new requirement exactly, but has no excess reserves for an outgoing loan.
It has a $30,000 reserve deficit and must obtain reserves just to comply.
It retains $30,000 of excess reserves because deposits have not changed.
It must shrink deposits by $90,000 even if it makes no new loan.
legendary.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more excess reserves
legendary.feedback: Required reserves rise from $60,000 to $90,000, exactly equal to actual reserves. The bank is compliant but the specified settlement constraint prevents further outgoing lending without adjustment.

legendary.q: The Fed cuts the discount rate, buys bonds, and lowers interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Bank borrowing and reserves rise, lending incentives strengthen, and the money supply tends to expand.
Bank reserves fall, lending incentives weaken, and the money supply contracts.
Taxes fall, consumption rises, and fiscal policy expands.
The money supply is unaffected because only fiscal policy matters.
legendary.commonError: treating Fed tools as unrelated one-off facts
legendary.feedback: All three actions push toward monetary expansion: cheaper Fed borrowing, more reserves, and less reward for holding reserves idle.

legendary.q: The Fed raises the discount rate, sells bonds, and raises interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Borrowing becomes costlier, reserves fall, banks may hold more reserves, and money creation weakens.
Borrowing becomes cheaper, reserves rise, and lending expands.
Government spending rises and taxes fall.
Money demand becomes zero.
legendary.commonError: missing that higher interest on reserves can be contractionary
legendary.feedback: That policy package tightens money through costlier borrowing, fewer reserves, and stronger incentives to hold reserves.

legendary.q: A bank has $10 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It holds $1.4 million in reserves. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 12 percent and banks lend all remaining excess reserves. How much can the bank lend after the change?
options: $1.2 million
$1.4 million
legendary.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the policy change
legendary.feedback: New required reserves are 0.12 x $10 million = $1.2 million. With $1.4 million in reserves, the bank can lend $200,000.

legendary.q: The Fed buys $80 million in bonds. The simple reserve ratio is 20 percent, but banks hold 25 percent of new reserves as excess reserves instead of lending them. Which answer best describes the result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $400 million simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $400 million.
The money supply rises by more than $400 million because excess reserves multiply.
The money supply falls because bond purchases are contractionary.
legendary.commonError: using the simple multiplier even when excess reserves are explicitly introduced
legendary.feedback: The simple multiplier maximum is 1/0.20 = 5, so $80 million could become $400 million. But excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

legendary.q: In a hypothetical fully loaned-up system with a fixed 10 percent reserve ratio and no excess reserves, the public permanently switches $36 million from deposits to currency. The monetary base stays fixed. Banks restore their reserve ratios through loan repayments that destroy deposits; there are no defaults or other changes. What are the final changes in deposits and in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $324 million.
Deposits fall $36 million; money is unchanged.
Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $396 million.
Deposits fall $324 million; money falls $360 million.
legendary.commonError: thinking currency withdrawal only changes the location of money with no multiplier effect
legendary.feedback: Currency rises $36 million and reserves fall $36 million. At reserves/deposits = 0.10, deposits must fall $360 million in total. Money changes by +$36 million − $360 million = −$324 million.

legendary.q: The Fed sells $75 million in bonds. The multiplier is 4, but the public responds by moving additional funds out of banks into currency. What should we expect relative to the simple multiplier result?
options: The contraction may exceed $300 million because currency drain further weakens deposit creation.
The contraction must equal exactly $300 million.
The money supply must increase because bond sales add reserves.
The contraction must be smaller because currency drain raises bank reserves.
legendary.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as exact even with added currency drain
legendary.feedback: The simple contraction is $75 million x 4 = $300 million, but currency drain can make the banking contraction larger.

legendary.q: A bank has a reserve shortfall of $20,000. The Fed lowers the discount rate, but the bank still refuses to borrow because it fears insolvency. What does this show?
options: A lower discount rate may not restore lending if bank risk concerns dominate.
The discount rate only affects fiscal policy.
Lower discount rates always force borrowing.
Reserve shortfalls increase lending capacity.
legendary.commonError: thinking a lower policy rate automatically fixes bank behavior
legendary.feedback: The Fed can make borrowing cheaper, but banks may still avoid borrowing or lending when risk dominates.

legendary.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. If the public deposits $30 million in currency into banks, the reserve ratio is 15 percent, and banks lend all excess reserves, what is the maximum total deposit expansion?
options: $200 million
$30 million
$25.5 million
$4.5 million
legendary.commonError: calculating only the first-round loan instead of total deposit expansion
legendary.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.15 = 6.666..., so $30 million can support about $200 million in total deposits. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

legendary.q: A student says, 'If banks create money through loans, loans must create real goods too.' What is the best correction?
options: Loans create deposits; real output still needs productive resources.
Loans automatically create real output one-for-one.
Deposits are not money.
Banks create commodity money with every loan.
legendary.commonError: thinking money creation equals real wealth creation
legendary.feedback: Bank lending can expand money and spending power, but it does not automatically create more real goods and services.

legendary.q: A new $100,000 deposit enters the banking system. The required reserve ratio is 10 percent, but the public withdraws 20 percent of every new loan as currency before redepositing the rest. What happens relative to the simple multiplier?
options: The final expansion is smaller than the simple $1,000,000 maximum.
The final expansion equals exactly $1,000,000.
The final expansion is larger because currency leakage increases reserves.
The money supply must contract because deposits increase.
legendary.commonError: using the simple multiplier despite a stated currency leakage
legendary.feedback: The simple maximum is $100,000 x 10 = $1,000,000, but currency leakage reduces redeposits and weakens money creation.

legendary.q: Which statement best combines Chapter 30's banking model with monetary-control limits?
options: Excess reserves and currency holdings weaken deposit multiplication.
Fractional reserve banking guarantees exact Fed control of M1.
The multiplier works only with commodity money.
Currency drain increases bank reserves and expands lending.
legendary.commonError: thinking the multiplier mechanism is automatic and exact
legendary.feedback: Fractional-reserve banking can multiply deposits, but excess reserves and currency holdings can make the actual expansion smaller than the simple model predicts.

legendary.q: Income rises, money demand shifts right, and the Fed holds money supply fixed. What memo is strongest?
options: Interest rates rise unless the Fed increases money supply.
Interest rates fall because higher income lowers money demand.
Interest rates stay fixed because money demand cannot shift.
Interest rates fall because fixed money supply means more lending.
legendary.commonError: Reversing income effects on money demand.
legendary.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; with fixed money supply, interest rates rise.

legendary.q: Money demand rises while the Fed increases money supply. Which conclusion is safest?
options: The interest-rate effect is ambiguous without knowing relative shift sizes.
Interest rates must rise because money demand always dominates.
Interest rates must fall because money supply always dominates.
Interest rates must stay fixed because both curves shifted.
legendary.commonError: Assuming one shift always dominates.
legendary.feedback: When money demand and money supply both increase, the interest-rate effect depends on which shift is larger.

legendary.q: Money demand rises because income rises, while the Fed cuts the money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates upward and pressure AD downward.
Both forces push interest rates downward and pressure AD upward.
Money demand raises rates, but lower money supply lowers rates.
Money demand lowers rates, but lower money supply raises rates.
legendary.commonError: Missing that both shifts raise interest rates.
legendary.feedback: Higher money demand and lower money supply both raise interest rates, weakening investment and AD.

legendary.q: Money demand falls while the Fed expands money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates downward and support AD.
Both forces push interest rates upward and weaken AD.
Money demand lowers rates, but higher money supply raises rates.
Money demand raises rates, but higher money supply lowers rates.
legendary.commonError: Missing that both shifts lower interest rates.
legendary.feedback: Lower money demand and higher money supply both push interest rates down, supporting investment and AD.

legendary.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. If the Fed wants to prevent the resulting interest-rate increase, what should it do?
options: Increase money supply enough to offset the rightward money-demand shift.
Decrease money supply to reinforce the money-demand shift.
Raise taxes because taxes directly shift money demand left.
Do nothing because r must fall when money demand rises.
legendary.commonError: thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
legendary.feedback: A rightward money-demand shift raises r if MS is fixed. Increasing MS can offset that pressure.

legendary.q: Real income rises and the central bank increases the money supply enough to leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged. What must be true?
options: Money demand stayed fixed even though higher income increased transaction volume.
The money supply shifted left by enough to offset the rise in money demand.
The price level fell to zero and eliminated the need to hold transaction balances.
The money-supply increase offset the rise in money demand.
legendary.commonError: Assuming an unchanged interest rate means neither curve shifted.
legendary.feedback: Higher income raises money demand. A sufficiently large increase in money supply can offset that pressure and leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged.

legendary.q: If the nominal interest rate were temporarily above point A while MS0 stayed fixed, what adjustment pressure would the graph imply?
options: Excess money demand pushes the rate farther above A.
Excess money supply pushes the rate down toward A.
Money supply shifts right until the rate rises above A.
Money demand shifts left until the rate remains above A.
legendary.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
legendary.feedback: Above equilibrium, the quantity of money demanded is less than the fixed money supply. Portfolio adjustment pushes the interest rate back down toward equilibrium.
legendary.imageAlt: Money market with downward-sloping money demand MD0 and vertical money supply MS0 intersecting at point A.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Money demand MD0 slopes downward from an interest rate of 12 at quantity 0 to 0 at quantity 200. Money supply MS0 is vertical at quantity 100. The curves intersect at point A, quantity of money 100 and nominal interest rate 6.

legendary.q: Starting from the money-market change shown, which downstream effect would normally follow?
options: Lower rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Higher rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
Higher rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
legendary.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
legendary.feedback: The standard transmission channel runs from more money to lower interest rates to more interest-sensitive spending and higher aggregate demand.
legendary.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 125; its MD0 intersection is at rate 2. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 2.

legendary.q: After the money-supply change from MS0 to MS1 shown in the graph, which spending-and-AD response should follow?
options: Higher rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
Higher rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates cut interest-sensitive spending and shift AD left.
Lower rates raise interest-sensitive spending and shift AD right.
legendary.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
legendary.feedback: The standard contractionary chain runs from less money to higher interest rates to less interest-sensitive spending and lower aggregate demand.
legendary.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 75; its MD0 intersection is at rate 6. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 6.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. The economy starts at B with MD0 and MS0. Money demand changes to MD1. The central bank increases money supply to MS1, but wants to restore B’s original nominal interest rate. If the straight MD1 line continues as drawn, approximately how much additional money beyond MS1 is needed?
options: 25 units; a total money quantity of 125.
No additional money; C already restores the original rate.
75 units; a total money quantity of 175.
12.5 units; a total money quantity of 112.5.
legendary.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
legendary.feedback: B’s rate is 3. MD1 passes through A at (75,6) and C at (100,4), a fall of 2 rate points per 25 money units. A further 1-point fall requires 12.5 additional units, beyond MS1 at 100.
legendary.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with two vertical MS lines, two downward MD lines and labeled points A, B, C and D.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money; the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Solid MS0 is vertical at 75 and dashed MS1 at 100. Solid MD0 is the lower straight downward line, through B (75,3) and D (100,1). Dashed MD1 is the upper parallel line, through A (75,6) and C (100,4). MD1 crosses the vertical axis at 12 and the horizontal axis at 150. MD0 crosses the vertical axis at 9. All four points are marked with black dots.

legendary.q: Which complete chain is consistent with the two-panel graph?
options: MD ↑; rate ↓; interest-sensitive spending ↑; AD →; GDP and prices ↑.
MD ↑; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↓; AD ←; GDP and prices ↓.
MS ↑; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↓; AD ←; GDP and prices ↑.
MD ↓; rate ↑; interest-sensitive spending ↑; AD →; GDP and prices ↑.
legendary.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
legendary.feedback: The panels show the full liquidity-preference transmission from a money-demand increase to a higher rate and lower aggregate demand.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with MS0, MD0 and MD1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. MS0 is vertical at 75. Solid downward MD0 passes through A (75,2); upper dashed MD1 passes through B (75,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 and SRAS meet at A (150,55); AD1 and SRAS meet at B (105,45). Dashed guides identify the point coordinates.

legendary.q: Refer to the money-market graph. Starting at point e (MS1 with MD1), both money demand and money supply shift right to MD2 and MS2. The new equilibrium is point d. What does the change from r2 to r3 imply?
options: The rightward money-demand shift exerts more upward pressure on the interest rate than the rightward money-supply shift offsets.
The money-supply shift must have dominated because any increase in money supply mechanically raises interest rates more than a simultaneous money-demand shift can affect them.
Both rightward shifts necessarily leave the interest rate unchanged.
The new equilibrium shows that money demand fell relative to money supply.
legendary.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
legendary.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.
legendary.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
legendary.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

legendary.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD2 and MS2, the equilibrium is point d at r3. If the interest rate is temporarily at point b on MS2 at r4, what adjustment should occur?
options: There is excess money demand, so households sell interest-bearing assets; bond prices fall and the interest rate rises farther above r4 before the market can clear.
Point b is already the equilibrium because it lies on MS2.
Money demand must shift right again before the interest rate can change.
There is excess money supply; people try to buy interest-bearing assets, putting downward pressure on the interest rate toward r3.
legendary.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
legendary.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
legendary.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
legendary.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

legendary.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD1 and MS1, equilibrium is point e at r2. If the interest rate is temporarily at r1, what pressure moves the market back toward equilibrium?
options: The market remains at r1 because a vertical money-supply curve prevents interest-rate adjustment.
The central bank must reduce the fixed money supply before households can obtain enough money balances and the interest rate can move back toward equilibrium.
Quantity of money demanded exceeds the fixed money supply, so attempts to raise money by selling interest-bearing assets put upward pressure on the interest rate.
Quantity of money supplied exceeds money demanded, so asset purchases push the interest rate lower.
legendary.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
legendary.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
legendary.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
legendary.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

legendary.q: Real income rises while the overall price level falls. With money supply fixed, what can be concluded about the equilibrium interest rate from liquidity-preference theory alone?
options: It cannot change because income and the price level never shift money demand.
The direction is ambiguous because higher income raises money demand while a lower price level reduces money demand.
It must rise because every increase in real income dominates every change in the price level.
It must fall because the price-level effect always dominates the income effect.
legendary.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
legendary.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.

legendary.q: The central bank increases the money supply and the equilibrium interest rate falls while income and the price level are unchanged. A student says, “Money demand shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: The fall in the interest rate is a movement along the existing money-demand curve unless a money-demand shifter also changed.
The student is correct because any fall in interest rates shifts the entire money-demand curve left at every quantity, even when income and the price level are unchanged.
Money demand shifts right whenever money supply increases.
Money demand becomes horizontal after an expansionary money-supply change.
legendary.commonError: Calls an interest-rate-induced movement along a money-demand curve a shift of the curve.
legendary.feedback: A change in the interest rate causes movement along a given money-demand curve. Income or the price level can shift the money-demand curve.

legendary.q: Refer to the money-market graph. The economy begins at e with MD1 and MS1. Money demand shifts to MD2, and the central bank also expands money supply to MS2. Is the increase in money supply large enough to keep the interest rate at r2?
options: Yes. Any rightward money-supply shift exactly offsets any rightward money-demand shift.
Yes. Point d lies on MS2, so the interest rate must still equal r2.
No. The central bank would need to reduce money supply to keep the interest rate from rising.
No. The new equilibrium d is at r3, so the central bank would need a larger rightward money-supply shift to hold the rate at r2.
legendary.commonError: Uses a contractionary money-supply response to offset a rightward money-demand shift.
legendary.feedback: If money demand shifts right and the central bank wants to prevent the interest rate from rising, it must increase money supply enough to accommodate the higher demand.
legendary.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
legendary.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

legendary.q: Real income rises, shifting money demand right, yet the observed equilibrium interest rate falls. Which inference is most consistent with the liquidity-preference model?
options: Money demand could not have risen because income never affects transaction demand.
The central bank must have held money supply fixed because a fixed supply guarantees a lower rate.
Money supply must have increased enough to more than offset the upward interest-rate pressure from higher money demand.
Money supply must have fallen because lower supply always lowers interest rates.
legendary.commonError: Ignores the opposing pressure from a money-demand increase when interpreting a falling interest rate.
legendary.feedback: If money demand rises but the equilibrium interest rate falls, money supply must have risen by enough to more than offset the upward interest-rate pressure from money demand.

legendary.q: The Fed shifts MS left while the economy is already below potential. What is the likely policy risk?
options: Interest rates rise, AD falls, and the recessionary gap worsens.
Interest rates fall, AD rises, and inflation disappears cleanly.
Interest rates rise, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to potential.
Interest rates fall, LRAS shifts left, and unemployment returns to natural.
legendary.commonError: Missing the danger of tightening into weak demand.
legendary.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates and shifts AD left, which can worsen a recessionary gap.

legendary.q: A student says expansionary monetary policy raises AD by directly increasing government purchases. What is the best correction?
options: Monetary policy works mainly through money supply, interest rates, and investment.
Monetary policy works by changing G before interest rates can move.
Monetary policy works only by shifting LRAS through technology.
Monetary policy works by raising taxes and lowering consumption.
legendary.commonError: Confusing monetary and fiscal policy channels.
legendary.feedback: Monetary policy affects AD primarily through money supply, interest rates, and investment spending.

legendary.q: A student says, 'If the Fed buys bonds, inflation must rise immediately and real output cannot move.' Which correction is strongest?
options: In the short run, lower rates can raise AD and output before long-run price adjustment dominates.
Bond purchases only change fiscal spending, so inflation and output are unaffected.
Bond purchases lower AD because reserves rise and lending must fall.
In the long run, bond purchases permanently reduce unemployment.
legendary.commonError: Skipping the short-run transmission channel.
legendary.feedback: Open-market purchases lower interest rates and can raise AD and output in the short run.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. What policy movement is shown across the two panels?
options: Money supply shifts left from MS1 to MS2, r rises from r1 to r2, AD shifts left from AD1 to AD2, and output falls from Y1 to Y2.
Money supply shifts right from MS2 to MS1, r falls from r2 to r1, AD shifts right from AD2 to AD1, and output rises from Y2 to Y1.
Money demand shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
The price level falls and the economy moves along AD1 from Y1 to Y2.
legendary.commonError: reading the leftward money-supply shift as expansionary policy
legendary.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy: MS shifts left, r rises, AD shifts left, and output falls.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment change caused by the MS1 to MS2 movement is $80 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct full AD effect?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $80 billion.
legendary.commonError: using the multiplier correctly but reading the graph direction backward
legendary.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left and r rising, so investment falls. MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5, so AD falls by $200 billion.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed moves the money supply from MS1 to MS2. If the resulting investment change is $60 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the correct full effect on AD?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $240 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $60 billion.
legendary.commonError: letting the arithmetic hide a bad graph read
legendary.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left from MS1 to MS2, which raises r and reduces investment. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so AD falls by $240 billion.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed moves MS from MS1 to MS2. If the investment response is $40 billion and MPC = 0.5, what is the correct AD result?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $80 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $80 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $40 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $20 billion.
legendary.commonError: stopping at the investment decrease instead of applying the multiplier
legendary.feedback: The graph shows tighter money. MPC = 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so a $40 billion investment fall lowers AD by $80 billion.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. If the MS1 to MS2 movement causes only a $20 billion investment response and MPC = 0.8, what is the correct AD interpretation?
options: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, and AD decreases by $100 billion.
The graph shows expansionary monetary policy, and AD increases by $100 billion.
The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, and AD decreases by only $20 billion.
The graph shows a movement along AD, and AD does not shift.
