legendary.commonError: thinking the graph shift alone gives the size of the AD effect
legendary.feedback: The graph shows MS left and AD left. MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so a $20 billion investment fall lowers AD by $100 billion.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment response to the MS1 to MS2 movement is $40 billion and MPC = 0.8, how far does AD shift?
options: AD shifts left by $200 billion.
AD shifts right by $200 billion.
AD shifts left by $40 billion.
AD shifts right by $50 billion.
legendary.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier or reading the AD shift backward
legendary.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, so AD shifts left. MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $40 billion becomes $200 billion.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. At price level P1, what happens when AD moves from AD1 to AD2?
options: Output falls from Y1 to Y2.
Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
Output stays at Y1.
The graph shows only an interest-rate change and no output change.
legendary.commonError: missing the output movement from AD1 to AD2 at P1
legendary.feedback: At P1, the leftward AD shift moves output from Y1 to Y2.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. A student says the graph shows a movement along AD caused by a lower price level. What is the best correction?
options: The graph shows AD shifting left because money supply falls and r rises.
The graph shows AD shifting right because money supply rises and r falls.
The graph shows a lower price level causing movement along AD1.
The graph shows fiscal expansion through higher government spending.
legendary.commonError: confusing an AD shift with movement along a fixed AD curve
legendary.feedback: This is not movement along AD. It is a leftward AD shift caused by tighter monetary policy.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. Which graph feature shows that the monetary policy is contractionary rather than expansionary?
options: MS moves left from MS1 to MS2 and AD moves left from AD1 to AD2.
MS moves right from MS2 to MS1 and AD moves right from AD2 to AD1.
Money demand moves left and AD stays fixed.
The price level falls along AD1.
legendary.commonError: not using the labels MS1, MS2, AD1, and AD2 to identify policy direction
legendary.feedback: The key evidence is MS1 to MS2 and AD1 to AD2, both leftward shifts.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.

A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. The policy direction shown needs to move AD left by $300 billion. If MPC = 0.5 and each 1-point increase in r lowers investment by $50 billion, how much must r rise?
options: 3 percentage points
6 percentage points
1.5 percentage points
2 percentage points
legendary.commonError: not dividing the AD target by the multiplier before solving for investment
legendary.feedback: The graph calls for a rise in r. MPC = 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so investment must fall $150 billion. At $50 billion per point, r must rise 3 points.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment response to the MS1 to MS2 movement is $50 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct order of effects?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls $50 billion, and AD shifts left by $125 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises $50 billion, and AD shifts right by $125 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises $50 billion, and AD shifts right by $125 billion.
MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls $50 billion, and AD shifts left by $50 billion only.
legendary.commonError: stopping at the investment decline instead of applying the multiplier
legendary.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left and r rising. MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5, so a $50 billion investment fall shifts AD left by $125 billion.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendary.q: Refer to the two-panel graph. Between A and B, the central bank expands money supply while SRAS stays fixed. A commentator says output and prices rose by the same percentage because they both rose. Which numerical comparison and inference are supported?
options: Output rises 12.5 percent and the price level 25 percent; their responses must be proportional.
Both rise 25 percent; equal directions establish equal percentage changes.
Both rise 6.25 percent; a common point label establishes a common percentage change.
Output rises 25 percent and the price level 12.5 percent; their responses need not be proportional.
legendary.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
legendary.feedback: Read output 100 to 125 and P 50 to 56.25. Their percentage changes are 25/100 = 25 percent and 6.25/50 = 12.5 percent. The diagram supplies distinct responses along fixed SRAS.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.

Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and upper dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (100,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (125,56.25). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

legendary.q: What macroeconomic conclusion is supported by the contractionary A-to-B movement across both panels?
options: The illustrated tightening lowers rates and raises both GDP and the price level.
The illustrated tightening raises rates and lowers both GDP and the price level.
The illustrated tightening lowers potential GDP by shifting LRAS to the left.
The illustrated tightening lowers GDP while raising the price level.
legendary.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
legendary.feedback: The graph supports the specific policy chain and depicted outcomes, not a universal mechanical coefficient.
legendary.imageAlt: Two panels with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
legendary.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. Downward MD0 meets solid MS0 at A (125,2.75) and dashed MS1 at B (100,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 meets SRAS at A (125,50); AD1 meets SRAS at B (100,45). Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those coordinates.

legendary.q: Money supply shifts from MS1 to MS2. If the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4, which price-level change and interpretation are correct?
options: P rises from 2 to 4; each dollar buys half as much.
P falls from 2 to 4; each dollar buys twice as much.
P rises from 1/2 to 1/4; each dollar buys more.
P stays at 2 because only money supply shifted.
legendary.commonError: treating the value of money as the price level
legendary.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. A fall from 1/2 to 1/4 means P rises from 2 to 4, so a dollar buys half as much.

legendary.q: Starting at the original equilibrium, the Fed doubles money supply. If output and velocity are unchanged, which answer matches quantity theory?
options: The price level doubles and the value of money halves.
The price level halves and the value of money doubles.
Real output doubles and the price level is unchanged.
Velocity doubles and money demand disappears.
legendary.commonError: thinking a doubled money supply doubles real output
legendary.feedback: With V and Y fixed, doubling M doubles P. Since value of money is 1/P, it falls by half.

legendary.q: After MS shifts right, there is excess money at the old price level. Which adjustment process restores equilibrium?
options: People spend or lend excess balances, raising demand for goods and pushing prices up until money demand equals supply.
People destroy excess balances, lowering prices until value of money falls.
The Fed automatically shifts money demand left.
Output permanently doubles, leaving prices unchanged.
legendary.commonError: identifying the shift but not explaining the adjustment process
legendary.feedback: People spend or lend excess balances, increasing demand for goods and services; prices rise until money demand equals the higher money supply.

legendary.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, and the value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, what happens to the price level?
options: It falls from 4 to 2.
It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays at 4.
legendary.commonError: thinking higher value of money means a higher price level
legendary.feedback: If the value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, P falls from 4 to 2.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. An analyst describes the move from a to b as a rightward shift of money demand and says that doubling the money quantity proves a doubling of the price level. Which diagnosis uses both curve evidence and the vertical-axis scale?
options: MD is unchanged; the price level rises by one-third, so constant output would require velocity to fall.
MD shifts right; the price level doubles, so velocity can remain fixed.
MD is unchanged; the price level falls by one-quarter, so velocity must rise.
MD shifts left; the price level is unchanged because the money supply is vertical.
legendary.commonError: mixing up which curve shifted
legendary.feedback: The same MD contains both a and b. Money doubles from 2,500 to 5,000, while P rises from 1/2 to 2/3, a factor of 4/3. With Y fixed, MV = PY requires velocity to change by (4/3)/2 = 2/3, so it falls.
legendary.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
legendary.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

legendary.q: An economy has M = 2,000, V = 3, and Y = 1,500. Next year M rises to 2,400, V falls to 2.5, and Y rises to 1,600. What happens to the price level?
options: It falls from 4.0 to 3.75.
It rises from 3.75 to 4.0.
It rises from 4.0 to 4.8.
It stays at 4.0.
legendary.commonError: assuming money growth raises prices without checking velocity and output

legendary.q: An economy plans for real output to grow 4 percent and the price level to grow 2 percent over one year. A payments change is expected to reduce velocity by 3 percent. Using the exact multiplicative quantity equation, approximately what money-growth rate meets both targets, and why would simply adding 2 and 4 be insufficient?
options: 9.36 percent; money must also offset the velocity decline.
6 percent; velocity has no effect when output growth is given.
3 percent; declining velocity reduces the money needed.
9 percent exactly; percentage growth rates always add exactly.
legendary.commonError: ignoring velocity growth even though it is given
legendary.feedback: The required money growth factor is (1.02 × 1.04)/0.97 = 1.093608..., so growth is about 9.36 percent. The sum approximation gives 9 percent, but is not the exact multiplicative result.

legendary.q: If the Fed contracts money supply and the value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, which statement correctly describes the result?
options: P falls from 4 to 2, so each dollar buys more.
P rises from 2 to 4, so each dollar buys less.
P stays fixed because money demand did not shift.
P falls from 1/2 to 1/4, so each dollar buys less.
legendary.commonError: forgetting that higher value of money means lower P
legendary.feedback: If value of money rises from 1/4 to 1/2, P falls from 4 to 2. Each dollar buys more.

legendary.q: A student says, 'Inflation means the money demand curve slopes up.' What is the best correction?
options: Inflation means a higher price level and lower value of money.
Inflation means money demand is always vertical.
Inflation means money supply must slope down.
Inflation means quantity of money cannot change.
legendary.commonError: misreading the value-of-money axis and money demand slope
legendary.feedback: The MD curve slopes downward against value of money because lower money value means higher P and more dollars demanded.

legendary.q: A student says nominal wages rose 8 percent, so workers are better off. Inflation was 11 percent. What correction survives?
options: Real wages fell because prices rose faster than nominal wages.
Real wages rose because nominal wages increased above zero.
Real wages were unchanged because all inflation is neutral immediately.
Real wages doubled because nominal wages are measured in dollars.
legendary.commonError: Confusing nominal wage growth with real wage growth.
legendary.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so workers lost purchasing power.

legendary.q: A student says, 'Since money is neutral, monetary policy cannot affect output during recessions.' Which correction is strongest?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run sticky prices allow AD effects on output.
Neutrality means money changes output permanently but not prices.
Neutrality applies only to fiscal policy and never to money.
Neutrality means the Phillips curve slopes downward in the long run.
legendary.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to every short-run case.
legendary.feedback: Money is neutral in the long run, but monetary policy can affect output in the short run through aggregate demand.

legendary.q: Nominal GDP rises 12 percent while real GDP rises 5 percent. What happened to the price level, and which kind of variable changed?
options: The price level rose about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level rose about 17 percent; that is a real change.
The price level fell about 7 percent; that is a nominal change.
The price level was unchanged; only real output changed.
legendary.commonError: adding nominal and real growth instead of subtracting
legendary.feedback: Nominal GDP growth is roughly inflation plus real GDP growth, so price growth is about 12 - 5 = 7 percent. The price level is nominal.

legendary.q: A worker's nominal wage rises from $24 to $30 while the price level rises from 6 to 10. What happens to the real wage?
options: It falls from 4 units to 3 units.
It rises from 4 units to 5 units.
It stays at 4 units.
It rises from 6 units to 10 units.
legendary.commonError: looking only at the nominal wage increase
legendary.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It falls from 24/6 = 4 to 30/10 = 3 units.

legendary.q: All nominal prices double except wages, which rise only 50 percent. What happens to real wages?
options: Real wages fall because nominal wages rise less than the price level.
Real wages rise because nominal wages rose.
Real wages are unchanged because all prices rose.
Real wages double because prices doubled.
legendary.commonError: thinking any nominal wage increase raises the real wage
legendary.feedback: Real wages depend on wages relative to prices. If wages rise 50 percent while prices double, real wages fall.

legendary.q: A country's price level rises from 100 to 140, nominal wages rise from $20 to $24, and workers complain their purchasing power fell. What happened to real wages?
options: They fell because wages rose 20 percent while prices rose 40 percent.
They rose because nominal wages rose.
They stayed the same because both wages and prices rose.
They doubled because the price level rose.
legendary.commonError: thinking nominal wage growth automatically raises purchasing power
legendary.feedback: Nominal wages rose 20 percent, but prices rose 40 percent. Real wages fell.

legendary.q: A policy causes all nominal prices, nominal wages, and nominal debts to double, but output and employment remain unchanged. Which outcome best fits long-run monetary neutrality?
options: Nominal variables changed while real variables stayed unchanged.
Real variables changed while nominal variables stayed unchanged.
Money had no effect on the price level.
Relative prices doubled.
legendary.commonError: thinking monetary neutrality means money has no nominal effects
legendary.feedback: Long-run monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real output or employment.

legendary.q: A lender’s one-year fixed nominal contract pays 12 percent. Expected inflation when written was 5 percent, but actual inflation is 9 percent. Use exact gross returns. What are the expected and realized real returns, and what nominal rate on a new loan would preserve the original expected real return if expected inflation is now 9 percent?
options: About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 16.27 percent.
7 percent, 3 percent, and 16 percent exactly.
About 2.75 percent, 6.67 percent, and 12 percent.
About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 12 percent.
legendary.commonError: using expected inflation for both expected and realized real rates
legendary.feedback: Expected real return is 1.12/1.05 − 1 = 6.67 percent; realized is 1.12/1.09 − 1 = 2.75 percent. Preserving the original gross real return on a new loan requires (1.12/1.05) × 1.09 − 1 = 16.27 percent nominal.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 11 percent. The real interest rate falls from 3 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 13 percent.
It rises from 4 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
legendary.commonError: assuming the real rate is constant when it is explicitly changed
legendary.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 3 + 4 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 11 = 13 percent.

legendary.q: A one-time monetary expansion lowers the value of money today. Credible guidance says the money-growth rate will then return to its previous path. The long-run real interest rate is unchanged. An analyst concludes that nominal interest rates must remain permanently higher. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: A one-time price-level rise does not establish permanently higher expected inflation, so the lasting nominal-rate claim is unsupported.
The higher price level guarantees permanently higher inflation, so the nominal-rate claim follows.
The lower value of money proves the real interest rate falls permanently, so nominal rates must fall.
Monetary neutrality makes expected inflation irrelevant to nominal rates, so the Fisher relationship does not apply.
legendary.commonError: confusing short-run liquidity effects with long-run Fisher effect
legendary.feedback: The Fisher effect relates nominal rates to expected inflation over the loan horizon. A level adjustment alone does not establish a continuing inflation-rate increase. The real-rate assumption therefore does not complete the analyst’s argument.

legendary.q: Money growth rises from 8 percent to 20 percent. Velocity growth is zero and output growth is 4 percent. If expected inflation adjusts fully, what happens to nominal rates when the real rate stays at 3 percent?
options: Nominal rates rise from about 7 percent to about 19 percent.
Nominal rates fall from 7 percent to 3 percent.
Nominal rates rise from 8 percent to 20 percent exactly.
Nominal rates stay at 3 percent.
legendary.commonError: not converting money growth into inflation before applying Fisher
legendary.feedback: Inflation rises from 8 - 4 = 4 percent to 20 - 4 = 16 percent. With real rate 3 percent, nominal rates rise from 7 to 19 percent.

legendary.q: A country establishes a credible low-inflation regime. Expected inflation falls from 9 percent to 3 percent, while saving and investment conditions leave the long-run real interest rate near 2 percent. Which outcome best fits the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate tends to fall from about 11 percent to about 5 percent.
The nominal interest rate tends to rise from about 5 percent to about 11 percent.
The real interest rate must fall from 2 percent to negative 4 percent.
The nominal interest rate should stay near 11 percent because credibility affects only actual inflation.
legendary.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
legendary.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

legendary.q: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?
options: It must be unchanged because identical expected inflation always forces identical nominal interest rates even when real saving and investment conditions differ.
It must be lower because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.
It must equal expected inflation because real rates disappear in the long run.
It should also be higher, showing that Fisher comparisons must account for the real-rate component as well as expected inflation.
legendary.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
legendary.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 3 percent inflation and charged 8 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 12 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
legendary.feedback: Actual inflation exceeded expected inflation, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 8 - 12 = -4 percent.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 8 percent inflation and charged 13 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 2 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking borrowers always gain when inflation is positive
legendary.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so lenders gain. The realized real rate is 13 - 2 = 11 percent.

legendary.q: If MS shifts right and the price level rises from 2 to 4, what inflation cost would become more likely if firms must repeatedly update prices?
options: Menu costs
Crowding out
Reserve shortfall
Liquidity preference equilibrium
legendary.commonError: identifying inflation but not connecting it to a specific cost
legendary.feedback: The graph shows inflation after monetary expansion. Firms repeatedly changing posted prices is menu cost.

legendary.q: If MS shifts right, the price level rises, and people reduce cash balances by making more frequent transfers, what inflation cost is described?
options: Shoeleather costs
Menu costs
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
legendary.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
legendary.feedback: When inflation makes people spend effort reducing money holdings, that is shoeleather cost.

legendary.q: A country experiences 18 percent money growth, 2 percent velocity growth, and 5 percent real output growth. Inflation is high, and borrowers with fixed-rate debt gain unexpectedly. What is the approximate inflation rate?
options: 15 percent
25 percent
21 percent
11 percent
legendary.commonError: forgetting velocity growth or subtracting it incorrectly
legendary.feedback: Inflation = money growth + velocity growth - output growth = 18 + 2 - 5 = 15 percent.

legendary.q: A country perfectly indexes many long-term contracts to the price level, greatly reducing unexpected debtor-creditor redistribution. Inflation nevertheless remains high and predictable. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Indexation can reduce redistribution without eliminating costs such as frequent repricing, cash management, or tax distortions.
Once contracts are indexed, high expected inflation becomes economically costless.
Indexation guarantees the price level stops rising because once nominal contracts are indexed, firms and households no longer face any inflation-related decisions.
Indexation converts inflation into deflation by raising the real value of money.
legendary.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

legendary.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth rises from 6 percent to 26 percent, output growth remains 3 percent, and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 3 percent to about 23 percent.
It rises from about 6 percent to about 26 percent exactly.
It falls from about 23 percent to about 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth did not change.
legendary.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth from money growth
legendary.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth. It rises from 3 percent to 23 percent.

legendary.q: A government uses inflation tax finance, expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates rise. Which concepts are being connected?
options: Inflation tax, expected inflation, and the Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and commodity money
Menu costs, M1, and fiscal multipliers
Liquidity trap, real wage, and barter
legendary.commonError: not connecting money finance to expected inflation and nominal rates
legendary.feedback: Printing money can create inflation expectations, and the Fisher effect links expected inflation to nominal interest rates.

legendary.q: Unexpected deflation reduces the price level from 1.25 to 1.00. A firm’s fixed nominal debt is $48,000. Its sales volume is unchanged, and its $12,000 nominal operating cash flow falls in the same proportion as the price level. Which pair describes the debt burden and the cash-flow pressure?
options: Real debt rises from 38,400 to 48,000 units; debt/cash flow rises from 4 to 5.
Real debt falls from 48,000 to 38,400 units; debt/cash flow falls from 5 to 4.
Real debt rises from 38,400 to 48,000 units; debt/cash flow stays at 4.
Real debt stays at 48,000 units; debt/cash flow rises from 4 to 5.
legendary.commonError: thinking falling prices always help borrowers
legendary.feedback: Real debt rises from 48,000/1.25 = 38,400 to 48,000/1 = 48,000. Nominal cash flow becomes 12,000 × 1/1.25 = 9,600. Debt/cash flow therefore rises from 4 to 5, despite unchanged sales volume.

legendary.q: A government increasingly finances deficits by creating money. As inflation expectations rise, households try to hold smaller real money balances. Why can continued reliance on seigniorage become increasingly disruptive?
options: The shrinking demand to hold real balances can require still more money creation to extract a given amount of real resources, worsening inflation pressure.
Lower money demand guarantees the government can finance the same amount of real spending with progressively less money creation and steadily less inflation forever.
Seigniorage becomes costless once households expect inflation.
The quantity theory implies real output must rise one-for-one with the extra money creation.
legendary.commonError: Treats money creation as a costless financing source regardless of public money demand.
legendary.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

legendary.q: A heavily indebted economy experiences an unexpected 6 percent fall in the overall price level while nominal debts are fixed. Which balance-sheet effect is most likely?
options: Debtors receive an automatic reduction in the nominal face value of their debts.
Creditors lose because every repayment dollar is worth less in real terms.
The fall in the price level is disinflation and therefore cannot affect real debt burdens.
Debtors face a higher real repayment burden, which can weaken spending and financial positions.
legendary.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
legendary.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

legendary.q: Inflation drops from 12 percent to 4 percent after a stabilization program, but the price level continues to rise. A student calls this deflation. What is the best evaluation?
options: The student is correct only if nominal interest rates also fall.
The student is wrong because disinflation requires inflation to become negative.
The student is wrong: inflation slowed, but deflation requires the overall price level to fall.
The student is correct because any decline in the inflation rate means the overall price level must also be falling.
legendary.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
legendary.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

easyBoss.q: Which statement correctly describes fiat money?
options: It has value because people accept it and government supports its use.
It has value because the material itself is valuable.
It can only serve as a store of value.
It is excluded from the money supply.
easyBoss.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
easyBoss.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. It works because people accept it.

easyBoss.q: A person uses dollars to buy groceries, compare prices, and save for next month. Which functions of money are being used?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value
Store of value only
Unit of account only
Reserve requirement and money multiplier
easyBoss.commonError: thinking money only has one function at a time
easyBoss.feedback: Buying, comparing prices, and saving line up with the three core functions of money.

easyBoss.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Currency held by the public is $900, checkable deposits are $1,100, savings deposits are $1,500, and small time deposits are $500. What are M1 and M2?
easyBoss.commonError: forgetting M2 includes M1 plus near monies
easyBoss.feedback: M1 is $900 + $1,100 = $2,000. M2 adds savings and small time deposits, so M2 = $4,000.

easyBoss.q: Which description correctly identifies the Federal Reserve?
options: the central bank of the United States
the agency that writes federal spending bills
the agency that collects income taxes
a private household lender
easyBoss.commonError: confusing the Fed with fiscal agencies
easyBoss.feedback: The Fed is the U.S. central bank. It handles monetary policy, not tax law.

easyBoss.q: The FOMC is most directly connected to
options: open-market operations and monetary policy
writing the federal budget
calculating the CPI
setting income tax brackets
easyBoss.commonError: confusing FOMC actions with fiscal policy
easyBoss.feedback: The FOMC conducts monetary policy largely through open-market operations.

easyBoss.q: A central bank faces political pressure to expand money before an election. Why does central bank independence matter here?
options: It limits political pressure for excessive money growth.
It lets the Fed set income tax rates.
It prevents all inflation forever.
It makes banks stop lending.
easyBoss.commonError: thinking Fed independence has nothing to do with inflation risk
easyBoss.feedback: Independence can help keep monetary policy from being pushed around for short-run political gain.

easyBoss.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, $110,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. How much can it lend?
easyBoss.commonError: treating all reserves as lendable reserves
easyBoss.feedback: Required reserves are $80,000. Excess reserves are $110,000 - $80,000 = $30,000.

easyBoss.q: In a fractional reserve system, banks
options: hold part of deposits as reserves and lend the rest
must hold 100 percent of deposits as reserves
cannot affect the money supply
create money by printing currency
easyBoss.commonError: thinking banks create money by printing cash
easyBoss.feedback: Banks create deposits through lending, not by printing currency.

easyBoss.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. A public cash deposit of $5,000 enters a banking system with a 20 percent reserve requirement. What is the first bank's initial loan and the simple maximum total deposit expansion?
options: Initial loan = $4,000; total expansion = $25,000
Initial loan = $1,000; total expansion = $5,000
Initial loan = $5,000; total expansion = $25,000
Initial loan = $4,000; total expansion = $20,000
easyBoss.commonError: confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion
easyBoss.feedback: The bank lends $4,000. The multiplier is 1/0.20 = 5, so total expansion can reach $25,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

easyBoss.q: If the Fed buys government bonds, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed
turn into commodity money
easyBoss.commonError: thinking bond purchases remove money from circulation
easyBoss.feedback: Buying bonds injects reserves and tends to increase the money supply.

easyBoss.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply using open-market operations, what should it do?
options: Sell government bonds.
Buy government bonds.
Lower reserve requirements.
Lower the discount rate.
easyBoss.commonError: thinking bond sales add reserves
easyBoss.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

easyBoss.q: The Fed sells $20 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 5. Under the simple model, what is the maximum decrease in the money supply?
options: $100 million
$20 million
$4 million
$25 million
easyBoss.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
easyBoss.feedback: A $20 million bond sale times multiplier 5 gives a maximum $100 million money-supply decrease.

easyBoss.q: Why is the Fed's control over the money supply imperfect?
options: Excess reserves and public currency holdings.
The Fed cannot influence reserves.
Banks cannot lend money.
Currency is not money.
easyBoss.commonError: assuming Fed control is mechanically perfect
easyBoss.feedback: The Fed can influence money creation, but banks and the public also matter.

easyBoss.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks choose not to lend because they are worried about risk. What happens relative to the simple multiplier?
options: Money creation is weaker than predicted.
Money creation is stronger than predicted.
The money supply must fall to zero.
The simple multiplier becomes infinite.
easyBoss.commonError: thinking reserves automatically become loans
easyBoss.feedback: If banks hold reserves instead of lending, deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

easyBoss.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks hold some excess reserves, and households keep some proceeds as currency. What is the best conclusion?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by exactly the simple multiplier amount.
The money supply must fall because households hold currency.
The Fed has perfect control over final money creation.
easyBoss.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed
easyBoss.feedback: Excess reserves and currency drain both weaken the multiplier. The Fed is powerful, not magical.

easyBoss.q: In the liquidity-preference model, the opportunity cost of holding money is the:
options: Interest income forgone by not holding interest-bearing assets.
The current price level paid for goods and services during the year.
The required reserve ratio applied to deposits held by commercial banks.
The previous year’s inflation rate reported by the statistical agency.
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing the opportunity cost of money with a price index or reserve rule.
easyBoss.feedback: Holding money sacrifices the interest that could have been earned on bonds or other interest-bearing assets.

easyBoss.q: If the money supply increases while money demand is unchanged, the equilibrium interest rate tends to:
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to the inflation rate.
easyBoss.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
easyBoss.feedback: More money supplied at each interest rate creates excess money balances until the interest rate falls.

easyBoss.q: Which event shifts money demand to the right?
options: An open-market purchase that increases money supply.
A decrease in the amount of currency printed.
An increase in real income and transactions.
A lower required reserve ratio by itself.
easyBoss.commonError: Selecting a money-supply event as a money-demand shifter.
easyBoss.feedback: Higher income generates more transactions and raises the quantity of money people want to hold at each interest rate.

easyBoss.q: The central bank buys government bonds from the public. What is the first link in the usual expansionary transmission chain?
options: Reserves and the money supply rise, pushing interest rates down.
Bank reserves fall and interest rates rise immediately.
Government purchases increase before the money market changes.
Aggregate supply shifts right because banks hold more bonds.
easyBoss.commonError: Skipping the money-supply and interest-rate links after an open-market purchase.
easyBoss.feedback: A bond purchase adds reserves to the banking system, supports money creation, and tends to lower market interest rates.

easyBoss.q: Why can lower interest rates increase aggregate demand in the short run?
options: They automatically reduce all product prices.
They increase investment and other rate-sensitive spending.
They raise required reserve ratios for banks.
They directly increase government purchases.
easyBoss.commonError: Treating monetary policy as a direct change in government spending or product prices.
easyBoss.feedback: Lower borrowing costs encourage investment and some durable consumption, shifting aggregate demand to the right.

easyBoss.q: Money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged. What happens at the new money-market equilibrium?
options: The equilibrium interest rate rises.
The price level must fall immediately.
The equilibrium interest rate falls.
Real output must remain permanently fixed.
easyBoss.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
easyBoss.feedback: With money demand fixed, a larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate.

easyBoss.q: In the equation MV = PY, what does velocity measure?
options: The percentage rate at which the overall price level changes.
The amount of real output produced by each unit of labor.
The interest rate the central bank pays on reserve balances.
The average turnover of money in purchases of final output.
easyBoss.commonError: Confusing velocity with inflation, productivity, or an interest rate.
easyBoss.feedback: Velocity links the money stock to nominal spending by measuring the average turnover of money.

easyBoss.q: Money grows 10 percent, real output grows 4 percent, and velocity is stable. What inflation rate is predicted?
options: Approximately 6 percent.
Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.
easyBoss.commonError: Failing to subtract real-output growth from money growth.
easyBoss.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is approximately money growth minus real-output growth: 10 - 4 = 6 percent.

easyBoss.q: If money supply and velocity are unchanged while real output rises, what must happen to the price level in MV = PY?
options: The price level rises.
The price level falls.
The price level stays fixed by definition.
Nominal GDP doubles.
easyBoss.commonError: Assuming higher real output always raises the price level when nominal spending is fixed.
easyBoss.feedback: If MV is unchanged and Y rises, P must fall so that PY continues to equal nominal spending.

easyBoss.q: Which outcome is most consistent with long-run monetary neutrality after a one-time increase in the money supply?
options: A higher price level with real output determined by real productive factors.
Permanently higher real output with no change in nominal prices.
Permanently lower prices because more money makes each dollar more valuable.
A permanently higher real wage solely because the number of dollars increased.
easyBoss.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
easyBoss.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

easyBoss.q: A worker’s nominal wage and the price level both rise 10 percent while productivity is unchanged. What happens to the worker’s real wage approximately?
options: It rises about 20 percent.
It rises exactly 10 percent.
It falls exactly 10 percent.
It is roughly unchanged.
easyBoss.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
easyBoss.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

easyBoss.q: Which variable is nominal rather than real?
options: Hours of labor used to produce haircuts.
Haircuts produced per worker.
The dollar price of a haircut.
The quantity of haircuts produced.
easyBoss.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
easyBoss.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

easyBoss.q: If expected inflation rises while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged, the Fisher effect predicts that the nominal interest rate will:
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to real GDP growth.
easyBoss.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
easyBoss.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

easyBoss.q: Which inflation rate matters when lenders set a nominal rate today for a future loan period?
options: Only last year’s inflation.
Only inflation observed after repayment.
The unemployment rate instead of inflation.
Expected inflation.
easyBoss.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
easyBoss.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

easyBoss.q: The real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 5 percent. The Fisher approximation gives a nominal rate near:
options: 3 percent.
15 percent.
8 percent.
2 percent.
easyBoss.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
easyBoss.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

easyBoss.q: A store must repeatedly change price labels because the overall price level is rising. This is primarily a:
options: Menu cost.
Shoeleather cost.
Natural-rate effect.
Money-multiplier effect.
easyBoss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
easyBoss.feedback: Repeatedly changing price labels is a menu cost because firms spend resources updating posted prices.

easyBoss.q: People make more frequent transfers so they can hold smaller cash balances during inflation. This is primarily a:
options: Menu cost.
Fisher-effect premium.
Reserve requirement.
Shoeleather cost.
easyBoss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
easyBoss.feedback: Extra transfers to keep smaller cash balances are shoeleather costs because households spend time and effort reducing money holdings.

easyBoss.q: Unexpected inflation is higher than lenders anticipated on fixed-rate loans. Who tends to gain?
options: Both sides equally, because unexpected inflation cannot redistribute purchasing power.
Only the central bank, because private contracts are unaffected by inflation.
Borrowers, because repayment dollars have less purchasing power than expected.
Lenders, because inflation always raises realized real returns.
easyBoss.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
easyBoss.feedback: Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between parties to fixed nominal contracts because the realized price level differs from what they expected.

easyBoss.q: When money-financed government spending reduces the purchasing power of existing money balances, the burden is called:
options: The inflation tax.
Crowding out.
The money multiplier.
The natural rate.
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
easyBoss.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

easyBoss.q: Inflation falls from 6 percent to 3 percent while prices continue to rise. This is:
options: Deflation.
Hyperinflation.
Monetary neutrality.
Disinflation.
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
easyBoss.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

easyBoss.q: If the overall price level falls, the value of money generally:
options: Becomes zero.
Equals the inflation rate.
Rises.
Falls.
easyBoss.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
easyBoss.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

mediumBoss.q: Which item belongs in M1 under standard textbook definitions?
options: A balance in a checking account.
A small time deposit.
A retail money-market mutual fund.
A long-term corporate bond.
mediumBoss.commonError: Including broad near-money assets in the narrow M1 measure.
mediumBoss.feedback: Checking deposits are immediately spendable and are included in M1.

mediumBoss.q: A restaurant posts every menu price in dollars. Which function of money is being used?
options: Medium of exchange.
Unit of account.
Store of value.
Commodity backing.
mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the act of quoting prices with settling a transaction.
mediumBoss.feedback: Money serves as a unit of account when it provides the common measurement used to state prices.

mediumBoss.q: A saver moves funds from checking to a small time deposit. Which result is correct?
options: M1 and M2 both decrease.
M1 does not change, but M2 increases.
M1 decreases, but M2 does not change.
M1 and M2 both increase.
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating an internal transfer within M2 as a change in M2.
mediumBoss.feedback: Checking is in M1 and M2; a small time deposit is in M2 only. The transfer lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

mediumBoss.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Federal Reserve from a commercial bank?
options: The Fed can create reserve balances; a commercial bank creates deposits when it makes loans
The commercial bank creates Federal Reserve reserve liabilities for the payment system, while the Fed creates private bank capital for each lender
Both institutions issue only physical currency and neither creates account balances
The Fed accepts household checking deposits in the same way as a retail bank
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
mediumBoss.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

mediumBoss.q: Which statement best distinguishes the Federal Reserve from the U.S. Treasury?
options: The Treasury conducts monetary policy and determines bank reserve conditions; the Fed sets federal tax rates for Congress
The two names refer to the same institution
The Fed manages congressional spending while the Treasury supplies bank reserves
The Fed conducts monetary policy; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
mediumBoss.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

mediumBoss.q: A central-bank committee decides to change monetary conditions. Which institutional description is most accurate?
options: The committee determines federal tax rates and appropriations for the entire national budget
The committee measures M1 but has no connection to monetary policy
The policy-making body chooses monetary actions within the central bank’s mandate
The committee directly approves household mortgages at commercial banks
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
mediumBoss.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

mediumBoss.q: Deposits are $600,000, the reserve requirement is 10 percent, and actual reserves are $90,000. Excess reserves are:
mediumBoss.commonError: Failing to subtract required reserves.
mediumBoss.feedback: Required reserves are $60,000, leaving $30,000.

mediumBoss.q: A bank makes a loan from excess reserves. On the bank’s balance sheet, the new loan is:
options: A withdrawal.
Capital.
An asset.
A liability.
mediumBoss.commonError: Misclassifying a bank loan.
mediumBoss.feedback: The borrower owes the bank, so the loan is an asset.

mediumBoss.q: A simple money multiplier of 4 corresponds to what reserve ratio?
options: 25 percent.
4 percent.
20 percent.
40 percent.
mediumBoss.commonError: Using the percentage rather than its reciprocal.
mediumBoss.feedback: The reserve ratio is the reciprocal of the multiplier: 1/4 = 25 percent.

mediumBoss.q: To increase banking-system reserves through open-market operations, the central bank should:
options: Sell government securities.
Buy government securities.
Raise taxes.
Increase reserve requirements.
mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the reserve effect of an open-market purchase.
mediumBoss.feedback: When the central bank buys securities, it pays by adding reserves to the banking system.

mediumBoss.q: What is the usual effect of lowering the discount rate?
options: Banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves.
The central bank removes reserves by selling bonds.
Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks.
Households are required to reduce currency holdings.
mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing the discount rate with reserve requirements or open-market sales.
mediumBoss.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost of borrowing reserves directly from the central bank.

mediumBoss.q: Which policy action is contractionary?
options: Buying government securities in the open market.
Lowering the interest paid on reserve balances.
Lowering reserve requirements.
Selling government securities in the open market.
mediumBoss.commonError: Selecting an expansionary tool as contractionary.
mediumBoss.feedback: An open-market sale withdraws reserves and tends to reduce money and credit expansion.

mediumBoss.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold much of them as excess reserves. What is the likely result?
options: Broad deposit creation is smaller than the simple multiplier maximum
Deposit creation must equal the maximum because reserves increased
The money supply must fall by the amount of the reserve injection
Required reserves disappear from bank balance sheets
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
mediumBoss.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

mediumBoss.q: Households convert part of each new bank deposit into currency rather than leaving the funds in banks. What happens to the deposit-multiplication process?
options: It strengthens because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves
It is unchanged because currency and bank reserves are identical
It guarantees a larger simple multiplier regardless of the reserve ratio
It weakens because less money is redeposited into banks for additional lending
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
mediumBoss.feedback: When households keep currency, less of each loan is redeposited; fewer redeposits support fewer subsequent lending rounds, weakening deposit multiplication.

mediumBoss.q: Banks have ample reserves and are willing to lend, but creditworthy firms postpone borrowing during a severe slump. Which limitation is illustrated?
options: Household currency holdings must have fallen to zero
Bank capital automatically rises whenever firms reject loans
Weak loan demand can keep money creation below the textbook maximum
The central bank has lost the legal authority to create reserves
mediumBoss.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
mediumBoss.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

mediumBoss.q: The price level rises while the nominal money supply is fixed. What happens in the money market?
options: Money demand falls and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Money supply rises and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Both curves remain fixed because only prices changed.
Money demand rises and the equilibrium interest rate increases.
mediumBoss.commonError: Ignoring the transaction-money demand created by a higher price level.
mediumBoss.feedback: A higher price level increases nominal transaction needs, shifting money demand right and raising the interest rate with fixed supply.

mediumBoss.q: The central bank increases the money supply. Through the interest-rate effect, what happens next?
options: The interest rate falls, encouraging investment and aggregate demand.
The interest rate rises, reducing investment and aggregate demand.
The price level falls before the interest rate changes.
Money demand shifts left because reserves increased.
mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the monetary-policy transmission chain.
mediumBoss.feedback: A larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate, which tends to increase interest-sensitive spending.

mediumBoss.q: Real income falls while the money supply is fixed. What is the likely equilibrium change?
options: Money demand rises and the interest rate increases.
Money demand falls and the interest rate decreases.
Money supply falls and the interest rate increases.
Money demand is unchanged because income is real.
mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the money-demand response to lower transaction volume.
mediumBoss.feedback: Lower real income reduces transactions, shifts money demand left, and lowers the equilibrium interest rate.

mediumBoss.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold most of them as excess reserves. How does this affect the transmission mechanism?
options: Money and credit expand more, making aggregate demand rise farther.
The policy becomes contractionary because excess reserves reduce taxes.
Aggregate demand rises by the same amount because reserve use never matters.
Money and credit expand less, weakening the interest-rate and aggregate-demand response.
mediumBoss.commonError: Assuming reserve injections always create the same money and credit expansion.
mediumBoss.feedback: When banks hold added reserves rather than lending them, money creation and the downstream spending response are weaker.

mediumBoss.q: Interest rates fall after an expansionary policy, but firms believe future sales will remain weak. What is the likely result?
options: Investment responds only modestly, so the rightward shift of aggregate demand is limited.
Investment surges because interest rates are the only influence on firms.
Aggregate demand shifts left because lower rates reduce borrowing.
The money supply contracts automatically when firms are pessimistic.
mediumBoss.commonError: Assuming lower rates guarantee a large investment response regardless of expectations.
mediumBoss.feedback: Weak expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing costs fall, weakening policy transmission.

mediumBoss.q: Which sequence correctly traces a contractionary open-market operation through aggregate demand?
options: Bond sales raise reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
Bond sales drain reserves, raise interest rates, reduce investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Bond purchases reduce reserves, raise investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Higher taxes reduce reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
mediumBoss.commonError: Reversing the reserve, interest-rate, or spending links in contractionary policy.
mediumBoss.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, contracts money and credit, raises rates, reduces interest-sensitive spending, and lowers aggregate demand.

mediumBoss.q: Which equation links the money supply, velocity, the price level, and real output?
options: M x V = P x Y
M + V = P + Y
P x M = V x Y
M / V = P / Y
mediumBoss.commonError: mixing up the parts of the quantity equation
mediumBoss.feedback: The quantity equation is M x V = P x Y.

mediumBoss.q: If M = 600, V = 5, and Y = 1,000, what is P?
mediumBoss.commonError: dividing by velocity instead of output
mediumBoss.feedback: M x V = P x Y, so 600 x 5 = P x 1,000. P = 3.

mediumBoss.q: If money supply shifts right and the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 2 to 4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays fixed.
mediumBoss.commonError: reading value of money as the price level
mediumBoss.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. A fall from 1/2 to 1/4 means P rises from 2 to 4.

mediumBoss.q: Which unit is used to express a nominal variable?
options: monetary units
physical units
real output units
labor hours only
mediumBoss.commonError: confusing nominal with real
mediumBoss.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in money terms, such as dollars.

mediumBoss.q: A nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 5 to 6 units.
It falls from 5 to 3.33 units.
It doubles.
mediumBoss.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
mediumBoss.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It starts at 20/4 = 5 and ends at 30/6 = 5.

mediumBoss.q: A country's money supply doubles, and in the long run all nominal prices and wages double while output is unchanged. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs
mediumBoss.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
mediumBoss.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

mediumBoss.q: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to
options: nominal interest rates
real GDP only
reserve requirements
M1 only
mediumBoss.commonError: thinking expected inflation is unrelated to nominal rates
mediumBoss.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

mediumBoss.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent, the nominal interest rate is about
options: 9 percent
5 percent
7 percent
14 percent
mediumBoss.commonError: subtracting expected inflation when solving for nominal rate
mediumBoss.feedback: Nominal interest is real interest plus expected inflation: 2 + 7 = 9 percent.

mediumBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent while the real interest rate falls from 4 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
mediumBoss.commonError: tracking only expected inflation and ignoring the real rate change
mediumBoss.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 3 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 8 = 10 percent.

mediumBoss.q: Shoeleather costs of inflation come from people
options: spending resources to reduce money holdings
changing posted prices
borrowing from the Fed
holding required reserves
mediumBoss.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
mediumBoss.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.

mediumBoss.q: A borrower expected inflation to be 2 percent, but actual inflation is 8 percent. Who benefits?
options: Borrowers benefit because they repay with less valuable dollars.
Lenders benefit because they receive more purchasing power.
No one is affected by unexpected inflation.
Only workers benefit because real wages rise.
mediumBoss.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
mediumBoss.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers because they repay with dollars worth less than expected.

mediumBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan has a 9 percent nominal interest rate. Expected inflation was 3 percent, but actual inflation was 10 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real interest rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 6 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 9 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
mediumBoss.commonError: using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate
mediumBoss.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. Realized real rate is 9 - 10 = -1 percent.

mediumBoss.q: When a government finances spending by printing money, this is called
options: an inflation tax
crowding out
a liquidity trap
a reserve requirement
mediumBoss.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit
mediumBoss.feedback: Printing money can act like an inflation tax by reducing the purchasing power of money.

mediumBoss.q: Use the quantity-equation growth approximation. A government prints money heavily to pay bills. Money growth rises to 18 percent, velocity is stable, and real output grows 4 percent. What inflation rate is predicted?
options: 14 percent
18 percent
22 percent
4 percent
mediumBoss.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth
mediumBoss.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is about money growth minus output growth: 18 - 4 = 14 percent.

mediumBoss.q: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates increase. Which concepts are linked?
options: Inflation tax, quantity theory, and Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and M1
Liquidity trap, real GDP, and commodity money
Menu costs, unemployment, and barter
mediumBoss.commonError: not connecting money creation to inflation expectations and nominal rates
mediumBoss.feedback: Money-financed deficits can raise inflation, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

finalBoss.q: A bank customer withdraws $500 from checking and holds the cash. What happens to M1?
options: M1 falls by $500 because checking deposits decline.
M1 rises by $500 because currency increases.
M1 falls while M2 rises by $500.
M1 is unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
finalBoss.commonError: Looking at one component change without accounting for the offsetting M1 component.
finalBoss.feedback: Currency held by the public and checking deposits are both in M1, so the transfer changes composition rather than the total.

finalBoss.q: An online service lets users pay merchants directly from savings accounts. What is the safest conclusion about money measurement?
options: Classification still depends on the official definition of the account.
Every savings balance automatically moves into M1 once direct payments are possible.
The payment service creates new money each time a customer completes a purchase.
Savings accounts must be removed from M2 because they are now easier to spend.
finalBoss.commonError: Assuming technology alone automatically changes official monetary definitions.
finalBoss.feedback: A new payment channel can make an asset more usable without automatically changing how statistical agencies classify the underlying account.

finalBoss.q: Prices are quoted in dollars, workers accept dollars as wages, and households save dollars for emergencies. What does this example show?
options: Money is performing only as a medium of exchange.
Money is performing all three primary functions.
Money is performing only as a unit of account.
Money is performing only as a store of value.
finalBoss.commonError: Selecting one function when the scenario demonstrates several.
finalBoss.feedback: The dollar measures value, settles transactions, and transfers purchasing power over time.

finalBoss.q: A solvent bank cannot obtain overnight funding during a panic, while an insolvent bank has losses larger than its capital. Which central-bank principle is most important?
options: Neither bank can receive liquidity because central banks deal only with government budgets
Liquidity lending can help the solvent bank, but it cannot by itself restore the insolvent bank’s capital
Both problems are identical and can be solved by unlimited reserve creation
Only the insolvent bank qualifies for lender-of-last-resort support because it has larger losses
finalBoss.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
finalBoss.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

finalBoss.q: The government establishes the central bank’s mandate, but elected officials cannot order a pre-election interest-rate change. The bank must explain its decisions publicly. What does this arrangement combine?
options: Instrument independence with democratic accountability
Complete independence from any public mandate
Fiscal dominance with no central-bank discretion
Commercial-bank control of the monetary-policy mandate
finalBoss.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
finalBoss.feedback: Elected institutions establish the public mandate, while the central bank retains day-to-day instrument choice and reports its decisions, combining operational independence with accountability.

finalBoss.q: The central bank adds reserves through an asset purchase, but banks and borrowers do not expand credit. What can still be said with confidence?
options: The asset purchase could not have occurred because every reserve increase must create the maximum amount of loans
Commercial banks must have created the reserve balances before the central bank could buy the asset
The lack of new lending means the action was fiscal rather than monetary
The central bank changed reserve conditions even though broader deposit creation did not respond mechanically
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
finalBoss.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

finalBoss.q: A bank has $1.5 million in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $240,000 in reserves. Its maximum immediate new lending is:
options: $1.32 million.
finalBoss.commonError: Confusing required reserves with excess reserves.
finalBoss.feedback: Required reserves are $180,000, so excess reserves are $60,000.

finalBoss.q: A bank has $30 million in assets and $28.5 million in liabilities. Assets fall 6 percent. New capital is:
options: $1.5 million.
-$1.8 million.
-$0.3 million.
$0.3 million.
finalBoss.commonError: Applying the asset loss to the wrong base.
finalBoss.feedback: Initial capital is $1.5 million; the asset loss is $1.8 million.

finalBoss.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. A $10,000 deposit enters a system with a 20 percent reserve requirement. If banks lend all excess reserves and loans are redeposited, maximum total deposits are:
finalBoss.commonError: Confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion.
finalBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 5, so total deposits can rise by $50,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

finalBoss.q: The central bank buys securities but simultaneously raises the interest paid on reserves. Why might lending rise by less than expected?
options: The purchase adds reserves, but the higher reserve return encourages banks to hold them.
Both actions remove reserves and directly reduce the banking system’s lending capacity.
The bond purchase automatically raises reserve requirements and blocks new loans.
The higher reserve return forces banks to lend every newly created reserve dollar.
finalBoss.commonError: Assuming every tool in a policy package pushes bank lending in the same direction.
finalBoss.feedback: The open-market purchase is expansionary, while a higher return on reserves can weaken the lending response.

finalBoss.q: A central bank wants to drain reserves quickly without changing reserve requirements. Which action is most direct?
options: Buy government securities and credit reserve accounts.
Sell government securities and debit reserve accounts.
Lower the discount rate to make reserve borrowing cheaper.
Lower interest paid on reserves to discourage reserve holding.
finalBoss.commonError: Choosing an expansionary action when the goal is to remove reserves.
finalBoss.feedback: An open-market sale receives payment from the banking system and reduces reserves directly.

finalBoss.q: Reserve requirements are lowered, but banks expect severe loan losses and keep the newly available reserves idle. What does this illustrate?
options: Lower reserve requirements always produce the full textbook deposit multiplier.
Banks lose the legal ability to hold excess reserves after requirements decline.
Policy can expand lending capacity without guaranteeing that banks will lend.
The central bank shifts aggregate supply left whenever it changes reserve rules.
finalBoss.commonError: Treating potential money creation as automatic actual money creation.
finalBoss.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free reserves for lending, but risk perceptions and bank choices can weaken the actual expansion.

finalBoss.q: After a reserve injection, banks hold extra reserves, the public keeps some loan proceeds as currency, and firms reduce borrowing. Relative to the simple multiplier model, what should we expect?
options: No change in broad money because reserve injections affect only bank capital
A substantially smaller expansion because several leakages interrupt repeated lending and redepositing
The exact simple multiplier maximum because the three effects cancel automatically
A larger expansion because every leakage creates additional bank reserves
finalBoss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
finalBoss.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

finalBoss.q: Which statement best describes what the central bank controls most directly?
options: Its own balance sheet and reserve conditions, not the exact final quantity of broad money
The exact quantity of bank loans made to every borrower
The public’s desired split between currency and deposits
The amount every commercial bank must want to lend regardless of risk
finalBoss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
finalBoss.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

finalBoss.q: The central bank lowers a policy-related borrowing rate, but banks still see borrowers as risky and firms do not want new loans. Why can the monetary response remain weak?
options: A lower central-bank lending rate automatically raises required reserves
The policy turns into a tax change when private borrowing is weak
Commercial banks are legally required to stop lending whenever the central bank lowers a rate
Cheaper central-bank liquidity does not eliminate bank risk concerns or weak credit demand
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
finalBoss.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

finalBoss.q: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate balances which two quantities?
options: money supply and money demand
taxes and government spending
exports and imports
labor supply and labor demand
finalBoss.commonError: confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
finalBoss.feedback: The interest rate balances money supply and money demand.

finalBoss.q: If the price level rises, what happens in the money market?
options: Money demand rises and interest rates rise.
Money demand falls and interest rates fall.
Money supply rises and interest rates fall.
Money supply falls and interest rates fall.
finalBoss.commonError: thinking higher prices reduce money demand
finalBoss.feedback: Higher prices mean people need more money for transactions, so money demand rises and interest rates rise.

finalBoss.q: A higher price level raises money demand, interest rates rise, and investment falls by $40 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what is the total AD decrease from this channel?
options: $160 billion
$40 billion
$53.3 billion
$30 billion
finalBoss.commonError: using MPC instead of the multiplier
finalBoss.feedback: MPC 0.75 gives multiplier 4. A $40 billion investment fall reduces AD by $160 billion.

finalBoss.q: Through the interest-rate channel, expansionary monetary policy shifts aggregate demand in which direction?
options: right
left
nowhere
only along short-run aggregate supply
finalBoss.commonError: thinking expansionary money shifts AD left
finalBoss.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

finalBoss.q: If the Fed increases money supply, what chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
Interest rates rise, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates fall, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates rise, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
finalBoss.commonError: thinking more money raises interest rates in this model
