finalBoss.feedback: More money lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

finalBoss.q: The Fed increases money supply and investment rises by $70 billion. If MPC = 0.6, what is the total AD increase?
options: $175 billion
$70 billion
$42 billion
$116.7 billion
finalBoss.commonError: stopping at the investment increase without applying the multiplier
finalBoss.feedback: MPC 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. A $70 billion investment increase raises AD by $175 billion.

finalBoss.q: Money supply grows 12 percent, velocity falls 2 percent, and real output grows 3 percent. What inflation rate follows from the quantity equation?
options: Approximately 3 percent.
Approximately 11 percent.
Approximately 7 percent.
Approximately 17 percent.
finalBoss.commonError: Adding all growth rates or ignoring the decline in velocity.
finalBoss.feedback: Inflation is 12 + (-2) - 3 = 7 percent.

finalBoss.q: Money supply grows 5 percent and velocity grows 1 percent. What is the implied growth rate of nominal GDP?
options: Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 5 percent.
Approximately 10 percent.
Approximately 6 percent.
finalBoss.commonError: Subtracting velocity growth from money growth when calculating nominal-spending growth.
finalBoss.feedback: Because MV equals nominal GDP, its growth is approximately money growth plus velocity growth: 5 + 1 = 6 percent.

finalBoss.q: A student claims that faster money growth can permanently raise real output at the same rate. What is the best long-run correction?
options: In the long run, sustained money growth mainly raises inflation, not real output.
Sustained money growth permanently raises real output but never prices.
Money growth has no effect on either nominal or real variables.
Velocity always adjusts to eliminate every effect of money growth.
finalBoss.commonError: Extending short-run output effects into a permanent long-run relationship.
finalBoss.feedback: In the long run, real output is determined mainly by real factors, so sustained excess money growth appears largely as inflation.

finalBoss.q: Money growth accelerates for several years. In the long-run neutrality framework, which comparison is most defensible?
options: Neutrality requires money growth to leave every nominal price and wage unchanged in the long run.
Nominal prices can be persistently higher even though money growth does not permanently raise productive capacity.
Productive capacity must rise one-for-one with the price level.
A higher price level proves long-run real output rose by the same percentage.
finalBoss.commonError: Treats a one-time nominal level change as permanent real growth.
finalBoss.feedback: A one-time monetary expansion can raise nominal levels; long-run real growth requires changes in real productive capacity.

finalBoss.q: A country redenominates so every old 100-unit price becomes 1 new unit, with contracts and wages converted proportionally. What has changed economically?
options: The nominal unit of account changed, while real quantities and relative prices need not change.
Real output fell by 99 percent because smaller numbers on price tags necessarily mean less production.
Productivity rose because fewer currency units are needed per transaction.
The natural rate of unemployment must fall because nominal wages were converted.
finalBoss.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
finalBoss.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

finalBoss.q: The central bank unexpectedly expands money, real activity rises for a time, and later output returns to potential while nominal prices remain higher. Which statement best reconciles the episode?
options: Long-run neutrality is disproved whenever any short-run real effect occurs.
Neutrality requires output to remain permanently above potential.
The episode can be neutral only if the price level eventually falls below its starting point.
Short-run real effects can coexist with long-run monetary neutrality.
finalBoss.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
finalBoss.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

finalBoss.q: Expected inflation rises from 4 to 10 percent while the equilibrium real rate falls from 3 to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal rate approximately?
options: It remains at about 7 percent because expected inflation and real rates always offset.
It rises from about 7 to about 11 percent.
It rises from about 7 to about 13 percent because the real-rate change is irrelevant.
It falls from about 7 to about 5 percent.
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
finalBoss.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

finalBoss.q: A fixed-rate loan was written when expected inflation was 2 percent, but actual inflation turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Expected inflation helped determine the original nominal rate; the surprise changes the realized real return.
The Fisher effect requires the bank to retroactively reset the nominal rate to actual inflation.
Unexpected inflation leaves the realized real return unchanged on a fixed-rate contract.
The nominal rate was based only on actual inflation, which was already known.
finalBoss.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
finalBoss.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

finalBoss.q: Nominal interest rates rise 3 percentage points while expected inflation rises 5 points. What does the Fisher decomposition imply about the real-rate component?
options: It rose by about 8 percentage points.
It rose by exactly 5 percentage points.
It must have remained unchanged because nominal rates increased.
It fell by about 2 percentage points.
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
finalBoss.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

finalBoss.q: Inflation is anticipated and nominal interest rates adjust, but firms still reprice frequently and households economize on cash balances. What does this show?
options: Anticipated inflation necessarily increases real output enough to offset every menu, cash-management, and redistribution cost.
Expected inflation can still impose menu and shoeleather costs even when some redistribution is avoided.
Expected inflation is costless whenever nominal interest rates adjust.
Menu and shoeleather costs occur only when inflation is unexpected.
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
finalBoss.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

finalBoss.q: A pension is fixed in nominal dollars and inflation is unexpectedly high. Which mechanism is most important?
options: The pension’s real purchasing power falls because the nominal payment buys less than expected.
The pension automatically rises one-for-one because every fixed nominal contract is indexed against unexpected inflation.
The price level falls, increasing the pension’s real value.
The inflation surprise affects only banks, not recipients of fixed nominal payments.
finalBoss.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
finalBoss.feedback: Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between parties to fixed nominal contracts because the realized price level differs from what they expected.

finalBoss.q: High inflation causes firms to reprice at different times, making it harder to distinguish relative-price changes from changes in the overall price level. Which cost is being described?
options: A larger money multiplier.
A lower natural unemployment rate by definition.
A statutory inflation-tax payment collected on a tax return.
Relative-price variability and signal confusion.
finalBoss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
finalBoss.feedback: When prices adjust at different times and by different amounts, inflation makes relative-price signals noisier; this is relative-price variability and signal confusion.

finalBoss.q: A government prints money to finance spending, expected inflation rises, and households reduce desired real cash balances. Which concern is most complete?
options: Households holding less money automatically raises real output enough to offset the inflation-tax burden and preserve seigniorage revenue.
Inflation-tax finance can erode real balances and become harder to sustain as people avoid holding money.
Lower money demand guarantees a stable price level despite continued money creation.
Printing money eliminates the need to consider inflation because seigniorage is a real resource.
finalBoss.commonError: Treats money creation as a costless financing source regardless of public money demand.
finalBoss.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

finalBoss.q: Unexpected deflation occurs while firms and households owe large fixed nominal debts. Which distributional effect is most likely?
options: The real burden shifts against debtors and toward creditors.
The real burden shifts against creditors because repayment dollars buy less.
Both sides are unaffected because nominal debt cannot have a real value.
All nominal debts automatically fall at the same rate as the price level.
finalBoss.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
finalBoss.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

finalBoss.q: A stabilization program reduces inflation from 20 percent to 5 percent without making inflation negative. Which statement is correct?
options: The program created deflation because any large decline in the inflation rate makes the price level fall.
The price level must have fallen 15 percent.
Disinflation requires the inflation rate to be below zero.
The program achieved disinflation; the price level can still be rising.
finalBoss.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
finalBoss.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

legendaryBoss.q: Use current U.S. definitions, in which savings deposits are part of M1. A household shifts $75,000 from checking to savings at the same bank. Later the bank originates a $12,000 loan by crediting another customer’s checking account; no loan is repaid and no other balance changes. Relative to the starting totals, how do M1 and M2 change?
options: Both rise by $12,000.
M1 falls by $63,000; M2 rises by $12,000.
Both rise by $87,000.
Both remain unchanged.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking moving funds within M2 must change M2
legendaryBoss.feedback: The checking-to-savings transfer changes neither aggregate and does not release reserves. The new loan adds a $12,000 deposit, raising both M1 and M2 by that amount.

legendaryBoss.q: M1 equals $900 billion and M2 equals $3.4 trillion. Households transfer $80 billion from checking deposits to small time deposits. What are the new values?
options: M1 remains $900 billion and M2 becomes $3.48 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 is $3.32 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
M1 becomes $980 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Subtracting the transfer from both aggregates instead of recognizing it remains inside M2.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The transfer leaves the broad M2 total unchanged but removes $80 billion from the narrower M1 measure.

legendaryBoss.q: A wallet provider reports $10 billion of customer balances that are fully backed by $10 billion already counted in bank checking deposits. What is the correct measurement treatment?
options: Add the full wallet balance to both M1 and M2 even though the deposit is counted.
Remove the bank deposit and count only the wallet balance in the money stock.
Exclude both balances because electronic monetary claims cannot be measured.
Do not add the wallet balance unless it is a separate monetary liability.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Double counting an access claim and the underlying deposit.
legendaryBoss.feedback: If the wallet balance is simply a claim on an already-counted deposit, adding both would overstate the money stock.

legendaryBoss.q: A central bank under political pressure buys bonds aggressively before an election. Banks lend most of the new reserves, and output is already near potential. Which long-run risk is most consistent with the chapter logic?
options: Excessive money growth creates inflation pressure without lasting real-output gains.
Real output permanently rises because more money creates more resources.
The price level falls because bond purchases reduce reserves.
Money demand becomes zero.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking money growth permanently raises real output
legendaryBoss.feedback: If output is near potential, aggressive money growth mainly risks inflation rather than permanent real gains.

legendaryBoss.q: A commercial bank makes a loan by crediting a deposit, while the Federal Reserve supplies reserve balances to banks. Which statement best separates the two forms of money creation?
options: Commercial banks create deposits; the central bank creates reserves and base money
Commercial banks issue reserve balances; the central bank issues all checking deposits
Both institutions can create only physical currency
Neither institution can create a financial liability
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank is solvent but temporarily unable to meet payments because short-term funding markets freeze. Which central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort principle?
options: Use tax revenue to replace every risky bank asset permanently
Refuse all liquidity because a funding shortage proves assets are worthless
Order the Treasury to guarantee every future bank loss
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral to an otherwise solvent bank
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has $80 million in assets and $74 million in liabilities. Asset values fall by 9 percent. What is the new capital position?
options: Negative $1.2 million
$6 million
$7.2 million
Negative $7.2 million
legendaryBoss.commonError: applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial capital is $6 million. A 9 percent loss on $80 million is $7.2 million, leaving capital at negative $1.2 million.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has actual reserves of $180,000 and excess reserves of $45,000. The reserve requirement is 9 percent. What are deposits?
legendaryBoss.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves

legendaryBoss.q: A bank begins with $5 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It has $700,000 in reserves. It lends all excess reserves, the loan is redeposited, and the next bank lends all excess reserves. What is the second bank's loan?
legendaryBoss.commonError: using original deposits instead of the redeposited loan
legendaryBoss.feedback: The first bank must hold $500,000, so it lends $200,000. The next bank keeps $20,000 and lends $180,000.

legendaryBoss.q: Use a hypothetical fixed-ratio reserve model with no currency drain: every loan payment is fully redeposited, credit demand is sufficient, and no other constraint binds. A bank has $10 million in deposits and $1.3 million in reserves. The reserve ratio is 10 percent. If the bank lends all excess reserves and every later bank does the same, what maximum total deposit expansion can the excess reserves support?
options: $3 million
$13 million
$1.3 million
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying all reserves instead of only excess reserves
legendaryBoss.feedback: Required reserves are $1 million, so excess reserves are $300,000. With multiplier 10, maximum expansion is $3 million.

legendaryBoss.q: A hypothetical system starts with no excess reserves. A public cash deposit of $25,000 enters the first bank. Each bank keeps the fixed 8 percent required reserve and lends the remainder. After each loan, 25 percent of its proceeds stays as public currency and 75 percent is deposited at the next bank. What is the second bank’s loan, and how much smaller is it than under full redepositing?
options: $21,160; no reduction.
legendaryBoss.commonError: forgetting the second bank also holds reserves
legendaryBoss.feedback: The first loan is $23,000. The next deposit is $23,000 × 0.75 = $17,250, of which 92 percent can be lent: $15,870. Full redepositing would permit $21,160, a difference of $5,290.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has $3,000,000 in deposits, $510,000 in reserves, and a 12 percent reserve requirement. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 15 percent. How much lending capacity remains after the change?
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the Fed changes policy
legendaryBoss.feedback: New required reserves are 0.15 x $3,000,000 = $450,000. With $510,000 in reserves, lending capacity is $60,000.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply by $480 million. The money multiplier is 6, but currency drain is expected to make the actual multiplier closer to 4. What bond sale is closest to the needed action?
options: Sell $120 million in bonds.
Sell $80 million in bonds.
Buy $120 million in bonds.
Buy $80 million in bonds.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the simple multiplier instead of the adjusted multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: With the actual multiplier closer to 4, the Fed sells $480 million / 4 = $120 million in bonds.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed buys bonds, lowers the discount rate, but raises interest on reserves sharply. Which answer best explains why the final lending response may be muted?
options: Reserve expansion may be offset if banks prefer earning interest on reserves.
All three actions are contractionary and must reduce reserves.
Higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend every dollar.
The discount rate only affects government spending.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming all listed Fed actions push lending the same way
legendaryBoss.feedback: Bond purchases and a lower discount rate are expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can weaken lending.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed wants a $900 million maximum money expansion. The reserve ratio is 12.5 percent. Under the simple model, how large should the bond purchase be?
options: $112.5 million
$900 million
$7.2 billion
$125 million
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying the target expansion by the multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.125 = 8. Required bond purchase is $900 million / 8 = $112.5 million.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed buys $120 million in bonds. The reserve ratio is 10 percent, but banks hold 30 percent of new reserves as excess reserves. Which result is most accurate?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $1.2 billion simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $1.2 billion.
The money supply falls because bond purchases drain reserves.
The money supply rises by more than $1.2 billion because excess reserves multiply faster.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the simple multiplier as exact when excess reserves are stated
legendaryBoss.feedback: The simple maximum is $120 million x 10 = $1.2 billion, but excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has $2 million in deposits, $260,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. The public then withdraws $100,000 in currency from deposits. If deposits and reserves both fall by $100,000, what is the bank's reserve position after the withdrawal?
options: It is short $30,000 in reserves.
It has $70,000 in excess reserves.
It has exactly required reserves.
It can lend $160,000.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not reducing both deposits and reserves after currency withdrawal
legendaryBoss.feedback: After withdrawal, deposits are $1.9 million and reserves are $160,000. Required reserves are $190,000, so the bank is short $30,000.

legendaryBoss.q: In a hypothetical banking system initially without excess reserves, the public deposits $56,000 of existing currency. The required-reserve ratio stays at 20 percent. Each bank lends all excess reserves; after every loan, 25 percent stays as currency and 75 percent reaches the next bank. No other constraint binds. Including the initial deposit, what is the eventual deposit increase, and what is the net increase in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $112,000.
Deposits rise $280,000; net money rises $224,000.
Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $140,000.
Deposits rise $112,000; net money rises $84,000.
legendaryBoss.commonError: ignoring the currency leakage stated in the question
legendaryBoss.feedback: Successive deposits have ratio 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60, so their sum is $56,000/(1 − 0.60) = $140,000. Total loans are 0.80 × $140,000 = $112,000; $28,000 returns to public currency. Currency changes by −$56,000 + $28,000, so net money rises $112,000.

legendaryBoss.q: A policy memo claims that supplying more reserves guarantees the full textbook deposit expansion, even when creditworthy firms postpone borrowing and banks retain excess reserves. Which correction addresses both breaks in the argument?
options: Banks must be willing to lend and borrowers willing to borrow; unused reserves do not guarantee new deposits.
Only the reserve requirement matters; banks and borrowers cannot alter the predicted expansion.
Borrower caution raises the multiplier because fewer loans consume fewer reserves.
Excess reserves are already customer deposits, so the predicted expansion has occurred.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming reserve injections guarantee full lending
legendaryBoss.feedback: The reserve injection is an input to a conditional model. Both bank decisions and credit demand can prevent the lending and redepositing needed to reach its maximum.

legendaryBoss.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. If the investment response to the interest-rate change is $50 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the correct AD effect?
options: Money demand shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $200 billion.
Money demand shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $200 billion.
Money supply shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $50 billion.
Money demand shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $50 billion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the multiplier but reading the money-market movement backward
legendaryBoss.feedback: With fixed MS, higher MD raises r and lowers investment. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so AD falls by $200 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: Money demand shifts left while money supply is fixed. If the investment response is $45 billion and MPC = 0.5, what is the correct AD effect?
options: MD shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $90 billion.
MD shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $90 billion.
MD shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $45 billion.
MD shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $45 billion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: claiming a price-level movement when the graph is a money-market shift
legendaryBoss.feedback: A leftward MD shift lowers r and raises investment. MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so AD rises $90 billion.

legendaryBoss.q: The price level rises and shifts money demand right. The central bank wants to keep the interest rate unchanged. What action fits the model?
options: Decrease the money supply by selling securities.
Hold money supply fixed and require less investment.
Increase the money supply enough to match the higher money demand.
Shift aggregate supply left to reduce money demand.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Using contractionary policy to offset a rightward money-demand shift.
legendaryBoss.feedback: To prevent the interest rate from rising when money demand shifts right, the central bank must shift money supply right as well.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD2 and MS2, point b is above the equilibrium interest rate at d. Which adjustment best explains movement toward equilibrium?
options: An excess supply of money leads people to buy interest-bearing assets, pushing the interest rate down toward r3.
An excess demand for money leads people to sell interest-bearing assets, lowering bond prices and pushing the interest rate farther above r4 until the central bank expands money supply.
Because MS2 is vertical, point b is an equilibrium regardless of money demand.
The central bank must shift MS2 left before any interest-rate adjustment can occur.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
legendaryBoss.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the money-market graph. The economy moves from e to d because both money demand and money supply shift right. Which conclusion is supported by the final interest rate?
options: The supply shift dominates, because every increase in money supply raises the interest rate.
The two shifts exactly offset, because both curves move right.
Money demand must have shifted left, because the equilibrium quantity of money rises.
The demand shift dominates the supply shift’s interest-rate effect, because the equilibrium rate rises from r2 to r3.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes the direction of one curve shift determines the interest rate even when both money demand and money supply move.
legendaryBoss.feedback: When money demand and money supply both shift, compare the new equilibrium with the old one; the interest-rate direction depends on their relative effects.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the graph showing MS1 to MS2. In a fixed-price spending model, the resulting investment loss is $90 billion, while an independent recovery in business expectations adds $30 billion of autonomous investment. MPC is 0.6; there are no taxes, imports or further interest-rate feedbacks. What is the net shift in aggregate demand, and what independent investment recovery would exactly cancel the monetary effect?
options: AD shifts left $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $225 billion; a $30 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $60 billion; a $150 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts right $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying before finding the net spending impulse or reading the graph backward
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph supplies contractionary direction. Net autonomous investment is −90 + 30 = −60. With multiplier 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5, AD shifts left $150 billion. Exact cancellation requires a $90 billion independent recovery, before multiplication.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed wants AD to move left by $300 billion using the policy direction shown. MPC = 0.75. Each 1-point rise in r lowers investment by $25 billion. How much must r rise?
options: 3 percentage points
4 percentage points
12 percentage points
1 percentage point
legendaryBoss.commonError: solving for a rate cut even though the graph shows a rate increase
legendaryBoss.feedback: The graph shows r rising. Multiplier is 4, so investment must fall $75 billion. At $25 billion per point, r must rise 3 points.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement best explains why this is not a liquidity-trap graph?
options: A leftward money-supply shift raises r from r1 to r2.
The graph shows money demand disappearing at low interest rates.
The graph shows investment rising when r rises.
The graph shows AD shifting right after a money-supply decrease.
legendaryBoss.commonError: calling any money-market graph a liquidity trap
legendaryBoss.feedback: A liquidity trap would show weak or flat interest-rate response. This graph shows r rising clearly from r1 to r2.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Two panels with vertical MS1 and MS2, downward MD, and downward AD1 and AD2.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.

legendaryBoss.q: An expansionary policy clearly lowers the market interest rate, but firms expect very weak future sales and barely change investment. Where does the usual transmission chain primarily weaken?
options: At the link from the lower interest rate to interest-sensitive spending, so aggregate demand shifts by less than the standard chain would predict.
At the initial money-supply link, because a lower interest rate proves money supply did not change.
At the price-level definition, because expectations about sales determine whether money is a medium of exchange.
At the long-run neutrality link, which requires aggregate demand to shift by a fixed amount immediately.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Assumes a change in the policy instrument guarantees a fixed-size aggregate-demand response.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Transmission can weaken if rates respond little or if households and firms are not very responsive to the resulting borrowing-cost change.

legendaryBoss.q: After MS shifts right, P rises from 2 to 4. If M doubled and Y was constant, what must have happened to velocity for these changes to satisfy the quantity equation?
options: Velocity stayed constant.
Velocity doubled.
Velocity fell by half.
Velocity became zero.
legendaryBoss.commonError: missing that doubled M and doubled P with fixed Y implies stable V
legendaryBoss.feedback: With Y constant, doubled M and doubled P are consistent with velocity staying constant.

legendaryBoss.q: Money growth rises from 7 percent to 22 percent, velocity growth rises from 0 to 3 percent, and real output growth stays at 4 percent. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 3 percent to about 21 percent.
It rises from about 7 percent to about 22 percent.
It falls from about 21 percent to about 3 percent.
It stays at 4 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: ignoring velocity growth in the second period
legendaryBoss.feedback: Inflation equals money growth plus velocity growth minus output growth. It rises from 7 + 0 - 4 = 3 percent to 22 + 3 - 4 = 21 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: A country has M = 1,500, V = 6, and Y = 3,000. Next year M = 2,100, V = 5, and Y = 3,500. What happens to the price level?
options: It stays at 3.
It rises from 3 to 3.5.
It falls from 3 to 2.5.
It rises from 5 to 6.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming higher M must raise P without checking V and Y

legendaryBoss.q: If the value of money falls from 1 to 1/2, then later to 1/4, what happens to the price level over those two moves?
options: It rises from 1 to 2 to 4.
It falls from 1 to 1/2 to 1/4.
It rises from 1/4 to 1/2 to 1.
It stays unchanged because value of money is not related to P.
legendaryBoss.commonError: reading the value-of-money axis as the price-level axis
legendaryBoss.feedback: P is the inverse of value of money. Values 1, 1/2, and 1/4 correspond to price levels 1, 2, and 4.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the value-of-money graph. A worker earns $24 at point a and $30 at point b. Treat each point’s price level as the reciprocal of its displayed value of money. What happens to the worker’s real wage, and what nominal wage at b would instead preserve the original purchasing power?
options: Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $32 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 12 to 20 output units; $18 would preserve it.
Real wage rises from 48 to 60 output units; $24 would preserve it.
Real wage falls from 48 to 45 output units; $36 would preserve it.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not converting value of money into price level before calculating real wage
legendaryBoss.feedback: P is 1/2 at a and 2/3 at b. Real wages are 24/(1/2) = 48 and 30/(2/3) = 45. To retain 48 units at b requires 48 × 2/3 = $32.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Money graph with downward-sloping MD, vertical MS1 and MS2, and labeled points a, b, and c.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Q_M and the vertical axis is V_M. MD slopes downward from upper left to lower right. MS1 is a vertical line at Q_M = 2,500 and MS2 is a vertical line at Q_M = 5,000. Point a lies where MS1 meets MD at V_M = 2. Point b lies where MS2 meets MD at V_M = 1.5. Point c lies on MD at Q_M = 7,500 and V_M = 1. Dashed guides mark the labeled V_M and Q_M values.

legendaryBoss.q: Nominal GDP rises 15 percent, real GDP rises 6 percent, and nominal wages rise 8 percent. What happens to the price level and real wages approximately?
options: P rises about 9 percent; real wages fall about 1 percent.
P rises about 21 percent; real wages rise about 8 percent.
P falls about 9 percent; real wages rise about 17 percent.
P rises about 6 percent; real wages rise about 2 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not comparing nominal wage growth to inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Inflation is about 15 - 6 = 9 percent. Nominal wages rise 8 percent, so real wages fall about 1 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: A country doubles the number of currency units used to quote every wage and price, while production technology, labor, and relative prices are unchanged. What is the best first inference?
options: The change is nominal; the economy has not doubled its real productive capacity.
Real productive capacity doubled because every nominal amount doubled.
The natural rate of unemployment doubled because the currency unit changed.
The country necessarily experienced a permanent doubling of output per worker because every quoted nominal price and wage also doubled.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If MS shifts right and the value of money falls, expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate stays at 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 5 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: forgetting to add the real interest rate to expected inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 9 = 11 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 10 percent while the real rate falls from 4 percent to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate, and why is this not a contradiction?
options: It rises from 6 percent to 11 percent because expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.
It falls from 6 percent to 1 percent because the real rate fell.
It stays at 6 percent because changes cancel exactly.
It rises from 2 percent to 10 percent because real rates do not matter.
legendaryBoss.commonError: tracking only the real rate or only expected inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 2 = 6 percent. New nominal rate is 1 + 10 = 11 percent. Expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.

legendaryBoss.q: A country’s nominal loan rate falls from 16 to 9 percent while expected inflation falls from 12 to 4 percent. Using the Fisher approximation, what happens to the expected real rate, and by how much would the new nominal rate have had to fall further to preserve its original expected real rate?
options: The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate falls from 4 to 3 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate stays at 4 percent; no further nominal change was needed.
The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 5-point nominal cut was needed.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming lower nominal rates always mean lower real rates
legendaryBoss.feedback: Subtract expected inflation: 16 − 12 = 4 initially and 9 − 4 = 5 later. Preserving a real rate of 4 with expected inflation of 4 requires a nominal rate of 8, one point below 9.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan has a 10 percent nominal interest rate. Expected inflation was 4 percent, but actual inflation was 11 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real interest rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 6 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 10 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. Realized real rate is 10 - 11 = -1 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: MS shifts right, P rises, and firms must update thousands of posted prices while households also reduce money balances. Which pair of inflation costs is described?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and the Fisher effect
Reserve shortfalls and capital losses
Liquidity trap and fiscal lag
legendaryBoss.commonError: identifying inflation but missing the specific costs
legendaryBoss.feedback: Updating posted prices is menu cost. Reducing money balances through extra effort is shoeleather cost.

legendaryBoss.q: MS shifts right, P rises from 2 to 5, and a fixed nominal debt of $10,000 is repaid. What happens to the real burden of that debt?
options: It falls because dollars are worth less when repaid.
It rises because dollars are worth more when repaid.
It is unchanged because the nominal debt is fixed.
It rises because inflation helps creditors.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking fixed nominal debt means unchanged real burden
legendaryBoss.feedback: When P rises, money is worth less. Fixed nominal repayments become easier in real terms, helping debtors.

legendaryBoss.q: All long-term debt is fully price-indexed, wage contracts adjust correctly, and inflation is perfectly anticipated. Firms still reprice at different times and households spend time moving funds out of non-interest-bearing cash. Which evaluation separates what indexation resolves from what it leaves?
options: Debt indexation limits surprise redistribution; asynchronous prices and cash management can still consume resources or distort signals.
Debt indexation eliminates all inflation costs because every relative price must adjust at the same instant.
The remaining cash-management costs transfer wealth from borrowers to lenders without using real resources.
Perfect anticipation eliminates repricing costs but creates unexpected redistribution on the indexed debt.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking only unexpected inflation is costly
legendaryBoss.feedback: Indexation protects the real value of the specified debt. It does not make repricing instantaneous or eliminate the effort spent economizing on non-interest-bearing cash.

legendaryBoss.q: If money demand shifts right while MS is fixed and the value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, what happens to P, and what inflation term does this imply?
options: P falls from 5 to 4; this is deflation.
P rises from 4 to 5; this is inflation.
P falls from 1/4 to 1/5; this is disinflation.
P is unchanged; this is monetary neutrality.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking higher value of money means higher price level
legendaryBoss.feedback: Value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, so P falls from 5 to 4. A falling price level is deflation.

legendaryBoss.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth jumps, expected inflation rises, nominal rates rise, and people hold less cash. Which chain is most complete?
options: Expected inflation raises nominal rates and shoeleather costs.
Crowding out lowers nominal rates and eliminates inflation costs.
Reserve requirements rise automatically and make money neutral.
Commodity money replaces fiat money and ends inflation.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not connecting money finance to expectations and behavior
legendaryBoss.feedback: Money finance can act as an inflation tax, raise expected inflation and nominal rates, and make people spend resources avoiding cash holdings.

legendaryBoss.q: A government finances part of its budget by creating money, and the public’s existing money balances lose purchasing power as prices rise. What is the core mechanism?
options: Money creation transfers real purchasing power away from holders of money balances through the inflation tax.
A statutory tax authority directly debits an inflation-tax line from every bank account.
Deflation raises the real value of balances and transfers purchasing power to debtors.
The policy can finance the same amount of real spending indefinitely without reducing the purchasing power of existing money balances held by the public.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

repairQuestions.q: What makes fiat money valuable?
options: Government acceptance and public trust, not intrinsic commodity value
Its gold content alone
A fixed reserve requirement
Its use only in foreign trade
repairQuestions.feedback: Fiat money has value because it is accepted in exchange, not because the paper itself is valuable.

repairQuestions.q: Which item belongs in M1?
options: Currency held by the public
Large time deposits
Credit card debt
Corporate bonds
repairQuestions.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

repairQuestions.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item is in M2 but not M1?
options: Savings deposits
Currency
Checkable deposits
Coins
repairQuestions.feedback: M2 includes near monies such as savings deposits.

repairQuestions.q: Money used to buy goods and services is serving which function?
options: Medium of exchange
Store of value
Unit of account
Reserve ratio
repairQuestions.feedback: Buying goods and services uses money as a medium of exchange.

repairQuestions.q: Money used to compare prices is serving which function?
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Discount rate
repairQuestions.feedback: Listing prices uses money as a unit of account.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A household owns a home and stocks and earns a salary, but keeps very little currency or checking deposits. Which statement is correct?
options: Wealth and income can be high even when the household holds little money
All household wealth is counted in M1 because it can eventually be sold
Salary income is automatically part of the money supply before it is paid
Only physical currency can count as money, so checking deposits are wealth instead
repairQuestions.feedback: Money is the stock of spendable balances, not total wealth or income; a household can own valuable assets and earn a high salary while holding little currency or checking deposits.

repairQuestions.commonError: Mixing up the three functions of money.
repairQuestions.q: Money used to list the price of a laptop is serving as:
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Federal funds rate
repairQuestions.feedback: Money is a unit of account when it is used to measure and quote value.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value.
repairQuestions.q: Fiat money has value mainly because:
options: People accept it and government supports its use
The paper itself is valuable
It is always backed by gold
It is never used in modern economies
repairQuestions.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. It works because people accept it.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing fiat money and commodity money.
repairQuestions.q: Which feature distinguishes commodity money from fiat money?
options: Has intrinsic value
Cannot be used to buy goods
Is created only by banks
Is excluded from M1
repairQuestions.feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself. Fiat money does not.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that M1 includes currency and checkable deposits.
repairQuestions.q: M1 includes:
options: Currency and checkable deposits
Savings deposits only
Small time deposits only
All financial assets
repairQuestions.feedback: M1 is the narrow money measure with currency and checkable deposits.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies.
repairQuestions.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. M2 equals:
options: M1 plus near monies like savings deposits
Only currency
Only checkable deposits
Only government bonds
repairQuestions.feedback: M2 includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

repairQuestions.q: What is the central bank of the United States?
options: The Federal Reserve
The Treasury
Congress
The IRS
repairQuestions.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.

repairQuestions.q: Which group directs open-market operations?
options: FOMC
IRS
BLS
CBO
repairQuestions.feedback: The Federal Open Market Committee directs open-market operations.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A solvent bank has sound assets but cannot obtain short-term funding during a panic. Which central-bank role is designed for this situation?
options: Lender of last resort
Collector of federal income taxes
Issuer of corporate stock
Manager of the congressional budget
repairQuestions.feedback: A lender of last resort provides temporary liquidity to a solvent bank facing a funding panic.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing monetary policy with fiscal policy.
repairQuestions.q: The Fed mainly conducts:
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Tax collection
repairQuestions.feedback: The Fed handles monetary policy, not taxes and government spending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing the FOMC with Congress.
repairQuestions.q: The FOMC is most closely tied to:
options: Open-market operations
Income tax rates
Federal spending bills
GDP measurement
repairQuestions.feedback: The FOMC helps direct monetary policy through open-market operations.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking FOMC decisions are fiscal policy.
repairQuestions.q: When the FOMC buys or sells bonds, it is using:
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Labor policy
repairQuestions.feedback: Buying and selling bonds is monetary policy.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: Elected officials establish a central bank’s mandate, while the bank chooses how to use its policy instruments and reports its decisions publicly. What principle does this arrangement illustrate?
options: Instrument independence combined with public accountability
Complete independence from any publicly established mandate
Fiscal dominance because elected officials choose tax rates
Abolition of central-bank discretion over policy instruments
repairQuestions.feedback: The arrangement gives the bank instrument independence within a public mandate and requires it to explain its decisions, preserving democratic accountability.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing the link between political pressure and inflation risk.
repairQuestions.q: Political pressure to print money can create risk of:
options: Inflation
Deflation always
Zero money demand
No nominal prices
repairQuestions.feedback: Politically driven money growth can create inflation pressure.

repairQuestions.q: A bank gets $1,000 in deposits and must hold $100. How much can it lend?
repairQuestions.feedback: The bank can lend deposits minus required reserves: $1,000 - $100 = $900.

repairQuestions.q: Deposits are $1,000 and the reserve requirement is 10 percent. Required reserves are:
repairQuestions.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement: $1,000 x 0.10 = $100.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A bank suffers a loss because some of its loan assets lose value. Which balance-sheet item absorbs the loss first?
options: Bank capital
Required reserves
Customer deposits automatically increase
New loans created after the loss
repairQuestions.feedback: Bank capital absorbs losses first because it is the difference between the bank’s assets and liabilities; a decline in asset value reduces that cushion.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating all reserves as excess reserves.
repairQuestions.q: Excess reserves equal:
options: Actual reserves minus required reserves
Deposits plus loans
Required reserves minus deposits
Currency plus M2
repairQuestions.feedback: Excess reserves are actual reserves beyond what the bank is required to hold.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating all reserves as lendable.
repairQuestions.q: If actual reserves are $150 and required reserves are $100, excess reserves are:
repairQuestions.feedback: Excess reserves are $150 - $100 = $50.

repairQuestions.q: If the reserve requirement is 20 percent, the simple money multiplier is:
repairQuestions.feedback: The simple multiplier is 1/reserve requirement, so 1/0.20 = 5.

repairQuestions.q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, what can happen next?
options: The loan can become a deposit elsewhere and support further lending
The money supply must shrink immediately
Required reserves disappear
The loan stops being an asset
repairQuestions.feedback: Loans can become deposits at other banks, allowing the deposit-creation process to continue.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A bank makes a new loan by crediting the borrower’s deposit account. Which statement best describes the textbook balance-sheet effect?
options: The bank adds a loan asset and a deposit liability; it does not hand the borrower a pile of reserves
The bank permanently loses required reserves equal to the full loan amount
The bank creates new capital equal to the loan and leaves deposits unchanged
The central bank must approve and create each commercial-bank loan individually
repairQuestions.feedback: When the bank credits the borrower’s account, it records a loan asset and a matching deposit liability; the bank does not hand over a preexisting pile of reserves.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using the reserve ratio as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: The simple money multiplier equals:
options: 1 divided by the reserve ratio
The reserve ratio divided by 1
Deposits minus reserves
M2 minus M1
repairQuestions.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1/r.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using 0.20 as the multiplier when the reserve ratio is 20%.
repairQuestions.q: If the reserve ratio is 20%, the simple multiplier is:
If the Fed buys bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: Fed bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

repairQuestions.q: If the Fed sells bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Fall
Rise
Double
Become M2
repairQuestions.feedback: Fed bond sales drain reserves from the banking system.

repairQuestions.q: Raising the interest rate paid on bank reserves tends to:
options: Encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend
Force banks to lend all reserves
Raise the money multiplier automatically
Shift SRAS right
repairQuestions.feedback: A higher return on reserves increases the incentive to hold reserves, which can restrain lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: If the reserve requirement is lowered, other things equal, what happens to the amount of deposits banks must hold as required reserves?
options: It falls, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending
It rises, leaving fewer reserves potentially available for lending
It is unchanged because reserve requirements affect only currency
It becomes equal to total bank capital
repairQuestions.feedback: A lower reserve requirement reduces the amount of deposits that must be held as required reserves, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing that bond purchases add reserves.
repairQuestions.q: A Fed bond purchase adds money to:
options: The banking system
The tax code
Imports only
Used goods markets only
repairQuestions.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
options: Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks
Required reserves automatically rise for every bank
The Treasury must reduce government spending
The public is forced to hold less currency
repairQuestions.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost to banks of borrowing directly from the central bank.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing that bond sales drain reserves.
repairQuestions.q: A Fed bond sale usually causes bank reserves to:
options: Fall
Rise
Double automatically
Become taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: When the public pays the Fed for bonds, reserves leave the banking system.

repairQuestions.q: If a bank’s assets fall, what absorbs the loss first?
options: Bank capital
Currency
M1
The CPI
repairQuestions.feedback: Losses reduce bank capital.

repairQuestions.q: Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?
options: Banks and depositors affect lending and reserves
The Fed cannot buy bonds
Currency is not money
Deposits never change
repairQuestions.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors also affect it.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
repairQuestions.q: The simple multiplier overpredicts money creation when banks:
options: Hold excess reserves
Lend all excess reserves
Face a lower reserve ratio
Receive new deposits
repairQuestions.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, less money is created through lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Ignoring public currency holdings.
repairQuestions.q: If people hold more currency instead of deposits, bank money creation usually:
options: Weakens
Strengthens
Becomes unlimited
Is unaffected by reserves
repairQuestions.feedback: Currency held outside banks cannot support deposit creation the same way bank deposits can.

repairQuestions.q: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate balances:
options: Money supply and money demand
Taxes and transfers
Exports and imports
Inflation and unemployment
repairQuestions.feedback: The interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

repairQuestions.q: If money demand rises and money supply is fixed, the interest rate tends to:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Become GDP
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher money demand pushes interest rates up when money supply is fixed.

repairQuestions.q: In the money market, the equilibrium interest rate occurs where:
options: Money demand equals money supply
AD equals SRAS
Saving equals investment only
Government spending equals taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: The money-market interest rate adjusts until the quantity of money demanded equals the quantity supplied.

repairQuestions.commonError: Calls an interest-rate-induced movement along a money-demand curve a shift of the curve.
repairQuestions.q: The central bank increases the money supply while income and the price level stay unchanged. The equilibrium interest rate falls. What happens to money demand in the standard diagram?
options: There is a movement down along the existing money-demand curve; the curve itself need not shift.
The money-demand curve shifts left because the lower interest rate changes households’ desired money holdings at every possible interest rate, not just at the new equilibrium.
The money-demand curve shifts right because the central bank supplied more money.
Money demand becomes vertical because the money supply changed.
repairQuestions.feedback: A change in the interest rate causes movement along a given money-demand curve. Income or the price level can shift the money-demand curve.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
repairQuestions.q: At the current interest rate, households want to hold more money than the fixed money supply provides. Which adjustment moves the market toward equilibrium?
options: People try to obtain money by selling interest-bearing assets, putting upward pressure on the interest rate.
People buy interest-bearing assets, pushing the interest rate downward.
The money-demand curve automatically shifts left until it equals money supply.
The central bank must change money supply because the interest rate cannot adjust.
repairQuestions.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.

repairQuestions.commonError: Reversing the effect of price level on money demand.
repairQuestions.q: When the price level rises, money demand usually:
options: Rises
Falls
Becomes zero
Turns into money supply
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher prices mean people need more money for transactions.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing the investment step in the interest-rate effect.
repairQuestions.q: Higher interest rates tend to make investment:
options: Fall
Rise
Become government spending
Equal money demand
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so investment falls.

repairQuestions.q: If the Fed decreases the money supply, aggregate demand usually:
options: Shifts left as interest rates rise and spending falls
Shifts right as interest rates fall
Does not change under any circumstance
Becomes vertical
repairQuestions.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy tends to raise interest rates and reduce interest-sensitive spending, shifting AD left.

repairQuestions.q: Expansionary monetary policy usually lowers interest rates and shifts AD:
options: Right
Left
Nowhere
Into SRAS
repairQuestions.feedback: Lower interest rates raise investment and shift AD right.

repairQuestions.q: If the money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged, the equilibrium interest rate tends to:
options: Fall
Rise
Stay fixed by definition
Equal the inflation rate
repairQuestions.feedback: More money supplied at each interest rate creates downward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking more money raises interest rates in liquidity preference theory.
repairQuestions.q: If the Fed increases money supply, interest rates usually:
options: Fall
Rise
Stay fixed forever
Become inflation
repairQuestions.feedback: More money lowers the equilibrium interest rate in the liquidity preference model.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing how lower rates shift AD.
repairQuestions.q: Lower interest rates usually shift AD right because they increase:
options: Investment
Taxes
Imports only
Required reserves
repairQuestions.feedback: Lower rates increase investment spending, shifting AD right.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking less money lowers interest rates.
repairQuestions.q: If the Fed decreases money supply, interest rates usually:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: Less money raises the equilibrium interest rate.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking tighter money shifts AD right.
repairQuestions.q: Higher interest rates usually shift AD left because they reduce:
options: Investment
Taxes
Money demand
Government purchases automatically
repairQuestions.feedback: Higher interest rates reduce investment, shifting AD left.

repairQuestions.q: A student writes only “the central bank increases money supply, so aggregate demand rises.” Which missing links are essential to the standard short-run transmission mechanism?
options: The equilibrium interest rate falls and interest-sensitive spending such as investment rises before aggregate demand shifts right.
Government purchases automatically rise and then the money supply increases.
The price level falls first, which directly forces aggregate demand to shift right.
The natural rate of unemployment falls permanently, which mechanically raises aggregate demand.
repairQuestions.commonError: Jumps directly from a central-bank action to aggregate demand and skips the interest-rate and spending links.
repairQuestions.feedback: Trace the chain explicitly: money conditions change, the interest rate changes, interest-sensitive spending responds, and aggregate demand shifts.

repairQuestions.q: If money grows while velocity and output are fixed, the price level should:
options: Rise
Fall
Stay zero
Become unemployment
repairQuestions.feedback: With velocity and output fixed, more money raises the price level.

repairQuestions.q: In MV = PY, what does P represent?
options: Price level
Population
Profit
Public debt
repairQuestions.feedback: P is the price level.

repairQuestions.q: In MV = PY, what does Y represent?
options: Real output
Nominal interest rate
Money supply
Expected inflation
repairQuestions.feedback: Y is real output.

repairQuestions.q: If the price level rises, the value of money:
options: Falls
Rises
Stays fixed
Becomes GDP
repairQuestions.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it falls when the price level rises.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking value of money equals the price level.
repairQuestions.q: The value of money equals:
options: 1 divided by the price level
The price level itself
Money supply times output
Velocity divided by GDP
repairQuestions.feedback: The value of money is 1/P.

repairQuestions.commonError: Getting the inverse relationship backward.
repairQuestions.q: What happens to money's purchasing power when the price level increases?
options: Falls
Rises
Stays fixed
Becomes velocity
repairQuestions.feedback: A higher price level means each dollar buys less, so the value of money falls.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting to subtract output growth from money growth.
repairQuestions.q: If velocity is stable, inflation is approximately:
options: Money growth minus real output growth
Money growth plus real output growth
Real output growth minus money growth
MPC times money growth
repairQuestions.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus real output growth.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using money growth alone as inflation.
repairQuestions.q: Money grows 10%, output grows 3%, and velocity is stable. Inflation is about:
repairQuestions.feedback: Inflation is about 10% - 3% = 7%.

repairQuestions.q: A student says, “If money is neutral, monetary policy can never affect real output.” What is the best correction?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run real effects can occur even if long-run real output returns to a level set by real factors.
Neutrality means money changes only real output and never prices at any horizon, so even temporary short-run changes in prices, spending, or production cannot occur.
Neutrality applies only during recessions, not in long-run comparisons of nominal and real economic variables.
Neutrality means every monetary-policy action has exactly zero effect on prices, output, employment, and interest rates at every horizon.
repairQuestions.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.

repairQuestions.q: A wage measured in dollars is:
options: Nominal
Real
Relative
Imported
repairQuestions.feedback: A dollar wage is a nominal variable.

repairQuestions.q: A wage adjusted for the price level is:
options: Real
Nominal
Fiat
Reserve
repairQuestions.feedback: A wage adjusted for prices is a real wage.

repairQuestions.commonError: Looking only at the nominal wage.
repairQuestions.q: Real wage equals:
options: Nominal wage divided by price level
Nominal wage times price level
Price level divided by nominal wage
Money supply divided by wage
repairQuestions.feedback: Real wage adjusts the dollar wage for the price level.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking a higher nominal wage always means higher purchasing power.
repairQuestions.q: If nominal wage is $20 and the price level is 4, real wage is:
options: 5 units
80 units
16 units
24 units
repairQuestions.feedback: Real wage is 20 / 4 = 5 units.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking neutrality means money has no effect on prices.
repairQuestions.q: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects:
options: Long-run nominal variables
Only real variables
Neither prices nor wages
Only unemployment
repairQuestions.feedback: Money neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking money neutrality means prices are fixed.
repairQuestions.q: If all nominal prices double but real output is unchanged, this fits:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs only
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

repairQuestions.q: A borrower says the Fisher effect is found by subtracting this year’s actual inflation from a loan rate set last year. What is the key mistake?
options: The Fisher effect concerns expected inflation when the nominal rate is set, not merely realized inflation afterward.
The Fisher effect uses only the unemployment rate when a loan is made, so expected inflation has no role in nominal-rate setting.
The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to stay fixed when expected inflation changes.
The Fisher effect says actual inflation and expected inflation must always be identical.
repairQuestions.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.

repairQuestions.q: A nominal interest rate is 8 percent and inflation is 3 percent. The approximate real interest rate is:
options: 5 percent
11 percent
8 percent
-5 percent
repairQuestions.feedback: Approximate real interest equals nominal interest minus inflation: 8% − 3% = 5%.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
repairQuestions.q: The Fisher equation says nominal interest is approximately:
options: Real interest plus expected inflation
Real interest minus expected inflation
Expected inflation minus money growth
MPC times inflation
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is approximately real interest plus expected inflation.

repairQuestions.commonError: Subtracting when solving for nominal interest.
repairQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If real interest is 3% and expected inflation is 5%, nominal interest is:
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is 3% + 5% = 8%.

repairQuestions.q: Unexpected inflation redistributes wealth toward borrowers when:
options: Loans have fixed nominal payments
All loans adjust instantly with inflation
Interest rates are always zero
Prices never change
repairQuestions.feedback: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers and hurting lenders.

repairQuestions.q: Menu costs are the costs of changing:
options: Posted prices
Reserve ratios
Real GDP
Natural unemployment
repairQuestions.feedback: Menu costs are costs firms face when changing posted prices.

repairQuestions.q: Shoeleather costs come from people trying to hold:
options: Less cash during inflation
More capital during recessions
More imports during booms
Less output during deflation
repairQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from efforts to reduce cash holdings during inflation.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation.
repairQuestions.q: Unexpectedly high inflation helps:
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Only banks
No one
repairQuestions.feedback: Borrowers repay with dollars worth less than expected.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking borrowers gain from unexpectedly low inflation.
repairQuestions.q: Unexpectedly low inflation helps:
options: Lenders
Borrowers
Only workers
Only importers
repairQuestions.feedback: Lenders are repaid with dollars worth more than expected.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
repairQuestions.q: A student says, “If everyone correctly expects 6 percent inflation, inflation has no economic costs.” Which response is best?
options: Anticipation reduces some redistribution, but cash-management, repricing, tax, and relative-price costs can remain.
Correct; expected inflation removes every resource and information cost.
Correct; only unexpected deflation can create economic costs.
Incorrect only because expected inflation always lowers real GDP by exactly 6 percent and therefore creates a predictable recession every year.
repairQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing shoeleather and menu costs.
repairQuestions.q: Shoeleather costs come from:
options: Effort spent reducing money holdings
Firms changing posted prices
Banks calculating reserves
The Fed selling bonds
repairQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the time and effort spent avoiding holding too much money during inflation.

repairQuestions.q: A student looks for an “inflation tax” line on a tax return. What is the best correction?
options: The inflation tax is the loss of purchasing power on money balances when money-financed spending contributes to inflation.
It is a statutory percentage surcharge collected only from commercial banks whenever the central bank expands the money supply to finance government spending.
It is the interest payment the Treasury makes on government bonds.
It is the fall in real debt burdens caused by unexpected deflation.
repairQuestions.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
Thinking printing money is costless government revenue.
repairQuestions.q: The inflation tax comes from government financing by:
options: Printing money
Cutting money supply
Lowering prices
Reducing nominal wages
repairQuestions.feedback: Printing money can act like a tax by reducing the value of money people already hold.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking heavy money creation has no inflation risk.
repairQuestions.q: Heavy reliance on printing money can lead to:
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
Permanent deflation
Zero nominal interest rates forever
A higher value of money
repairQuestions.feedback: Persistent money creation can create high inflation.

bridgeQuestions.q: Households move cash from wallets into checking accounts. The composition of M1 changes little, but what banking consequence can the shift create?
options: Banks receive deposits and reserves that can support lending under the banking model
The deposits stop counting in M1 because checking accounts are not money
The central bank must create matching bank capital before any deposit can be accepted
The shift guarantees the maximum simple money multiplier regardless of bank behavior
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Moving cash into checking changes little in M1, but it gives banks deposits and reserves that can support lending under the banking model.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

bridgeQuestions.q: A grocery store accepts dollars for food, lists prices in dollars, and saves cash overnight. Which set matches the functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, money multiplier
Unit of account, discount rate, federal funds rate
Medium of exchange, LRAS, inflation tax
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and stores purchasing power over time.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Mixing up the three functions of money.
bridgeQuestions.q: A store lists coffee at $6, accepts dollars for payment, and the owner saves some cash for later. Which functions appear?
options: Unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value
Medium of exchange only
Store of value only
Reserve requirement and multiplier
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The price is unit of account, payment is medium of exchange, and saving is store of value.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting M2 includes M1 plus near monies.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Currency is $800, checkable deposits are $1,200, and savings deposits are $1,500. What are M1 and M2?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: M1 = currency + checkable deposits = $2,000. M2 adds savings deposits, so M2 = $3,500.

bridgeQuestions.q: A financial panic hits and the banking system needs a lender-of-last-resort institution. Which institution fits?
options: Federal Reserve
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Congressional Budget Office
Internal Revenue Service
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The Fed acts as the central bank and lender of last resort.

bridgeQuestions.q: The FOMC decides that monetary conditions should be easier and authorizes purchases of securities. What connection is being made?
options: The FOMC is choosing a monetary-policy tool that adds reserves
The Treasury is using fiscal policy to change government purchases
A commercial bank is deciding how much capital to issue to shareholders
Households are changing M1 by moving funds from checking to savings
bridgeQuestions.feedback: When the FOMC authorizes securities purchases, it is using an expansionary monetary-policy tool that adds reserve balances to banks.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Confusing the Fed with Congress or the Treasury.
bridgeQuestions.q: If a policy changes bank reserves and interest rates, it is most likely:
options: Monetary policy by the Fed
Fiscal policy by Congress
Trade policy
GDP accounting
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Changes in reserves and interest rates are monetary policy territory.

bridgeQuestions.q: A bank gets $4,000 in new deposits and must hold 25 percent in reserves. First-round lending can be:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are $1,000, so the bank can lend $3,000.

bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $8,000 in deposits and a 12.5 percent reserve requirement. Required reserves are:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are $8,000 x 0.125 = $1,000.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Using the wrong reserve calculation.
