bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $900,000 in deposits and a 12% reserve requirement. Required reserves are:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are 0.12 x $900,000 = $108,000.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treating all reserves as lendable.
bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $900,000 in deposits, a 10% reserve requirement, and $140,000 in reserves. How much can it lend?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are $90,000, so excess reserves are $50,000.

bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank adds reserves to the banking system through an asset purchase. Why does this not mean the central bank itself makes every new commercial loan?
options: The central bank supplies reserves; commercial banks and borrowers determine later lending and deposit creation
The central bank directly selects every commercial borrower and dictates the size of each loan after the asset purchase
Commercial banks can lend only currency printed during the same transaction
Asset purchases increase bank capital rather than reserve balances
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The central bank supplies reserve balances; commercial banks and borrowers determine whether those reserves support subsequent loans and deposit creation.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Confusing initial lending with total expansion.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. A $10,000 deposit enters a system with a 20% reserve ratio. What is the maximum total deposit expansion?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 5, so total expansion can reach $50,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank buys securities and bank reserves rise, but banks choose to hold much of the new reserves idle. What does this show about the policy chain?
options: The tool can increase reserves even when the resulting expansion of bank deposits is smaller than the simple model predicts
The asset purchase failed to change reserves, so it was not a monetary-policy action
Holding excess reserves forces the money multiplier above its simple maximum
A central-bank asset purchase automatically becomes fiscal policy when banks do not lend
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The asset purchase raises bank reserves, but banks’ decision to hold excess reserves can leave deposit creation below the simple-multiplier prediction.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank buys securities, increasing reserves and the money supply. In the liquidity-preference money-market model, what is the next directional step, other things equal?
options: The equilibrium interest rate tends to fall
The equilibrium interest rate must rise because reserves increased
Aggregate supply immediately shifts left before any interest-rate change
The federal budget deficit automatically falls by the amount of the purchase
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With money demand unchanged, the increase in money supply creates excess balances and puts downward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank sells securities, reducing reserves and the money supply. In the liquidity-preference money-market model, what is the next directional step, other things equal?
options: The equilibrium interest rate tends to rise
The equilibrium interest rate must fall because reserves decreased
Aggregate supply immediately shifts right before any interest-rate change
The federal budget surplus automatically rises by the amount of the sale
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With money demand unchanged, the decrease in money supply creates excess money demand and puts upward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $500,000 in assets and $30,000 in capital. If assets fall by $20,000, capital becomes:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Losses reduce capital, so $30,000 - $20,000 = $10,000.

bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold excess reserves. What should happen to deposit creation?
options: It is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts
It reaches the full multiplier automatically
It becomes unrelated to lending
It eliminates currency from M1
bridgeQuestions.feedback: If banks do not lend excess reserves, the deposit expansion process weakens.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks hold half of them as excess reserves. What happens?
options: Money creation is less than the simple multiplier predicts
Money creation is exactly the simple maximum
Money creation is larger than the simple maximum
Money supply must fall
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Excess reserve holding weakens the multiplier process.

bridgeQuestions.q: In the money market, if the interest rate is too low, quantity of money demanded is usually:
options: Greater than money supplied
Less than money supplied
Equal to zero
Equal to LRAS
bridgeQuestions.feedback: At too low an interest rate, people demand more money than is supplied, pushing rates up.

bridgeQuestions.q: Income rises, so people want to hold more money. If money supply is fixed, interest rates:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Become inflation
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher money demand with fixed money supply raises interest rates.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing money-market and AD-AS equilibrium.
bridgeQuestions.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. What happens to the interest rate?
options: It rises
It falls
It becomes zero
It turns into the price level
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes the interest rate up.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
bridgeQuestions.q: A higher price level shifts money demand right while money supply is fixed, so the equilibrium interest rate rises. To carry that money-market result into the policy-transmission model, what happens next?
options: Interest-sensitive investment falls, putting downward pressure on aggregate demand.
Investment rises because higher rates make borrowing cheaper, shifting aggregate demand right.
Aggregate demand shifts left directly because the price level changed, with no spending channel involved.
The higher interest rate shifts money demand farther right but has no effect on spending.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

bridgeQuestions.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, raising the equilibrium interest rate. What is the next step if the student is bridging from the money market to monetary-policy transmission?
options: Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive investment and put downward pressure on aggregate demand.
Higher borrowing costs raise investment because firms earn more interest.
The higher interest rate directly increases government purchases.
Aggregate demand is unaffected because interest rates matter only inside the money-market graph.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed increases the money supply. Which chain is correct?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates fall, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates rise, investment rises, AD shifts right
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Reversing the monetary-policy chain.
bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed increases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Taxes fall, consumption rises, AD shifts right
Money demand disappears, AD is unchanged
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Reversing contractionary monetary policy.
bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed decreases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Taxes rise, consumption falls, AD shifts left
Money demand disappears, AD rises
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

bridgeQuestions.q: Money grows 6 percent, velocity is stable, and output grows 2 percent. Approximate inflation is:
options: 4 percent
6 percent
8 percent
2 percent
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth minus output growth: 6 - 2 = 4 percent.

bridgeQuestions.q: If M = 200, V = 5, and Y = 500, then P equals:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: MV = PY, so 200 x 5 = P x 500, which gives P = 2.

bridgeQuestions.q: If the price level rises from 2 to 5, the value of money changes from:
options: 2 to 5
5 to 2
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it falls from 1/2 to 1/5.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Reading value of money as the price level.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use value of money = 1/P. If value falls from 1/2 to 1/4, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4
It falls from 2 to 4
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4
It stays fixed
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Value of money is 1/P, so 1/2 means P = 2 and 1/4 means P = 4.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting to subtract output growth.
bridgeQuestions.q: Money grows 12%, output grows 4%, and velocity is stable. Inflation is about:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Inflation is about 12% - 4% = 8%.

bridgeQuestions.q: If all nominal prices and wages double but real output is unchanged, this supports:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky wage theory only
A liquidity trap
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run.

bridgeQuestions.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 5 percent while inflation is 8 percent. The real wage:
options: Falls by about 3 percent
Rises by about 3 percent
Rises by about 13 percent
Does not change
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation: 5 - 8 = -3 percent.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Looking only at nominal wage growth.
bridgeQuestions.q: Nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 and the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units
It rises to 6 units
It falls to 3.33 units
It doubles
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Real wage is 20/4 = 5 and 30/6 = 5.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Thinking neutrality means no price changes.
bridgeQuestions.q: Money supply doubles, all nominal prices double, and real output is unchanged. This illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

bridgeQuestions.q: The quantity theory predicts that sustained money growth faster than real output growth can raise inflation. In the long-run neutrality framework, what should a student infer about real productive capacity?
options: Faster money growth can raise nominal prices without permanently increasing productive capacity.
Faster money growth must permanently raise productive capacity by the same percentage.
Higher inflation proves output per worker rose by the same amount.
Long-run neutrality requires inflation to be zero whenever money growth exceeds output growth.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Stops after predicting the price-level effect and does not separate nominal from real outcomes.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Use the quantity-theory result for nominal spending and prices, then apply long-run neutrality to ask which real variables need not rise permanently.

bridgeQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is:
options: 8 percent
6 percent
4 percent
2 percent
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting expected inflation in nominal rates.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Real interest is 2% and expected inflation is 6%. Nominal interest is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is 2% + 6% = 8%.

bridgeQuestions.q: Suppose long-run money growth raises expected inflation while real productive conditions leave the real interest rate unchanged. Which next step connects monetary neutrality to the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate rises to incorporate the higher expected inflation while the real-rate component stays unchanged.
The real interest rate must rise one-for-one because all nominal variables are neutral and expected inflation cannot influence nominal contract rates.
The nominal interest rate stays fixed because expected inflation affects only the price level.
Actual inflation must be known before lenders can set any nominal interest rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Recognizes nominal neutrality but does not connect expected inflation to nominal interest rates.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Once long-run real and nominal variables are separated, the Fisher effect explains why higher expected inflation is reflected in higher nominal interest rates.

bridgeQuestions.q: A restaurant reprints menus every week because prices keep changing. This is:
options: Menu cost
Shoeleather cost
Inflation tax
Money neutrality
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Menu costs are costs of changing posted prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: Inflation makes a household transfer money more often to avoid holding cash. This is:
options: Shoeleather cost
Menu cost
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the costs of reducing money holdings during inflation.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate.
bridgeQuestions.q: Nominal interest is 9%, expected inflation was 3%, but actual inflation is 10%. Who gains?
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Both equally
No one
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers repay with less valuable dollars.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing inflation cost examples.
bridgeQuestions.q: Firms repeatedly update posted prices while households make more transfers to avoid holding cash. Which costs are shown?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and liquidity trap
Reserve shortfall and bank capital loss
M1 and M2
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Price updates are menu costs; reducing cash balances creates shoeleather costs.

bridgeQuestions.q: A government prints money to pay bills and the value of existing money falls. This is closest to:
options: Inflation tax
Reserve requirement
Crowding out
Sacrifice ratio
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
bridgeQuestions.q: A government relies heavily on money creation. Inflation rises, households reduce cash balances, and they make more frequent transfers to avoid holding money. Which connection is most accurate?
options: Money finance creates an inflation-tax burden on money balances and also generates shoeleather costs.
Money finance eliminates the inflation tax because households hold less cash.
Shoeleather costs occur only during deflation, so the two effects cannot occur together.
The policy changes only real output and has no effect on nominal money balances, cash-management decisions, or the purchasing power of money.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Money creation erodes the purchasing power of money balances (the inflation tax) and encourages people to make more frequent transfers or otherwise avoid holding cash (shoeleather costs).

options: Government acceptance and public trust, not intrinsic commodity value
Its gold content alone
A fixed reserve requirement
Its use only in foreign trade
commodity_vs_fiat_money.feedback: Fiat money has value because it is accepted in exchange, not because the paper itself is valuable.

deposit_creation.q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, what can happen next?
options: The loan can become a deposit elsewhere and support further lending
The money supply must shrink immediately
Required reserves disappear
The loan stops being an asset
deposit_creation.feedback: Loans can become deposits at other banks, allowing the deposit-creation process to continue.

interest_on_reserves_policy.q: Raising the interest rate paid on bank reserves tends to:
options: Encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend
Force banks to lend all reserves
Raise the money multiplier automatically
Shift SRAS right
interest_on_reserves_policy.feedback: A higher return on reserves increases the incentive to hold reserves, which can restrain lending.

read_money_market_equilibrium.q: In the money market, the equilibrium interest rate occurs where:
options: Money demand equals money supply
AD equals SRAS
Saving equals investment only
Government spending equals taxes
read_money_market_equilibrium.feedback: The money-market interest rate adjusts until the quantity of money demanded equals the quantity supplied.

monetary_policy_ad_shift.q: If the Fed decreases the money supply, aggregate demand usually:
options: Shifts left as interest rates rise and spending falls
Shifts right as interest rates fall
Does not change under any circumstance
Becomes vertical
monetary_policy_ad_shift.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy tends to raise interest rates and reduce interest-sensitive spending, shifting AD left.

read_money_market_shift.q: If the money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged, the equilibrium interest rate tends to:
options: Fall
Rise
Stay fixed by definition
Equal the inflation rate
read_money_market_shift.feedback: More money supplied at each interest rate creates downward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

nominal_real_interest_rate.q: A nominal interest rate is 8 percent and inflation is 3 percent. The approximate real interest rate is:
options: 5 percent
11 percent
8 percent
-5 percent
nominal_real_interest_rate.feedback: Approximate real interest equals nominal interest minus inflation: 8% − 3% = 5%.

inflation_redistribution.q: Unexpected inflation redistributes wealth toward borrowers when:
options: Loans have fixed nominal payments
All loans adjust instantly with inflation
Interest rates are always zero
Prices never change
inflation_redistribution.feedback: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers and hurting lenders.

fiat_money_definition.commonError: Thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value.
fiat_money_definition.q: Fiat money has value mainly because:
options: People accept it and government supports its use
The paper itself is valuable
It is always backed by gold
It is never used in modern economies
fiat_money_definition.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. It works because people accept it.

fiat_money_definition.commonError: Confusing fiat money and commodity money.
fiat_money_definition.q: Which feature distinguishes commodity money from fiat money?
options: Has intrinsic value
Cannot be used to buy goods
Is created only by banks
Is excluded from M1
fiat_money_definition.feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself. Fiat money does not.

functions_of_money.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
functions_of_money.q: A household owns a home and stocks and earns a salary, but keeps very little currency or checking deposits. Which statement is correct?
options: Wealth and income can be high even when the household holds little money
All household wealth is counted in M1 because it can eventually be sold
Salary income is automatically part of the money supply before it is paid
Only physical currency can count as money, so checking deposits are wealth instead
functions_of_money.feedback: Money is the stock of spendable balances, not total wealth or income; a household can own valuable assets and earn a high salary while holding little currency or checking deposits.

functions_of_money.commonError: Mixing up the three functions of money.
functions_of_money.q: Money used to list the price of a laptop is serving as:
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Federal funds rate

Store of value
Discount rate
identify_money_functions.feedback: Listing prices uses money as a unit of account.

All financial assets

fed_independence.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

Deflation always
Zero money demand
No nominal prices

required_reserves_formula.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
required_reserves_formula.q: A bank suffers a loss because some of its loan assets lose value. Which balance-sheet item absorbs the loss first?

Required reserves
Customer deposits automatically increase
New loans created after the loss

required_reserves_formula.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
required_reserves_formula.q: A bank makes a new loan by crediting the borrower’s deposit account. Which statement best describes the textbook balance-sheet effect?
options: The bank adds a loan asset and a deposit liability; it does not hand the borrower a pile of reserves
The bank permanently loses required reserves equal to the full loan amount
The bank creates new capital equal to the loan and leaves deposits unchanged
The central bank must approve and create each commercial-bank loan individually
required_reserves_formula.feedback: When the bank credits the borrower’s account, it records a loan asset and a matching deposit liability; the bank does not hand over a preexisting pile of reserves.

calculate_required_reserves.q: Deposits are $1,000 and the reserve requirement is 10 percent. Required reserves are:
calculate_required_reserves.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement: $1,000 x 0.10 = $100.

calculate_excess_reserves.feedback: The bank can lend deposits minus required reserves: $1,000 - $100 = $900.

excess_reserves_formula.commonError: Treating all reserves as excess reserves.
options: Actual reserves minus required reserves
Deposits plus loans
Required reserves minus deposits
Currency plus M2
excess_reserves_formula.feedback: Excess reserves are actual reserves beyond what the bank is required to hold.

excess_reserves_formula.q: If actual reserves are $150 and required reserves are $100, excess reserves are:

money_multiplier_application.commonError: Using the reserve ratio as the multiplier.
options: 1 divided by the reserve ratio
The reserve ratio divided by 1
Deposits minus reserves
M2 minus M1

money_multiplier_application.commonError: Using 0.20 as the multiplier when the reserve ratio is 20%.
money_multiplier_application.q: If the reserve ratio is 20%, the simple multiplier is:

calculate_money_multiplier_effect.q: If the reserve requirement is 20 percent, the simple money multiplier is:
calculate_money_multiplier_effect.feedback: The simple multiplier is 1/reserve requirement, so 1/0.20 = 5.

fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.q: If the reserve requirement is lowered, other things equal, what happens to the amount of deposits banks must hold as required reserves?
options: It falls, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending
It rises, leaving fewer reserves potentially available for lending
It is unchanged because reserve requirements affect only currency
It becomes equal to total bank capital
fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.feedback: A lower reserve requirement reduces the amount of deposits that must be held as required reserves, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending.

fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.commonError: Missing that bond purchases add reserves.
fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.q: A Fed bond purchase adds money to:
options: The banking system
The tax code
Imports only
Used goods markets only
fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.q: If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
options: Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks
Required reserves automatically rise for every bank
The Treasury must reduce government spending
The public is forced to hold less currency
fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost to banks of borrowing directly from the central bank.

fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.commonError: Missing that bond sales drain reserves.
fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.q: A Fed bond sale usually causes bank reserves to:
options: Fall
Rise
Double automatically
Become taxes
fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.feedback: When the public pays the Fed for bonds, reserves leave the banking system.

choose_fed_tool_effect.q: If the Fed buys bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
choose_fed_tool_effect.feedback: Fed bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

choose_fed_tool_effect.q: If the Fed sells bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Fall
Rise
Double
Become M2
choose_fed_tool_effect.feedback: Fed bond sales drain reserves from the banking system.

actual_vs_simple_multiplier.q: If people hold more currency instead of deposits, bank money creation usually:
options: Weakens
Strengthens
Becomes unlimited
Is unaffected by reserves
actual_vs_simple_multiplier.feedback: Currency held outside banks cannot support deposit creation the same way bank deposits can.

actual_vs_simple_multiplier.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
actual_vs_simple_multiplier.q: The simple multiplier overpredicts money creation when banks:

Lend all excess reserves
Face a lower reserve ratio
Receive new deposits
actual_vs_simple_multiplier.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, less money is created through lending.

limits_of_monetary_control.q: Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?

The Fed cannot buy bonds
Currency is not money
Deposits never change
limits_of_monetary_control.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors also affect it.

bank_leverage_risk.q: If a bank’s assets fall, what absorbs the loss first?

Currency
M1
The CPI

interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.commonError: Missing the investment step in the interest-rate effect.
interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.q: Higher interest rates tend to make investment:

Rise
Become government spending
Equal money demand

interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.commonError: Reversing the effect of price level on money demand.
interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.q: When the price level rises, money demand usually:
options: Rises
Falls
Becomes zero
Turns into money supply
interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.feedback: Higher prices mean people need more money for transactions.

money_demand_interest_rate.feedback: Higher money demand pushes interest rates up when money supply is fixed.

liquidity_preference_definition.commonError: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
liquidity_preference_definition.q: At the current interest rate, households want to hold more money than the fixed money supply provides. Which adjustment moves the market toward equilibrium?
options: People try to obtain money by selling interest-bearing assets, putting upward pressure on the interest rate.
People buy interest-bearing assets, pushing the interest rate downward.
The money-demand curve automatically shifts left until it equals money supply.
The central bank must change money supply because the interest rate cannot adjust.
liquidity_preference_definition.feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.

liquidity_preference_definition.commonError: Calls an interest-rate-induced movement along a money-demand curve a shift of the curve.
liquidity_preference_definition.q: The central bank increases the money supply while income and the price level stay unchanged. The equilibrium interest rate falls. What happens to money demand in the standard diagram?
options: There is a movement down along the existing money-demand curve; the curve itself need not shift.
The money-demand curve shifts left because the lower interest rate changes households’ desired money holdings at every possible interest rate, not just at the new equilibrium.
The money-demand curve shifts right because the central bank supplied more money.
Money demand becomes vertical because the money supply changed.
liquidity_preference_definition.feedback: A change in the interest rate causes movement along a given money-demand curve. Income or the price level can shift the money-demand curve.

liquidity_preference_theory.q: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate balances:
options: Money supply and money demand
Taxes and transfers
Exports and imports
Inflation and unemployment
liquidity_preference_theory.feedback: The interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

contractionary_monetary_policy_chain.commonError: Thinking tighter money shifts AD right.

options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
contractionary_monetary_policy_chain.feedback: Less money raises the equilibrium interest rate.

expansionary_monetary_policy_chain.commonError: Missing how lower rates shift AD.
expansionary_monetary_policy_chain.q: Lower interest rates usually shift AD right because they increase:

Imports only

Nowhere
Into SRAS
monetary_policy_transmission.feedback: Lower interest rates raise investment and shift AD right.

omitted_transmission_link.q: A student writes only “the central bank increases money supply, so aggregate demand rises.” Which missing links are essential to the standard short-run transmission mechanism?

Government purchases automatically rise and then the money supply increases.
The price level falls first, which directly forces aggregate demand to shift right.

Menu costs only

monetary_neutrality_definition.commonError: Thinking neutrality means money has no effect on prices.
monetary_neutrality_definition.q: Monetary neutrality means money growth affects:
options: Long-run nominal variables
Only real variables
Neither prices nor wages
Only unemployment
monetary_neutrality_definition.feedback: Money neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

fisher_effect.q: A borrower says the Fisher effect is found by subtracting this year’s actual inflation from a loan rate set last year. What is the key mistake?

The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to stay fixed when expected inflation changes.

unexpected_inflation_debtors_creditors.feedback: Borrowers repay with dollars worth less than expected.

The Fed selling bonds

Real GDP
Natural unemployment

Less output during deflation
shoeleather_costs.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from efforts to reduce cash holdings during inflation.

inflation_tax_policy_risk.commonError: Thinking heavy money creation has no inflation risk.
inflation_tax_policy_risk.q: Heavy reliance on printing money can lead to:
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
Permanent deflation
Zero nominal interest rates forever
A higher value of money
inflation_tax_policy_risk.feedback: Persistent money creation can create high inflation.

inflation_tax_policy_risk.commonError: Thinking printing money is costless government revenue.

Medium of exchange only
Store of value only

identify_money_functions.q: A grocery store accepts dollars for food, lists prices in dollars, and saves cash overnight. Which set matches the functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, money multiplier
Unit of account, discount rate, federal funds rate
Medium of exchange, LRAS, inflation tax
identify_money_functions.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and stores purchasing power over time.

distinguish_m1_m2.q: Households move cash from wallets into checking accounts. The composition of M1 changes little, but what banking consequence can the shift create?

distinguish_m1_m2.feedback: Moving cash into checking changes little in M1, but it gives banks deposits and reserves that can support lending under the banking model.
distinguish_m1_m2.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

The Treasury is using fiscal policy to change government purchases
A commercial bank is deciding how much capital to issue to shareholders
Households are changing M1 by moving funds from checking to savings
fomc_role.feedback: When the FOMC authorizes securities purchases, it is using an expansionary monetary-policy tool that adds reserve balances to banks.
fomc_role.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

central_bank_role.q: A financial panic hits and the banking system needs a lender-of-last-resort institution. Which institution fits?
options: Federal Reserve
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Congressional Budget Office
Internal Revenue Service
central_bank_role.feedback: The Fed acts as the central bank and lender of last resort.

calculate_excess_reserves.feedback: Required reserves are $1,000, so the bank can lend $3,000.

money_multiplier_application.commonError: Confusing initial lending with total expansion.
money_multiplier_application.q: A $10,000 deposit enters a system with a 20% reserve ratio. What is the maximum total deposit expansion?

calculate_money_multiplier_effect.q: The central bank adds reserves to the banking system through an asset purchase. Why does this not mean the central bank itself makes every new commercial loan?
options: The central bank supplies reserves; commercial banks and borrowers determine later lending and deposit creation
The central bank directly selects every commercial borrower and dictates the size of each loan after the asset purchase
Commercial banks can lend only currency printed during the same transaction
Asset purchases increase bank capital rather than reserve balances
calculate_money_multiplier_effect.feedback: The central bank supplies reserve balances; commercial banks and borrowers determine whether those reserves support subsequent loans and deposit creation.
calculate_money_multiplier_effect.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

Holding excess reserves forces the money multiplier above its simple maximum
A central-bank asset purchase automatically becomes fiscal policy when banks do not lend

choose_fed_tool_effect.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.

fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.q: The central bank buys securities, increasing reserves and the money supply. In the liquidity-preference money-market model, what is the next directional step, other things equal?
options: The equilibrium interest rate tends to fall
The equilibrium interest rate must rise because reserves increased
Aggregate supply immediately shifts left before any interest-rate change
The federal budget deficit automatically falls by the amount of the purchase
fed_buys_bonds_money_supply.feedback: With money demand unchanged, the increase in money supply creates excess balances and puts downward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.q: The central bank sells securities, reducing reserves and the money supply. In the liquidity-preference money-market model, what is the next directional step, other things equal?
options: The equilibrium interest rate tends to rise
The equilibrium interest rate must fall because reserves decreased
Aggregate supply immediately shifts right before any interest-rate change
The federal budget surplus automatically rises by the amount of the sale
fed_sells_bonds_money_supply.feedback: With money demand unchanged, the decrease in money supply creates excess money demand and puts upward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

bank_leverage_risk.q: A bank has $500,000 in assets and $30,000 in capital. If assets fall by $20,000, capital becomes:

limits_of_monetary_control.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold excess reserves. What should happen to deposit creation?
options: It is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts
It reaches the full multiplier automatically
It becomes unrelated to lending
It eliminates currency from M1
limits_of_monetary_control.feedback: If banks do not lend excess reserves, the deposit expansion process weakens.

actual_vs_simple_multiplier.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
actual_vs_simple_multiplier.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks hold half of them as excess reserves. What happens?
options: Money creation is less than the simple multiplier predicts
Money creation is exactly the simple maximum
Money creation is larger than the simple maximum
Money supply must fall
actual_vs_simple_multiplier.feedback: Excess reserve holding weakens the multiplier process.

interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.commonError: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.q: A higher price level shifts money demand right while money supply is fixed, so the equilibrium interest rate rises. To carry that money-market result into the policy-transmission model, what happens next?
options: Interest-sensitive investment falls, putting downward pressure on aggregate demand.
Investment rises because higher rates make borrowing cheaper, shifting aggregate demand right.
Aggregate demand shifts left directly because the price level changed, with no spending channel involved.
The higher interest rate shifts money demand farther right but has no effect on spending.
interest_rate_effect_ad_slope.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

money_demand_interest_rate.q: Income rises, so people want to hold more money. If money supply is fixed, interest rates:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Become inflation
money_demand_interest_rate.feedback: Higher money demand with fixed money supply raises interest rates.

liquidity_preference_theory.q: In the money market, if the interest rate is too low, quantity of money demanded is usually:
options: Greater than money supplied
Less than money supplied
Equal to zero
Equal to LRAS
liquidity_preference_theory.feedback: At too low an interest rate, people demand more money than is supplied, pushing rates up.

liquidity_preference_definition.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. What happens to the interest rate?
options: It rises
It falls
It becomes zero
It turns into the price level
liquidity_preference_definition.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes the interest rate up.

bridge_money_market_transmission.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, raising the equilibrium interest rate. What is the next step if the student is bridging from the money market to monetary-policy transmission?
options: Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive investment and put downward pressure on aggregate demand.
Higher borrowing costs raise investment because firms earn more interest.
The higher interest rate directly increases government purchases.
Aggregate demand is unaffected because interest rates matter only inside the money-market graph.
bridge_money_market_transmission.commonError: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
bridge_money_market_transmission.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

expansionary_monetary_policy_chain.q: The Fed increases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Taxes fall, consumption rises, AD shifts right
Money demand disappears, AD is unchanged
expansionary_monetary_policy_chain.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

monetary_policy_transmission.q: The Fed increases the money supply. Which chain is correct?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates fall, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates rise, investment rises, AD shifts right
monetary_policy_transmission.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

contractionary_monetary_policy_chain.q: The Fed decreases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Taxes rise, consumption falls, AD shifts left
Money demand disappears, AD rises
contractionary_monetary_policy_chain.feedback: Contractionary monetary policy raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

value_of_money.q: If the price level rises from 2 to 5, the value of money changes from:
options: 2 to 5
5 to 2
value_of_money.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, so it falls from 1/2 to 1/5.

quantity_theory_growth_rates.q: Money grows 12%, output grows 4%, and velocity is stable. Inflation is about:

quantity_equation.q: If M = 200, V = 5, and Y = 500, then P equals:
quantity_equation.feedback: MV = PY, so 200 x 5 = P x 500, which gives P = 2.

money_growth_to_inflation.q: Money grows 6 percent, velocity is stable, and output grows 2 percent. Approximate inflation is:
options: 4 percent
6 percent
8 percent
2 percent
money_growth_to_inflation.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth minus output growth: 6 - 2 = 4 percent.

value_of_money_formula.commonError: Reading value of money as the price level.
value_of_money_formula.q: Use value of money = 1/P. If value falls from 1/2 to 1/4, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4
It falls from 2 to 4
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4
It stays fixed
value_of_money_formula.feedback: Value of money is 1/P, so 1/2 means P = 2 and 1/4 means P = 4.

real_wage_formula.commonError: Looking only at nominal wage growth.
real_wage_formula.q: Nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 and the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units
It rises to 6 units
It falls to 3.33 units
It doubles

monetary_neutrality_definition.commonError: Thinking neutrality means no price changes.
monetary_neutrality_definition.q: Money supply doubles, all nominal prices double, and real output is unchanged. This illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
monetary_neutrality_definition.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

nominal_vs_real_variables.q: A worker’s nominal wage rises 5 percent while inflation is 8 percent. The real wage:
options: Falls by about 3 percent
Rises by about 3 percent
Rises by about 13 percent
Does not change
nominal_vs_real_variables.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation: 5 - 8 = -3 percent.

monetary_neutrality.q: If all nominal prices and wages double but real output is unchanged, this supports:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky wage theory only
A liquidity trap
monetary_neutrality.feedback: Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run.

monetary_neutrality.q: The quantity theory predicts that sustained money growth faster than real output growth can raise inflation. In the long-run neutrality framework, what should a student infer about real productive capacity?
options: Faster money growth can raise nominal prices without permanently increasing productive capacity.
Faster money growth must permanently raise productive capacity by the same percentage.
Higher inflation proves output per worker rose by the same amount.
Long-run neutrality requires inflation to be zero whenever money growth exceeds output growth.
monetary_neutrality.commonError: Stops after predicting the price-level effect and does not separate nominal from real outcomes.
monetary_neutrality.feedback: Use the quantity-theory result for nominal spending and prices, then apply long-run neutrality to ask which real variables need not rise permanently.

fisher_effect.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is:
options: 8 percent
6 percent
4 percent
2 percent
fisher_effect.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

fisher_effect.q: Suppose long-run money growth raises expected inflation while real productive conditions leave the real interest rate unchanged. Which next step connects monetary neutrality to the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate rises to incorporate the higher expected inflation while the real-rate component stays unchanged.
The real interest rate must rise one-for-one because all nominal variables are neutral and expected inflation cannot influence nominal contract rates.
The nominal interest rate stays fixed because expected inflation affects only the price level.
Actual inflation must be known before lenders can set any nominal interest rate.
fisher_effect.commonError: Recognizes nominal neutrality but does not connect expected inflation to nominal interest rates.
fisher_effect.feedback: Once long-run real and nominal variables are separated, the Fisher effect explains why higher expected inflation is reflected in higher nominal interest rates.

fisher_equation_simple.commonError: Forgetting expected inflation in nominal rates.
fisher_equation_simple.q: Real interest is 2% and expected inflation is 6%. Nominal interest is:

inflation_costs_overview.q: Firms repeatedly update posted prices while households make more transfers to avoid holding cash. Which costs are shown?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and liquidity trap
Reserve shortfall and bank capital loss
M1 and M2
inflation_costs_overview.feedback: Price updates are menu costs; reducing cash balances creates shoeleather costs.

menu_costs.q: A restaurant reprints menus every week because prices keep changing. This is:
options: Menu cost
Shoeleather cost
Inflation tax
Money neutrality
menu_costs.feedback: Menu costs are costs of changing posted prices.

unexpected_inflation_debtors_creditors.commonError: Using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate.
unexpected_inflation_debtors_creditors.q: Nominal interest is 9%, expected inflation was 3%, but actual inflation is 10%. Who gains?
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Both equally
No one
unexpected_inflation_debtors_creditors.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers repay with less valuable dollars.

shoeleather_costs.q: Inflation makes a household transfer money more often to avoid holding cash. This is:
options: Shoeleather cost
Menu cost
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
shoeleather_costs.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the costs of reducing money holdings during inflation.

inflation_tax.q: A government prints money to pay bills and the value of existing money falls. This is closest to:
options: Inflation tax
Reserve requirement
Crowding out
Sacrifice ratio
inflation_tax.feedback: The inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.

inflation_tax_policy_risk.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
inflation_tax_policy_risk.q: A government relies heavily on money creation. Inflation rises, households reduce cash balances, and they make more frequent transfers to avoid holding money. Which connection is most accurate?
options: Money finance creates an inflation-tax burden on money balances and also generates shoeleather costs.
Money finance eliminates the inflation tax because households hold less cash.
Shoeleather costs occur only during deflation, so the two effects cannot occur together.
The policy changes only real output and has no effect on nominal money balances, cash-management decisions, or the purchasing power of money.
inflation_tax_policy_risk.feedback: Money creation erodes the purchasing power of money balances (the inflation tax) and encourages people to make more frequent transfers or otherwise avoid holding cash (shoeleather costs).

money-functions-and-measures.title: Money Functions and Measures
money-functions-and-measures.description: Identify money’s functions, forms, and M1/M2 measurement.

easy.q: Which function of money is being used when dollars are accepted to buy groceries?
options: Store of value
Medium of exchange
Unit of account
Reserve requirement
easy.commonError: Confusing the functions of money.
easy.feedback: Money is a medium of exchange when it is used to buy goods and services.

easy.q: Which function of money is being used when a store lists a phone price as $900?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
easy.commonError: Confusing pricing with payment.
easy.feedback: Money is a unit of account when it measures and compares prices.

easy.q: Which item is counted in M1?
options: Large time deposits
Currency held by the public
Credit card balances
Money market mutual funds held by businesses
easy.commonError: Counting credit cards as money.
easy.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item is included in M2 but not M1?
options: Checkable deposits
Coins held by households
Savings deposits
Currency held by the public
easy.commonError: Treating M1 and M2 as identical.
easy.feedback: M2 includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

easy.q: What is fiat money?
options: Money backed fully by gold
Accepted money with no intrinsic value
Money used only by banks
Money that cannot lose value
easy.commonError: Thinking fiat money must be backed by gold.
easy.feedback: Fiat money has value because people accept it, not because it has intrinsic value.

easy.q: A farmer wants shoes, but the shoemaker does not want wheat. Both are willing to accept dollars. Which feature of money solves the immediate trading problem?
options: It serves as a medium of exchange, so the two traders do not need a double coincidence of wants
It serves only as a store of value, so neither trader has to exchange anything
It makes every good part of M1, so barter becomes unnecessary
It guarantees that the relative price of wheat and shoes never changes
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Money serves as a medium of exchange because dollars let the farmer trade without finding a shoemaker who wants wheat.

easy.q: A repair shop compares a $450 used laptop with a $900 new laptop before deciding which to buy. Which function of money makes that comparison straightforward?
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Bank reserve
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Money serves as a unit of account because quoting both laptops in dollars provides a common measure for comparing their prices.

easy.q: A household keeps $600 in cash for emergencies. If prices rise substantially before the cash is spent, which statement is most accurate?
options: The cash serves as a store of value, but its purchasing power can fall
The cash stops being money because a store of value must keep purchasing power constant
The cash is serving only as a unit of account because it is not being spent today
Inflation converts the cash from M1 into a nonmonetary financial asset
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: Cash is a store of value because it carries purchasing power into the future, although inflation can reduce that purchasing power before it is spent.

easy.q: Customers accept paper currency even though the paper itself has little intrinsic value and cannot be redeemed for a commodity. Which explanation best fits?
options: It is fiat money whose usefulness depends on general acceptance rather than commodity value
It is commodity money because the paper can be physically held
It is bank capital because it supports financial transactions
It is not money unless every note is backed one-for-one by gold
easy.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
easy.feedback: The currency is fiat money: it is accepted as payment even though the paper has little intrinsic value and is not redeemable for a commodity.

easy.q: Commodity money differs from fiat money because commodity money
options: has intrinsic value
is created only through bank lending
cannot be used as a medium of exchange
is always part of M2 but never M1
easy.commonError: treating all money as fiat money
easy.feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself, like gold or silver. Fiat money does not.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is included in M1?
options: Currency held by the public
Small time deposits
Savings deposits
Money market mutual funds held by individuals
easy.commonError: including all near monies in M1
easy.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public, checkable deposits, and similar highly liquid transaction balances.

easy.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which of the following is part of M2 but not M1?
options: Savings deposits
Currency
Checkable deposits
Traveler's checks
easy.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes near monies
easy.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies, so they are included in M2 but not M1.

medium.q: A student says credit card balances should be counted in M1 because people use cards to buy goods. What is the best correction?
options: Credit cards are borrowing, not money balances
Credit cards are currency held by the public
Credit cards are checkable deposits
Credit cards are savings deposits
medium.commonError: Counting credit cards as money.
medium.feedback: Credit cards allow borrowing. They are not money balances like currency or checkable deposits.

medium.q: A household keeps cash because it wants to make purchases quickly, compare prices, and save some value for later. Which answer matches all three functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, fiat money
Unit of account, leverage, discount rate
Medium of exchange, multiplier, bank capital
medium.commonError: Mixing money functions with banking tools.
medium.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and can transfer purchasing power into the future.

medium.q: A student says, 'Money is valuable because the dollar bill itself has valuable paper.' What is the best correction?
options: Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
Fiat money has value because its paper is worth more than its face value.
Commodity money and fiat money are the same thing.
Money only has value if it can be exchanged for gold.
medium.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
medium.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. Its value comes from general acceptance and government backing.

medium.q: A grocery store lists apples at $2 per pound. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Fractional reserve
medium.commonError: choosing medium of exchange whenever prices involve money
medium.feedback: The price tag uses money to measure value, so money is acting as a unit of account.

medium.q: A person keeps $500 in cash for emergencies. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Store of value
Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
medium.commonError: thinking money only matters when it is spent immediately
medium.feedback: The cash is preserving purchasing power for later, so it is serving as a store of value.

medium.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item would be counted in M2 but not in M1?
options: A savings deposit
Currency in your wallet
A checking account deposit
A traveler's check
medium.commonError: putting all liquid assets into M1
medium.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies. They belong in M2, not M1.

medium.q: Why does money make specialization easier?
options: It removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
It makes all goods cost the same amount.
It prevents prices from changing.
It eliminates scarcity.
medium.commonError: thinking money eliminates scarcity rather than reducing transaction costs
medium.feedback: Money reduces transaction costs because people no longer need to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.

medium.q: Which statement best explains why currency held by a bank does not count the same way as currency held by the public?
options: Currency held by banks is part of bank reserves, not currency circulating among the public.
Currency held by banks is automatically counted twice in M1.
Currency held by banks is commodity money.
Currency held by banks is never money.
medium.commonError: double-counting currency held inside banks
medium.feedback: Currency held by banks is treated as reserves. Currency in the money supply refers to currency held by the public.

hard.q: A student says M2 is smaller than M1 because M2 excludes currency. What is the best correction?
options: M2 includes M1 plus near monies
M2 includes only bank reserves
M1 includes savings deposits only
M1 equals credit card balances
hard.commonError: Reversing the relationship between M1 and M2.
hard.feedback: M2 is broader than M1 because it includes M1 plus near monies such as savings deposits.

hard.q: A farmer accepts dollars for corn, uses dollars to compare seed prices, and saves some dollars for next month. Which answer correctly matches the three functions of money?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, medium of exchange, unit of account
Unit of account, store of value, medium of exchange
Money multiplier, reserve requirement, federal funds rate
hard.commonError: mixing up using money to buy with using money to measure value
hard.feedback: Buying uses money as a medium of exchange, comparing prices uses it as a unit of account, and saving it uses it as a store of value.

hard.q: A country uses paper currency that has no intrinsic value, is not convertible into gold, but is accepted for payment. What kind of money is this?
options: Fiat money
Commodity money
Barter money
Reserve money only
hard.commonError: thinking money must be backed by a commodity to have value
hard.feedback: That is fiat money: it has value because it is accepted, not because the paper itself has intrinsic value.

hard.q: Currency held by the public rises because households withdraw funds from checking accounts. What happens to banks' ability to create deposits, other things equal?
options: It falls because banks have fewer deposits to support lending.
It rises because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves.
It is unchanged because currency and deposits are identical for banks.
It becomes unlimited because reserve requirements no longer matter.
hard.commonError: thinking public currency holdings help banks lend more
hard.feedback: When households hold more currency and fewer deposits, banks have fewer deposits available to support loans.

hard.q: A household moves $4,000 from a checking account into a retail money-market mutual fund. Under standard textbook definitions, what happens?
options: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.
hard.commonError: Treating movement between M1 and non-M1 M2 assets as a change in total M2.
hard.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.

hard.q: Which asset is included in M2 but normally excluded from M1?
options: Currency held by the public.
A small-denomination time deposit.
Funds in a checking account.
Traveler’s checks held by households.
hard.commonError: Placing every liquid financial asset in M1.
hard.feedback: Small time deposits are near-money assets included in M2 but not in the narrower M1 measure.

elite.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists public currency as $600, checkable deposits as $1,400, savings deposits as $1,800, small time deposits as $500, and retail money market mutual funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
elite.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
elite.feedback: M1 is currency plus checkable deposits: $600 + $1,400 = $2,000. M2 adds savings, small time deposits, and retail money market funds: $4,600.

elite.q: A payment app transfers balances instantly from users’ checking accounts but holds no separate monetary balance. How should the app affect measured money?
options: Every transfer through the app permanently increases the measured M1 stock.
The app balance enters M2 even though no separate monetary balance exists.
It changes payment convenience without creating a new money balance.
Using the app removes the linked checking deposits from measured money.
elite.commonError: Counting a payment method as a separate stock of money when it only accesses an existing deposit.
elite.feedback: A payment platform that merely accesses checking deposits changes how money is used, not how much money exists.

elite.q: A store lists prices in dollars, accepts dollars at checkout, and households keep dollars for future purchases. Which statement is correct?
options: Money is serving only as a medium of exchange during the checkout transaction.
Money is serving as a unit of account and barter device, but not as stored value.
Money is serving only as a store of value because households retain some dollars.
Money is serving as unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value.
elite.commonError: Assuming one transaction can illustrate only one function of money.
elite.feedback: Money can perform all three functions in the same setting: quoting prices, settling purchases, and carrying purchasing power forward.

elite.q: Inflation accelerates, but dollars remain widely accepted and prices continue to be quoted in dollars. Which money function is most directly weakened?
options: Store of value, because purchasing power erodes more quickly.
Medium of exchange, because dollars can no longer buy anything.
Unit of account, because prices cannot be stated in dollars.
Standard of deferred payment, because all credit disappears.
elite.commonError: Assuming inflation eliminates every function of money equally.
elite.feedback: Rapid inflation most directly weakens money’s ability to preserve purchasing power over time.

legendary.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $3,000, savings deposits are $2,500, small time deposits are $1,200, retail money market funds are $800, and large time deposits are $900. If large time deposits are not counted in M2, what is M2?
legendary.commonError: including large time deposits when the course definition excludes them
legendary.feedback: M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $3,000 + $2,500 + $1,200 + $800 = $7,500.

legendary.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A household moves $10,000 from a checking account to a savings account. What happens to M1 and M2, using standard course definitions?
options: M1 falls, while M2 is unchanged.
Both M1 and M2 fall.
M1 is unchanged, while M2 rises.
Both M1 and M2 rise.
legendary.commonError: thinking every movement between accounts changes M2
legendary.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2; savings deposits are in M2 but not M1. Moving funds to savings lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

legendary.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks lend more, and the public redeposits most loan proceeds. Which money measures are most likely affected first?
options: Bank deposits and M1 rise, with broader effects on M2 depending on where funds are held.
Commodity-money holdings rise because bond purchases convert financial assets into physical commodity money
Real GDP rises immediately while the quantity of bank deposits is unaffected by the lending and redeposit process
M1 falls because additional bank lending reduces the checkable deposits held by households and businesses
legendary.commonError: thinking bank-created deposits are not part of money measures
legendary.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits, and checkable deposits are part of M1. M2 can also be affected depending on where funds are held.

legendary.q: Currency held by the public rises by $20 billion, checking deposits fall by $20 billion, and small time deposits are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2?
options: M1 rises by $20 billion while M2 remains unchanged because currency is broader money.
Both aggregates are unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
M1 and M2 both fall by $20 billion because checking deposits decline.
M1 remains unchanged while M2 rises by $20 billion because currency increases.
legendary.commonError: Adding gross component changes without recognizing an offset within both aggregates.
legendary.feedback: Currency and checking deposits are both in M1 and M2. An equal transfer between them changes composition but not either total.

legendary.q: A new digital wallet stores claims on bank checking deposits and the same balances are still reported as checking deposits. How should statisticians avoid double counting?
options: Count both the checking deposit and the wallet claim as separate M1 balances.
Exclude the checking deposit and count only the wallet claim as part of M2.
Count the underlying deposit once and do not add the wallet claim again.
Remove both records because digitally accessed balances cannot qualify as money.
legendary.commonError: Counting two records of the same underlying monetary claim as two balances.
legendary.feedback: A wallet claim backed one-for-one by an already-counted checking deposit is another access channel, not a second stock of money.

legendary.q: An economy replaces an unstable commodity money with fiat currency. Which condition is most important for the fiat currency to function well?
options: The currency must possess substantial nonmonetary commodity value in every use.
Every note must remain redeemable for a fixed quantity of gold or silver.
The government must prohibit bank deposits and all competing payment methods.
Users must trust its acceptance and the institutions supporting its value.
legendary.commonError: Assuming fiat money requires intrinsic commodity value.
legendary.feedback: Fiat money works because of general acceptability, legal and institutional support, and confidence in its purchasing power.

calculation.q: Currency held by the public is $800 billion and checkable deposits are $1,200 billion. Assume these are the only M1 components with nonzero balances. What is M1?
options: $2,000 billion
$1,200 billion
$800 billion
$400 billion
calculation.commonError: leaving out either currency or checkable deposits
calculation.feedback: M1 includes currency plus checkable deposits: $800 billion + $1,200 billion = $2,000 billion.

calculation.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $2,000 billion, savings deposits are $900 billion, small time deposits are $300 billion, and retail money market mutual funds are $200 billion. M2 is
options: $3,400 billion
$2,000 billion
$1,400 billion
$2,300 billion
calculation.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
calculation.feedback: M2 equals M1 plus near monies: $2,000 + $900 + $300 + $200 = $3,400 billion.

calculation.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A table lists currency held by the public as $900, checkable deposits as $1,600, savings deposits as $2,000, small time deposits as $700, and retail money market funds as $300. What are M1 and M2?
calculation.commonError: forgetting that M2 includes M1 plus near monies
calculation.feedback: M1 = currency + checkable deposits = $2,500. M2 = M1 + savings + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $5,500.

boss.q: Which statement correctly describes fiat money?
options: It has value because people accept it and government supports its use.
It has value because the material itself is valuable.
It can only serve as a store of value.
It is excluded from the money supply.
boss.commonError: thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
boss.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. It works because people accept it.

boss.q: A person uses dollars to buy groceries, compare prices, and save for next month. Which functions of money are being used?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value
Store of value only
Unit of account only
Reserve requirement and money multiplier
boss.commonError: thinking money only has one function at a time
boss.feedback: Buying, comparing prices, and saving line up with the three core functions of money.

boss.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Currency held by the public is $900, checkable deposits are $1,100, savings deposits are $1,500, and small time deposits are $500. What are M1 and M2?
boss.commonError: forgetting M2 includes M1 plus near monies
boss.feedback: M1 is $900 + $1,100 = $2,000. M2 adds savings and small time deposits, so M2 = $4,000.

boss.q: Which item belongs in M1 under standard textbook definitions?
options: A balance in a checking account.
A small time deposit.
A retail money-market mutual fund.
A long-term corporate bond.
boss.commonError: Including broad near-money assets in the narrow M1 measure.
boss.feedback: Checking deposits are immediately spendable and are included in M1.

boss.q: A restaurant posts every menu price in dollars. Which function of money is being used?
options: Medium of exchange.
Unit of account.
Store of value.
Commodity backing.
boss.commonError: Confusing the act of quoting prices with settling a transaction.
boss.feedback: Money serves as a unit of account when it provides the common measurement used to state prices.

boss.q: A saver moves funds from checking to a small time deposit. Which result is correct?
options: M1 and M2 both decrease.
M1 does not change, but M2 increases.
M1 decreases, but M2 does not change.
M1 and M2 both increase.
boss.commonError: Treating an internal transfer within M2 as a change in M2.
boss.feedback: Checking is in M1 and M2; a small time deposit is in M2 only. The transfer lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

boss.q: A bank customer withdraws $500 from checking and holds the cash. What happens to M1?
options: M1 falls by $500 because checking deposits decline.
M1 rises by $500 because currency increases.
M1 falls while M2 rises by $500.
M1 is unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
boss.commonError: Looking at one component change without accounting for the offsetting M1 component.
boss.feedback: Currency held by the public and checking deposits are both in M1, so the transfer changes composition rather than the total.

boss.q: An online service lets users pay merchants directly from savings accounts. What is the safest conclusion about money measurement?
options: Classification still depends on the official definition of the account.
Every savings balance automatically moves into M1 once direct payments are possible.
The payment service creates new money each time a customer completes a purchase.
Savings accounts must be removed from M2 because they are now easier to spend.
boss.commonError: Assuming technology alone automatically changes official monetary definitions.
boss.feedback: A new payment channel can make an asset more usable without automatically changing how statistical agencies classify the underlying account.

boss.q: Prices are quoted in dollars, workers accept dollars as wages, and households save dollars for emergencies. What does this example show?
options: Money is performing only as a medium of exchange.
Money is performing all three primary functions.
Money is performing only as a unit of account.
Money is performing only as a store of value.
boss.commonError: Selecting one function when the scenario demonstrates several.
boss.feedback: The dollar measures value, settles transactions, and transfers purchasing power over time.

legendaryBoss.q: Use current U.S. definitions, in which savings deposits are part of M1. A household shifts $75,000 from checking to savings at the same bank. Later the bank originates a $12,000 loan by crediting another customer’s checking account; no loan is repaid and no other balance changes. Relative to the starting totals, how do M1 and M2 change?
options: Both rise by $12,000.
M1 falls by $63,000; M2 rises by $12,000.
Both rise by $87,000.
Both remain unchanged.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking moving funds within M2 must change M2
legendaryBoss.feedback: The checking-to-savings transfer changes neither aggregate and does not release reserves. The new loan adds a $12,000 deposit, raising both M1 and M2 by that amount.

legendaryBoss.q: M1 equals $900 billion and M2 equals $3.4 trillion. Households transfer $80 billion from checking deposits to small time deposits. What are the new values?
options: M1 remains $900 billion and M2 becomes $3.48 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 is $3.32 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
M1 becomes $980 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Subtracting the transfer from both aggregates instead of recognizing it remains inside M2.
legendaryBoss.feedback: The transfer leaves the broad M2 total unchanged but removes $80 billion from the narrower M1 measure.

legendaryBoss.q: A wallet provider reports $10 billion of customer balances that are fully backed by $10 billion already counted in bank checking deposits. What is the correct measurement treatment?
options: Add the full wallet balance to both M1 and M2 even though the deposit is counted.
Remove the bank deposit and count only the wallet balance in the money stock.
Exclude both balances because electronic monetary claims cannot be measured.
Do not add the wallet balance unless it is a separate monetary liability.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Double counting an access claim and the underlying deposit.
legendaryBoss.feedback: If the wallet balance is simply a claim on an already-counted deposit, adding both would overstate the money stock.

repairQuestions.q: What makes fiat money valuable?
options: Government acceptance and public trust, not intrinsic commodity value
Its gold content alone
A fixed reserve requirement
Its use only in foreign trade
repairQuestions.feedback: Fiat money has value because it is accepted in exchange, not because the paper itself is valuable.

repairQuestions.q: Which item belongs in M1?
options: Currency held by the public
Large time deposits
Credit card debt
Corporate bonds
repairQuestions.feedback: M1 includes currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

repairQuestions.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item is in M2 but not M1?
options: Savings deposits
Currency
Checkable deposits
Coins
repairQuestions.feedback: M2 includes near monies such as savings deposits.

repairQuestions.q: Money used to buy goods and services is serving which function?
options: Medium of exchange
Store of value
Unit of account
Reserve ratio
repairQuestions.feedback: Buying goods and services uses money as a medium of exchange.

repairQuestions.q: Money used to compare prices is serving which function?
options: Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Store of value
Discount rate
repairQuestions.feedback: Listing prices uses money as a unit of account.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A household owns a home and stocks and earns a salary, but keeps very little currency or checking deposits. Which statement is correct?
options: Wealth and income can be high even when the household holds little money
All household wealth is counted in M1 because it can eventually be sold
Salary income is automatically part of the money supply before it is paid
Only physical currency can count as money, so checking deposits are wealth instead
repairQuestions.feedback: Money is the stock of spendable balances, not total wealth or income; a household can own valuable assets and earn a high salary while holding little currency or checking deposits.

repairQuestions.commonError: Mixing up the three functions of money.
