Sell government bonds to the public.
Raise taxes on households.
Reduce government purchases.
medium.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases remove money from circulation
medium.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it pays money into the economy, increasing the money supply.

medium.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Sell government bonds to the public.
Buy government bonds from the public.
Cut the discount rate.
Lower reserve requirements.
medium.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales inject money
medium.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, the public pays money to the Fed, reducing the money supply.

medium.q: If the Fed lowers the discount rate, which effect is most likely?
options: Banks find it cheaper to borrow from the Fed.
Banks are required to hold more reserves.
The money supply must fall.
Currency becomes commodity money.
medium.commonError: thinking a lower discount rate discourages borrowing
medium.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper for banks.

medium.q: If the Fed raises reserve requirements, the banking system's ability to create money usually
options: decreases
increases
becomes unlimited
does not depend on deposits anymore
medium.commonError: thinking higher required reserves create more lending
medium.feedback: Higher reserve requirements force banks to hold more reserves and lend less, reducing money creation.

medium.q: If the Fed pays a higher interest rate on reserves, banks may respond by
options: holding more reserves and lending less
holding fewer reserves and lending more
creating commodity money
eliminating demand deposits
medium.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending
medium.feedback: Higher interest on reserves can make banks more willing to hold reserves instead of lending.

hard.q: Which sequence best describes a contractionary open-market operation?
options: Sell bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Buy bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Sell bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Buy bonds, reserves rise, lending contracts
hard.commonError: Reversing bond sales and purchases.
hard.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, weakens lending, and reduces money creation.

hard.q: The Fed raises the discount rate and also raises interest on reserves. Which combined effect is most likely?
options: Banks borrow less from the Fed and may hold more reserves.
Banks borrow more from the Fed and lend every reserve.
Households automatically hold fewer dollars because taxes fall.
The money multiplier becomes infinite.
hard.commonError: treating all Fed tools as expansionary regardless of direction
hard.feedback: A higher discount rate discourages bank borrowing, and higher interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves.

hard.q: Which Fed action is most clearly contractionary?
options: Selling bonds and raising reserve requirements
Buying bonds and lowering reserve requirements
Buying bonds and lowering the discount rate
Lowering interest on reserves and buying bonds
hard.commonError: mixing expansionary and contractionary tools
hard.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out, and raising reserve requirements restricts lending. That is contractionary.

hard.q: Which Fed action is most clearly expansionary?
options: Buying bonds and lowering reserve requirements
Selling bonds and raising reserve requirements
Raising the discount rate and raising interest on reserves
Selling bonds and lowering bank lending
hard.commonError: thinking bond purchases are contractionary
hard.feedback: Buying bonds injects money, and lower reserve requirements support more lending. That is expansionary.

hard.q: If the Fed wants looser money but also raises interest on reserves, what tension does this create?
options: It injects reserves but may also encourage banks to hold them instead of lending.
It lowers reserves and forces banks to lend more.
It turns deposits into commodity money.
It makes fiscal policy impossible.
hard.commonError: assuming all policy tools point in the same direction
hard.feedback: More reserves can support lending, but higher interest on reserves may make banks sit on those reserves.

hard.q: The central bank raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. What response is most likely, other things equal?
options: Banks are more willing to hold reserves and less willing to expand lending.
Banks reduce reserve holdings and expand lending because reserves now pay more.
Households move currency directly into government spending when reserves earn more.
The required reserve ratio automatically falls when reserve interest increases.
hard.commonError: Reversing the incentive effect of higher interest paid on reserves.
hard.feedback: A higher return on reserve balances makes reserve holding more attractive and tends to restrain lending and money creation.

elite.q: The Fed wants the money supply to fall by $180 million. If the money multiplier is 6 and banks fully lend according to the simple model, what open-market operation should the Fed conduct?
options: Sell $30 million in bonds.
Buy $30 million in bonds.
Sell $180 million in bonds.
Buy $1.08 billion in bonds.
elite.commonError: multiplying the desired money change by the multiplier instead of dividing
elite.feedback: To reduce money by $180 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $30 million in bonds.

elite.q: The Fed buys bonds while also increasing interest on reserves. Which answer best captures the policy conflict?
options: Bond purchases add reserves, but higher interest on reserves may reduce banks' willingness to lend them.
Bond purchases remove reserves, while higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend more.
Both actions clearly reduce reserves and contract lending.
Both actions clearly eliminate money demand.
elite.commonError: assuming every Fed action in a scenario pushes the same direction
elite.feedback: Buying bonds is expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

elite.q: Which policy package most strongly reduces bank lending capacity?
options: Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds and lowers the discount rate.
Fed lowers reserve requirements and buys bonds.
elite.commonError: failing to combine multiple contractionary tools
elite.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, higher reserve requirements restrict lending, and higher interest on reserves encourages banks to hold reserves.

elite.q: Which policy package most strongly expands bank lending capacity?
options: Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds and raises the discount rate.
Fed raises reserve requirements and pays banks more to hold reserves.
elite.commonError: missing that lower interest on reserves can encourage lending
elite.feedback: Buying bonds adds reserves, lower reserve requirements free reserves, and lower interest on reserves weakens the incentive to sit on reserves.

elite.q: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio rises from 10 percent to 20 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $40,000 to $0.
They rise from $40,000 to $80,000.
They fall from $80,000 to $40,000.
They stay at $80,000.
elite.commonError: forgetting required reserves change when the ratio changes
elite.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $40,000 and excess reserves are $40,000. At 20 percent, required reserves are $80,000 and excess reserves are $0.

elite.q: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio falls from 20 percent to 10 percent. What new lending capacity is created?
elite.commonError: thinking lower reserve requirements reduce excess reserves
elite.feedback: Required reserves fall from $80,000 to $40,000, creating $40,000 in excess reserves.

elite.q: If the Fed sells bonds and the public pays with checking deposits, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Bank reserves rise, strengthening deposit creation.
Bank reserves stay fixed, but taxes rise.
Bank reserves become commodity money.
elite.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales add reserves to banks
elite.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, payment leaves bank deposits and reserves fall, reducing money creation.

elite.q: If the Fed buys bonds from the public and sellers deposit the proceeds, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves rise, supporting deposit creation.
Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Taxes rise, reducing consumption.
Reserve requirements automatically rise to 100 percent.
elite.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases drain reserves
elite.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, money enters bank deposits and reserves rise, supporting lending and deposit creation.

legendary.q: A bank has $2,400,000 in deposits, $360,000 in reserves, and a reserve requirement of 10 percent. The reserve requirement then rises to 15 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $120,000 to $0.
They rise from $120,000 to $360,000.
They fall from $360,000 to $240,000.
They rise from $0 to $120,000.
legendary.commonError: forgetting to recalculate required reserves after the policy change
legendary.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $240,000, so excess reserves are $120,000. At 15 percent, required reserves are $360,000, leaving zero excess reserves.

legendary.q: In a hypothetical steady-state banking model, the required-reserve ratio is 10 percent, banks hold excess reserves equal to 5 percent of deposits, and the public holds currency equal to 25 percent of deposits. These ratios remain fixed. Money is currency plus deposits; the monetary base is currency plus total reserves. What base increase is needed for a $250 million money increase, and why is the simple 1/required-ratio estimate too small?
options: $80 million; both currency holdings and excess reserves absorb base money.
$25 million; every base dollar supports ten dollars of money.
$100 million; currency is excluded from the money measure.
$62.5 million; retaining a fixed fraction once describes every lending round.
legendary.commonError: ignoring the 80 percent lending adjustment
legendary.feedback: With deposits D, money is 1.25D and the base is (0.25 + 0.10 + 0.05)D = 0.40D. The money/base ratio is 3.125, so the base must rise $250/3.125 = $80 million. The simple multiplier ignores both leakages.

legendary.q: A hypothetical bank has $600,000 in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The required-reserve ratio rises from 10 to 15 percent. The bank cannot obtain new reserves, and any additional loan payment would settle at another bank. Which conclusion distinguishes its reserve position from its ability to expand?
options: It meets the new requirement exactly, but has no excess reserves for an outgoing loan.
It has a $30,000 reserve deficit and must obtain reserves just to comply.
It retains $30,000 of excess reserves because deposits have not changed.
It must shrink deposits by $90,000 even if it makes no new loan.
legendary.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more excess reserves
legendary.feedback: Required reserves rise from $60,000 to $90,000, exactly equal to actual reserves. The bank is compliant but the specified settlement constraint prevents further outgoing lending without adjustment.

legendary.q: The Fed cuts the discount rate, buys bonds, and lowers interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Bank borrowing and reserves rise, lending incentives strengthen, and the money supply tends to expand.
Bank reserves fall, lending incentives weaken, and the money supply contracts.
Taxes fall, consumption rises, and fiscal policy expands.
The money supply is unaffected because only fiscal policy matters.
legendary.commonError: treating Fed tools as unrelated one-off facts
legendary.feedback: All three actions push toward monetary expansion: cheaper Fed borrowing, more reserves, and less reward for holding reserves idle.

legendary.q: The Fed raises the discount rate, sells bonds, and raises interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Borrowing becomes costlier, reserves fall, banks may hold more reserves, and money creation weakens.
Borrowing becomes cheaper, reserves rise, and lending expands.
Government spending rises and taxes fall.
Money demand becomes zero.
legendary.commonError: missing that higher interest on reserves can be contractionary
legendary.feedback: That policy package tightens money through costlier borrowing, fewer reserves, and stronger incentives to hold reserves.

legendary.q: A bank has $10 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It holds $1.4 million in reserves. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 12 percent and banks lend all remaining excess reserves. How much can the bank lend after the change?
options: $1.2 million
$1.4 million
legendary.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the policy change
legendary.feedback: New required reserves are 0.12 x $10 million = $1.2 million. With $1.4 million in reserves, the bank can lend $200,000.

calculation.q: If the Fed buys $40 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 4, what is the maximum possible increase in the money supply?
options: $160 million
$40 million
$10 million
$44 million
calculation.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
calculation.feedback: A bond purchase injects reserves. Maximum money expansion is $40 million x 4 = $160 million.

calculation.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply by exactly $120 million and the money multiplier is 6, how many bonds should it sell?
options: $20 million
$120 million
$720 million
$6 million
calculation.commonError: multiplying target money change by the multiplier instead of dividing
calculation.feedback: To reduce money by $120 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $20 million in bonds.

boss.q: If the Fed buys government bonds, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed
turn into commodity money
boss.commonError: thinking bond purchases remove money from circulation
boss.feedback: Buying bonds injects reserves and tends to increase the money supply.

boss.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply using open-market operations, what should it do?
options: Sell government bonds.
Buy government bonds.
Lower reserve requirements.
Lower the discount rate.
boss.commonError: thinking bond sales add reserves
boss.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

boss.q: The Fed sells $20 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 5. Under the simple model, what is the maximum decrease in the money supply?
options: $100 million
$20 million
$4 million
$25 million
boss.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
boss.feedback: A $20 million bond sale times multiplier 5 gives a maximum $100 million money-supply decrease.

boss.q: To increase banking-system reserves through open-market operations, the central bank should:
options: Sell government securities.
Buy government securities.
Raise taxes.
Increase reserve requirements.
boss.commonError: Reversing the reserve effect of an open-market purchase.
boss.feedback: When the central bank buys securities, it pays by adding reserves to the banking system.

boss.q: What is the usual effect of lowering the discount rate?
options: Banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves.
The central bank removes reserves by selling bonds.
Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks.
Households are required to reduce currency holdings.
boss.commonError: Confusing the discount rate with reserve requirements or open-market sales.
boss.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost of borrowing reserves directly from the central bank.

boss.q: Which policy action is contractionary?
options: Buying government securities in the open market.
Lowering the interest paid on reserve balances.
Lowering reserve requirements.
Selling government securities in the open market.
boss.commonError: Selecting an expansionary tool as contractionary.
boss.feedback: An open-market sale withdraws reserves and tends to reduce money and credit expansion.

boss.q: The central bank buys securities but simultaneously raises the interest paid on reserves. Why might lending rise by less than expected?
options: The purchase adds reserves, but the higher reserve return encourages banks to hold them.
Both actions remove reserves and directly reduce the banking system’s lending capacity.
The bond purchase automatically raises reserve requirements and blocks new loans.
The higher reserve return forces banks to lend every newly created reserve dollar.
boss.commonError: Assuming every tool in a policy package pushes bank lending in the same direction.
boss.feedback: The open-market purchase is expansionary, while a higher return on reserves can weaken the lending response.

boss.q: A central bank wants to drain reserves quickly without changing reserve requirements. Which action is most direct?
options: Buy government securities and credit reserve accounts.
Sell government securities and debit reserve accounts.
Lower the discount rate to make reserve borrowing cheaper.
Lower interest paid on reserves to discourage reserve holding.
boss.commonError: Choosing an expansionary action when the goal is to remove reserves.
boss.feedback: An open-market sale receives payment from the banking system and reduces reserves directly.

boss.q: Reserve requirements are lowered, but banks expect severe loan losses and keep the newly available reserves idle. What does this illustrate?
options: Lower reserve requirements always produce the full textbook deposit multiplier.
Banks lose the legal ability to hold excess reserves after requirements decline.
Policy can expand lending capacity without guaranteeing that banks will lend.
The central bank shifts aggregate supply left whenever it changes reserve rules.
boss.commonError: Treating potential money creation as automatic actual money creation.
boss.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free reserves for lending, but risk perceptions and bank choices can weaken the actual expansion.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has $3,000,000 in deposits, $510,000 in reserves, and a 12 percent reserve requirement. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 15 percent. How much lending capacity remains after the change?
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the Fed changes policy
legendaryBoss.feedback: New required reserves are 0.15 x $3,000,000 = $450,000. With $510,000 in reserves, lending capacity is $60,000.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply by $480 million. The money multiplier is 6, but currency drain is expected to make the actual multiplier closer to 4. What bond sale is closest to the needed action?
options: Sell $120 million in bonds.
Sell $80 million in bonds.
Buy $120 million in bonds.
Buy $80 million in bonds.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the simple multiplier instead of the adjusted multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: With the actual multiplier closer to 4, the Fed sells $480 million / 4 = $120 million in bonds.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed buys bonds, lowers the discount rate, but raises interest on reserves sharply. Which answer best explains why the final lending response may be muted?
options: Reserve expansion may be offset if banks prefer earning interest on reserves.
All three actions are contractionary and must reduce reserves.
Higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend every dollar.
The discount rate only affects government spending.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming all listed Fed actions push lending the same way
legendaryBoss.feedback: Bond purchases and a lower discount rate are expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can weaken lending.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed wants a $900 million maximum money expansion. The reserve ratio is 12.5 percent. Under the simple model, how large should the bond purchase be?
options: $112.5 million
$900 million
$7.2 billion
$125 million
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying the target expansion by the multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.125 = 8. Required bond purchase is $900 million / 8 = $112.5 million.

repairQuestions.q: If the Fed buys bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: Fed bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

repairQuestions.q: If the Fed sells bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Fall
Rise
Double
Become M2
repairQuestions.feedback: Fed bond sales drain reserves from the banking system.

repairQuestions.q: Raising the interest rate paid on bank reserves tends to:
options: Encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend
Force banks to lend all reserves
Raise the money multiplier automatically
Shift SRAS right
repairQuestions.feedback: A higher return on reserves increases the incentive to hold reserves, which can restrain lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: If the reserve requirement is lowered, other things equal, what happens to the amount of deposits banks must hold as required reserves?
options: It falls, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending
It rises, leaving fewer reserves potentially available for lending
It is unchanged because reserve requirements affect only currency
It becomes equal to total bank capital
repairQuestions.feedback: A lower reserve requirement reduces the amount of deposits that must be held as required reserves, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing that bond purchases add reserves.
repairQuestions.q: A Fed bond purchase adds money to:
options: The banking system
The tax code
Imports only
Used goods markets only
repairQuestions.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
options: Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks
Required reserves automatically rise for every bank
The Treasury must reduce government spending
The public is forced to hold less currency
repairQuestions.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost to banks of borrowing directly from the central bank.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing that bond sales drain reserves.
repairQuestions.q: A Fed bond sale usually causes bank reserves to:
options: Fall
Rise
Double automatically
Become taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: When the public pays the Fed for bonds, reserves leave the banking system.

bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank buys securities and bank reserves rise, but banks choose to hold much of the new reserves idle. What does this show about the policy chain?
options: The tool can increase reserves even when the resulting expansion of bank deposits is smaller than the simple model predicts
The asset purchase failed to change reserves, so it was not a monetary-policy action
Holding excess reserves forces the money multiplier above its simple maximum
A central-bank asset purchase automatically becomes fiscal policy when banks do not lend
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The asset purchase raises bank reserves, but banks’ decision to hold excess reserves can leave deposit creation below the simple-multiplier prediction.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank buys securities, increasing reserves and the money supply. In the liquidity-preference money-market model, what is the next directional step, other things equal?
options: The equilibrium interest rate tends to fall
The equilibrium interest rate must rise because reserves increased
Aggregate supply immediately shifts left before any interest-rate change
The federal budget deficit automatically falls by the amount of the purchase
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With money demand unchanged, the increase in money supply creates excess balances and puts downward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank sells securities, reducing reserves and the money supply. In the liquidity-preference money-market model, what is the next directional step, other things equal?
options: The equilibrium interest rate tends to rise
The equilibrium interest rate must fall because reserves decreased
Aggregate supply immediately shifts right before any interest-rate change
The federal budget surplus automatically rises by the amount of the sale
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With money demand unchanged, the decrease in money supply creates excess money demand and puts upward pressure on the equilibrium interest rate.

monetary-control-limits.title: Limits of Monetary Control
monetary-control-limits.description: Evaluate currency drain, excess reserves, leverage risk, and multiplier slippage.

easy.q: Why is the Fed's control over the money supply not perfect?
options: M1 and M2 are always equal
Currency is not money
The Fed cannot buy bonds
Banks and depositors also influence lending
easy.commonError: Assuming the Fed controls every dollar directly.
easy.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits.

easy.q: The Fed's control over the money supply is imperfect partly because
options: banks may choose to hold excess reserves
Congress directly controls every bank loan
money demand is always zero
currency cannot be held by the public
easy.commonError: thinking the Fed can force banks to lend every excess reserve
easy.feedback: The Fed can influence lending conditions, but banks may still choose to hold excess reserves.

easy.q: The Fed's control over the money supply is imperfect partly because households can choose to hold more money as
options: currency instead of deposits
real GDP instead of inflation
tax revenue instead of government spending
imports instead of exports
easy.commonError: forgetting that currency held by the public affects bank reserves and deposit creation
easy.feedback: If people hold more currency instead of deposits, banks have fewer deposits to lend out, limiting money creation.

easy.q: If banks become nervous and stop lending excess reserves, the money multiplier will
options: be smaller than the simple multiplier predicts
be larger than the simple multiplier predicts
be exactly equal to the inflation rate
stop depending on reserves
easy.commonError: thinking the simple multiplier always predicts the exact real-world result
easy.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves instead of lending them, deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier suggests.

easy.q: Why might a Fed policy action fail to increase the money supply as much as expected?
options: Banks may not lend all available excess reserves.
The Fed cannot buy government bonds.
Fiat money must have intrinsic value.
The price level is always fixed.
easy.commonError: assuming central bank policy mechanically creates lending one-for-one
easy.feedback: Fed actions influence the money supply, but the final effect depends partly on bank lending decisions.

easy.q: Interest on reserves can affect monetary control because it changes banks' incentive to
options: hold reserves instead of lending them
calculate real GDP
set tax rates
issue commodity money
easy.commonError: thinking interest on reserves has nothing to do with bank lending
easy.feedback: Paying interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend them, affecting money creation.

medium.q: If banks decide to hold more excess reserves, the money creation process becomes:
options: Stronger because lending rises
Weaker because lending falls
Unchanged because reserves do not matter
Infinite because deposits disappear
medium.commonError: Ignoring bank behavior in monetary control.
medium.feedback: When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.

medium.q: Why is the simple money multiplier only a rough prediction in the real world?
options: Banks may hold excess reserves and people may hold currency.
The Fed cannot affect reserves in any way.
Deposits are not part of the money supply.
Banks always lend exactly zero.
medium.commonError: thinking the simple multiplier always predicts the exact result
medium.feedback: The simple multiplier assumes banks lend all excess reserves and the public holds no currency; excess reserves and currency holdings make actual money creation smaller.

medium.q: If households decide to hold more currency and fewer bank deposits, banks will have
options: fewer deposits available to support loans
more deposits available to support loans
no reserve requirement
a larger required reserve ratio automatically
medium.commonError: thinking currency holdings do not affect bank lending
medium.feedback: When people hold more currency, fewer funds sit in deposits, which limits bank lending and money creation.

medium.q: A bank holds excess reserves during a financial panic. What happens to deposit creation compared with the simple multiplier prediction?
options: Deposit creation is weaker.
Deposit creation is stronger.
Deposit creation is exactly unchanged.
Deposit creation becomes unrelated to reserves.
medium.commonError: ignoring bank behavior in money creation
medium.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

medium.q: Which situation makes the Fed's control over the money supply less precise?
options: Banks change how much they want to lend.
The Fed exists as a central bank.
Money has three functions.
Prices are quoted in dollars.
medium.commonError: thinking central bank control is mechanically perfect
medium.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but bank lending decisions affect the final amount of money created.

medium.q: The central bank supplies ample reserves and banks are willing to lend, but households and firms become reluctant to borrow. What happens to deposit creation relative to the simple multiplier maximum?
options: Weak loan demand can keep deposit creation below the simple-multiplier maximum
It must equal the maximum because reserve supply alone determines every loan
It must exceed the maximum because unborrowed reserves count twice
It becomes fiscal policy because borrowers are not requesting loans
medium.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
medium.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

hard.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold the new reserves instead of lending them. What happens to the money multiplier process?
options: It weakens despite higher reserves
It strengthens despite no lending
It becomes unrelated to banks
It eliminates currency from M1
hard.commonError: Assuming Fed purchases always create full deposit expansion.
hard.feedback: Fed purchases raise reserves, but deposit expansion is weaker if banks do not lend those reserves.

hard.q: A student says, 'The Fed can perfectly control the money supply because it controls reserves.' What is the best correction?
options: Bank reserves and public currency choices affect final money creation.
The Fed cannot influence reserves at all.
Banks cannot create money in a fractional reserve system.
Currency held by the public always increases deposits.
hard.commonError: assuming Fed control over reserves equals perfect control over money supply
hard.feedback: The Fed has powerful tools, but final money creation depends partly on banks and the public.

hard.q: During a panic, banks hold excess reserves and households withdraw deposits into currency. What happens to the money multiplier?
options: It falls below the simple multiplier prediction.
It rises above the simple multiplier prediction.
It becomes equal to the reserve requirement.
It becomes unrelated to bank behavior.
hard.commonError: using the simple multiplier mechanically during financial stress
hard.feedback: Both excess reserves and currency withdrawals weaken deposit creation, so the actual multiplier falls.

hard.q: If the Fed injects reserves but banks choose not to lend them, why might the money supply grow less than expected?
options: The reserves remain idle instead of supporting new deposits.
The reserve requirement must have become 100 percent by law.
The public must have stopped using money entirely.
The Fed's bond purchase automatically reduced deposits.
hard.commonError: assuming injected reserves are always fully multiplied
hard.feedback: Reserves only multiply into deposits if banks lend and borrowers redeposit. If banks sit on reserves, the multiplier weakens.

hard.q: A higher interest rate paid on reserves can make monetary policy tighter because it
options: raises the reward for banks to hold reserves instead of lending
forces households to hold more commodity money
automatically lowers all taxes
makes money demand zero
hard.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending incentives
hard.feedback: If reserves pay more, banks may prefer holding reserves over making loans, which can restrain money creation.

hard.q: If the public suddenly deposits more currency into banks and banks lend excess reserves, what happens to the banking system's ability to create money?
options: It increases because deposits and reserves available for lending rise.
It decreases because deposits destroy reserves.
It stays unchanged because deposits are never lent.
It disappears because money becomes fiat.
hard.commonError: thinking moving currency into banks weakens lending
hard.feedback: When currency becomes bank deposits, banks have more deposits and reserves to support lending.

hard.q: A central bank wants to expand lending but banks are already holding large excess reserves. Which issue is most relevant?
options: Bank willingness to lend may limit money creation.
Commodity money must replace fiat money.
M1 must exclude checking deposits.
Velocity must be exactly zero.
hard.commonError: thinking more reserves automatically guarantees more loans
hard.feedback: More reserves do not guarantee more lending if banks are unwilling to lend.

hard.q: A Fed bond purchase increases reserves, but households convert much of the new deposits into currency. What is the likely result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by more than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply cannot rise at all because bonds were purchased.
Currency holdings make the reserve requirement negative.
hard.commonError: ignoring leakages from deposits into currency
hard.feedback: Currency drain limits redepositing, so the multiplier effect is weaker.

hard.q: Which statement best explains why banks cannot make society rich simply by creating more money through lending?
options: Money creation can increase nominal balances, but it does not automatically create real goods and services.
Every bank loan creates new factories instantly.
Money creation permanently increases real output without limits.
The money supply is unrelated to prices or output.
hard.commonError: thinking more money means more real wealth automatically
hard.feedback: Banks can help create money, but real wealth depends on real goods, services, labor, capital, and productivity.

elite.q: A bank receives new deposits, the Fed pays higher interest on reserves, and banks choose to hold more excess reserves. What is the likely result?
options: Money creation weakens because lending falls
Money creation strengthens because deposits rose
The multiplier becomes unrelated to reserves
M1 falls because deposits are excluded
elite.commonError: Assuming deposits automatically create full lending expansion.
elite.feedback: Deposits increase lending potential, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

elite.q: The Fed buys bonds during a banking panic, but households increase currency holdings and banks increase excess reserves. What should students infer?
options: Fed control is limited by depositor and bank behavior
The money multiplier must rise to its maximum
Open-market purchases cannot affect reserves
Currency holdings are excluded from M1
elite.commonError: Ignoring leakage from currency holdings and excess reserves.
elite.feedback: Fed purchases add reserves, but currency withdrawals and excess reserve holdings can weaken money creation.

elite.q: The Fed buys $30 million in bonds. The reserve ratio is 10 percent, but banks hold half of new reserves as excess reserves. Which answer best describes the actual result compared with the simple multiplier maximum?
options: The actual money increase is less than the $300 million simple multiplier maximum.
The actual money increase equals exactly $300 million.
The actual money increase exceeds $300 million because excess reserves multiply faster.
The money supply must fall because bond purchases are contractionary.
elite.commonError: using the simple multiplier even when banks hold excess reserves
elite.feedback: The simple maximum would be $30 million x 10 = $300 million, but excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

elite.q: A student says, 'If the Fed lowers reserve requirements, the money supply must always rise by the maximum multiplier amount.' What is the best correction?
options: The maximum depends on banks lending excess reserves and borrowers redepositing funds.
Lower reserve requirements always eliminate excess reserves.
The money supply must fall when reserve requirements fall.
Reserve requirements affect only fiscal policy.
elite.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as a guaranteed result
elite.feedback: The simple multiplier is a maximum under strict assumptions. Banks and the public can weaken the actual money creation process.

elite.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. The public moves $50 million from currency into checking deposits. The reserve ratio is 10 percent and banks lend all excess reserves. What is the maximum total deposit expansion supported by this shift?
options: $500 million
$50 million
$45 million
$5 million
elite.commonError: thinking currency deposited into banks cannot support money creation
elite.feedback: Moving currency into deposits gives banks reserves to support lending. With a multiplier of 10, $50 million can support up to $500 million in deposits. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

elite.q: The public withdraws $50 million from checking deposits into currency. The reserve ratio is 10 percent. Why can the final money supply fall by more than $50 million?
options: The withdrawal removes reserves from banks and reduces further deposit creation.
Currency automatically multiplies faster than deposits.
Banks gain excess reserves from the withdrawal.
Reserve requirements become negative.
elite.commonError: thinking a currency withdrawal affects only the first $50 million
elite.feedback: A currency drain reduces bank reserves and shrinks the base for additional lending, so the total effect can exceed the initial withdrawal.

elite.q: Which scenario best illustrates why Fed control is powerful but not perfect?
options: The Fed injects reserves, but banks hold them because loan risk is high.
The Fed buys bonds and every bank must lend every reserve by law.
The Fed sets M1 exactly by counting every dollar daily.
The Fed controls household spending by setting tax brackets.
elite.commonError: assuming Fed reserve injections automatically become loans
elite.feedback: Fed tools matter, but banks still decide whether they are willing to lend.

elite.q: If the Fed buys $100 million in bonds but the public holds all proceeds as currency instead of depositing them, which part of the simple multiplier process breaks?
options: Redepositing into banks, which limits further lending.
The initial Fed injection, which never occurs.
The definition of fiat money.
The unit of account function.
elite.commonError: thinking currency held by the public supports the same lending as deposits
elite.feedback: The money enters the public's hands, but if it is not deposited, banks cannot use it as reserves for further lending.

elite.q: Which answer best explains why lowering the discount rate may not create much lending during a crisis?
options: Banks may still avoid borrowing or lending if they see borrowers as too risky.
Lower borrowing costs always force banks to lend.
The discount rate controls tax rates, not bank borrowing.
Lower discount rates automatically create commodity money.
elite.commonError: assuming cheaper Fed credit guarantees private lending
elite.feedback: Lowering the discount rate helps only if banks are willing to borrow and lend.

legendary.q: The Fed buys $80 million in bonds. The simple reserve ratio is 20 percent, but banks hold 25 percent of new reserves as excess reserves instead of lending them. Which answer best describes the result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $400 million simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $400 million.
The money supply rises by more than $400 million because excess reserves multiply.
The money supply falls because bond purchases are contractionary.
legendary.commonError: using the simple multiplier even when excess reserves are explicitly introduced
legendary.feedback: The simple multiplier maximum is 1/0.20 = 5, so $80 million could become $400 million. But excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

legendary.q: In a hypothetical fully loaned-up system with a fixed 10 percent reserve ratio and no excess reserves, the public permanently switches $36 million from deposits to currency. The monetary base stays fixed. Banks restore their reserve ratios through loan repayments that destroy deposits; there are no defaults or other changes. What are the final changes in deposits and in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $324 million.
Deposits fall $36 million; money is unchanged.
Deposits fall $360 million; money falls $396 million.
Deposits fall $324 million; money falls $360 million.
legendary.commonError: thinking currency withdrawal only changes the location of money with no multiplier effect
legendary.feedback: Currency rises $36 million and reserves fall $36 million. At reserves/deposits = 0.10, deposits must fall $360 million in total. Money changes by +$36 million − $360 million = −$324 million.

legendary.q: The Fed sells $75 million in bonds. The multiplier is 4, but the public responds by moving additional funds out of banks into currency. What should we expect relative to the simple multiplier result?
options: The contraction may exceed $300 million because currency drain further weakens deposit creation.
The contraction must equal exactly $300 million.
The money supply must increase because bond sales add reserves.
The contraction must be smaller because currency drain raises bank reserves.
legendary.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as exact even with added currency drain
legendary.feedback: The simple contraction is $75 million x 4 = $300 million, but currency drain can make the banking contraction larger.

legendary.q: A bank has a reserve shortfall of $20,000. The Fed lowers the discount rate, but the bank still refuses to borrow because it fears insolvency. What does this show?
options: A lower discount rate may not restore lending if bank risk concerns dominate.
The discount rate only affects fiscal policy.
Lower discount rates always force borrowing.
Reserve shortfalls increase lending capacity.
legendary.commonError: thinking a lower policy rate automatically fixes bank behavior
legendary.feedback: The Fed can make borrowing cheaper, but banks may still avoid borrowing or lending when risk dominates.

legendary.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. If the public deposits $30 million in currency into banks, the reserve ratio is 15 percent, and banks lend all excess reserves, what is the maximum total deposit expansion?
options: $200 million
$30 million
$25.5 million
$4.5 million
legendary.commonError: calculating only the first-round loan instead of total deposit expansion
legendary.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.15 = 6.666..., so $30 million can support about $200 million in total deposits. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

legendary.q: A student says, 'If banks create money through loans, loans must create real goods too.' What is the best correction?
options: Loans create deposits; real output still needs productive resources.
Loans automatically create real output one-for-one.
Deposits are not money.
Banks create commodity money with every loan.
legendary.commonError: thinking money creation equals real wealth creation
legendary.feedback: Bank lending can expand money and spending power, but it does not automatically create more real goods and services.

legendary.q: A new $100,000 deposit enters the banking system. The required reserve ratio is 10 percent, but the public withdraws 20 percent of every new loan as currency before redepositing the rest. What happens relative to the simple multiplier?
options: The final expansion is smaller than the simple $1,000,000 maximum.
The final expansion equals exactly $1,000,000.
The final expansion is larger because currency leakage increases reserves.
The money supply must contract because deposits increase.
legendary.commonError: using the simple multiplier despite a stated currency leakage
legendary.feedback: The simple maximum is $100,000 x 10 = $1,000,000, but currency leakage reduces redeposits and weakens money creation.

legendary.q: Which statement best combines Chapter 30's banking model with monetary-control limits?
options: Excess reserves and currency holdings weaken deposit multiplication.
Fractional reserve banking guarantees exact Fed control of M1.
The multiplier works only with commodity money.
Currency drain increases bank reserves and expands lending.
legendary.commonError: thinking the multiplier mechanism is automatic and exact
legendary.feedback: Fractional-reserve banking can multiply deposits, but excess reserves and currency holdings can make the actual expansion smaller than the simple model predicts.

calculation.q: A bank has $2 million in assets and $120,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 4 percent, capital falls to:
calculation.commonError: Applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets.
calculation.feedback: A 4 percent asset loss is $80,000, so capital falls from $120,000 to $40,000.

calculation.q: A bank has assets of $1,000,000 and capital of $80,000. If assets fall by $40,000, bank capital becomes:
calculation.commonError: Thinking losses reduce liabilities first.
calculation.feedback: Losses reduce bank capital. $80,000 - $40,000 = $40,000.

boss.q: Why is the Fed's control over the money supply imperfect?
options: Excess reserves and public currency holdings.
The Fed cannot influence reserves.
Banks cannot lend money.
Currency is not money.
boss.commonError: assuming Fed control is mechanically perfect
boss.feedback: The Fed can influence money creation, but banks and the public also matter.

boss.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks choose not to lend because they are worried about risk. What happens relative to the simple multiplier?
options: Money creation is weaker than predicted.
Money creation is stronger than predicted.
The money supply must fall to zero.
The simple multiplier becomes infinite.
boss.commonError: thinking reserves automatically become loans
boss.feedback: If banks hold reserves instead of lending, deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

boss.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks hold some excess reserves, and households keep some proceeds as currency. What is the best conclusion?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by exactly the simple multiplier amount.
The money supply must fall because households hold currency.
The Fed has perfect control over final money creation.
boss.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed
boss.feedback: Excess reserves and currency drain both weaken the multiplier. The Fed is powerful, not magical.

boss.q: After a reserve injection, banks hold extra reserves, the public keeps some loan proceeds as currency, and firms reduce borrowing. Relative to the simple multiplier model, what should we expect?
options: No change in broad money because reserve injections affect only bank capital
A substantially smaller expansion because several leakages interrupt repeated lending and redepositing
The exact simple multiplier maximum because the three effects cancel automatically
A larger expansion because every leakage creates additional bank reserves
boss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
boss.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

boss.q: Which statement best describes what the central bank controls most directly?
options: Its own balance sheet and reserve conditions, not the exact final quantity of broad money
The exact quantity of bank loans made to every borrower
The public’s desired split between currency and deposits
The amount every commercial bank must want to lend regardless of risk
boss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
boss.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

boss.q: The central bank lowers a policy-related borrowing rate, but banks still see borrowers as risky and firms do not want new loans. Why can the monetary response remain weak?
options: A lower central-bank lending rate automatically raises required reserves
The policy turns into a tax change when private borrowing is weak
Commercial banks are legally required to stop lending whenever the central bank lowers a rate
Cheaper central-bank liquidity does not eliminate bank risk concerns or weak credit demand
boss.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
boss.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

boss.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold much of them as excess reserves. What is the likely result?
options: Broad deposit creation is smaller than the simple multiplier maximum
Deposit creation must equal the maximum because reserves increased
The money supply must fall by the amount of the reserve injection
Required reserves disappear from bank balance sheets
boss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
boss.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

boss.q: Households convert part of each new bank deposit into currency rather than leaving the funds in banks. What happens to the deposit-multiplication process?
options: It strengthens because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves
It is unchanged because currency and bank reserves are identical
It guarantees a larger simple multiplier regardless of the reserve ratio
It weakens because less money is redeposited into banks for additional lending
boss.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
boss.feedback: When households keep currency, less of each loan is redeposited; fewer redeposits support fewer subsequent lending rounds, weakening deposit multiplication.

boss.q: Banks have ample reserves and are willing to lend, but creditworthy firms postpone borrowing during a severe slump. Which limitation is illustrated?
options: Household currency holdings must have fallen to zero
Bank capital automatically rises whenever firms reject loans
Weak loan demand can keep money creation below the textbook maximum
The central bank has lost the legal authority to create reserves
boss.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
boss.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed buys $120 million in bonds. The reserve ratio is 10 percent, but banks hold 30 percent of new reserves as excess reserves. Which result is most accurate?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $1.2 billion simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $1.2 billion.
The money supply falls because bond purchases drain reserves.
The money supply rises by more than $1.2 billion because excess reserves multiply faster.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the simple multiplier as exact when excess reserves are stated
legendaryBoss.feedback: The simple maximum is $120 million x 10 = $1.2 billion, but excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has $2 million in deposits, $260,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. The public then withdraws $100,000 in currency from deposits. If deposits and reserves both fall by $100,000, what is the bank's reserve position after the withdrawal?
options: It is short $30,000 in reserves.
It has $70,000 in excess reserves.
It has exactly required reserves.
It can lend $160,000.
legendaryBoss.commonError: not reducing both deposits and reserves after currency withdrawal
legendaryBoss.feedback: After withdrawal, deposits are $1.9 million and reserves are $160,000. Required reserves are $190,000, so the bank is short $30,000.

legendaryBoss.q: In a hypothetical banking system initially without excess reserves, the public deposits $56,000 of existing currency. The required-reserve ratio stays at 20 percent. Each bank lends all excess reserves; after every loan, 25 percent stays as currency and 75 percent reaches the next bank. No other constraint binds. Including the initial deposit, what is the eventual deposit increase, and what is the net increase in currency plus deposits?
options: Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $112,000.
Deposits rise $280,000; net money rises $224,000.
Deposits rise $140,000; net money rises $140,000.
Deposits rise $112,000; net money rises $84,000.
legendaryBoss.commonError: ignoring the currency leakage stated in the question
legendaryBoss.feedback: Successive deposits have ratio 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60, so their sum is $56,000/(1 − 0.60) = $140,000. Total loans are 0.80 × $140,000 = $112,000; $28,000 returns to public currency. Currency changes by −$56,000 + $28,000, so net money rises $112,000.

legendaryBoss.q: A policy memo claims that supplying more reserves guarantees the full textbook deposit expansion, even when creditworthy firms postpone borrowing and banks retain excess reserves. Which correction addresses both breaks in the argument?
options: Banks must be willing to lend and borrowers willing to borrow; unused reserves do not guarantee new deposits.
Only the reserve requirement matters; banks and borrowers cannot alter the predicted expansion.
Borrower caution raises the multiplier because fewer loans consume fewer reserves.
Excess reserves are already customer deposits, so the predicted expansion has occurred.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming reserve injections guarantee full lending
legendaryBoss.feedback: The reserve injection is an input to a conditional model. Both bank decisions and credit demand can prevent the lending and redepositing needed to reach its maximum.

repairQuestions.q: If a bank’s assets fall, what absorbs the loss first?
options: Bank capital
Currency
M1
The CPI
repairQuestions.feedback: Losses reduce bank capital.

repairQuestions.q: Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?
options: Banks and depositors affect lending and reserves
The Fed cannot buy bonds
Currency is not money
Deposits never change
repairQuestions.feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors also affect it.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
repairQuestions.q: The simple multiplier overpredicts money creation when banks:
options: Hold excess reserves
Lend all excess reserves
Face a lower reserve ratio
Receive new deposits
repairQuestions.feedback: If banks hold excess reserves, less money is created through lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Ignoring public currency holdings.
repairQuestions.q: If people hold more currency instead of deposits, bank money creation usually:
options: Weakens
Strengthens
Becomes unlimited
Is unaffected by reserves
repairQuestions.feedback: Currency held outside banks cannot support deposit creation the same way bank deposits can.

bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $500,000 in assets and $30,000 in capital. If assets fall by $20,000, capital becomes:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Losses reduce capital, so $30,000 - $20,000 = $10,000.

bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold excess reserves. What should happen to deposit creation?
options: It is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts
It reaches the full multiplier automatically
It becomes unrelated to lending
It eliminates currency from M1
bridgeQuestions.feedback: If banks do not lend excess reserves, the deposit expansion process weakens.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
bridgeQuestions.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks hold half of them as excess reserves. What happens?
options: Money creation is less than the simple multiplier predicts
Money creation is exactly the simple maximum
Money creation is larger than the simple maximum
Money supply must fall
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Excess reserve holding weakens the multiplier process.

liquidity-preference-and-money-market.title: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
liquidity-preference-and-money-market.description: Determine money-market equilibrium and interest-rate adjustment.

easy.q: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate adjusts to balance:
options: Money supply and money demand
Taxes and spending
Imports and exports
Inflation and unemployment
easy.commonError: Confusing money-market equilibrium with fiscal balance.
easy.feedback: Liquidity preference theory says the interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

easy.q: Liquidity preference theory says the interest rate adjusts to balance
options: money supply and money demand
aggregate supply and aggregate demand
tax revenue and government spending
exports and imports
easy.commonError: confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
easy.feedback: Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the price that balances money supply and money demand.

easy.q: In liquidity preference theory, the money supply is assumed to be fixed by
options: the central bank
household income
the price level alone
consumer confidence
easy.commonError: thinking money supply slopes downward like money demand
easy.feedback: In this model, the central bank fixes the money supply.

easy.q: When the interest rate rises, the opportunity cost of holding money
options: rises
falls
disappears
becomes the price level
easy.commonError: forgetting that bonds pay more when interest rates rise
easy.feedback: A higher interest rate raises the opportunity cost of holding money instead of bonds.

easy.q: When the interest rate rises, money demand tends to
options: fall
rise
become vertical
equal government spending
easy.commonError: thinking higher interest rates increase money demand
easy.feedback: Higher interest rates make holding money more costly, so money demand falls.

easy.q: When real income rises, money demand tends to
options: rise
fall
stay fixed by the Fed
turn into money supply
easy.commonError: thinking higher income reduces transaction demand for money
easy.feedback: Higher income means people buy more goods and services, so they demand more money for transactions.

easy.q: When the price level rises, money demand tends to
options: rise
fall
stay unchanged because prices do not matter
become equal to investment
easy.commonError: thinking a higher price level reduces the dollars needed for purchases
easy.feedback: A higher price level means people need more dollars to buy the same goods, so money demand rises.

easy.q: At point A in the money market, what is the equilibrium nominal interest rate?
options: 6 percent
4 percent
8 percent
12 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: Point A is where MD0 intersects MS0, at a nominal interest rate of 6 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Money market with downward-sloping money demand MD0 and vertical money supply MS0 intersecting at point A.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Money demand MD0 slopes downward from an interest rate of 12 at quantity 0 to 0 at quantity 200. Money supply MS0 is vertical at quantity 100. The curves intersect at point A, quantity of money 100 and nominal interest rate 6.

easy.q: The money-supply curve moves from MS0 at 100 to MS1 at 125. What happens to the equilibrium nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
It stays at 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: With money demand fixed, the larger money supply moves equilibrium down MD0 from 4 percent to 2 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 125; its MD0 intersection is at rate 2. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 2.

easy.q: When the money-supply line moves left from 100 to 75, how does the equilibrium interest rate respond?
options: It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
It falls from 6 percent to 4 percent
It stays at 4 percent
It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: With money demand fixed, the smaller money supply moves equilibrium up MD0 from 4 percent to 6 percent.
easy.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with MD0 and vertical MS0 and MS1.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money and the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. The straight downward MD0 line runs from (0,12) to (150,0). Solid MS0 is vertical at quantity 100; its MD0 intersection is at rate 4. Dashed MS1 is vertical at quantity 75; its MD0 intersection is at rate 6. Horizontal dashed guides mark rates 4 and 6.

easy.q: Which labeled point is the original equilibrium where MD0 intersects MS0?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
Point D
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: The original curves MD0 and MS0 intersect at point B, quantity 75 and interest rate 3.
easy.imageAlt: Money-market diagram with two vertical MS lines, two downward MD lines and labeled points A, B, C and D.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is quantity of money; the vertical axis is nominal interest rate. Solid MS0 is vertical at 75 and dashed MS1 at 100. Solid MD0 is the lower straight downward line, through B (75,3) and D (100,1). Dashed MD1 is the upper parallel line, through A (75,6) and C (100,4). MD1 crosses the vertical axis at 12 and the horizontal axis at 150. MD0 crosses the vertical axis at 9. All four points are marked with black dots.

easy.q: In the left panel, money demand rises from MD0 to MD1 while MS0 stays fixed. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 2 percent to 4 percent
It falls from 4 percent to 2 percent
It stays at 2 percent
It rises from 4 percent to 6 percent
easy.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
easy.feedback: With fixed money supply, the higher money-demand curve raises the equilibrium interest rate from point A to point B.
easy.imageAlt: Two panels with MS0, MD0 and MD1 on the left and AD0, AD1 and SRAS on the right.
easy.graphDescription: Left panel axes: quantity of money horizontally and nominal interest rate (%) vertically. MS0 is vertical at 75. Solid downward MD0 passes through A (75,2); upper dashed MD1 passes through B (75,4). Right panel axes: real GDP horizontally and price level vertically. Solid AD0 and lower dashed AD1 slope downward; red SRAS slopes upward. AD0 and SRAS meet at A (150,55); AD1 and SRAS meet at B (105,45). Dashed guides identify the point coordinates.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD1 unchanged, money supply increases from MS1 to MS2. Which equilibrium movement follows?
options: g to e
e to g
a to d
c to f
medium.commonError: Using the wrong money demand curve.
medium.feedback: MD1 intersects MS1 at e and MS2 at g. Increasing supply moves equilibrium from e to g and lowers the nominal interest rate.
medium.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
medium.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market graph. If money demand shifts from MD1 to MD2 while money supply remains MS1, equilibrium moves from:
options: e to a
a to e
g to d
f to c
medium.commonError: Confusing money demand shifts with money supply shifts.
medium.feedback: At MS1, MD1 intersects at e and MD2 intersects at a, so the interest rate rises.
medium.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
medium.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

medium.q: Refer to the money-market graph. Which point shows MS2 and MD2 in equilibrium?
options: a
b
d
g
medium.commonError: Reading a non-intersection point as equilibrium.
medium.feedback: MS2 and MD2 intersect at point d.
medium.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves and two downward-sloping money-demand curves.
medium.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right/up and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.

medium.q: If real income rises, money demand increases. In the liquidity preference model, this tends to:
options: Raise the interest rate
Lower the interest rate
Reduce money supply automatically
Shift AD left directly
medium.commonError: Thinking more money demand lowers interest rates.
medium.feedback: Higher money demand pushes the interest rate up when money supply is fixed.

medium.q: Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the variable that balances
options: money supply and money demand
labor supply and labor demand
exports and imports
taxes and spending
medium.commonError: confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
medium.feedback: The interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

medium.q: Which curve shows the amount of money fixed by the central bank?
options: The vertical money supply curve
The downward-sloping money demand curve
The aggregate demand curve
The multiplier curve
medium.commonError: thinking money demand is fixed by the central bank
medium.feedback: The central bank fixes the money supply in this model, so money supply is vertical.

medium.q: Which curve slopes downward because higher interest rates reduce the quantity of money demanded?
options: Money demand
Money supply
Aggregate demand
Long-run aggregate supply
medium.commonError: thinking money supply slopes downward
medium.feedback: Money demand slopes downward because higher interest rates raise the opportunity cost of holding money.

medium.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, the equilibrium interest rate should
options: rise
fall
stay unchanged
become the price level
medium.commonError: thinking higher money demand lowers the interest rate
medium.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes the equilibrium interest rate up.

medium.q: If real income rises, money demand increases because households
options: need more money for transactions
want fewer goods and services
face a lower price level automatically
stop holding liquid assets
medium.commonError: thinking higher income lowers transaction demand for money
medium.feedback: Higher income usually means more buying and selling, so people demand more money for transactions.

medium.q: If the price level rises while output is unchanged, money demand increases because people
options: need more dollars to buy the same goods
need fewer dollars to buy the same goods
earn no income
stop buying bonds forever
medium.commonError: thinking higher prices reduce the dollars needed for transactions
medium.feedback: Higher prices mean people need more money to buy the same amount of goods and services.

medium.q: At point A, what quantity of money clears the market?
medium.commonError: misreads_money_market_or_transmission
medium.feedback: The vertical money-supply curve MS0 is fixed at quantity 100, and MD0 intersects it at point A.

Money demand falls, interest rates fall, and investment rises.

Money demand rises, interest rates fall, and investment rises.

hard.feedback: Higher prices increase money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment.

hard.q: Why does a lower price level increase the quantity of goods and services demanded?
options: Lower prices reduce money demand, lower interest rates, and increase investment.
Lower prices increase money demand, raise interest rates, and lower investment.
Lower prices reduce money supply and shift AD left.
Lower prices eliminate the need for investment.
hard.commonError: thinking lower prices raise money demand
hard.feedback: Lower prices reduce money demand, which lowers interest rates and raises investment spending.

hard.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply stays fixed, what must happen to restore money-market equilibrium?
options: The interest rate rises.
The interest rate falls.
Money supply shifts left automatically.
Aggregate demand becomes vertical.

hard.feedback: With fixed money supply, stronger money demand pushes the equilibrium interest rate up.

hard.q: A rise in real income shifts money demand right. If the Fed holds money supply fixed, what happens next?
options: Interest rates rise.
Interest rates fall.
Money supply rises automatically.
Investment rises because borrowing is cheaper.
hard.commonError: thinking higher income lowers transaction demand for money
hard.feedback: Higher income increases money demand. With fixed money supply, the interest rate rises.

hard.q: A fall in the price level shifts money demand left. If money supply is fixed, what happens to the interest rate?
options: It falls.
It rises.
It stays fixed because money demand cannot shift.
It becomes the inflation rate.
hard.commonError: thinking a lower price level increases money demand
hard.feedback: A lower price level reduces the dollars needed for transactions, so money demand falls and interest rates fall.

hard.q: Moving downward along MD0 from a higher to a lower interest rate, what happens to the quantity of money demanded?

The quantity of money supplied rises.
The money-demand curve shifts left.
The quantity of money demanded rises.

hard.feedback: Holding other determinants fixed, lower interest rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding money, so quantity of money demanded rises.

elite.q: If income rises and the Fed prevents interest rates from rising, what policy shift is needed?
options: Increase money supply as money demand rises
Decrease money supply as money demand rises
Increase money demand as money supply falls
Decrease money demand as interest rates rise
elite.commonError: Forgetting the Fed must offset higher money demand.
elite.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; to hold rates down, the Fed must increase money supply.

elite.q: If the Fed cuts money supply while money demand rises, what happens to the interest rate pressure?
options: It rises from both forces
It falls from both forces
It rises from supply but falls from demand
It falls from supply but rises from demand
elite.commonError: Missing that both shifts raise rates.
elite.feedback: Lower money supply and higher money demand both push the interest rate upward.

elite.q: Starting in money-market equilibrium, the price level rises. Which full chain explains the interest-rate effect on aggregate demand?
options: Higher P raises money demand, raises r, lowers investment, and lowers quantity of goods and services demanded.
Higher P lowers money demand, lowers r, raises investment, and raises quantity demanded.
Higher P raises money supply, lowers r, raises investment, and shifts AD right.
Higher P lowers money supply, raises r, and shifts money demand left.
elite.commonError: reversing the price-level effect on money demand
elite.feedback: Higher prices require more money for transactions. That raises money demand, raises interest rates, lowers investment, and reduces quantity demanded.

elite.q: Starting at P1 and r1, the price level falls to P2. What happens in the money market and AD model?
options: Money demand falls, r falls, investment rises, and output demanded rises.
Money demand rises, r rises, investment falls, and output demanded falls.
Money supply falls, r rises, and AD shifts left.
Money demand falls, r rises, and investment falls.
elite.commonError: thinking lower prices increase money demand
elite.feedback: A lower price level reduces money demand, lowers interest rates, raises investment, and increases quantity demanded.

elite.q: Money demand shifts from MD1 to MD2 while money supply remains fixed. What is the likely effect on r and investment?
options: r rises and investment falls.
r falls and investment rises.
r rises and investment rises.
r falls and investment falls.
elite.commonError: thinking higher money demand lowers the interest rate
elite.feedback: With fixed money supply, a rightward shift in money demand raises the interest rate, which lowers investment.

elite.q: Money demand shifts left while money supply remains fixed. What chain follows?
options: r falls, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
r rises, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r falls, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r rises, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
elite.commonError: missing the investment response after the money-market movement
elite.feedback: Lower money demand reduces the equilibrium interest rate, which supports investment and AD.

elite.q: If a rise in the price level shifts money demand right and the Fed does not change money supply, why does this help explain the downward slope of AD?
options: Higher P raises r and lowers investment, reducing quantity demanded.
Higher P lowers r and raises investment, increasing quantity demanded.
Higher P shifts AD right by increasing investment.
Higher P makes money supply rise automatically.
elite.commonError: missing that this is movement along AD, not an AD shift
elite.feedback: Higher P raises money demand and interest rates, lowering investment and quantity demanded along the AD curve.

elite.q: If an increase in Y raises money demand and the Fed wants to prevent r from rising, what should the Fed do?
options: Increase money supply to match the higher money demand.
Decrease money supply to reduce money demand.
Raise taxes because money supply cannot shift.
Reduce government spending to make MD vertical.
elite.commonError: thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
elite.feedback: If money demand rises, increasing money supply can prevent the equilibrium interest rate from rising.

elite.q: If P rises, money demand shifts right. If the Fed also increases money supply enough to hold r constant, what happens to the interest-rate effect on AD?
options: It is offset because r does not rise to reduce investment.
It becomes stronger because r rises more.
It reverses because investment must fall more.
It disappears because AD is no longer related to spending.
elite.commonError: ignoring that Fed policy can offset money-demand pressure on r
elite.feedback: If the Fed accommodates the higher money demand, r does not rise, so the investment channel behind the interest-rate effect is muted.

elite.q: A student says a fall in the interest rate from 8 percent to 6 percent would shift MD0 to the right. What is the best correction?
