fisher-effect.title: Fisher Effect
fisher-effect.description: Connect expected inflation to nominal and real interest rates.

easy.q: If expected inflation rises and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should:
options: Fall
Rise
Become zero
Equal real GDP
easy.commonError: Reversing the Fisher effect.
easy.feedback: Nominal interest rates include expected inflation, so they rise when expected inflation rises.

easy.q: The Fisher effect says that when expected inflation rises, the nominal interest rate tends to
options: rise
fall
stay fixed forever
become equal to real GDP growth
easy.commonError: thinking inflation lowers nominal interest rates
easy.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

easy.q: The Fisher equation is most commonly written as
options: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation
real interest rate = nominal interest rate + expected inflation
expected inflation = real GDP + money supply
nominal interest rate = velocity divided by output
easy.commonError: adding inflation to the wrong side of the equation
easy.feedback: The Fisher equation links nominal rates, real rates, and expected inflation: nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation.

easy.q: If expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent and the real interest rate is unchanged, the nominal interest rate should
options: rise by about 3 percentage points
fall by about 3 percentage points
stay exactly the same
fall to zero
easy.commonError: thinking nominal rates ignore expected inflation
easy.feedback: If the real rate is unchanged, a 3-point rise in expected inflation raises the nominal rate by about 3 points.

easy.q: Under the Fisher effect, a country with persistently higher inflation will tend to have
options: higher nominal interest rates
lower nominal interest rates
no nominal interest rates
unchanged price levels forever
easy.commonError: thinking high inflation means low nominal rates
easy.feedback: Higher expected inflation tends to be built into higher nominal interest rates.

easy.q: Lenders begin expecting inflation to be 4 percentage points higher, while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Nominal interest rates tend to rise by about 4 percentage points.
Nominal interest rates tend to fall by about 4 percentage points.
Real interest rates must rise by exactly 4 percentage points.
Actual inflation must immediately equal the new nominal interest rate.
easy.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
easy.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

easy.q: A bank sets a fixed nominal loan rate today for next year. Which inflation concept is most relevant to the Fisher effect when that rate is chosen?
options: Only inflation that has already occurred.
The current unemployment rate by itself.
Only the realized inflation rate known after repayment.
Expected inflation over the loan period.
easy.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
easy.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

medium.q: If expected inflation rises while the real interest rate is unchanged, lenders will require
options: a higher nominal interest rate
a lower nominal interest rate
no repayment
a lower price level
medium.commonError: thinking lenders ignore expected inflation
medium.feedback: Lenders care about purchasing power, so higher expected inflation is built into higher nominal interest rates.

medium.q: Two otherwise similar economies have the same long-run real interest rate, but expected inflation is 2 percent in one and 7 percent in the other. What should differ under the Fisher effect?
options: The second economy should tend to have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher.
The first economy should have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher instead because lower expected inflation raises nominal rates.
Both nominal rates must be identical because real rates match.
The second economy must have a real rate 5 points higher.
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
medium.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

medium.q: Expected inflation falls from 6 percent to 2 percent while the long-run real interest rate remains 3 percent. What nominal-rate change is predicted?
options: The nominal rate rises from about 5 percent to about 9 percent.
The real rate falls from 3 percent to negative 1 percent automatically.
The nominal rate stays at 9 percent because only actual inflation matters.
The nominal rate falls from about 9 percent to about 5 percent.
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
medium.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

medium.q: A one-year loan is priced when inflation is expected to be 3 percent. Actual inflation later turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement separates the Fisher effect from the realized return?
options: The Fisher effect uses actual inflation only and ignores expectations.
Unexpected inflation raises both parties’ realized real returns by the same amount.
The nominal rate reflected expected inflation when set; the unexpectedly high actual inflation changes the ex post real return.
The nominal rate must be rewritten after actual inflation is observed so the original expected rate no longer matters.
medium.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
medium.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

hard.q: Expected inflation rises 6 percentage points while the equilibrium real interest rate falls 2 percentage points. What happens to the nominal interest rate approximately?
options: It rises about 4 percentage points because both expected inflation and the real rate matter.
It rises exactly 6 percentage points because the Fisher effect requires the real rate to remain fixed in every comparison.
It falls about 8 percentage points because expected inflation lowers nominal rates.
It is unchanged because the two components must always offset completely.
hard.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
hard.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

hard.q: Country A has expected inflation of 8 percent and a real interest rate of 1 percent. Country B has expected inflation of 3 percent and a real interest rate of 5 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Country A must have a nominal rate exactly 5 points above Country B.
Country B must have the lower nominal interest rate because lower expected inflation always dominates any real-rate difference.
The Fisher effect says real interest rates are always identical across countries.
A one-for-one comparison of nominal rates cannot use expected inflation alone because the real rates differ too.
hard.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
hard.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

hard.q: Expected inflation falls sharply after a credible long-run policy change, but productive opportunities and saving behavior leave the real rate roughly unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Real interest rates must fall by exactly the same amount as expected inflation.
Nominal rates should stay fixed because only realized inflation affects contracts.
Nominal interest rates should fall as the inflation premium falls.
Nominal interest rates should rise because lower expected inflation raises the inflation premium.
hard.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
hard.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

hard.q: A lender receives a 10 percent nominal rate that was set when expected inflation was 4 percent. Actual inflation is later 9 percent. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Expected inflation is irrelevant once a fixed nominal rate has been written.
The ex ante pricing reflected roughly a 6 percent real return, but the realized real return is much lower.
The Fisher effect predicted a 1 percent real return when the loan was made.
The nominal rate automatically rises to 15 percent after inflation is observed because fixed-rate contracts always adjust retroactively after the fact.
hard.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
hard.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

hard.q: Nominal interest rates rise from 7 to 11 percent at the same time expected inflation rises from 3 to 8 percent. Can we conclude the real rate was unchanged?
options: No. The nominal rate rose 4 points while expected inflation rose 5, so the implied real rate actually fell about 1 point.
Yes. Any rise in nominal rates alongside expected inflation proves the real rate is unchanged.
Yes. The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to rise exactly half as much as expected inflation regardless of changes in real rates.
No. The implied real rate rose about 9 percentage points.
hard.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
hard.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

elite.q: A lender expected 4 percent inflation and charged 9 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 8 percent. What happened to the realized real return?
options: It was lower than expected
It was higher than expected
It was unchanged
It became nominal GDP
elite.commonError: Ignoring unexpected inflation after a loan is written.
elite.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real return to lenders.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower signs a loan at 9 percent nominal interest when expected inflation is 4 percent. Actual inflation is 7 percent. What happened to the realized real interest rate compared with what the lender expected?
options: It fell from 5 percent expected to 2 percent realized.
It rose from 5 percent expected to 7 percent realized.
It stayed at 5 percent because nominal interest was fixed.
It fell from 9 percent expected to 4 percent realized.
elite.commonError: using expected inflation for the realized real rate
elite.feedback: Expected real rate was 9 - 4 = 5 percent. Realized real rate was 9 - 7 = 2 percent.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate is stable at 3 percent, what should happen to the nominal interest rate under the Fisher effect?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 12 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 3 percent.
It rises from 2 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 3 percent.
elite.commonError: forgetting the real interest rate is part of nominal interest
elite.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 3 + 2 = 5 to 3 + 9 = 12 percent.

legendary.q: A lender’s one-year fixed nominal contract pays 12 percent. Expected inflation when written was 5 percent, but actual inflation is 9 percent. Use exact gross returns. What are the expected and realized real returns, and what nominal rate on a new loan would preserve the original expected real return if expected inflation is now 9 percent?
options: About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 16.27 percent.
7 percent, 3 percent, and 16 percent exactly.
About 2.75 percent, 6.67 percent, and 12 percent.
About 6.67 percent, 2.75 percent, and 12 percent.
legendary.commonError: using expected inflation for both expected and realized real rates
legendary.feedback: Expected real return is 1.12/1.05 − 1 = 6.67 percent; realized is 1.12/1.09 − 1 = 2.75 percent. Preserving the original gross real return on a new loan requires (1.12/1.05) × 1.09 − 1 = 16.27 percent nominal.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 11 percent. The real interest rate falls from 3 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 13 percent.
It rises from 4 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
legendary.commonError: assuming the real rate is constant when it is explicitly changed
legendary.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 3 + 4 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 11 = 13 percent.

legendary.q: A one-time monetary expansion lowers the value of money today. Credible guidance says the money-growth rate will then return to its previous path. The long-run real interest rate is unchanged. An analyst concludes that nominal interest rates must remain permanently higher. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: A one-time price-level rise does not establish permanently higher expected inflation, so the lasting nominal-rate claim is unsupported.
The higher price level guarantees permanently higher inflation, so the nominal-rate claim follows.
The lower value of money proves the real interest rate falls permanently, so nominal rates must fall.
Monetary neutrality makes expected inflation irrelevant to nominal rates, so the Fisher relationship does not apply.
legendary.commonError: confusing short-run liquidity effects with long-run Fisher effect
legendary.feedback: The Fisher effect relates nominal rates to expected inflation over the loan horizon. A level adjustment alone does not establish a continuing inflation-rate increase. The real-rate assumption therefore does not complete the analyst’s argument.

legendary.q: Money growth rises from 8 percent to 20 percent. Velocity growth is zero and output growth is 4 percent. If expected inflation adjusts fully, what happens to nominal rates when the real rate stays at 3 percent?
options: Nominal rates rise from about 7 percent to about 19 percent.
Nominal rates fall from 7 percent to 3 percent.
Nominal rates rise from 8 percent to 20 percent exactly.
Nominal rates stay at 3 percent.
legendary.commonError: not converting money growth into inflation before applying Fisher
legendary.feedback: Inflation rises from 8 - 4 = 4 percent to 20 - 4 = 16 percent. With real rate 3 percent, nominal rates rise from 7 to 19 percent.

legendary.q: A country establishes a credible low-inflation regime. Expected inflation falls from 9 percent to 3 percent, while saving and investment conditions leave the long-run real interest rate near 2 percent. Which outcome best fits the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate tends to fall from about 11 percent to about 5 percent.
The nominal interest rate tends to rise from about 5 percent to about 11 percent.
The real interest rate must fall from 2 percent to negative 4 percent.
The nominal interest rate should stay near 11 percent because credibility affects only actual inflation.
legendary.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
legendary.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

legendary.q: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?
options: It must be unchanged because identical expected inflation always forces identical nominal interest rates even when real saving and investment conditions differ.
It must be lower because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.
It must equal expected inflation because real rates disappear in the long run.
It should also be higher, showing that Fisher comparisons must account for the real-rate component as well as expected inflation.
legendary.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
legendary.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 9 percent, the Fisher effect predicts the nominal rate rises by:
options: 3 points
4 points
5 points
9 points
calculation.commonError: Using the final inflation rate instead of the change.
calculation.feedback: Expected inflation rises by 5 percentage points, so the nominal rate rises by 5 points.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 6 percent while the real interest rate stays at 2 percent. The nominal rate becomes:
options: 3 percent
5 percent
6 percent
8 percent
calculation.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
calculation.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

calculation.q: If the nominal interest rate is 9 percent and expected inflation is 4 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
13 percent
4 percent
36 percent
calculation.commonError: adding inflation when solving for the real rate
calculation.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal rate minus expected inflation: 9 - 4 = 5 percent.

calculation.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 8 percent
4 percent
3 percent
12 percent
calculation.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
calculation.feedback: Nominal interest rate is approximately real interest rate plus expected inflation: 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. The nominal interest rate is 11 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent. If actual inflation turns out to be 10 percent, what is the realized real interest rate?
options: 1 percent
4 percent
3 percent
21 percent
calculation.commonError: using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate
calculation.feedback: The realized real rate uses actual inflation: 11 - 10 = 1 percent.

calculation.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent and the real interest rate remains 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 2 percent.
calculation.commonError: forgetting to include the real interest rate in both periods
calculation.feedback: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 8 = 10.

calculation.q: If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 2 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
1 percent
2 percent
6 percent
calculation.commonError: subtracting inflation from the real rate when solving for nominal rate
calculation.feedback: The nominal interest rate is approximately the real interest rate plus expected inflation: 3 + 2 = 5 percent.

calculation.q: If the nominal interest rate is 7 percent and expected inflation is 3 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 4 percent
10 percent
3 percent
21 percent
calculation.commonError: adding expected inflation when solving for the real interest rate
calculation.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal interest rate minus expected inflation: 7 - 3 = 4 percent.

boss.q: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to
options: nominal interest rates
real GDP only
reserve requirements
M1 only
boss.commonError: thinking expected inflation is unrelated to nominal rates
boss.feedback: The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.

boss.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent, the nominal interest rate is about
options: 9 percent
5 percent
7 percent
14 percent
boss.commonError: subtracting expected inflation when solving for nominal rate
boss.feedback: Nominal interest is real interest plus expected inflation: 2 + 7 = 9 percent.

boss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent while the real interest rate falls from 4 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
boss.commonError: tracking only expected inflation and ignoring the real rate change
boss.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 3 = 7 percent. New nominal rate is 2 + 8 = 10 percent.

boss.q: If expected inflation rises while the long-run real interest rate is unchanged, the Fisher effect predicts that the nominal interest rate will:
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to real GDP growth.
boss.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
boss.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

boss.q: Which inflation rate matters when lenders set a nominal rate today for a future loan period?
options: Only last year’s inflation.
Only inflation observed after repayment.
The unemployment rate instead of inflation.
Expected inflation.
boss.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
boss.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

boss.q: The real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation is 5 percent. The Fisher approximation gives a nominal rate near:
options: 3 percent.
15 percent.
8 percent.
2 percent.
boss.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.
boss.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

boss.q: Expected inflation rises from 4 to 10 percent while the equilibrium real rate falls from 3 to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal rate approximately?
options: It remains at about 7 percent because expected inflation and real rates always offset.
It rises from about 7 to about 11 percent.
It rises from about 7 to about 13 percent because the real-rate change is irrelevant.
It falls from about 7 to about 5 percent.
boss.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
boss.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

boss.q: A fixed-rate loan was written when expected inflation was 2 percent, but actual inflation turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement is correct?
options: Expected inflation helped determine the original nominal rate; the surprise changes the realized real return.
The Fisher effect requires the bank to retroactively reset the nominal rate to actual inflation.
Unexpected inflation leaves the realized real return unchanged on a fixed-rate contract.
The nominal rate was based only on actual inflation, which was already known.
boss.commonError: Uses realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made.
boss.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

boss.q: Nominal interest rates rise 3 percentage points while expected inflation rises 5 points. What does the Fisher decomposition imply about the real-rate component?
options: It rose by about 8 percentage points.
It rose by exactly 5 percentage points.
It must have remained unchanged because nominal rates increased.
It fell by about 2 percentage points.
boss.commonError: Assumes nominal rates must move one-for-one with expected inflation even when the real rate also changes.
boss.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If MS shifts right and the value of money falls, expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 9 percent. If the real interest rate stays at 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 11 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 9 percent.
It stays at 5 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: forgetting to add the real interest rate to expected inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Nominal rate equals real rate plus expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 9 = 11 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 10 percent while the real rate falls from 4 percent to 1 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate, and why is this not a contradiction?
options: It rises from 6 percent to 11 percent because expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.
It falls from 6 percent to 1 percent because the real rate fell.
It stays at 6 percent because changes cancel exactly.
It rises from 2 percent to 10 percent because real rates do not matter.
legendaryBoss.commonError: tracking only the real rate or only expected inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial nominal rate is 4 + 2 = 6 percent. New nominal rate is 1 + 10 = 11 percent. Expected inflation rose more than the real rate fell.

legendaryBoss.q: A country’s nominal loan rate falls from 16 to 9 percent while expected inflation falls from 12 to 4 percent. Using the Fisher approximation, what happens to the expected real rate, and by how much would the new nominal rate have had to fall further to preserve its original expected real rate?
options: The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate falls from 4 to 3 percent; a further 1-point nominal cut was needed.
The expected real rate stays at 4 percent; no further nominal change was needed.
The expected real rate rises from 4 to 5 percent; a further 5-point nominal cut was needed.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming lower nominal rates always mean lower real rates
legendaryBoss.feedback: Subtract expected inflation: 16 − 12 = 4 initially and 9 − 4 = 5 later. Preserving a real rate of 4 with expected inflation of 4 requires a nominal rate of 8, one point below 9.

repairQuestions.q: A borrower says the Fisher effect is found by subtracting this year’s actual inflation from a loan rate set last year. What is the key mistake?
options: The Fisher effect concerns expected inflation when the nominal rate is set, not merely realized inflation afterward.
The Fisher effect uses only the unemployment rate when a loan is made, so expected inflation has no role in nominal-rate setting.
The Fisher effect requires nominal rates to stay fixed when expected inflation changes.
The Fisher effect says actual inflation and expected inflation must always be identical.
repairQuestions.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.
repairQuestions.commonError: Uses actual inflation instead of expected inflation when applying the Fisher effect.

repairQuestions.q: A nominal interest rate is 8 percent and inflation is 3 percent. The approximate real interest rate is:
options: 5 percent
11 percent
8 percent
-5 percent
repairQuestions.feedback: Approximate real interest equals nominal interest minus inflation: 8% − 3% = 5%.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting to add expected inflation to the real rate.
repairQuestions.q: The Fisher equation says nominal interest is approximately:
options: Real interest plus expected inflation
Real interest minus expected inflation
Expected inflation minus money growth
MPC times inflation
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is approximately real interest plus expected inflation.

repairQuestions.commonError: Subtracting when solving for nominal interest.
repairQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If real interest is 3% and expected inflation is 5%, nominal interest is:
repairQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is 3% + 5% = 8%.

bridgeQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is:
options: 8 percent
6 percent
4 percent
2 percent
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting expected inflation in nominal rates.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Real interest is 2% and expected inflation is 6%. Nominal interest is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nominal interest is 2% + 6% = 8%.

bridgeQuestions.q: Suppose long-run money growth raises expected inflation while real productive conditions leave the real interest rate unchanged. Which next step connects monetary neutrality to the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate rises to incorporate the higher expected inflation while the real-rate component stays unchanged.
The real interest rate must rise one-for-one because all nominal variables are neutral and expected inflation cannot influence nominal contract rates.
The nominal interest rate stays fixed because expected inflation affects only the price level.
Actual inflation must be known before lenders can set any nominal interest rate.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Recognizes nominal neutrality but does not connect expected inflation to nominal interest rates.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Once long-run real and nominal variables are separated, the Fisher effect explains why higher expected inflation is reflected in higher nominal interest rates.

inflation-costs.title: Costs of Inflation
inflation-costs.description: Analyze redistribution, shoeleather costs, menu costs, and price distortions.

easy.q: Shoeleather costs of inflation come from:
options: Changing menus often
Holding less cash and making more transactions
Higher unemployment benefits
Falling expected prices
easy.commonError: Confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs.
easy.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from efforts to reduce money holdings when inflation is high.

easy.q: Menu costs of inflation refer to the cost of:
options: Printing more money
Changing posted prices
Measuring real GDP
Buying bonds
easy.commonError: Confusing menu costs with restaurant spending.
easy.feedback: Menu costs are the costs firms face when changing listed prices.

easy.q: Shoe-leather costs of inflation come from people
options: trying to reduce money holdings when inflation is high
wearing out shoes because factories produce less
paying higher menu prices at restaurants
borrowing less because taxes are lower
easy.commonError: taking shoe-leather costs literally
easy.feedback: Shoe-leather costs refer to the time and effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high.

easy.q: Menu costs of inflation are the costs of
options: changing listed prices
buying more food at restaurants
holding too many government bonds
printing money at the central bank
easy.commonError: thinking menu costs only apply to restaurants
easy.feedback: Menu costs are the costs firms face when they change posted prices.

easy.q: Unexpected inflation tends to help
options: debtors
creditors
people holding only cash
workers with fixed nominal wages and no adjustment
easy.commonError: thinking lenders always benefit from inflation
easy.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps debtors because they repay loans with dollars that are worth less than expected.

easy.q: Unexpected inflation tends to hurt
options: creditors
debtors
borrowers with fixed-rate loans
people whose debts are repaid with cheaper dollars
easy.commonError: forgetting that creditors are repaid in money with lower value
easy.feedback: Unexpected inflation hurts creditors because the dollars they are repaid have less purchasing power than expected.

medium.q: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders when:
options: Loans were written before the inflation surprise
All contracts are indexed perfectly
Real wages rise automatically
Nominal prices cannot change
medium.commonError: Missing redistribution from unexpected inflation.
medium.feedback: Borrowers repay with dollars that are worth less than lenders expected.

medium.q: Which example best fits menu costs?
options: A firm pays to update price lists after inflation rises
A household visits the bank more often
A lender loses from unexpected inflation
A central bank buys bonds
medium.commonError: Confusing menu costs with shoeleather costs.
medium.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices.

medium.q: Which example best fits shoeleather costs?
options: A firm prints new menus
A worker compares nominal and real wages
A household makes extra bank transfers to hold less cash
A creditor gains from unexpected deflation
medium.commonError: Confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs.
medium.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from actions people take to reduce money holdings during inflation.

medium.q: Unexpected inflation benefits borrowers because
options: they repay loans with dollars worth less than expected
they repay loans with dollars worth more than expected
their nominal debt automatically disappears
creditors receive more purchasing power than expected
medium.commonError: thinking inflation always hurts borrowers
medium.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers because their fixed nominal repayments are made with less valuable dollars.

medium.q: Unexpectedly low inflation hurts borrowers because
options: they repay loans with dollars worth more than expected
they repay loans with dollars worth less than expected
their debts are erased
nominal interest rates instantly become negative
medium.commonError: forgetting that unexpectedly low inflation benefits creditors
medium.feedback: When inflation is lower than expected, borrowers repay with dollars that have more purchasing power than expected.

medium.q: Which situation is the clearest example of menu costs?
options: A firm spends money updating price tags and online menus after inflation.
A worker walks to the bank more often to avoid holding cash.
A borrower repays debt with less valuable dollars.
A bank holds excess reserves.
medium.commonError: confusing menu costs with shoeleather costs
medium.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices.

medium.q: Which situation is the clearest example of shoeleather costs?
options: People make more frequent trips to reduce cash holdings during high inflation.
A restaurant prints new menus after raising prices.
A debtor repays a fixed loan with less valuable dollars.
A firm buys new equipment because interest rates fall.
medium.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
medium.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from the effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high.

medium.q: Inflation is fully anticipated, so fixed-rate contracts are written with the expected inflation built in. Which cost can still remain?
options: Firms may still spend resources changing posted prices more often.
Unexpected borrower-creditor redistribution must become larger even though the inflation rate was correctly anticipated by both sides.
The nominal interest rate must become zero.
All relative prices become permanently fixed.
medium.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
medium.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

hard.q: A borrower signs a loan expecting 2 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 7 percent. Who is helped?
options: The borrower
The lender
Both equally
Neither side
hard.commonError: Reversing unexpected inflation redistribution.
hard.feedback: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers because they repay in dollars worth less than expected.

hard.q: A lender expected 2 percent inflation and charged 6 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 5 percent. Who is helped by the surprise, and why?
options: Borrowers, because they repay with dollars worth less than expected.
Lenders, because they receive dollars worth more than expected.
Borrowers, because the nominal interest rate rises after the loan is signed.
Lenders, because real repayment rises automatically.
hard.commonError: thinking lenders benefit from unexpectedly high inflation
hard.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders because repayment occurs in less valuable dollars.

hard.q: A lender expected 6 percent inflation and charged 10 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 2 percent. Who is helped by the surprise?
options: Lenders
Borrowers
Both equally because nominal interest was fixed
Neither because inflation never redistributes wealth
hard.commonError: thinking all inflation outcomes help borrowers
hard.feedback: Lower-than-expected inflation helps lenders because they are repaid with dollars worth more than expected.

hard.q: Which sequence best explains shoeleather costs during high inflation?
options: Inflation raises the cost of holding money, so people spend resources reducing cash balances.
Inflation lowers interest rates, so people hold more cash forever.
Inflation makes all prices stable, so no one changes behavior.
Inflation eliminates the need for banks.
hard.commonError: treating shoeleather costs as literal shoe damage only
hard.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the wasted time and effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.

hard.q: Which sequence best explains menu costs during inflation?
options: Inflation changes desired prices, so firms spend resources updating posted prices.
Inflation reduces borrowing costs, so firms buy more menus.
Inflation eliminates relative price changes.
Inflation makes prices unnecessary.
hard.commonError: thinking menu costs apply only to restaurants
hard.feedback: Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices, not just restaurant menus.

hard.q: Why can inflation make relative prices harder to interpret?
options: Because not all prices adjust at the same time or by the same amount.
Because all real prices are legally fixed.
Because inflation makes money demand disappear.
Because every nominal price changes perfectly together every second.
hard.commonError: thinking inflation only changes the average price level without affecting signals
hard.feedback: Inflation can distort price signals because different prices adjust unevenly.

hard.q: If all prices rise but incomes rise by the same percentage, why can inflation still be costly?
options: It causes shoe-leather, menu, tax, signal, and redistribution costs.
It has no costs if incomes rise at all.
It only affects people who never buy goods.
It permanently raises real wages.
hard.commonError: thinking inflation is harmless whenever nominal incomes rise
hard.feedback: Inflation can still impose real costs through behavior changes, price adjustment costs, distortions, and redistribution.

hard.q: A fixed-rate lender expected 3 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 8 percent. At the same time firms repeatedly update prices. Which statement separates the two costs?
options: The inflation surprise redistributes toward the borrower, while repricing uses real resources even if inflation had been anticipated.
Both effects are examples only of shoeleather costs.
The surprise benefits the lender, while repricing raises real output automatically.
Neither effect is an inflation cost unless the price level actually falls, because rising prices cannot redistribute purchasing power or use real resources.
hard.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
hard.feedback: The surprise redistributes purchasing power toward the borrower, while repeated price changes are menu costs that use real resources even when inflation is anticipated.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 6 percent inflation and charged 11 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 3 percent. Who gains from the surprise and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 14 percent.
elite.commonError: missing that lower-than-expected inflation helps lenders
elite.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so the lender gains. Realized real rate is 11 - 3 = 8 percent.

elite.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A borrower expected 3 percent inflation on a loan with a 7 percent nominal rate. Actual inflation was 10 percent. Who gains and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 4 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 7 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -3 percent.
elite.commonError: thinking borrowers are hurt by unexpectedly high inflation
elite.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 7 - 10 = -3 percent.

elite.q: Why can high inflation distort relative prices even if the average price level is what gets reported?
options: Individual prices do not all adjust instantly or proportionally, so signals get noisy.
All individual prices change by exactly the same amount every second.
Relative prices are nominal variables only.
Inflation eliminates scarcity.
elite.commonError: thinking inflation only changes the average price level with no signal distortion
elite.feedback: Inflation can make price signals harder to read because prices adjust unevenly across goods and time.

elite.q: A government funds a deficit by printing money. People respond by holding less cash and visiting banks more often. Which inflation cost is most directly shown?
options: Shoeleather costs from reducing money holdings
Menu costs from changing posted prices
Crowding out from higher interest rates
Monetary neutrality from unchanged real variables
elite.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
elite.feedback: The extra effort to reduce money holdings is the shoeleather cost of inflation.

elite.q: A government funds a deficit by printing money. Firms then repeatedly update catalogs, labels, and online prices. Which inflation cost is most directly shown?
options: Menu costs
Shoeleather costs
Unexpected inflation redistribution
Liquidity trap
elite.commonError: thinking menu costs are only restaurant costs
elite.feedback: The cost of updating prices is menu cost. Not glamorous. Still real.

elite.q: A student says inflation makes everyone poorer because all prices rise. What is the best elite-level correction?
options: Inflation still causes distortions, behavior changes, and redistribution.
Inflation never has costs if any wage rises.
Inflation only affects creditors and no one else.
Inflation lowers all nominal incomes by definition.
elite.commonError: thinking inflation's only effect is higher prices with no nominal income adjustment
elite.feedback: Inflation is costly, but not simply because prices rise. The real damage comes through distortions, wasted effort, confusion, and redistribution.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 3 percent inflation and charged 8 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 12 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 8 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -4 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
legendary.feedback: Actual inflation exceeded expected inflation, so borrowers gain. The realized real rate is 8 - 12 = -4 percent.

legendary.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A lender expected 8 percent inflation and charged 13 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 2 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real rate?
options: Lender gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 5 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 11 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking borrowers always gain when inflation is positive
legendary.feedback: Actual inflation was lower than expected, so lenders gain. The realized real rate is 13 - 2 = 11 percent.

legendary.q: If MS shifts right and the price level rises from 2 to 4, what inflation cost would become more likely if firms must repeatedly update prices?
options: Menu costs
Crowding out
Reserve shortfall
Liquidity preference equilibrium
legendary.commonError: identifying inflation but not connecting it to a specific cost
legendary.feedback: The graph shows inflation after monetary expansion. Firms repeatedly changing posted prices is menu cost.

legendary.q: If MS shifts right, the price level rises, and people reduce cash balances by making more frequent transfers, what inflation cost is described?
options: Shoeleather costs
Menu costs
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
legendary.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
legendary.feedback: When inflation makes people spend effort reducing money holdings, that is shoeleather cost.

legendary.q: A country experiences 18 percent money growth, 2 percent velocity growth, and 5 percent real output growth. Inflation is high, and borrowers with fixed-rate debt gain unexpectedly. What is the approximate inflation rate?
options: 15 percent
25 percent
21 percent
11 percent
legendary.commonError: forgetting velocity growth or subtracting it incorrectly
legendary.feedback: Inflation = money growth + velocity growth - output growth = 18 + 2 - 5 = 15 percent.

legendary.q: A country perfectly indexes many long-term contracts to the price level, greatly reducing unexpected debtor-creditor redistribution. Inflation nevertheless remains high and predictable. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Indexation can reduce redistribution without eliminating costs such as frequent repricing, cash management, or tax distortions.
Once contracts are indexed, high expected inflation becomes economically costless.
Indexation guarantees the price level stops rising because once nominal contracts are indexed, firms and households no longer face any inflation-related decisions.
Indexation converts inflation into deflation by raising the real value of money.
legendary.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

boss.q: Shoeleather costs of inflation come from people
options: spending resources to reduce money holdings
changing posted prices
borrowing from the Fed
holding required reserves
boss.commonError: confusing shoeleather costs with menu costs
boss.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.

boss.q: A borrower expected inflation to be 2 percent, but actual inflation is 8 percent. Who benefits?
options: Borrowers benefit because they repay with less valuable dollars.
Lenders benefit because they receive more purchasing power.
No one is affected by unexpected inflation.
Only workers benefit because real wages rise.
boss.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
boss.feedback: Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers because they repay with dollars worth less than expected.

boss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan has a 9 percent nominal interest rate. Expected inflation was 3 percent, but actual inflation was 10 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real interest rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 6 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 9 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
boss.commonError: using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate
boss.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. Realized real rate is 9 - 10 = -1 percent.

boss.q: A store must repeatedly change price labels because the overall price level is rising. This is primarily a:
options: Menu cost.
Shoeleather cost.
Natural-rate effect.
Money-multiplier effect.
boss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
boss.feedback: Repeatedly changing price labels is a menu cost because firms spend resources updating posted prices.

boss.q: People make more frequent transfers so they can hold smaller cash balances during inflation. This is primarily a:
options: Menu cost.
Fisher-effect premium.
Reserve requirement.
Shoeleather cost.
boss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
boss.feedback: Extra transfers to keep smaller cash balances are shoeleather costs because households spend time and effort reducing money holdings.

boss.q: Unexpected inflation is higher than lenders anticipated on fixed-rate loans. Who tends to gain?
options: Both sides equally, because unexpected inflation cannot redistribute purchasing power.
Only the central bank, because private contracts are unaffected by inflation.
Borrowers, because repayment dollars have less purchasing power than expected.
Lenders, because inflation always raises realized real returns.
boss.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
boss.feedback: Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between parties to fixed nominal contracts because the realized price level differs from what they expected.

boss.q: Inflation is anticipated and nominal interest rates adjust, but firms still reprice frequently and households economize on cash balances. What does this show?
options: Anticipated inflation necessarily increases real output enough to offset every menu, cash-management, and redistribution cost.
Expected inflation can still impose menu and shoeleather costs even when some redistribution is avoided.
Expected inflation is costless whenever nominal interest rates adjust.
Menu and shoeleather costs occur only when inflation is unexpected.
boss.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
boss.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

boss.q: A pension is fixed in nominal dollars and inflation is unexpectedly high. Which mechanism is most important?
options: The pension’s real purchasing power falls because the nominal payment buys less than expected.
The pension automatically rises one-for-one because every fixed nominal contract is indexed against unexpected inflation.
The price level falls, increasing the pension’s real value.
The inflation surprise affects only banks, not recipients of fixed nominal payments.
boss.commonError: Ignores that unexpected inflation changes the realized real value of fixed nominal payments.
boss.feedback: Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between parties to fixed nominal contracts because the realized price level differs from what they expected.

boss.q: High inflation causes firms to reprice at different times, making it harder to distinguish relative-price changes from changes in the overall price level. Which cost is being described?
options: A larger money multiplier.
A lower natural unemployment rate by definition.
A statutory inflation-tax payment collected on a tax return.
Relative-price variability and signal confusion.
boss.commonError: Labels inflation as costly without identifying the mechanism.
boss.feedback: When prices adjust at different times and by different amounts, inflation makes relative-price signals noisier; this is relative-price variability and signal confusion.

legendaryBoss.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan has a 10 percent nominal interest rate. Expected inflation was 4 percent, but actual inflation was 11 percent. Who gains, and what is the realized real interest rate?
options: Borrower gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is 6 percent.
Borrower gains; realized real rate is 10 percent.
Lender gains; realized real rate is -1 percent.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation
legendaryBoss.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers gain. Realized real rate is 10 - 11 = -1 percent.

legendaryBoss.q: MS shifts right, P rises, and firms must update thousands of posted prices while households also reduce money balances. Which pair of inflation costs is described?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and the Fisher effect
Reserve shortfalls and capital losses
Liquidity trap and fiscal lag
legendaryBoss.commonError: identifying inflation but missing the specific costs
legendaryBoss.feedback: Updating posted prices is menu cost. Reducing money balances through extra effort is shoeleather cost.

legendaryBoss.q: MS shifts right, P rises from 2 to 5, and a fixed nominal debt of $10,000 is repaid. What happens to the real burden of that debt?
options: It falls because dollars are worth less when repaid.
It rises because dollars are worth more when repaid.
It is unchanged because the nominal debt is fixed.
It rises because inflation helps creditors.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking fixed nominal debt means unchanged real burden
legendaryBoss.feedback: When P rises, money is worth less. Fixed nominal repayments become easier in real terms, helping debtors.

legendaryBoss.q: All long-term debt is fully price-indexed, wage contracts adjust correctly, and inflation is perfectly anticipated. Firms still reprice at different times and households spend time moving funds out of non-interest-bearing cash. Which evaluation separates what indexation resolves from what it leaves?
options: Debt indexation limits surprise redistribution; asynchronous prices and cash management can still consume resources or distort signals.
Debt indexation eliminates all inflation costs because every relative price must adjust at the same instant.
The remaining cash-management costs transfer wealth from borrowers to lenders without using real resources.
Perfect anticipation eliminates repricing costs but creates unexpected redistribution on the indexed debt.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking only unexpected inflation is costly
legendaryBoss.feedback: Indexation protects the real value of the specified debt. It does not make repricing instantaneous or eliminate the effort spent economizing on non-interest-bearing cash.

repairQuestions.q: Unexpected inflation redistributes wealth toward borrowers when:
options: Loans have fixed nominal payments
All loans adjust instantly with inflation
Interest rates are always zero
Prices never change
repairQuestions.feedback: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers and hurting lenders.

repairQuestions.q: Menu costs are the costs of changing:
options: Posted prices
Reserve ratios
Real GDP
Natural unemployment
repairQuestions.feedback: Menu costs are costs firms face when changing posted prices.

repairQuestions.q: Shoeleather costs come from people trying to hold:
options: Less cash during inflation
More capital during recessions
More imports during booms
Less output during deflation
repairQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs come from efforts to reduce cash holdings during inflation.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking lenders gain from unexpectedly high inflation.
repairQuestions.q: Unexpectedly high inflation helps:
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Only banks
No one
repairQuestions.feedback: Borrowers repay with dollars worth less than expected.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking borrowers gain from unexpectedly low inflation.
repairQuestions.q: Unexpectedly low inflation helps:
options: Lenders
Borrowers
Only workers
Only importers
repairQuestions.feedback: Lenders are repaid with dollars worth more than expected.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assumes perfectly anticipated inflation has no resource cost.
repairQuestions.q: A student says, “If everyone correctly expects 6 percent inflation, inflation has no economic costs.” Which response is best?
options: Anticipation reduces some redistribution, but cash-management, repricing, tax, and relative-price costs can remain.
Correct; expected inflation removes every resource and information cost.
Correct; only unexpected deflation can create economic costs.
Incorrect only because expected inflation always lowers real GDP by exactly 6 percent and therefore creates a predictable recession every year.
repairQuestions.feedback: Expected inflation can still create shoeleather, menu, tax-system, and relative-price costs even when debtor-creditor redistribution is reduced.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing shoeleather and menu costs.
repairQuestions.q: Shoeleather costs come from:
options: Effort spent reducing money holdings
Firms changing posted prices
Banks calculating reserves
The Fed selling bonds
repairQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the time and effort spent avoiding holding too much money during inflation.

bridgeQuestions.q: A restaurant reprints menus every week because prices keep changing. This is:
options: Menu cost
Shoeleather cost
Inflation tax
Money neutrality
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Menu costs are costs of changing posted prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: Inflation makes a household transfer money more often to avoid holding cash. This is:
options: Shoeleather cost
Menu cost
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the costs of reducing money holdings during inflation.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate.
bridgeQuestions.q: Nominal interest is 9%, expected inflation was 3%, but actual inflation is 10%. Who gains?
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Both equally
No one
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers repay with less valuable dollars.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing inflation cost examples.
bridgeQuestions.q: Firms repeatedly update posted prices while households make more transfers to avoid holding cash. Which costs are shown?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and liquidity trap
Reserve shortfall and bank capital loss
M1 and M2
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Price updates are menu costs; reducing cash balances creates shoeleather costs.
