The Fed accepts household checking deposits in the same way as a retail bank
boss.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
boss.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

boss.q: Which statement best distinguishes the Federal Reserve from the U.S. Treasury?
options: The Treasury conducts monetary policy and determines bank reserve conditions; the Fed sets federal tax rates for Congress
The two names refer to the same institution
The Fed manages congressional spending while the Treasury supplies bank reserves
The Fed conducts monetary policy; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations
boss.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
boss.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

boss.q: A central-bank committee decides to change monetary conditions. Which institutional description is most accurate?
options: The committee determines federal tax rates and appropriations for the entire national budget
The committee measures M1 but has no connection to monetary policy
The policy-making body chooses monetary actions within the central bank’s mandate
The committee directly approves household mortgages at commercial banks
boss.commonError: Treats the Federal Reserve and Treasury as interchangeable agencies.
boss.feedback: The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.

legendaryBoss.q: A central bank under political pressure buys bonds aggressively before an election. Banks lend most of the new reserves, and output is already near potential. Which long-run risk is most consistent with the chapter logic?
options: Excessive money growth creates inflation pressure without lasting real-output gains.
Real output permanently rises because more money creates more resources.
The price level falls because bond purchases reduce reserves.
Money demand becomes zero.
legendaryBoss.commonError: thinking money growth permanently raises real output
legendaryBoss.feedback: If output is near potential, aggressive money growth mainly risks inflation rather than permanent real gains.

legendaryBoss.q: A commercial bank makes a loan by crediting a deposit, while the Federal Reserve supplies reserve balances to banks. Which statement best separates the two forms of money creation?
options: Commercial banks create deposits; the central bank creates reserves and base money
Commercial banks issue reserve balances; the central bank issues all checking deposits
Both institutions can create only physical currency
Neither institution can create a financial liability
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank is solvent but temporarily unable to meet payments because short-term funding markets freeze. Which central-bank response best fits the lender-of-last-resort principle?
options: Use tax revenue to replace every risky bank asset permanently
Refuse all liquidity because a funding shortage proves assets are worthless
Order the Treasury to guarantee every future bank loss
Provide temporary liquidity against sound collateral to an otherwise solvent bank
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats emergency central-bank liquidity as a way to erase losses at an insolvent institution.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Lender-of-last-resort support addresses temporary liquidity problems; insolvency requires losses to be recognized and capital restored through other mechanisms.

repairQuestions.q: What is the central bank of the United States?
options: The Federal Reserve
The Treasury
Congress
The IRS
repairQuestions.feedback: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.

repairQuestions.q: Which group directs open-market operations?
options: FOMC
IRS
BLS
CBO
repairQuestions.feedback: The Federal Open Market Committee directs open-market operations.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A solvent bank has sound assets but cannot obtain short-term funding during a panic. Which central-bank role is designed for this situation?
options: Lender of last resort
Collector of federal income taxes
Issuer of corporate stock
Manager of the congressional budget
repairQuestions.feedback: A lender of last resort provides temporary liquidity to a solvent bank facing a funding panic.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing monetary policy with fiscal policy.
repairQuestions.q: The Fed mainly conducts:
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Tax collection
repairQuestions.feedback: The Fed handles monetary policy, not taxes and government spending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing the FOMC with Congress.
repairQuestions.q: The FOMC is most closely tied to:
options: Open-market operations
Income tax rates
Federal spending bills
GDP measurement
repairQuestions.feedback: The FOMC helps direct monetary policy through open-market operations.

repairQuestions.commonError: Thinking FOMC decisions are fiscal policy.
repairQuestions.q: When the FOMC buys or sells bonds, it is using:
options: Monetary policy
Fiscal policy
Trade policy
Labor policy
repairQuestions.feedback: Buying and selling bonds is monetary policy.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: Elected officials establish a central bank’s mandate, while the bank chooses how to use its policy instruments and reports its decisions publicly. What principle does this arrangement illustrate?
options: Instrument independence combined with public accountability
Complete independence from any publicly established mandate
Fiscal dominance because elected officials choose tax rates
Abolition of central-bank discretion over policy instruments
repairQuestions.feedback: The arrangement gives the bank instrument independence within a public mandate and requires it to explain its decisions, preserving democratic accountability.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing the link between political pressure and inflation risk.
repairQuestions.q: Political pressure to print money can create risk of:
options: Inflation
Deflation always
Zero money demand
No nominal prices
repairQuestions.feedback: Politically driven money growth can create inflation pressure.

bridgeQuestions.q: A financial panic hits and the banking system needs a lender-of-last-resort institution. Which institution fits?
options: Federal Reserve
Bureau of Labor Statistics
Congressional Budget Office
Internal Revenue Service
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The Fed acts as the central bank and lender of last resort.

bridgeQuestions.q: The FOMC decides that monetary conditions should be easier and authorizes purchases of securities. What connection is being made?
options: The FOMC is choosing a monetary-policy tool that adds reserves
The Treasury is using fiscal policy to change government purchases
A commercial bank is deciding how much capital to issue to shareholders
Households are changing M1 by moving funds from checking to savings
bridgeQuestions.feedback: When the FOMC authorizes securities purchases, it is using an expansionary monetary-policy tool that adds reserve balances to banks.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Confusing the Fed with Congress or the Treasury.
bridgeQuestions.q: If a policy changes bank reserves and interest rates, it is most likely:
options: Monetary policy by the Fed
Fiscal policy by Congress
Trade policy
GDP accounting
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Changes in reserves and interest rates are monetary policy territory.

bank-balance-sheets-reserves-and-capital.title: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
bank-balance-sheets-reserves-and-capital.description: Analyze bank assets and liabilities, required and excess reserves, lending capacity, capital, leverage, and losses.

objectiveLabels.bank-balance-sheets-reserves-and-capital: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital

easy.q: In a fractional reserve banking system, banks
options: hold only part of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest
must keep 100 percent of deposits as cash
cannot affect the money supply
create money by printing currency
easy.commonError: thinking banks create money by printing currency
easy.feedback: Fractional reserve banking means banks keep some deposits as reserves and lend the rest.

easy.q: The money multiplier becomes larger when the reserve ratio
options: falls
rises
equals the inflation rate
equals the nominal interest rate
easy.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more lending
easy.feedback: A lower reserve ratio lets banks lend more of each deposit, which increases the money multiplier.

easy.q: For a commercial bank, customer deposits are recorded as:
options: Revenue because deposits increase cash.
Liabilities because the bank owes the funds to depositors.
Bank capital because deposits belong to shareholders.
Assets because the bank physically holds the money.
easy.commonError: Treating deposits as bank-owned assets.
easy.feedback: Deposits are liabilities: the bank has an obligation to repay depositors.

easy.q: A 10 percent reserve rule applies to a $50,000 deposit base. How much must the bank keep rather than lend?
easy.commonError: Multiplying by the lending share instead of the reserve ratio.
easy.feedback: Ten percent of $50,000 is $5,000.

easy.q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, the loan is recorded as:
options: Bank capital only.
An asset of the bank.
A reduction in deposits with no matching asset.
A liability of the bank.
easy.commonError: Classifying loans as liabilities.
easy.feedback: Borrowers owe repayment to the bank, so loans are bank assets.

medium.q: A bank has $300,000 in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $50,000 in actual reserves. Excess reserves are:
medium.commonError: Forgetting to subtract required reserves from actual reserves.
medium.feedback: Required reserves are $36,000, leaving $14,000 in excess reserves.

medium.q: A new $2,000 deposit enters a bank with a 20 percent reserve requirement. The bank’s maximum first-round loan is:
medium.commonError: Using required reserves as lending or applying the multiplier to the first round.
medium.feedback: The bank keeps $400 and may lend $1,600.

medium.q: A bank reports $14 million in assets and $12.9 million in liabilities. What is its capital cushion?
options: $26.9 million.
$1.1 million.
$14 million.
$12.9 million.
medium.commonError: Adding assets and liabilities or using liabilities alone.
medium.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $1.1 million.

hard.q: Why does leverage make banks riskier?
options: A small percentage loss on assets can wipe out a large share of capital.
It guarantees assets never fall in value.
It prevents banks from making loans.
It makes reserves unnecessary.
hard.commonError: thinking leverage only increases returns and not risk
hard.feedback: Leverage magnifies gains and losses. A small asset loss can hit capital hard.

hard.q: A bank originates a loan by crediting its borrower’s checking account. The borrower then pays a supplier at a different bank, and the payment settles in reserves. Which comparison correctly separates origination from settlement?
options: Origination adds a loan and a deposit; settlement reduces the originating bank’s reserves and its borrower’s deposit.
Origination reduces reserves; settlement creates the loan and increases bank capital.
Origination adds reserves and a deposit; settlement leaves both banks’ reserves unchanged.
Origination reduces deposits; settlement cancels the originating bank’s loan asset.
hard.commonError: thinking loans reduce assets instead of changing asset composition
hard.feedback: Crediting the account initially adds a loan asset and a deposit liability. The later outgoing payment reduces reserves and the deposit liability; the loan remains an asset.

hard.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a 10 percent reserve requirement, and $95,000 in reserves. If deposits increase by $100,000 and reserves rise by $20,000, the bank’s new excess reserves are:
hard.commonError: Updating deposits or reserves but not both.
hard.feedback: New deposits are $900,000, required reserves are $90,000, and actual reserves are $115,000.

hard.q: A bank has $25 million in assets and $1.5 million in capital. An 8 percent asset loss occurs. What is the new capital position?
options: $0.5 million.
-$0.5 million.
-$2.0 million.
$1.5 million.
hard.commonError: Applying the loss to capital instead of assets.
hard.feedback: An 8 percent asset loss is $2 million, reducing $1.5 million of capital to -$0.5 million.

hard.q: A banking system has a 10 percent reserve requirement, but banks hold an additional 5 percent of deposits as excess reserves and the public holds no currency. A simple effective deposit multiplier is closest to:
hard.commonError: Ignoring voluntary excess reserves.
hard.feedback: If 15 percent of deposits is retained, the simple effective multiplier is about 1/0.15 = 6.67.

elite.q: Assume the bank cannot obtain extra reserves, sell assets, or retain any new loan proceeds as deposits; every new loan payment would leave the bank. A bank has $900,000 in deposits, a 15 percent reserve requirement, and $135,000 in actual reserves. What can the bank do immediately?
options: It cannot lend more because actual reserves equal required reserves.
It can lend $135,000 because all reserves are excess reserves.
It can lend $765,000 because deposits minus reserves are lendable.
It must borrow $15,000 from the Fed.
elite.commonError: treating required reserves as lendable reserves
elite.feedback: Required reserves are 0.15 x $900,000 = $135,000. Actual reserves equal required reserves, so there are no excess reserves to lend.

elite.q: A bank has $1,200,000 in deposits, $210,000 in reserves, and a 12.5 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, how much can it lend?
elite.commonError: lending all reserves instead of only excess reserves
elite.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $1,200,000 = $150,000. Excess reserves are $210,000 - $150,000 = $60,000.

elite.q: A bank has assets of $50 million and liabilities of $47 million. Asset values fall by 8 percent. What happens to bank capital?
options: Capital falls from $3 million to negative $1 million.
Capital falls from $3 million to $2.76 million.
Capital rises from $3 million to $7 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb losses first.
elite.commonError: applying the percentage loss to capital instead of assets
elite.feedback: Initial capital is $3 million. An 8 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4 million, so capital becomes negative $1 million.

elite.q: A bank has $100 million in assets and $92 million in liabilities. If asset values fall by 6 percent, what percentage of initial capital is lost?
options: 75 percent
6 percent
8 percent
60 percent
elite.commonError: thinking a 6 percent asset loss means a 6 percent capital loss
elite.feedback: Initial capital is $8 million. A 6 percent asset loss is $6 million, which is 75 percent of capital.

elite.q: A bank has $1 million in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The reserve requirement is 10 percent. What is the bank's reserve problem?
options: It is short $10,000 in required reserves.
It has $90,000 in excess reserves.
It can lend $10,000 immediately.
It has exactly enough reserves.
elite.commonError: thinking reserves below required levels are still lendable
elite.feedback: Required reserves are $100,000. The bank has $90,000, so it is short $10,000.

elite.q: If required reserves are $75,000 and the reserve ratio is 15 percent, what are deposits?
elite.commonError: multiplying required reserves by the reserve ratio instead of dividing
elite.feedback: Required reserves = r x deposits, so deposits = $75,000 / 0.15 = $500,000.

elite.q: If excess reserves are $25,000, actual reserves are $85,000, and the reserve ratio is 12 percent, what are deposits?
elite.commonError: forgetting to find required reserves before solving deposits
elite.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $85,000 - $25,000 = $60,000. Deposits = $60,000 / 0.12 = $500,000.

elite.q: A commercial bank wants to increase lending but is below its required reserves. Which action most directly fixes the reserve shortfall?
options: Borrow reserves or attract new deposits before expanding loans.
Make new loans immediately from required reserves.
Reduce assets by increasing liabilities.
Ignore reserve requirements because lending creates reserves.
elite.commonError: thinking banks can lend when already short of required reserves
elite.feedback: A bank below required reserves needs reserves before it can safely expand lending.

legendary.q: A bank has $50 million in assets, $46 million in liabilities, and then suffers a 9 percent asset loss. What is the new capital position?
options: Capital falls from $4 million to negative $500,000.
Capital falls from $4 million to $3.64 million.
Capital rises from $4 million to $8.5 million.
Capital is unchanged because liabilities absorb asset losses first.
legendary.commonError: applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets
legendary.feedback: Initial capital is $4 million. A 9 percent asset loss on $50 million is $4.5 million, so capital becomes negative $500,000.

legendary.q: A bank has actual reserves of $96,000, excess reserves of $24,000, and a reserve requirement of 12 percent. What are deposits?
legendary.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves
legendary.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $96,000 - $24,000 = $72,000. Deposits are $72,000 / 0.12 = $600,000.

legendary.q: A bank's assets fall by 4 percent. Its capital ratio before the loss was 5 percent of assets. What happens to most of the bank's capital?
options: Most capital is wiped out because the asset loss is almost as large as the capital cushion.
Capital falls by only 4 percent.
Capital rises because liabilities fall first.
Capital is unaffected because reserves absorb all losses.
legendary.commonError: thinking a 4 percent asset loss means only 4 percent of capital is lost
legendary.feedback: If capital is only 5 percent of assets, a 4 percent asset loss wipes out four-fifths of the capital cushion.

calculation.q: If a bank receives a $1,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 20 percent, required reserves are:
calculation.commonError: Subtracting instead of multiplying by the reserve requirement.
calculation.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement, so $1,000 x 0.20 = $200.

calculation.q: A bank receives $5,000 in new deposits, holds 15 percent required reserves, and lends the rest. What is the maximum first-round loan?
calculation.commonError: Lending required reserves or using the multiplier too early.
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are $750, so the bank can lend $4,250 in the first round.

calculation.q: A bank receives $2,000 in new deposits and faces a 10 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, its first new loan can be:
calculation.commonError: Lending required reserves.
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are $200, so excess reserves are $1,800.

calculation.q: A bank has $50,000 in deposits and must hold 8 percent in reserves. Required reserves equal:
calculation.commonError: Dividing deposits by the reserve requirement.
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are $50,000 x 0.08 = $4,000.

calculation.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Required reserves equal
calculation.commonError: using 10 instead of 0.10
calculation.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve ratio: $500,000 x 0.10 = $50,000.

calculation.q: A bank has $500,000 in deposits, $80,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Excess reserves equal
calculation.commonError: treating all reserves as excess reserves
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are $50,000, so excess reserves are $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000.

calculation.q: A bank receives a new $2,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 25 percent. How much can the bank initially lend?
calculation.commonError: lending the entire deposit despite reserve requirements
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are 0.25 x $2,000 = $500, so the bank can initially lend $1,500.

calculation.q: If a bank has $1,000 in deposits and the reserve requirement is 10 percent, required reserves are
calculation.commonError: multiplying by 10 instead of 0.10
calculation.feedback: Required reserves equal the reserve ratio times deposits: 0.10 x $1,000 = $100.

calculation.q: If a bank receives a new $1,000 deposit and must hold $100 in required reserves, the bank can initially lend
calculation.commonError: thinking the full deposit can be lent when reserves are required
calculation.feedback: The bank can lend excess reserves. $1,000 minus $100 leaves $900 available to lend.

calculation.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a required reserve ratio of 12.5 percent, and actual reserves of $140,000. How much can it lend before hitting its required reserve level?
calculation.commonError: treating all actual reserves as lendable reserves
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $800,000 = $100,000. Excess reserves are $140,000 - $100,000 = $40,000.

calculation.q: Use the textbook reserve-constrained model, with no other changes. A bank has $300,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It currently holds $45,000 in reserves. If it lends all excess reserves, what will its reserves and loans change by? Assume the borrower immediately pays someone at another bank and the entire payment settles in reserves.
options: Reserves fall by $15,000 and loans rise by $15,000.
Reserves fall by $30,000 and loans rise by $30,000.
Reserves fall by $45,000 and loans rise by $45,000.
Reserves rise by $15,000 and loans fall by $15,000.
calculation.commonError: lending required reserves as if they were excess reserves
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are $30,000, so excess reserves are $15,000. Lending those lowers reserves by $15,000 and raises loans by $15,000.

calculation.q: A bank has assets of $10 million and liabilities of $9.4 million. What is bank capital?
options: $9.4 million
$10 million
$19.4 million
calculation.commonError: adding assets and liabilities instead of subtracting
calculation.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $10 million - $9.4 million = $600,000.

calculation.q: A bank has $2 million in assets and $100,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 5 percent, what happens to capital?
options: It falls to zero.
It falls by $5,000.
It rises to $200,000.
It stays at $100,000.
calculation.commonError: applying the percentage loss to capital instead of assets
calculation.feedback: Five percent of $2 million is $100,000. That wipes out the bank's $100,000 in capital.

calculation.q: A 10 percent reserve rule applies to a $50,000 deposit base. How much must the bank keep rather than lend?
calculation.commonError: Multiplying by the lending share instead of the reserve ratio.
calculation.feedback: Ten percent of $50,000 is $5,000.

calculation.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a 10 percent reserve requirement, and $95,000 in reserves. If deposits increase by $100,000 and reserves rise by $20,000, the bank’s new excess reserves are:
calculation.commonError: Updating deposits or reserves but not both.
calculation.feedback: New deposits are $900,000, required reserves are $90,000, and actual reserves are $115,000.

calculation.q: A bank has $25 million in assets and $1.5 million in capital. An 8 percent asset loss occurs. What is the new capital position?
options: $0.5 million.
-$0.5 million.
-$2.0 million.
$1.5 million.
calculation.commonError: Applying the loss to capital instead of assets.
calculation.feedback: An 8 percent asset loss is $2 million, reducing $1.5 million of capital to -$0.5 million.

calculation.q: A banking system has a 10 percent reserve requirement, but banks hold an additional 5 percent of deposits as excess reserves and the public holds no currency. A simple effective deposit multiplier is closest to:
calculation.commonError: Ignoring voluntary excess reserves.
calculation.feedback: If 15 percent of deposits is retained, the simple effective multiplier is about 1/0.15 = 6.67.

calculation.q: A bank has $300,000 in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $50,000 in actual reserves. Excess reserves are:
calculation.commonError: Forgetting to subtract required reserves from actual reserves.
calculation.feedback: Required reserves are $36,000, leaving $14,000 in excess reserves.

calculation.q: A new $2,000 deposit enters a bank with a 20 percent reserve requirement. The bank’s maximum first-round loan is:
calculation.commonError: Using required reserves as lending or applying the multiplier to the first round.
calculation.feedback: The bank keeps $400 and may lend $1,600.

calculation.q: A bank reports $14 million in assets and $12.9 million in liabilities. What is its capital cushion?
options: $26.9 million.
$1.1 million.
$14 million.
$12.9 million.
calculation.commonError: Adding assets and liabilities or using liabilities alone.
calculation.feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $1.1 million.

boss.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, $110,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. How much can it lend?
boss.commonError: treating all reserves as lendable reserves
boss.feedback: Required reserves are $80,000. Excess reserves are $110,000 - $80,000 = $30,000.

boss.q: Deposits are $600,000, the reserve requirement is 10 percent, and actual reserves are $90,000. Excess reserves are:
boss.commonError: Failing to subtract required reserves.
boss.feedback: Required reserves are $60,000, leaving $30,000.

boss.q: A bank makes a loan from excess reserves. On the bank’s balance sheet, the new loan is:
options: A withdrawal.
Capital.
An asset.
A liability.
boss.commonError: Misclassifying a bank loan.
boss.feedback: The borrower owes the bank, so the loan is an asset.

boss.q: A bank has $1.5 million in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $240,000 in reserves. Its maximum immediate new lending is:
options: $1.32 million.
boss.commonError: Confusing required reserves with excess reserves.
boss.feedback: Required reserves are $180,000, so excess reserves are $60,000.

boss.q: A bank has $30 million in assets and $28.5 million in liabilities. Assets fall 6 percent. New capital is:
options: $1.5 million.
-$1.8 million.
-$0.3 million.
$0.3 million.
boss.commonError: Applying the asset loss to the wrong base.
boss.feedback: Initial capital is $1.5 million; the asset loss is $1.8 million.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has $80 million in assets and $74 million in liabilities. Asset values fall by 9 percent. What is the new capital position?
options: Negative $1.2 million
$6 million
$7.2 million
Negative $7.2 million
legendaryBoss.commonError: applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial capital is $6 million. A 9 percent loss on $80 million is $7.2 million, leaving capital at negative $1.2 million.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has actual reserves of $180,000 and excess reserves of $45,000. The reserve requirement is 9 percent. What are deposits?
legendaryBoss.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves

repairQuestions.q: A bank gets $1,000 in deposits and must hold $100. How much can it lend?
repairQuestions.feedback: The bank can lend deposits minus required reserves: $1,000 - $100 = $900.

repairQuestions.q: Deposits are $1,000 and the reserve requirement is 10 percent. Required reserves are:
repairQuestions.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement: $1,000 x 0.10 = $100.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A bank suffers a loss because some of its loan assets lose value. Which balance-sheet item absorbs the loss first?
options: Bank capital
Required reserves
Customer deposits automatically increase
New loans created after the loss
repairQuestions.feedback: Bank capital absorbs losses first because it is the difference between the bank’s assets and liabilities; a decline in asset value reduces that cushion.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating all reserves as excess reserves.
repairQuestions.q: Excess reserves equal:
options: Actual reserves minus required reserves
Deposits plus loans
Required reserves minus deposits
Currency plus M2
repairQuestions.feedback: Excess reserves are actual reserves beyond what the bank is required to hold.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating all reserves as lendable.
repairQuestions.q: If actual reserves are $150 and required reserves are $100, excess reserves are:
repairQuestions.feedback: Excess reserves are $150 - $100 = $50.

bridgeQuestions.q: A bank gets $4,000 in new deposits and must hold 25 percent in reserves. First-round lending can be:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are $1,000, so the bank can lend $3,000.

bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $8,000 in deposits and a 12.5 percent reserve requirement. Required reserves are:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are $8,000 x 0.125 = $1,000.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Using the wrong reserve calculation.
bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $900,000 in deposits and a 12% reserve requirement. Required reserves are:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are 0.12 x $900,000 = $108,000.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treating all reserves as lendable.
bridgeQuestions.q: A bank has $900,000 in deposits, a 10% reserve requirement, and $140,000 in reserves. How much can it lend?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Required reserves are $90,000, so excess reserves are $50,000.

deposit-creation-and-money-multiplier.title: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
deposit-creation-and-money-multiplier.description: Analyze fractional-reserve deposit creation, redeposit chains, multiplier mechanics, and reserve-ratio reasoning.

objectiveLabels.deposit-creation-and-money-multiplier: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier

easy.q: If the reserve requirement rises, the simple money multiplier generally:
options: Rises.
Stays equal to one.
Falls.
Becomes unrelated to reserves.
easy.commonError: Reversing the relationship between the reserve ratio and multiplier.
easy.feedback: The simple multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio.

medium.q: The simple money multiplier is 5. The implied reserve ratio is:
options: 50 percent.
25 percent.
20 percent.
5 percent.
medium.commonError: Using the multiplier itself as the reserve percentage.
medium.feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/5, or 20 percent.

medium.q: A bank receives a new deposit and holds all of it as excess reserves instead of lending. Compared with the simple multiplier prediction:
options: Deposit expansion will be larger.
The reserve requirement becomes zero.
Deposit expansion will be smaller.
Deposit expansion must equal the full multiplier.
medium.commonError: Assuming banks always lend all excess reserves.
medium.feedback: The simple multiplier is a maximum that depends on lending and redepositing.

medium.q: A borrower spends a newly created bank loan, and the recipient deposits the payment at another bank. This process:
options: Eliminates the original loan under the stated conditions.
Creates a new deposit that can support another round of lending.
Prevents any further money creation as the relevant economic conclusion.
Turns the loan into bank capital.
medium.commonError: Failing to connect lending, spending, and redepositing.
medium.feedback: Loan proceeds commonly become deposits elsewhere, allowing additional lending.

hard.q: If banks lend more aggressively from excess reserves, the money supply rises mainly because
options: new loans create new deposits as funds are spent and redeposited
the Fed prints commodity money for each loan
M1 excludes bank deposits
borrowers destroy checking accounts when they borrow
hard.commonError: thinking bank lending only transfers existing money without deposit creation
hard.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits as loan proceeds are spent and redeposited through the banking system.

elite.q: If banks become more cautious while the Fed is trying to expand the money supply, which link in the chain is most likely to weaken?
options: Reserves to loans and deposits
Currency to fiat money
Prices to real output in the long run
Expected inflation to nominal rates
elite.commonError: Thinking reserves and loans always move one-for-one.
elite.feedback: The money creation chain weakens when banks do not convert excess reserves into new loans and deposits.

elite.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. A public cash deposit of $8,000 enters a banking system with a 20 percent reserve requirement. What is the first bank's initial loan and the maximum total deposit expansion?
options: Initial loan = $6,400; total expansion = $40,000
Initial loan = $1,600; total expansion = $8,000
Initial loan = $8,000; total expansion = $40,000
Initial loan = $6,400; total expansion = $32,000
elite.commonError: confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion
elite.feedback: The first bank keeps 20 percent, or $1,600, and lends $6,400. The multiplier is 5, so total deposit expansion can reach $40,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

elite.q: A bank receives $5,000 in new deposits. The reserve ratio is 10 percent. The borrower spends the loan, and the next bank also lends all excess reserves. What are the first two rounds of new lending?
elite.commonError: forgetting each new bank keeps reserves before lending
elite.feedback: The first bank lends 90 percent of $5,000, or $4,500. The second bank lends 90 percent of $4,500, or $4,050.

elite.q: A bank has $2 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It has $260,000 in reserves. If it lends all excess reserves and the borrower deposits the funds in another bank, what is the next bank's required reserve on that new deposit?
elite.commonError: using original deposits instead of the new loan as the next bank's deposit
elite.feedback: Required reserves at the first bank are $200,000, so it lends $60,000. The next bank must hold 10 percent of $60,000, or $6,000.

elite.q: If the simple money multiplier falls from 10 to 4, what happened to the reserve ratio?
options: It rose from 10 percent to 25 percent.
It fell from 25 percent to 10 percent.
It rose from 4 percent to 10 percent.
It fell from 10 percent to 4 percent.
elite.commonError: thinking a smaller multiplier means a smaller reserve ratio
elite.feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/multiplier. A multiplier of 10 means 10 percent; a multiplier of 4 means 25 percent.

legendary.q: In a hypothetical system with a fixed 12.5 percent reserve ratio, a household deposits $28,000 of existing public currency. Banks initially have no excess reserves. Every bank lends all new excess reserves, all loan payments are redeposited, and no other constraint binds. An analyst counts the first deposit as new money and reports the full deposit increase as money creation. Which set of results diagnoses the error?
options: First loan $24,500; deposit increase $224,000; net money increase $196,000.
First loan $24,500; deposit increase $196,000; net money increase $224,000.
First loan $3,500; deposit increase $224,000; net money increase $224,000.
First loan $28,000; deposit increase $196,000; net money increase $168,000.
legendary.commonError: confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion
legendary.feedback: The first loan is $28,000 × 0.875 = $24,500. Deposits rise by $28,000/0.125 = $224,000. Subtract the $28,000 decline in public currency to obtain $196,000 of net money creation.

legendary.q: A bank has $1,000,000 in deposits and $140,000 in reserves. The reserve requirement is 10 percent. The bank lends all excess reserves, and that loan is redeposited in another bank facing the same reserve requirement. What is the second bank's maximum loan?
legendary.commonError: using the original deposit instead of the first loan as the second bank's deposit
legendary.feedback: The first bank's required reserves are $100,000, so it lends $40,000. The second bank keeps 10 percent, or $4,000, and can lend $36,000.

legendary.q: In two hypothetical steady states, the public holds no currency and banks have a fixed required-reserve ratio of 10 percent. The observed deposit-to-reserve ratio falls from 8 to 5. Assume all reserves are either required or deliberately held as excess reserves. Which diagnosis fits both observations?
options: The excess-reserve share of deposits rose from 2.5 to 10 percent.
The required-reserve ratio rose from 12.5 to 20 percent.
The excess-reserve share of deposits fell from 10 to 2.5 percent.
The public currency-to-deposit ratio rose from 2.5 to 10 percent.
legendary.commonError: thinking a lower multiplier means a lower reserve ratio
legendary.feedback: Total reserves/deposits are the reciprocal of deposits/reserves: 12.5 percent, then 20 percent. Subtract the unchanged 10 percent requirement to infer excess-reserve shares of 2.5 and 10 percent.

legendary.q: Use a hypothetical fixed-ratio reserve model with no currency drain: every loan payment is fully redeposited, credit demand is sufficient, and no other constraint binds. A bank has $5 million in deposits, $700,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It lends all excess reserves, and every later bank does the same. What is the maximum total money expansion created by the excess reserves?
options: $2 million
$5 million
legendary.commonError: multiplying total reserves instead of excess reserves
legendary.feedback: Required reserves are $500,000, so excess reserves are $200,000. With multiplier 10, maximum expansion from excess reserves is $2 million.

calculation.q: If the reserve requirement is 10 percent, the simple money multiplier is:
calculation.commonError: Using the reserve ratio instead of its reciprocal.
calculation.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve requirement, so 1/0.10 = 10.

calculation.q: If the reserve requirement is 12.5 percent, the simple money multiplier is:
calculation.commonError: Using the reserve requirement instead of its reciprocal.
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.125 = 8.

calculation.q: If the reserve requirement falls from 20 percent to 10 percent, the simple money multiplier:
options: Falls from 10 to 5
Rises from 5 to 10
Stays fixed at 20
Falls from 20 to 10
calculation.commonError: Thinking a lower reserve requirement lowers the multiplier.
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1/rr. It rises from 5 to 10 when the reserve requirement falls from 0.20 to 0.10.

calculation.q: If the reserve ratio is 12.5 percent, the simple money multiplier is
calculation.commonError: using the reserve ratio itself as the multiplier
calculation.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1 / 0.125 = 8.

calculation.q: If the money multiplier is 5 and the Fed injects $20 million of reserves, the maximum possible increase in the money supply is
options: $100 million
$20 million
$25 million
$4 million
calculation.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
calculation.feedback: The maximum increase equals multiplier times reserves: 5 x $20 million = $100 million.

calculation.q: If the reserve ratio is 20 percent, the simple money multiplier is
calculation.commonError: using the reserve ratio as the multiplier
calculation.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio: 1 / 0.20 = 5.

calculation.q: In a hypothetical system, a household deposits $10,000 of currency previously held outside banks. Banks initially meet a fixed 20 percent reserve ratio exactly, lend every new excess reserve dollar, and all loan payments are redeposited without currency drain. No other constraint binds. What are the first bank’s loan and the eventual net increase in currency plus checking deposits?
options: First loan $8,000; net money increase $40,000.
First loan $8,000; net money increase $50,000.
First loan $2,000; net money increase $40,000.
First loan $10,000; net money increase $50,000.
calculation.commonError: confusing initial lending with total possible deposit creation
calculation.feedback: Required reserves on the initial deposit are $2,000, leaving an $8,000 first loan. Total deposits rise by $10,000/0.20 = $50,000, but public currency falls by $10,000. Net money creation is $40,000.

calculation.q: If the reserve requirement falls from 20 percent to 10 percent, what happens to the simple money multiplier?
options: It rises from 5 to 10.
It falls from 10 to 5.
It rises from 0.2 to 0.1.
It stays fixed at 20.
calculation.commonError: thinking the multiplier moves in the same direction as the reserve ratio
calculation.feedback: The multiplier is 1/r. At 20 percent it is 5; at 10 percent it is 10.

calculation.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. Suppose the reserve ratio is 25 percent and a public cash deposit of $4,000 enters the banking system. What is the maximum total deposit expansion and the first bank's initial loan?
options: Maximum expansion = $16,000; initial loan = $3,000
Maximum expansion = $4,000; initial loan = $1,000
Maximum expansion = $3,000; initial loan = $16,000
Maximum expansion = $1,000; initial loan = $4,000
calculation.commonError: confusing first-round loan with total deposit expansion
calculation.feedback: Multiplier is 1 / 0.25 = 4, so total expansion is $16,000. First bank keeps $1,000 and lends $3,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

calculation.q: The simple money multiplier is 5. The implied reserve ratio is:
options: 50 percent.
25 percent.
20 percent.
5 percent.
calculation.commonError: Using the multiplier itself as the reserve percentage.
calculation.feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/5, or 20 percent.

boss.q: In a fractional reserve system, banks
options: hold part of deposits as reserves and lend the rest
must hold 100 percent of deposits as reserves
cannot affect the money supply
create money by printing currency
boss.commonError: thinking banks create money by printing cash
boss.feedback: Banks create deposits through lending, not by printing currency.

boss.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. A public cash deposit of $5,000 enters a banking system with a 20 percent reserve requirement. What is the first bank's initial loan and the simple maximum total deposit expansion?
options: Initial loan = $4,000; total expansion = $25,000
Initial loan = $1,000; total expansion = $5,000
Initial loan = $5,000; total expansion = $25,000
Initial loan = $4,000; total expansion = $20,000
boss.commonError: confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion
boss.feedback: The bank lends $4,000. The multiplier is 1/0.20 = 5, so total expansion can reach $25,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

boss.q: A simple money multiplier of 4 corresponds to what reserve ratio?
options: 25 percent.
4 percent.
20 percent.
40 percent.
boss.commonError: Using the percentage rather than its reciprocal.
boss.feedback: The reserve ratio is the reciprocal of the multiplier: 1/4 = 25 percent.

boss.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. A $10,000 deposit enters a system with a 20 percent reserve requirement. If banks lend all excess reserves and loans are redeposited, maximum total deposits are:
boss.commonError: Confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion.
boss.feedback: The multiplier is 5, so total deposits can rise by $50,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank begins with $5 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It has $700,000 in reserves. It lends all excess reserves, the loan is redeposited, and the next bank lends all excess reserves. What is the second bank's loan?
legendaryBoss.commonError: using original deposits instead of the redeposited loan
legendaryBoss.feedback: The first bank must hold $500,000, so it lends $200,000. The next bank keeps $20,000 and lends $180,000.

legendaryBoss.q: Use a hypothetical fixed-ratio reserve model with no currency drain: every loan payment is fully redeposited, credit demand is sufficient, and no other constraint binds. A bank has $10 million in deposits and $1.3 million in reserves. The reserve ratio is 10 percent. If the bank lends all excess reserves and every later bank does the same, what maximum total deposit expansion can the excess reserves support?
options: $3 million
$13 million
$1.3 million
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying all reserves instead of only excess reserves
legendaryBoss.feedback: Required reserves are $1 million, so excess reserves are $300,000. With multiplier 10, maximum expansion is $3 million.

legendaryBoss.q: A hypothetical system starts with no excess reserves. A public cash deposit of $25,000 enters the first bank. Each bank keeps the fixed 8 percent required reserve and lends the remainder. After each loan, 25 percent of its proceeds stays as public currency and 75 percent is deposited at the next bank. What is the second bank’s loan, and how much smaller is it than under full redepositing?
options: $21,160; no reduction.
legendaryBoss.commonError: forgetting the second bank also holds reserves
legendaryBoss.feedback: The first loan is $23,000. The next deposit is $23,000 × 0.75 = $17,250, of which 92 percent can be lent: $15,870. Full redepositing would permit $21,160, a difference of $5,290.

repairQuestions.q: If the reserve requirement is 20 percent, the simple money multiplier is:
repairQuestions.feedback: The simple multiplier is 1/reserve requirement, so 1/0.20 = 5.

repairQuestions.q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, what can happen next?
options: The loan can become a deposit elsewhere and support further lending
The money supply must shrink immediately
Required reserves disappear
The loan stops being an asset
repairQuestions.feedback: Loans can become deposits at other banks, allowing the deposit-creation process to continue.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: A bank makes a new loan by crediting the borrower’s deposit account. Which statement best describes the textbook balance-sheet effect?
options: The bank adds a loan asset and a deposit liability; it does not hand the borrower a pile of reserves
The bank permanently loses required reserves equal to the full loan amount
The bank creates new capital equal to the loan and leaves deposits unchanged
The central bank must approve and create each commercial-bank loan individually
repairQuestions.feedback: When the bank credits the borrower’s account, it records a loan asset and a matching deposit liability; the bank does not hand over a preexisting pile of reserves.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using the reserve ratio as the multiplier.
repairQuestions.q: The simple money multiplier equals:
options: 1 divided by the reserve ratio
The reserve ratio divided by 1
Deposits minus reserves
M2 minus M1
repairQuestions.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1/r.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using 0.20 as the multiplier when the reserve ratio is 20%.
repairQuestions.q: If the reserve ratio is 20%, the simple multiplier is:

bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank adds reserves to the banking system through an asset purchase. Why does this not mean the central bank itself makes every new commercial loan?
options: The central bank supplies reserves; commercial banks and borrowers determine later lending and deposit creation
The central bank directly selects every commercial borrower and dictates the size of each loan after the asset purchase
Commercial banks can lend only currency printed during the same transaction
Asset purchases increase bank capital rather than reserve balances
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The central bank supplies reserve balances; commercial banks and borrowers determine whether those reserves support subsequent loans and deposit creation.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Confusing initial lending with total expansion.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. A $10,000 deposit enters a system with a 20% reserve ratio. What is the maximum total deposit expansion?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The multiplier is 5, so total expansion can reach $50,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

monetary-policy-tools.title: Monetary-Policy Tools
monetary-policy-tools.description: Apply open-market operations, administered rates, and reserve tools.

easy.q: If the Fed buys bonds in open-market operations, what happens first?
options: Bank reserves tend to fall
Bank reserves tend to rise
SRAS shifts left
The natural rate falls
easy.commonError: Reversing bond purchases and bond sales.
easy.feedback: Fed bond purchases inject reserves into the banking system.

easy.q: When the Fed buys government bonds in open-market operations, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed by law
turn into commodity money
easy.commonError: thinking bond purchases reduce the money supply
easy.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it injects money into the banking system, so the money supply tends to increase.

easy.q: When the Fed sells government bonds in open-market operations, the money supply tends to
options: decrease
increase
become equal to real GDP
stop depending on banks
easy.commonError: thinking bond sales add money to the economy
easy.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, buyers pay money to the Fed, so money is pulled out of circulation.

easy.q: A lower discount rate tends to make banks
options: more willing to borrow from the Fed
less willing to lend
hold exactly 100 percent reserves
stop creating deposits
easy.commonError: thinking a lower borrowing cost discourages borrowing
easy.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper, which can encourage bank lending.

easy.q: If the Fed wants to expand the money supply using open-market operations, it should
options: buy government bonds
sell government bonds
raise taxes
cut government purchases
easy.commonError: thinking bond purchases take money out of circulation
easy.feedback: Buying government bonds injects money into the banking system and expands the money supply.

easy.q: If the Fed wants to contract the money supply using open-market operations, it should
options: sell government bonds
buy government bonds
increase government spending
lower income taxes
easy.commonError: thinking bond sales add money to banks
easy.feedback: Selling government bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

easy.q: If the Fed lowers reserve requirements, banks can usually create
options: more money through lending
less money through lending
no deposits at all
commodity money instead of fiat money
easy.commonError: thinking lower reserve requirements reduce bank lending
easy.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free up reserves, allowing banks to lend more and expand deposits.

medium.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply through open-market operations, it should:
options: Buy bonds from banks
Sell bonds to the public
Lower reserve requirements
Lower the discount rate
medium.commonError: Reversing open-market purchases and sales.
medium.feedback: Selling bonds pulls reserves out of the banking system and reduces the money supply.

medium.q: Which sequence correctly describes an open-market purchase?
options: Fed buys bonds, reserves rise, money supply can expand
Fed sells bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Fed buys bonds, reserves fall, money supply contracts
Fed sells bonds, reserves fall, money demand vanishes
medium.commonError: Breaking the reserves-to-money-supply chain.
medium.feedback: A Fed bond purchase adds reserves and can support money supply expansion.

medium.q: A higher interest rate paid on reserves most directly encourages banks to:
options: Hold more reserves
Hold fewer reserves
Ignore the Fed
Create commodity money
medium.commonError: Thinking interest on reserves always increases lending.
medium.feedback: Paying more on reserves makes holding reserves more attractive to banks.

medium.q: The Fed wants to increase the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Buy government bonds from the public.
Sell government bonds to the public.
Raise taxes on households.
Reduce government purchases.
medium.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases remove money from circulation
medium.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, it pays money into the economy, increasing the money supply.

medium.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply. Which open-market operation matches that goal?
options: Sell government bonds to the public.
Buy government bonds from the public.
Cut the discount rate.
Lower reserve requirements.
medium.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales inject money
medium.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, the public pays money to the Fed, reducing the money supply.

medium.q: If the Fed lowers the discount rate, which effect is most likely?
options: Banks find it cheaper to borrow from the Fed.
Banks are required to hold more reserves.
The money supply must fall.
Currency becomes commodity money.
medium.commonError: thinking a lower discount rate discourages borrowing
medium.feedback: A lower discount rate makes borrowing from the Fed cheaper for banks.

medium.q: If the Fed raises reserve requirements, the banking system's ability to create money usually
options: decreases
increases
becomes unlimited
does not depend on deposits anymore
medium.commonError: thinking higher required reserves create more lending
medium.feedback: Higher reserve requirements force banks to hold more reserves and lend less, reducing money creation.

medium.q: If the Fed pays a higher interest rate on reserves, banks may respond by
options: holding more reserves and lending less
holding fewer reserves and lending more
creating commodity money
eliminating demand deposits
medium.commonError: thinking interest on reserves cannot affect lending
medium.feedback: Higher interest on reserves can make banks more willing to hold reserves instead of lending.

hard.q: Which sequence best describes a contractionary open-market operation?
options: Sell bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Buy bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Sell bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Buy bonds, reserves rise, lending contracts
hard.commonError: Reversing bond sales and purchases.
hard.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, weakens lending, and reduces money creation.

hard.q: The Fed raises the discount rate and also raises interest on reserves. Which combined effect is most likely?
options: Banks borrow less from the Fed and may hold more reserves.
Banks borrow more from the Fed and lend every reserve.
Households automatically hold fewer dollars because taxes fall.
The money multiplier becomes infinite.
hard.commonError: treating all Fed tools as expansionary regardless of direction
hard.feedback: A higher discount rate discourages bank borrowing, and higher interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves.

hard.q: Which Fed action is most clearly contractionary?
options: Selling bonds and raising reserve requirements
Buying bonds and lowering reserve requirements
Buying bonds and lowering the discount rate
Lowering interest on reserves and buying bonds
hard.commonError: mixing expansionary and contractionary tools
hard.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out, and raising reserve requirements restricts lending. That is contractionary.

hard.q: Which Fed action is most clearly expansionary?
options: Buying bonds and lowering reserve requirements
Selling bonds and raising reserve requirements
Raising the discount rate and raising interest on reserves
Selling bonds and lowering bank lending
hard.commonError: thinking bond purchases are contractionary
hard.feedback: Buying bonds injects money, and lower reserve requirements support more lending. That is expansionary.

hard.q: If the Fed wants looser money but also raises interest on reserves, what tension does this create?
options: It injects reserves but may also encourage banks to hold them instead of lending.
It lowers reserves and forces banks to lend more.
It turns deposits into commodity money.
It makes fiscal policy impossible.
hard.commonError: assuming all policy tools point in the same direction
hard.feedback: More reserves can support lending, but higher interest on reserves may make banks sit on those reserves.

hard.q: The central bank raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. What response is most likely, other things equal?
options: Banks are more willing to hold reserves and less willing to expand lending.
Banks reduce reserve holdings and expand lending because reserves now pay more.
Households move currency directly into government spending when reserves earn more.
The required reserve ratio automatically falls when reserve interest increases.
hard.commonError: Reversing the incentive effect of higher interest paid on reserves.
hard.feedback: A higher return on reserve balances makes reserve holding more attractive and tends to restrain lending and money creation.

elite.q: The Fed wants the money supply to fall by $180 million. If the money multiplier is 6 and banks fully lend according to the simple model, what open-market operation should the Fed conduct?
options: Sell $30 million in bonds.
Buy $30 million in bonds.
Sell $180 million in bonds.
Buy $1.08 billion in bonds.
elite.commonError: multiplying the desired money change by the multiplier instead of dividing
elite.feedback: To reduce money by $180 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $30 million in bonds.

elite.q: The Fed buys bonds while also increasing interest on reserves. Which answer best captures the policy conflict?
options: Bond purchases add reserves, but higher interest on reserves may reduce banks' willingness to lend them.
Bond purchases remove reserves, while higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend more.
Both actions clearly reduce reserves and contract lending.
Both actions clearly eliminate money demand.
elite.commonError: assuming every Fed action in a scenario pushes the same direction
elite.feedback: Buying bonds is expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

elite.q: Which policy package most strongly reduces bank lending capacity?
options: Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds and lowers the discount rate.
Fed lowers reserve requirements and buys bonds.
elite.commonError: failing to combine multiple contractionary tools
elite.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, higher reserve requirements restrict lending, and higher interest on reserves encourages banks to hold reserves.

elite.q: Which policy package most strongly expands bank lending capacity?
options: Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds and raises the discount rate.
Fed raises reserve requirements and pays banks more to hold reserves.
elite.commonError: missing that lower interest on reserves can encourage lending
elite.feedback: Buying bonds adds reserves, lower reserve requirements free reserves, and lower interest on reserves weakens the incentive to sit on reserves.

elite.q: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio rises from 10 percent to 20 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $40,000 to $0.
They rise from $40,000 to $80,000.
They fall from $80,000 to $40,000.
They stay at $80,000.
elite.commonError: forgetting required reserves change when the ratio changes
elite.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $40,000 and excess reserves are $40,000. At 20 percent, required reserves are $80,000 and excess reserves are $0.

elite.q: A bank has $400,000 in deposits and $80,000 in reserves. The required reserve ratio falls from 20 percent to 10 percent. What new lending capacity is created?
elite.commonError: thinking lower reserve requirements reduce excess reserves
elite.feedback: Required reserves fall from $80,000 to $40,000, creating $40,000 in excess reserves.

elite.q: If the Fed sells bonds and the public pays with checking deposits, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Bank reserves rise, strengthening deposit creation.
Bank reserves stay fixed, but taxes rise.
Bank reserves become commodity money.
elite.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales add reserves to banks
elite.feedback: When the Fed sells bonds, payment leaves bank deposits and reserves fall, reducing money creation.

elite.q: If the Fed buys bonds from the public and sellers deposit the proceeds, what is the direct effect on bank reserves and the money supply process?
options: Bank reserves rise, supporting deposit creation.
Bank reserves fall, weakening deposit creation.
Taxes rise, reducing consumption.
Reserve requirements automatically rise to 100 percent.
elite.commonError: thinking Fed bond purchases drain reserves
elite.feedback: When the Fed buys bonds, money enters bank deposits and reserves rise, supporting lending and deposit creation.

legendary.q: A bank has $2,400,000 in deposits, $360,000 in reserves, and a reserve requirement of 10 percent. The reserve requirement then rises to 15 percent. What happens to excess reserves?
options: They fall from $120,000 to $0.
They rise from $120,000 to $360,000.
They fall from $360,000 to $240,000.
They rise from $0 to $120,000.
legendary.commonError: forgetting to recalculate required reserves after the policy change
legendary.feedback: At 10 percent, required reserves are $240,000, so excess reserves are $120,000. At 15 percent, required reserves are $360,000, leaving zero excess reserves.

legendary.q: In a hypothetical steady-state banking model, the required-reserve ratio is 10 percent, banks hold excess reserves equal to 5 percent of deposits, and the public holds currency equal to 25 percent of deposits. These ratios remain fixed. Money is currency plus deposits; the monetary base is currency plus total reserves. What base increase is needed for a $250 million money increase, and why is the simple 1/required-ratio estimate too small?
options: $80 million; both currency holdings and excess reserves absorb base money.
$25 million; every base dollar supports ten dollars of money.
$100 million; currency is excluded from the money measure.
$62.5 million; retaining a fixed fraction once describes every lending round.
legendary.commonError: ignoring the 80 percent lending adjustment
legendary.feedback: With deposits D, money is 1.25D and the base is (0.25 + 0.10 + 0.05)D = 0.40D. The money/base ratio is 3.125, so the base must rise $250/3.125 = $80 million. The simple multiplier ignores both leakages.

legendary.q: A hypothetical bank has $600,000 in deposits and $90,000 in reserves. The required-reserve ratio rises from 10 to 15 percent. The bank cannot obtain new reserves, and any additional loan payment would settle at another bank. Which conclusion distinguishes its reserve position from its ability to expand?
options: It meets the new requirement exactly, but has no excess reserves for an outgoing loan.
It has a $30,000 reserve deficit and must obtain reserves just to comply.
It retains $30,000 of excess reserves because deposits have not changed.
It must shrink deposits by $90,000 even if it makes no new loan.
legendary.commonError: thinking a higher reserve requirement creates more excess reserves
legendary.feedback: Required reserves rise from $60,000 to $90,000, exactly equal to actual reserves. The bank is compliant but the specified settlement constraint prevents further outgoing lending without adjustment.

legendary.q: The Fed cuts the discount rate, buys bonds, and lowers interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Bank borrowing and reserves rise, lending incentives strengthen, and the money supply tends to expand.
Bank reserves fall, lending incentives weaken, and the money supply contracts.
Taxes fall, consumption rises, and fiscal policy expands.
The money supply is unaffected because only fiscal policy matters.
legendary.commonError: treating Fed tools as unrelated one-off facts
legendary.feedback: All three actions push toward monetary expansion: cheaper Fed borrowing, more reserves, and less reward for holding reserves idle.

legendary.q: The Fed raises the discount rate, sells bonds, and raises interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Borrowing becomes costlier, reserves fall, banks may hold more reserves, and money creation weakens.
Borrowing becomes cheaper, reserves rise, and lending expands.
Government spending rises and taxes fall.
Money demand becomes zero.
legendary.commonError: missing that higher interest on reserves can be contractionary
legendary.feedback: That policy package tightens money through costlier borrowing, fewer reserves, and stronger incentives to hold reserves.

legendary.q: A bank has $10 million in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It holds $1.4 million in reserves. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 12 percent and banks lend all remaining excess reserves. How much can the bank lend after the change?
options: $1.2 million
$1.4 million
legendary.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the policy change
legendary.feedback: New required reserves are 0.12 x $10 million = $1.2 million. With $1.4 million in reserves, the bank can lend $200,000.

calculation.q: If the Fed buys $40 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 4, what is the maximum possible increase in the money supply?
options: $160 million
$40 million
$10 million
$44 million
calculation.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
calculation.feedback: A bond purchase injects reserves. Maximum money expansion is $40 million x 4 = $160 million.

calculation.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply by exactly $120 million and the money multiplier is 6, how many bonds should it sell?
options: $20 million
$120 million
$720 million
$6 million
calculation.commonError: multiplying target money change by the multiplier instead of dividing
calculation.feedback: To reduce money by $120 million with a multiplier of 6, the Fed sells $20 million in bonds.

boss.q: If the Fed buys government bonds, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed
turn into commodity money
boss.commonError: thinking bond purchases remove money from circulation
boss.feedback: Buying bonds injects reserves and tends to increase the money supply.

boss.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply using open-market operations, what should it do?
options: Sell government bonds.
Buy government bonds.
Lower reserve requirements.
Lower the discount rate.
boss.commonError: thinking bond sales add reserves
boss.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

boss.q: The Fed sells $20 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 5. Under the simple model, what is the maximum decrease in the money supply?
options: $100 million
$20 million
$4 million
$25 million
boss.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
boss.feedback: A $20 million bond sale times multiplier 5 gives a maximum $100 million money-supply decrease.

boss.q: To increase banking-system reserves through open-market operations, the central bank should:
options: Sell government securities.
Buy government securities.
Raise taxes.
Increase reserve requirements.
boss.commonError: Reversing the reserve effect of an open-market purchase.
boss.feedback: When the central bank buys securities, it pays by adding reserves to the banking system.

boss.q: What is the usual effect of lowering the discount rate?
options: Banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves.
The central bank removes reserves by selling bonds.
Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks.
Households are required to reduce currency holdings.
boss.commonError: Confusing the discount rate with reserve requirements or open-market sales.
boss.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost of borrowing reserves directly from the central bank.

boss.q: Which policy action is contractionary?
options: Buying government securities in the open market.
Lowering the interest paid on reserve balances.
Lowering reserve requirements.
Selling government securities in the open market.
boss.commonError: Selecting an expansionary tool as contractionary.
boss.feedback: An open-market sale withdraws reserves and tends to reduce money and credit expansion.

boss.q: The central bank buys securities but simultaneously raises the interest paid on reserves. Why might lending rise by less than expected?
options: The purchase adds reserves, but the higher reserve return encourages banks to hold them.
Both actions remove reserves and directly reduce the banking system’s lending capacity.
The bond purchase automatically raises reserve requirements and blocks new loans.
The higher reserve return forces banks to lend every newly created reserve dollar.
boss.commonError: Assuming every tool in a policy package pushes bank lending in the same direction.
boss.feedback: The open-market purchase is expansionary, while a higher return on reserves can weaken the lending response.

boss.q: A central bank wants to drain reserves quickly without changing reserve requirements. Which action is most direct?
options: Buy government securities and credit reserve accounts.
Sell government securities and debit reserve accounts.
Lower the discount rate to make reserve borrowing cheaper.
Lower interest paid on reserves to discourage reserve holding.
boss.commonError: Choosing an expansionary action when the goal is to remove reserves.
boss.feedback: An open-market sale receives payment from the banking system and reduces reserves directly.

boss.q: Reserve requirements are lowered, but banks expect severe loan losses and keep the newly available reserves idle. What does this illustrate?
options: Lower reserve requirements always produce the full textbook deposit multiplier.
Banks lose the legal ability to hold excess reserves after requirements decline.
Policy can expand lending capacity without guaranteeing that banks will lend.
The central bank shifts aggregate supply left whenever it changes reserve rules.
boss.commonError: Treating potential money creation as automatic actual money creation.
boss.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free reserves for lending, but risk perceptions and bank choices can weaken the actual expansion.

legendaryBoss.q: A bank has $3,000,000 in deposits, $510,000 in reserves, and a 12 percent reserve requirement. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 15 percent. How much lending capacity remains after the change?
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the Fed changes policy
legendaryBoss.feedback: New required reserves are 0.15 x $3,000,000 = $450,000. With $510,000 in reserves, lending capacity is $60,000.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply by $480 million. The money multiplier is 6, but currency drain is expected to make the actual multiplier closer to 4. What bond sale is closest to the needed action?
options: Sell $120 million in bonds.
Sell $80 million in bonds.
Buy $120 million in bonds.
Buy $80 million in bonds.
legendaryBoss.commonError: using the simple multiplier instead of the adjusted multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: With the actual multiplier closer to 4, the Fed sells $480 million / 4 = $120 million in bonds.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed buys bonds, lowers the discount rate, but raises interest on reserves sharply. Which answer best explains why the final lending response may be muted?
options: Reserve expansion may be offset if banks prefer earning interest on reserves.
All three actions are contractionary and must reduce reserves.
Higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend every dollar.
The discount rate only affects government spending.
legendaryBoss.commonError: assuming all listed Fed actions push lending the same way
legendaryBoss.feedback: Bond purchases and a lower discount rate are expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can weaken lending.

legendaryBoss.q: The Fed wants a $900 million maximum money expansion. The reserve ratio is 12.5 percent. Under the simple model, how large should the bond purchase be?
options: $112.5 million
$900 million
$7.2 billion
$125 million
legendaryBoss.commonError: multiplying the target expansion by the multiplier
legendaryBoss.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.125 = 8. Required bond purchase is $900 million / 8 = $112.5 million.

repairQuestions.q: If the Fed buys bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Rise
Fall
Become zero
Turn into taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: Fed bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

repairQuestions.q: If the Fed sells bonds, bank reserves usually:
options: Fall
Rise
Double
Become M2
repairQuestions.feedback: Fed bond sales drain reserves from the banking system.

repairQuestions.q: Raising the interest rate paid on bank reserves tends to:
options: Encourage banks to hold reserves rather than lend
Force banks to lend all reserves
Raise the money multiplier automatically
Shift SRAS right
repairQuestions.feedback: A higher return on reserves increases the incentive to hold reserves, which can restrain lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: If the reserve requirement is lowered, other things equal, what happens to the amount of deposits banks must hold as required reserves?
options: It falls, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending
It rises, leaving fewer reserves potentially available for lending
It is unchanged because reserve requirements affect only currency
It becomes equal to total bank capital
repairQuestions.feedback: A lower reserve requirement reduces the amount of deposits that must be held as required reserves, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing that bond purchases add reserves.
repairQuestions.q: A Fed bond purchase adds money to:
options: The banking system
The tax code
Imports only
Used goods markets only
repairQuestions.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

repairQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
repairQuestions.q: If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
options: Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks
Required reserves automatically rise for every bank
The Treasury must reduce government spending
The public is forced to hold less currency
repairQuestions.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost to banks of borrowing directly from the central bank.

repairQuestions.commonError: Missing that bond sales drain reserves.
repairQuestions.q: A Fed bond sale usually causes bank reserves to:
options: Fall
Rise
Double automatically
Become taxes
repairQuestions.feedback: When the public pays the Fed for bonds, reserves leave the banking system.

bridgeQuestions.q: The central bank buys securities and bank reserves rise, but banks choose to hold much of the new reserves idle. What does this show about the policy chain?
options: The tool can increase reserves even when the resulting expansion of bank deposits is smaller than the simple model predicts
The asset purchase failed to change reserves, so it was not a monetary-policy action
Holding excess reserves forces the money multiplier above its simple maximum
A central-bank asset purchase automatically becomes fiscal policy when banks do not lend
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The asset purchase raises bank reserves, but banks’ decision to hold excess reserves can leave deposit creation below the simple-multiplier prediction.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
